docs.text: Accessibility # Contour reports where the terminal caret is to the operating system, so assistive technology can follow it. This is what makes a screen magnifier keep the cursor in view while you type, and what lets a screen reader know where it should be reading. There is nothing to switch on. Reporting is always available and costs effectively nothing while no assistive client is attached; the platform activates it when one appears. Should you ever need to rule the caret reports out — when diagnosing input latency, say — set accessibility_caret_reporting: false in contour.yml . That silences the caret reports only; the announcements below have their own setting. What is reported # Reported Meaning The caret's position and screen rectangle Where the cursor is, updated whenever it moves. The visible screen's text The grid contents, addressed by offset, rows separated by newlines. The shell prompt region Where the current prompt is — see below. The caret is reported whenever it moves and is visible , and also whenever it becomes visible after having been hidden — so an application that hides the cursor while it redraws and then shows it again does not leave a client pointing at a stale position. A blinking cursor is not reported on every blink. Only the focused pane reports, so a split window does not make a magnifier jump between panes. The prompt region # When your shell has OSC 133 shell integration enabled, Contour additionally exposes the live shell prompt — the one you are typing at — as its own focusable region. Assistive technology that follows focus (rather than the text caret) uses this to keep the prompt itself in view, which is usually what you want while typing a command. While a command is running there is no prompt to report, and Contour says so rather than pointing at a stale one. Without shell integration, or with a shell that marks only prompt starts, the caret is still reported as usual — only the prompt region is unavailable. This needs no opt-in beyond the shell integration itself: it is driven by the OSC 133 marks directly and does not require DEC mode 2034 . The window around the terminal # The tab bar is exposed as a tab list whose tabs announce themselves as you switch between them, the window and tab buttons say what they do rather than naming the glyph they are drawn with, and every field on the settings page carries its own label. Keyboard access to the window chrome # With defaults_edition: native2026 , Ctrl+F6 moves keyboard focus out of the terminal and into the window's chrome, and on through it: the terminal, then the tab bar, then the toolbar (the daemon control that heads a shown sidebar or the location chip, the daemon version chip and the new-tab button), then back to the terminal. Ctrl+Shift+F6 walks the other way. On macOS Ctrl+F5 goes straight to the toolbar and Ctrl+F6 moves between the areas. An area that is not shown, such as a tab bar hidden by tab_bar_visibility , is skipped. The location chip is a menu button named for what it shows, "Workspace billing on starfive"; the daemon control that heads a shown sidebar is named "Daemon local". The description carries the connection state when the daemon is not connected, what another workspace asks while the chip's marker shows ("Another workspace needs you"), then whether the switcher is open or closed ("Reconnecting, collapsed"), so a screen reader hears the state even where the chip has no room to spell it. Space or Return opens the switcher and Escape closes it. A ring marks the item that has focus: a 3 pt outline in the accent on macOS and 2 pt on Windows and Linux, and a run of selection-coloured cells under ui_style: terminal . It appears for keyboard focus only, so clicking a tab never draws it. Where Key What it does Tab bar Left, Right Move to the previous or next tab; Home and End jump to the first or last Tab bar Return, Space Activate the tab Tab bar Backspace, Delete Close the tab; Contour asks first when a program may still be running in it Tab bar Alt+Left, Alt+Right Move the tab left or right Toolbar Left, Right Move to the previous or next item Toolbar Return, Space Press the item Either Escape Return to the terminal A bare F6 is never taken: it reaches the shell, so mc , vim and htop keep it. The three actions, FocusNextArea , FocusPreviousArea and FocusToolbar , can be bound to other chords, on any key, and those chords keep working from inside the chrome. When the window shows no tab bar and no toolbar there is nowhere to go, and Ctrl+F6 reaches the program like any other key. Closing a tab asks whenever its foreground program is not its shell, and also when Contour cannot tell (every pane of a daemon-hosted window), because closing the tab would end whatever runs in it. While the chrome has focus, every key binding keeps working, such as the command palette, opening a new tab or one of your own, except the keys the chrome takes for itself: the arrow keys, Home, End, Return, Space, Escape, Backspace, Delete and Tab, with no modifier or with Shift or Alt alone. A chord with Ctrl on one of those keys is still yours. Plain typing is not sent to the shell until you press Escape to return to the terminal. The workspace sidebar # Each row of the workspace sidebar is a list item whose name says what a sighted user reads off the tree: its title, its kind, whether it is expanded or collapsed, how many panes under it need you or work, and whether it is the current tab: billing, workspace, expanded, 1 needs you . Qt's accessibility has no expanded state of its own, so it is part of the name. A tab or pane that failed or finished is named failed or done . The footer's counts are one text, and the sidebar's list and filter field have their own names. Ctrl+Shift+D ( ⇧⌘E on macOS) moves keyboard focus into the tree, which then answers the arrow keys, Return, F2 and typing as the sidebar guide lists. When a pane in a workspace other than the one you are looking at starts needing you, Contour announces it, Polite, once. Reduce Motion is honoured: rows fold and unfold at once. Things that are only announced # Some of what a terminal does has no representation in the accessibility tree at all — nothing's state changed, so nothing is reported unless it is said explicitly. Contour announces: Event Politeness The bell Polite — it waits for your screen reader to finish its sentence A desktop notification (OSC 99, OSC 777 or OSC 9) Polite A pane in another workspace starts needing you (see the sidebar ) Polite Read-only mode being switched on or off Assertive — it interrupts, because it changes what typing does Set accessibility_announcements: false in contour.yml to switch these off. They cost nothing while no assistive client is attached. Reading a selection aloud # Select some text and press ++ctrl+shift+s++, or pick Read Aloud from the right-click menu, to have the operating system's speech synthesizer read it. ++ctrl+shift+s++ again reads the new selection. Text is prepared before it is spoken: the blank padding every terminal line carries out to the right margin is dropped, runs of empty lines collapse to a single pause, and a very long selection is cut at a line boundary so that selecting a build log gives a readable excerpt rather than many minutes of speech. This needs a speech engine, and it is optional Reading aloud needs Qt's TextToSpeech module at build time and a speech engine with an installed voice at run time — on Linux that means speech-dispatcher or flite . Where either is missing the feature is simply not offered: the menu row does not appear and the shortcut does nothing, rather than appearing and staying silent. Whether a voice is available is checked once, in the background, as soon as Contour starts, so opening a menu never waits for the speech engine. Until that check has answered — usually well under a few seconds — the menu row is not offered yet. A build that omitted it says so in its own build log, so a packager can see it without having to run the application. Platform notes # Platform Technology Notes Linux AT-SPI 2 Works with Orca and with KDE Plasma's zoom — see the note below. Windows UI Automation Works with Magnifier's follow keyboard focus / text cursor modes. macOS NSAccessibility Qt maps the text interface to AXTextArea . Not verified. KDE Plasma: caret tracking is off by default Plasma's zoom ( Meta + + / Meta + - / Meta + 0 ) follows the mouse pointer out of the box and ignores the text caret until you say otherwise. Turn on Enable caret tracking in System Settings → Accessibility → Screen Magnifier ; without it the zoom will not follow the cursor in Contour — or in any other application — no matter what the application reports. KWin consumes the AT-SPI object:text-caret-moved signal for this. If tracking still does not follow after enabling the option, KWIN_WAYLAND_ZOOM_FORCE_LEGACY_TEXT_CARET_TRACKING=1 forces KWin onto that AT-SPI path rather than its newer one. Qt's own environment variables apply. In particular QT_ACCESSIBILITY=0 disables accessibility for the process, and on Linux QT_LINUX_ACCESSIBILITY_ALWAYS_ON=1 forces the AT-SPI bridge on even when no client has announced itself. Verifying it # To inspect what Contour actually exposes: Linux — Accerciser . Select the Contour window; the terminal appears with a text interface, and the caret offset updates as you type. A shell prompt child appears while you are at a prompt and disappears while a command runs. Windows — Accessibility Insights, or Inspect.exe from the Windows SDK.

docs.text: Control API # Every workspace, tab and pane a Contour daemon hosts can be listed, driven and watched from the shell, from scripts and from coding agents, with the same contour binary that runs the terminal. The verbs below talk to the daemon's control API; contour api list shows everything the API offers, including what has no verb yet. Where you are # A shell hosted by the daemon finds its surroundings in four environment variables: Variable Holds $CONTOUR_PANE The shell's own pane, pane:<uuid> . The default target of every verb. $CONTOUR_TAB Its tab, tab:<uuid> . $CONTOUR_WORKSPACE Its workspace, workspace:<uuid> . $CONTOUR_DAEMON The daemon's socket path. Targets # Wherever a verb takes a pane, tab or workspace ( --pane P ), P is resolved in this order, and the first kind of match wins: a full id ( pane:018f3c4e-... ); a name, compared case-insensitively (see contour rename ); a 1-based position, for tabs and workspaces; an id suffix of at least four hex digits. More than one match is an error that lists the candidates, one per line. Without --pane , a verb acts on $CONTOUR_PANE ; a pane that has since closed is an error (exit status 3), never a silent fallback to another pane. Verbs # Verb What it does contour ls [--workspace W] Lists workspaces, tabs and panes as a tree; ids are shortened to their last 8 hex digits and * marks the active ones. contour new [--workspace W \| --new-workspace] [--cwd DIR] [--name NAME] [--no-focus] [-- CMD...] Opens a tab, named NAME with --name , and prints its pane id. Without --cwd the shell starts in the calling pane's directory, when run from one. contour split [--pane P] [--right \| --below] [--ratio PCT] [--cwd DIR] [--name NAME] [--no-focus] [-- CMD...] Splits a pane, naming the new one NAME with --name , and prints the new pane's id. Without --cwd the shell starts in the split pane's directory. contour send [--pane P] [--enter] [--wait] TEXT...\|- Types text into a pane. --enter appends a carriage return, - reads standard input, --wait waits for the command the text starts and exits with that command's own status. contour pane capture [--pane P] [--scrollback N \| --all] Prints a pane's text. contour close [--pane P \| --tab T] Closes a pane, or a tab with all its panes. contour rename OBJECT NAME Names a workspace, tab or pane ( contour rename pane:018f logs ); an empty name clears it. A workspace's or a tab's name is what its windows show for it, in the sidebar, the tab strip and the switcher, over its title; cleared, it shows its title again. The window's Rename… sets this same name. contour workspace new [--cwd DIR] [--name NAME] Opens a workspace with one tab and prints its id. The shell starts in --cwd , and the workspace is named after that folder (its repository's, inside one) unless --name names it. contour workspace close WORKSPACE Closes a workspace with all its tabs and panes, and ends their shells. Whatever it holds at that moment goes, in one step, and the workspace is removed. The daemon's last workspace cannot be closed. contour workspace move --to N WORKSPACE Moves a workspace to position N of the workspace order, counted from 1 as contour ls lists them; a position past the end puts it last. contour tab move [--workspace W] --to N TAB Moves a tab to position N of a workspace, counted from 1: another workspace to take it there, its own to reorder it. Its panes keep running, and a workspace left without tabs is closed. Without --workspace , the calling pane's workspace. contour pane move (--tab T \| --workspace W [--to N] \| --new-workspace) PANE Moves a pane: into tab T as a split beside its active pane, into workspace W as a tab of its own (at position N , counted from 1, or last), or into a new workspace. It keeps running; a tab or a workspace left empty is closed. Prints the workspace it is in now. contour block list [--pane P] [--limit N] Lists a pane's recent command blocks, newest first: id exit duration command . contour block read [BLOCK] [--pane P] [--prompt \| --output] Prints a block's text; without BLOCK , the pane's last finished block. With neither flag, the prompt and then the output. contour switch [--workspace W] (--to-name N \| --to-host H \| --to-workspace W2) [--to-workspace W2] Asks one window to switch to another workspace or daemon, in place. See Switching a window . contour wait [BLOCK] [--pane P] [--timeout SECONDS] Waits for a block to finish and exits with the command's own status. contour events [--follow] [--kind K[,K...]] [--pane P] Prints the first matching event and exits, or with --follow every event until Ctrl+C (exit status 130). contour api list [-q] Lists the API's methods and events; -q prints names only. contour api describe NAME Prints one method's or event's schemas and examples. contour api call NAME [JSON\|@FILE\|-] Calls any method with the given request, sent as is and without context. The output is indented on a terminal and one line otherwise. contour api wit Prints the API as the WIT package terminal-extensions:control@0.1.0 a WebAssembly extension imports, exactly as wit/control/world.wit holds it. Reaches no daemon and takes none of the connection options. contour pane capture is spelled that way because contour capture is the older verb that captures the screen of the terminal it runs in. Until 0.9.0 the older spellings still work, each with a note on standard error naming its replacement: contour label OBJECT NAME and contour workspace rename WORKSPACE NAME run contour rename , and contour switch --to-label is --to-name . Across an upgrade, the daemon and its clients agree on the words: a Contour older than this one is answered in its own spelling ( label keys, object.setLabel , workspace.rename , the event workspace.labelChanged ), and this one speaks that spelling to an older daemon. The MCP tool object_setLabel stays listed, as a deprecated alias of object_rename . Options that look like words ( --pane , but also the bare pane ) can be mistaken for typed text, and a word that starts with a dash but names no option is refused rather than typed: put -- before text that starts with the name of an option or with a dash, as in contour send --enter -- wait or contour send -- -x . Connection options # Every verb takes: Option Meaning --json Prints the reply JSON as received, plus a newline, instead of the human form. --daemon PATH\|HOST:PORT\|URL\|NAME The daemon. Defaults to $CONTOUR_DAEMON , then the default socket. A verb never starts a daemon. On every verb --daemon picks the daemon; the verbs that make a workspace, tab or pane name it with --name . --token-file FILE The token a HOST:PORT daemon expects. --tls-ca FILE The CA certificate (PEM) a HOST:PORT daemon is verified against. A HOST:PORT daemon without --tls-ca is refused before anything is sent, with a message naming the option: control requests, which can type into panes, never travel over an unverified connection. A bare word ( --daemon work ) names a local daemon by its name ( contour daemon --name work ), else a saved host of the configuration's hosts: section. A word that names both is refused (exit status 2) with the two spellings that pick one: --daemon name:work and --daemon host:work , which are accepted everywhere. An ssh:// URL names an ad-hoc host. A host is read exactly as contour client --host reads it (see Remote hosts ): the host's own token_file and tls_ca apply, and --token-file and --tls-ca do not. A saved tls:// host without tls_ca is refused like a HOST:PORT daemon without --tls-ca . A word that names neither a local daemon nor a saved host exits 4 with the names that are saved. Until 0.9.0, --label L is still accepted, as --daemon name:L , with a note on standard error. Workspace order # The workspaces are listed in an order the user can change, and workspace.list reports it as each workspace's position (from 1). workspace.move changes it, and a workspace addressed by its position ( contour ls --workspace 2 ) means the one that holds that place now. tab.move is to tabs what workspace.move is to workspaces, and moves a tab between workspaces as well. pane.move moves one pane out of its tab: into another tab as a split beside that tab's active pane (on the side a drop on a tab takes), into a workspace as a tab of its own, or into a new workspace, which it replies with. Its own tab, or a new workspace for a workspace's only pane, is refused as failed , and changes nothing. Method Request Grant workspace.create {"cwd":"/home/me/src/contour","name":""} , both optional write workspace.close {"workspace":"build"} write workspace.move {"workspace":"build","toPosition":1} write tab.move {"tab":"logs","toWorkspace":"build","toPosition":1} write pane.move {"pane":"logs","to":"tab","toTab":"build"} ; to is tab , workspace (with toWorkspace and an optional toPosition ) or newWorkspace write workspace.create replies with the workspace , tab and pane ids. object.rename names a workspace, as it does a tab or a pane, and publishes object.renamed . A toPosition of 0 , which a missing key reads as, is a bad request (in pane.move too, where a missing key is the end instead), one past the end is clamped, and a target no object matches is notFound . contour api describe NAME prints the schemas and an example of each. Workspaces opened by contour new --new-workspace # A workspace created by a control connection is selected by no window yet. It appears in the open GUI's workspace list as hidden , and any window can select it. With no GUI attached it is there for the next launch to find. Switching a window # workspace.switch asks one window to switch to another workspace, or to another daemon, in place: a window shows one workspace at a time and moves between a daemon's workspaces without opening another window. It is a socket method (an extension cannot call it) and needs write ; it is not an MCP tool, because an agent in a pane must not re-point the window it runs in. { "toName" : "admin" , "toHost" : "" , "toWorkspace" : "build" } Field Meaning workspace Optional. The workspace whose window switches (id, name, position or suffix): the window selecting it that was focused last. Absent: the window selecting the caller's pane's workspace, and from outside any pane the window that rings and raises for the daemon (the most recently focused one). toName A local daemon, by name. toHost A saved host, or an ssh:// URL. Not together with toName ; with neither, the window stays on this daemon. toWorkspace The destination workspace, as a spec the window resolves against the destination daemon (id, name, position or suffix). Empty lets the window decide. From the command line: contour switch --to-name admin # this pane's window goes to the daemon named admin contour switch --to-host homepc --to-workspace build # a saved host, and its workspace build contour switch --to-workspace 2 # another workspace of the same daemon contour switch --daemon work --workspace w1 --to-name admin # the window selecting w1, from outside any pane --daemon chooses the daemon the window is on now, and --workspace , optionally, the workspace its window selects (default: the workspace of $CONTOUR_PANE , so inside a pane no flags are needed; outside a pane, the window focused last). --to-host takes a saved host's name or an ssh:// URL; any other URL is refused with exit status 2, and must be saved in the configuration's hosts: section first. Without --to-workspace , a destination with exactly one workspace (or none, which creates one) is used; with several, the window asks which in its switcher popup (outcome picker ). contour switch waits for the window's answer and prints the outcome; switched , focused and picker exit 0, refused exits 5, failed exits 1, and a workspace that no window selects (or a daemon with no window attached) exits 3 with the reason. To open a window on another daemon instead of re-pointing one, use contour client --daemon NAME --workspace W or contour client --host H --workspace W (see Remote hosts ). The window asks its user before it switches: a prompt names the destination in full and offers Deny or Switch, with Don't ask again , which keeps the answer for switches between the same two daemons until Contour exits; a remembered Deny is answered refused at once. The daemon tells the window how long it waits for the answer (30 seconds), and the prompt stays up only while an allowed switch could still land before then: the wait less the 10 seconds a switch may take to show its destination, less 2 seconds for the answer to travel back -- 18 seconds. A prompt left unanswered that long is taken down and answered refused ("the user did not answer in time"). An allowed switch must then land within the wait less those 2 seconds, counted from the request's arrival, whatever it waits for first (the destination daemon's workspaces are listed before anything moves): one that could no longer start in time fails, and one still landing then gives up, so a window never switches after contour switch gave up. A daemon on another host may state a longer wait; the window takes at most 5 minutes of it. A destination given as an ssh:// URL is asked every time (see Persistent sessions ). The reply is {"outcome":"switched","detail":""} . outcome is switched , focused (another window already shows the destination, and was focused), picker (the window asked its user which workspace), refused (the user declined: "the user declined the switch") or failed ; detail says why in a sentence. A window that no longer selects the workspace answers failed ("no window here shows workspace N"). A window that does not answer within 30 seconds is reported as failed ("no answer from the window"), and one whose client predates switching as failed ("the window cannot switch (client too old)"). Which window switches is decided by the daemon, always to exactly one. With workspace , it is the window selecting that workspace that was focused last; without it, the window selecting the workspace of the caller's pane; without a pane either, the window that rings and raises. When no window selects the named workspace the call fails as notFound ("no window selects workspace ..."), and with no window attached at all as notFound ("no window is attached"). Two windows selecting the same workspace therefore never make a call fail: the one focused last is asked. workspace.list tells what a switch can act on. Each workspace carries visibility ( shown : some window selects it; hidden : none does), clients (how many windows select it) and native (the daemon's own id for it, in decimal, which a window selects it by). It also says what a switcher shows of a workspace on another daemon. git is the workspace's repository, where its active pane's directory is: branch (the branch or ref name, or a detached HEAD's short object id), kind ( branch , detached or otherRef ), and ahead and behind its upstream where it has one. The daemon looks it up whenever the pane's directory changes or a command finishes, and every 30 seconds, whether or not a window is attached; git is absent outside a repository and until the pane's directory is known. Each pane's lastFinished is its newest finished command block (as block.list reports one: the command, its exit code, when it started and how long it ran), absent until a command has finished; it needs screen , as programStatus does. Waiting # contour wait and contour send --wait exit with the finished command's own status, clamped to 0..255. A block without an exit code, with a negative one, or that was superseded by a newer prompt exits 1, with a note on standard error. contour wait with no BLOCK waits for the next block of the pane to finish; one that already finished is read with contour block read . --timeout SECONDS is kept by the client: when it runs out, contour wait prints Error: timed out and exits 1, and the command in the pane carries on. contour send --enter 'make' && contour wait --timeout 600 || echo "make failed or took too long" Events # contour events subscribes to the daemon's events. A line reads HH:MM:SS type pane details (times are UTC; the pane is the last 8 hex digits of its id behind an ellipsis). With --json each event is printed as received, one per line, which is what scripts read: contour events --follow --json --kind block.finished | jq -r '.payload.block | "\(.exitCode) \(.command)"' An event of a type this release does not know, from a newer daemon, is printed raw. --kind takes a comma separated list of: Event Fires when block.finished A command block finished. pane.bell A pane rang the bell. pane.titleChanged A pane's title changed. pane.cwdChanged A pane's working directory changed. object.renamed A workspace, tab or pane was renamed ( object.rename , or a window's Rename… ); the payload carries its object id and its name , empty when it was cleared. pane.programStatusChanged A pane's program status changed. pane.created , pane.closed A pane was created or closed. tab.created , tab.closed A tab was created or closed. client.attached , client.detached A GUI client attached or detached. events.dropped The subscriber was too slow and events were dropped. Exit statuses # Status Meaning 0 Done. 1 The call failed; the reason is on standard error as Error: <message> . 2 The command line was malformed, or a setting it names cannot be used (a --tls-ca that does not parse). 3 The pane, tab, workspace or block named does not exist, or the name matches several. 4 No daemon could be reached. 5 The daemon declined; the reason is on standard error. 130 Interrupted by Ctrl+C. contour send --wait exits with the command's own status instead (0 to 255). A command with no exit code, or one that was superseded, exits 1 with a note on standard error. Permissions # A daemon's TCP tokens carry grants ( contour daemon --access-file ): read for listing, screen for capturing, reading blocks and program status ( pane.programStatusChanged , and the programStatus and lastFinished of contour ls --json ), input for typing, and write for changing the workspace. A call outside the token's grants is refused as forbidden (exit status 1). The daemon's socket grants everything to its owner. daemon.info reports the connection's own grants in its grants array (by name, in the order above), so a client can tell what it may call before it tries. A connection holds at most 64 subscriptions and 256 pending waits; one more is refused as limitReached (exit status 1). Each verb opens a connection of its own, so only a script driving contour api call over one connection meets it. Reporting a pane's status # An integration, such as a coding agent's hook, tells the daemon what a pane's program is doing with two methods. Both need the input grant, and both are reachable with contour api call : Method What it does pane.reportStatus Sets the integration's own record of a pane: {"pane": "...", "integration": "claude-code", "state": "blocked", "kind": "permission", "title": "...", "message": "...", "progress": 40} . integration is [a-z0-9-]{1,32} and becomes the record's id; state is idle , working , done , blocked or error ; kind ( none , permission , question , auth ) is for blocked only. An empty pane is the caller's own. pane.clearStatus Removes the record that integration set: {"pane": "...", "integration": "claude-code"} . Records a program sent by OSC 7501 are not touched. The title and message are untrusted text: control and invisible formatting characters are removed, and each is cut to 200 bytes. Records the integration sets list as origin: "integration" , apart from a program's origin: "program" , with since (when the state or kind last changed) and a generation that rises whenever the state or kind changes (not when only the title, message or progress does). When someone types or pastes into the pane in a Contour window, the integration's blocked records become working : the person has answered. Input sent with pane.send does not do that, nor do the focus and mouse reports a window sends by itself, nor does input from a client too old to say which of its input was typed. These methods need a daemon. In-process mode (no contour daemon ) has no control socket, so a hook finds none and does nothing. Upgrading the daemon # daemon.upgrade replaces the running daemon with a newer release, keeping every program running (see Live upgrade ); contour daemon upgrade is its verb. contour api call daemon.upgrade '{"image":""}' image names a staged image of the daemon's store; empty, the daemon upgrades to its own installed executable, the file a package upgrade replaced. The call needs write and a connection on the daemon's own machine, through the daemon's Unix socket: over a TCP token it is refused. It is not offered to extensions or to the agent's tools. The reply, {"started":true,"toRelease":"0.9.1"} , is sent before the daemon tells its clients it is upgrading and closes every connection, this one included; the clients reconnect to the same daemon. It is provisional: the daemon may still decline after it, while it waits for its clients and sessions to settle, and the switch to the new binary may fail. Either way the daemon then resumes and serves on as before, and the connection that asked is gone by then. contour daemon status tells how it ended: its upgrades count is one higher once the new release serves, and a last upgrade line names the failure otherwise. contour daemon upgrade reads it there for you. A refusal before the reply is an error with code failed whose message leads with a stable name, then says why: sandboxed: the daemon runs in a sandbox that cannot reach the new release . The names are inProgress , notStaged , sandboxed , formatUnreadable , inFlightTailTooLarge , targetUnresponsive , notSupported , unsupportedSession , sessionStarting , quiesceTimedOut , imageTooLarge , configUnreadable and localOnly . execFailed , an exec that failed after the daemon stopped its sessions' pumps and resumed them, always comes after the reply, so this call never returns it; it is the name contour daemon status reports such a failure under. A connection that breaks before the reply leaves the outcome unknown: ask contour daemon status again. A workflow: run the tests beside you # pane = $( contour split --below --no-focus --json | jq -r .pane ) contour send --pane " $pane " --enter --wait -- 'make test' # exits with make's status contour block read --pane " $pane " --output # what it printed Agents # contour agent setup writes a skill that teaches coding agents to operate Contour panes: where they are, how targets resolve, every verb with its usage, the exit statuses, the run-the-tests workflow, and the whole API. The skill is generated from the verb table and the API catalog, so it always matches the binary. contour agent setup # every agent found, and ~/.agents contour agent setup --agent claude-code --dry-run Agent Skill file claude-code (Claude Code) ~/.claude/skills/contour/SKILL.md , or beneath $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that is set agents (Codex, OpenCode and other agents reading ~/.agents ) ~/.agents/skills/contour/SKILL.md Without --agent , an agent is set up only when its configuration directory exists ( ~/.claude or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR ; ~/.codex or $CODEX_HOME ), so nothing is created for an agent you do not use; the report says which were skipped. Naming an agent with --agent sets it up whether or not it is found. The names are the ones contour agent report --agent takes. Rerun it after upgrading Contour: a file it generated is updated, one that is already current is left alone, and a file it did not generate is kept unless you pass --force . --dry-run reports what would happen, and --json prints the outcomes as an array. Status hooks # contour agent setup also installs the hooks that let a coding agent tell Contour what it is doing, so that the pane shows a working, blocked (waiting for you) or done status. The hooks run contour agent report --agent <claude-code|codex> , which turns the agent's hook payload into pane.reportStatus or pane.clearStatus on the daemon hosting the pane. It prints nothing, always exits 0, gives up after two seconds (reading the payload included), ignores a payload larger than 1 MiB, and does nothing outside a pane of a Contour daemon (no $CONTOUR_DAEMON or $CONTOUR_PANE ; a window running its sessions in process does not pass those on to its own shells). The contour binary is written into the hooks by its absolute path (under an AppImage, the AppImage's), so rerun contour agent setup after moving it. Agent Hook file What is installed claude-code (Claude Code) ~/.claude/settings.json , or beneath $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR one hook group for each of UserPromptSubmit , PreToolUse , PermissionRequest , Notification , Elicitation , PostToolUse , PostToolUseFailure , Stop , StopFailure and SessionEnd codex (Codex) ~/.codex/hooks.json , or beneath $CODEX_HOME (which must already exist) one hook group for each of UserPromptSubmit , PreToolUse , PermissionRequest , PostToolUse , Stop , Interrupt and SessionEnd Your own hooks and settings are kept, and a file is replaced in one step (a symlinked one through its link, which stays). A hook of ours is one whose command is exactly the binary followed by agent report --agent <claude-code|codex> ; a command of yours that merely mentions it is left alone. A hook file that is not valid JSON is left alone and reported, and so is a $CODEX_HOME that names a directory that does not exist (it is not created). Codex runs only hooks you have reviewed: after contour agent setup , open Codex once and trust the new hooks (its hooks review), or they never run and the pane shows no status. contour agent setup --uninstall removes exactly these hooks (and leaves the skill file as it is), and the groups and event arrays that held only them; --dry-run reports what would change. Limits: Both agents show working (prompt, tool use), needs-you (a permission request; for Claude also a question) and done. Claude also shows an error ( StopFailure ); Codex shows idle after an interrupt. Claude's "idle, waiting for your input" notification is ignored. The event names and payload fields were checked against the agents' hook documentation on 2026-11-11; a renamed event shows up as a pane that never changes status. The hooks need the daemon. In in-process mode there is no control socket, and the hooks do nothing. MCP # contour mcp serves the control API to coding agents that speak the Model Context Protocol (MCP): it reads JSON-RPC requests, one per line, on standard input and writes the replies, one per line, on standard output. Nothing else is ever written to standard output; diagnostics go to standard error. Register it once: claude mcp add contour -- contour mcp An agent started in a Contour pane inherits $CONTOUR_PANE , which is its own pane. The server offers these tools (an agent sees only those the daemon's grants permit, see daemon.info ): Tool Does Needs workspace_list Lists workspaces, tabs and panes, marking your own read daemon_info Reports the daemon and the connection's grants read pane_capture Reads a pane's screen screen block_list , block_read Lists and reads command blocks screen pane_run Runs a command in a pane and waits for its result input , screen pane_type Types into a pane input pane_split , tab_create Opens a split or a tab write pane_close , tab_close , object_rename Closes or names write pane_run needs OSC 133 shell integration in the pane. It types one command line (join several with && or ; ), waits, and returns the exit code and the last 64 KiB of output ( maxOutputBytes changes that). A result of timedOut means the command is still running; fetch its output later with block_read . It refuses the agent's own pane, as does pane_type : use pane_split to get a shell pane. By default the agent acts only on the panes of its own tab: an action aimed at another tab is refused, and a name or id suffix is matched within the own tab only. workspace_list still lists every tab, so the agent can tell you what exists; scoping limits what it may do, not what it can see. Without $CONTOUR_PANE the server refuses to start (exit status 2) unless you pass --allow-all-tabs , which lets the agent act on every tab and enables tab_create and tab_close . --read-only leaves out the tools that type or change the workspace. --daemon , --token-file and --tls-ca work as for every verb. The scoping is a guardrail against an agent wandering into the wrong tab, not a sandbox: an agent that can run shell commands can run contour itself, with the same connection. The real boundary is what the daemon's token grants ( contour daemon --access-file ); give an agent a token that can do no more than you want it to.
docs.title: control api

docs.text: Every workspace, tab and pane a Contour daemon hosts can be listed, driven and watched from the shell, from scripts and from coding agents, with the same contour binary that runs the terminal. The verbs below talk to the daemon's control API; contour api list shows everything the API offers, including what has no verb yet.
docs.title: Control API

docs.text: A shell hosted by the daemon finds its surroundings in four environment variables: Variable Holds $CONTOUR_PANE The shell's own pane, pane:<uuid> . The default target of every verb. $CONTOUR_TAB Its tab, tab:<uuid> . $CONTOUR_WORKSPACE Its workspace, workspace:<uuid> . $CONTOUR_DAEMON The daemon's socket path.
docs.title: Where you are

docs.text: Wherever a verb takes a pane, tab or workspace ( --pane P ), P is resolved in this order, and the first kind of match wins: a full id ( pane:018f3c4e-... ); a name, compared case-insensitively (see contour rename ); a 1-based position, for tabs and workspaces; an id suffix of at least four hex digits. More than one match is an error that lists the candidates, one per line. Without --pane , a verb acts on $CONTOUR_PANE ; a pane that has since closed is an error (exit status 3), never a silent fallback to another pane.
docs.title: Targets

docs.text: Verb What it does contour ls [--workspace W] Lists workspaces, tabs and panes as a tree; ids are shortened to their last 8 hex digits and * marks the active ones. contour new [--workspace W \| --new-workspace] [--cwd DIR] [--name NAME] [--no-focus] [-- CMD...] Opens a tab, named NAME with --name , and prints its pane id. Without --cwd the shell starts in the calling pane's directory, when run from one. contour split [--pane P] [--right \| --below] [--ratio PCT] [--cwd DIR] [--name NAME] [--no-focus] [-- CMD...] Splits a pane, naming the new one NAME with --name , and prints the new pane's id. Without --cwd the shell starts in the split pane's directory. contour send [--pane P] [--enter] [--wait] TEXT...\|- Types text into a pane. --enter appends a carriage return, - reads standard input, --wait waits for the command the text starts and exits with that command's own status. contour pane capture [--pane P] [--scrollback N \| --all] Prints a pane's text. contour close [--pane P \| --tab T] Closes a pane, or a tab with all its panes. contour rename OBJECT NAME Names a workspace, tab or pane ( contour rename pane:018f logs ); an empty name clears it. A workspace's or a tab's name is what its windows show for it, in the sidebar, the tab strip and the switcher, over its title; cleared, it shows its title again. The window's Rename… sets this same name. contour workspace new [--cwd DIR] [--name NAME] Opens a workspace with one tab and prints its id. The shell starts in --cwd , and the workspace is named after that folder (its repository's, inside one) unless --name names it. contour workspace close WORKSPACE Closes a workspace with all its tabs and panes, and ends their shells. Whatever it holds at that moment goes, in one step, and the workspace is removed. The daemon's last workspace cannot be closed. contour workspace move --to N WORKSPACE Moves a workspace to position N of the workspace order, counted from 1 as contour ls lists them; a position past the end puts it last. contour tab move [--workspace W] --to N TAB Moves a tab to position N of a workspace, counted from 1: another workspace to take it there, its own to reorder it. Its panes keep running, and a workspace left without tabs is closed. Without --workspace , the calling pane's workspace. contour pane move (--tab T \| --workspace W [--to N] \| --new-workspace) PANE Moves a pane: into tab T as a split beside its active pane, into workspace W as a tab of its own (at position N , counted from 1, or last), or into a new workspace. It keeps running; a tab or a workspace left empty is closed. Prints the workspace it is in now. contour block list [--pane P] [--limit N] Lists a pane's recent command blocks, newest first: id exit duration command . contour block read [BLOCK] [--pane P] [--prompt \| --output] Prints a block's text; without BLOCK , the pane's last finished block. With neither flag, the prompt and then the output. contour switch [--workspace W] (--to-name N \| --to-host H \| --to-workspace W2) [--to-workspace W2] Asks one window to switch to another workspace or daemon, in place. See Switching a window . contour wait [BLOCK] [--pane P] [--timeout SECONDS] Waits for a block to finish and exits with the command's own status. contour events [--follow] [--kind K[,K...]] [--pane P] Prints the first matching event and exits, or with --follow every event until Ctrl+C (exit status 130). contour api list [-q] Lists the API's methods and events; -q prints names only. contour api describe NAME Prints one method's or event's schemas and examples. contour api call NAME [JSON\|@FILE\|-] Calls any method with the given request, sent as is and without context. The output is indented on a terminal and one line otherwise. contour api wit Prints the API as the WIT package terminal-extensions:control@0.1.0 a WebAssembly extension imports, exactly as wit/control/world.wit holds it. Reaches no daemon and takes none of the connection options. contour pane capture is spelled that way because contour capture is the older verb that captures the screen of the terminal it runs in. Until 0.9.0 the older spellings still work, each with a note on standard error naming its replacement: contour label OBJECT NAME and contour workspace rename WORKSPACE NAME run contour rename , and contour switch --to-label is --to-name . Across an upgrade, the daemon and its clients agree on the words: a Contour older than this one is answered in its own spelling ( label keys, object.setLabel , workspace.rename , the event workspace.labelChanged ), and this one speaks that spelling to an older daemon. The MCP tool object_setLabel stays listed, as a deprecated alias of object_rename . Options that look like words ( --pane , but also the bare pane ) can be mistaken for typed text, and a word that starts with a dash but names no option is refused rather than typed: put -- before text that starts with the name of an option or with a dash, as in contour send --enter -- wait or contour send -- -x .
docs.title: Verbs

docs.text: Every verb takes: Option Meaning --json Prints the reply JSON as received, plus a newline, instead of the human form. --daemon PATH\|HOST:PORT\|URL\|NAME The daemon. Defaults to $CONTOUR_DAEMON , then the default socket. A verb never starts a daemon. On every verb --daemon picks the daemon; the verbs that make a workspace, tab or pane name it with --name . --token-file FILE The token a HOST:PORT daemon expects. --tls-ca FILE The CA certificate (PEM) a HOST:PORT daemon is verified against. A HOST:PORT daemon without --tls-ca is refused before anything is sent, with a message naming the option: control requests, which can type into panes, never travel over an unverified connection. A bare word ( --daemon work ) names a local daemon by its name ( contour daemon --name work ), else a saved host of the configuration's hosts: section. A word that names both is refused (exit status 2) with the two spellings that pick one: --daemon name:work and --daemon host:work , which are accepted everywhere. An ssh:// URL names an ad-hoc host. A host is read exactly as contour client --host reads it (see Remote hosts ): the host's own token_file and tls_ca apply, and --token-file and --tls-ca do not. A saved tls:// host without tls_ca is refused like a HOST:PORT daemon without --tls-ca . A word that names neither a local daemon nor a saved host exits 4 with the names that are saved. Until 0.9.0, --label L is still accepted, as --daemon name:L , with a note on standard error.
docs.title: Connection options

docs.text: The workspaces are listed in an order the user can change, and workspace.list reports it as each workspace's position (from 1). workspace.move changes it, and a workspace addressed by its position ( contour ls --workspace 2 ) means the one that holds that place now. tab.move is to tabs what workspace.move is to workspaces, and moves a tab between workspaces as well. pane.move moves one pane out of its tab: into another tab as a split beside that tab's active pane (on the side a drop on a tab takes), into a workspace as a tab of its own, or into a new workspace, which it replies with. Its own tab, or a new workspace for a workspace's only pane, is refused as failed , and changes nothing. Method Request Grant workspace.create {"cwd":"/home/me/src/contour","name":""} , both optional write workspace.close {"workspace":"build"} write workspace.move {"workspace":"build","toPosition":1} write tab.move {"tab":"logs","toWorkspace":"build","toPosition":1} write pane.move {"pane":"logs","to":"tab","toTab":"build"} ; to is tab , workspace (with toWorkspace and an optional toPosition ) or newWorkspace write workspace.create replies with the workspace , tab and pane ids. object.rename names a workspace, as it does a tab or a pane, and publishes object.renamed . A toPosition of 0 , which a missing key reads as, is a bad request (in pane.move too, where a missing key is the end instead), one past the end is clamped, and a target no object matches is notFound . contour api describe NAME prints the schemas and an example of each.
docs.title: Workspace order

docs.text: A workspace created by a control connection is selected by no window yet. It appears in the open GUI's workspace list as hidden , and any window can select it. With no GUI attached it is there for the next launch to find.
docs.title: Workspaces opened by contour new --new-workspace

docs.text: workspace.switch asks one window to switch to another workspace, or to another daemon, in place: a window shows one workspace at a time and moves between a daemon's workspaces without opening another window. It is a socket method (an extension cannot call it) and needs write ; it is not an MCP tool, because an agent in a pane must not re-point the window it runs in. { "toName" : "admin" , "toHost" : "" , "toWorkspace" : "build" } Field Meaning workspace Optional. The workspace whose window switches (id, name, position or suffix): the window selecting it that was focused last. Absent: the window selecting the caller's pane's workspace, and from outside any pane the window that rings and raises for the daemon (the most recently focused one). toName A local daemon, by name. toHost A saved host, or an ssh:// URL. Not together with toName ; with neither, the window stays on this daemon. toWorkspace The destination workspace, as a spec the window resolves against the destination daemon (id, name, position or suffix). Empty lets the window decide. From the command line: contour switch --to-name admin # this pane's window goes to the daemon named admin contour switch --to-host homepc --to-workspace build # a saved host, and its workspace build contour switch --to-workspace 2 # another workspace of the same daemon contour switch --daemon work --workspace w1 --to-name admin # the window selecting w1, from outside any pane --daemon chooses the daemon the window is on now, and --workspace , optionally, the workspace its window selects (default: the workspace of $CONTOUR_PANE , so inside a pane no flags are needed; outside a pane, the window focused last). --to-host takes a saved host's name or an ssh:// URL; any other URL is refused with exit status 2, and must be saved in the configuration's hosts: section first. Without --to-workspace , a destination with exactly one workspace (or none, which creates one) is used; with several, the window asks which in its switcher popup (outcome picker ). contour switch waits for the window's answer and prints the outcome; switched , focused and picker exit 0, refused exits 5, failed exits 1, and a workspace that no window selects (or a daemon with no window attached) exits 3 with the reason. To open a window on another daemon instead of re-pointing one, use contour client --daemon NAME --workspace W or contour client --host H --workspace W (see Remote hosts ). The window asks its user before it switches: a prompt names the destination in full and offers Deny or Switch, with Don't ask again , which keeps the answer for switches between the same two daemons until Contour exits; a remembered Deny is answered refused at once. The daemon tells the window how long it waits for the answer (30 seconds), and the prompt stays up only while an allowed switch could still land before then: the wait less the 10 seconds a switch may take to show its destination, less 2 seconds for the answer to travel back -- 18 seconds. A prompt left unanswered that long is taken down and answered refused ("the user did not answer in time"). An allowed switch must then land within the wait less those 2 seconds, counted from the request's arrival, whatever it waits for first (the destination daemon's workspaces are listed before anything moves): one that could no longer start in time fails, and one still landing then gives up, so a window never switches after contour switch gave up. A daemon on another host may state a longer wait; the window takes at most 5 minutes of it. A destination given as an ssh:// URL is asked every time (see Persistent sessions ). The reply is {"outcome":"switched","detail":""} . outcome is switched , focused (another window already shows the destination, and was focused), picker (the window asked its user which workspace), refused (the user declined: "the user declined the switch") or failed ; detail says why in a sentence. A window that no longer selects the workspace answers failed ("no window here shows workspace N"). A window that does not answer within 30 seconds is reported as failed ("no answer from the window"), and one whose client predates switching as failed ("the window cannot switch (client too old)"). Which window switches is decided by the daemon, always to exactly one. With workspace , it is the window selecting that workspace that was focused last; without it, the window selecting the workspace of the caller's pane; without a pane either, the window that rings and raises. When no window selects the named workspace the call fails as notFound ("no window selects workspace ..."), and with no window attached at all as notFound ("no window is attached"). Two windows selecting the same workspace therefore never make a call fail: the one focused last is asked. workspace.list tells what a switch can act on. Each workspace carries visibility ( shown : some window selects it; hidden : none does), clients (how many windows select it) and native (the daemon's own id for it, in decimal, which a window selects it by). It also says what a switcher shows of a workspace on another daemon. git is the workspace's repository, where its active pane's directory is: branch (the branch or ref name, or a detached HEAD's short object id), kind ( branch , detached or otherRef ), and ahead and behind its upstream where it has one. The daemon looks it up whenever the pane's directory changes or a command finishes, and every 30 seconds, whether or not a window is attached; git is absent outside a repository and until the pane's directory is known. Each pane's lastFinished is its newest finished command block (as block.list reports one: the command, its exit code, when it started and how long it ran), absent until a command has finished; it needs screen , as programStatus does.
