A block without an exit code, with a negative one, or that was superseded by a newer prompt exits 1, with a note on standard error. contour wait with no BLOCK waits for the next block of the pane to finish; one that already finished is read with contour block read . --timeout SECONDS is kept by the client: when it runs out, contour wait prints Error: timed out and exits 1, and the command in the pane carries on. contour send --enter 'make' && contour wait --timeout 600 || echo "make failed or took too long"
docs.title: Waiting

docs.text: contour events subscribes to the daemon's events. A line reads HH:MM:SS type pane details (times are UTC; the pane is the last 8 hex digits of its id behind an ellipsis). With --json each event is printed as received, one per line, which is what scripts read: contour events --follow --json --kind block.finished | jq -r '.payload.block | "\(.exitCode) \(.command)"' An event of a type this release does not know, from a newer daemon, is printed raw. --kind takes a comma separated list of: Event Fires when block.finished A command block finished. pane.bell A pane rang the bell. pane.titleChanged A pane's title changed. pane.cwdChanged A pane's working directory changed. object.renamed A workspace, tab or pane was renamed ( object.rename , or a window's Rename… ); the payload carries its object id and its name , empty when it was cleared. pane.programStatusChanged A pane's program status changed. pane.created , pane.closed A pane was created or closed. tab.created , tab.closed A tab was created or closed. client.attached , client.detached A GUI client attached or detached. events.dropped The subscriber was too slow and events were dropped.
docs.title: Events

docs.text: Status Meaning 0 Done. 1 The call failed; the reason is on standard error as Error: <message> . 2 The command line was malformed, or a setting it names cannot be used (a --tls-ca that does not parse). 3 The pane, tab, workspace or block named does not exist, or the name matches several. 4 No daemon could be reached. 5 The daemon declined; the reason is on standard error. 130 Interrupted by Ctrl+C. contour send --wait exits with the command's own status instead (0 to 255). A command with no exit code, or one that was superseded, exits 1 with a note on standard error.
docs.title: Exit statuses

docs.text: A daemon's TCP tokens carry grants ( contour daemon --access-file ): read for listing, screen for capturing, reading blocks and program status ( pane.programStatusChanged , and the programStatus and lastFinished of contour ls --json ), input for typing, and write for changing the workspace. A call outside the token's grants is refused as forbidden (exit status 1). The daemon's socket grants everything to its owner. daemon.info reports the connection's own grants in its grants array (by name, in the order above), so a client can tell what it may call before it tries. A connection holds at most 64 subscriptions and 256 pending waits; one more is refused as limitReached (exit status 1). Each verb opens a connection of its own, so only a script driving contour api call over one connection meets it.
docs.title: Permissions

docs.text: An integration, such as a coding agent's hook, tells the daemon what a pane's program is doing with two methods. Both need the input grant, and both are reachable with contour api call : Method What it does pane.reportStatus Sets the integration's own record of a pane: {"pane": "...", "integration": "claude-code", "state": "blocked", "kind": "permission", "title": "...", "message": "...", "progress": 40} . integration is [a-z0-9-]{1,32} and becomes the record's id; state is idle , working , done , blocked or error ; kind ( none , permission , question , auth ) is for blocked only. An empty pane is the caller's own. pane.clearStatus Removes the record that integration set: {"pane": "...", "integration": "claude-code"} . Records a program sent by OSC 7501 are not touched. The title and message are untrusted text: control and invisible formatting characters are removed, and each is cut to 200 bytes. Records the integration sets list as origin: "integration" , apart from a program's origin: "program" , with since (when the state or kind last changed) and a generation that rises whenever the state or kind changes (not when only the title, message or progress does). When someone types or pastes into the pane in a Contour window, the integration's blocked records become working : the person has answered. Input sent with pane.send does not do that, nor do the focus and mouse reports a window sends by itself, nor does input from a client too old to say which of its input was typed. These methods need a daemon. In-process mode (no contour daemon ) has no control socket, so a hook finds none and does nothing.
docs.title: Reporting a pane's status

docs.text: daemon.upgrade replaces the running daemon with a newer release, keeping every program running (see Live upgrade ); contour daemon upgrade is its verb. contour api call daemon.upgrade '{"image":""}' image names a staged image of the daemon's store; empty, the daemon upgrades to its own installed executable, the file a package upgrade replaced. The call needs write and a connection on the daemon's own machine, through the daemon's Unix socket: over a TCP token it is refused. It is not offered to extensions or to the agent's tools. The reply, {"started":true,"toRelease":"0.9.1"} , is sent before the daemon tells its clients it is upgrading and closes every connection, this one included; the clients reconnect to the same daemon. It is provisional: the daemon may still decline after it, while it waits for its clients and sessions to settle, and the switch to the new binary may fail. Either way the daemon then resumes and serves on as before, and the connection that asked is gone by then. contour daemon status tells how it ended: its upgrades count is one higher once the new release serves, and a last upgrade line names the failure otherwise. contour daemon upgrade reads it there for you. A refusal before the reply is an error with code failed whose message leads with a stable name, then says why: sandboxed: the daemon runs in a sandbox that cannot reach the new release . The names are inProgress , notStaged , sandboxed , formatUnreadable , inFlightTailTooLarge , targetUnresponsive , notSupported , unsupportedSession , sessionStarting , quiesceTimedOut , imageTooLarge , configUnreadable and localOnly . execFailed , an exec that failed after the daemon stopped its sessions' pumps and resumed them, always comes after the reply, so this call never returns it; it is the name contour daemon status reports such a failure under. A connection that breaks before the reply leaves the outcome unknown: ask contour daemon status again.
docs.title: Upgrading the daemon

docs.text: pane = $( contour split --below --no-focus --json | jq -r .pane ) contour send --pane " $pane " --enter --wait -- 'make test' # exits with make's status contour block read --pane " $pane " --output # what it printed
docs.title: A workflow: run the tests beside you

docs.text: contour agent setup writes a skill that teaches coding agents to operate Contour panes: where they are, how targets resolve, every verb with its usage, the exit statuses, the run-the-tests workflow, and the whole API. The skill is generated from the verb table and the API catalog, so it always matches the binary. contour agent setup # every agent found, and ~/.agents contour agent setup --agent claude-code --dry-run Agent Skill file claude-code (Claude Code) ~/.claude/skills/contour/SKILL.md , or beneath $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that is set agents (Codex, OpenCode and other agents reading ~/.agents ) ~/.agents/skills/contour/SKILL.md Without --agent , an agent is set up only when its configuration directory exists ( ~/.claude or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR ; ~/.codex or $CODEX_HOME ), so nothing is created for an agent you do not use; the report says which were skipped. Naming an agent with --agent sets it up whether or not it is found. The names are the ones contour agent report --agent takes. Rerun it after upgrading Contour: a file it generated is updated, one that is already current is left alone, and a file it did not generate is kept unless you pass --force . --dry-run reports what would happen, and --json prints the outcomes as an array.
docs.title: Agents

docs.text: contour agent setup also installs the hooks that let a coding agent tell Contour what it is doing, so that the pane shows a working, blocked (waiting for you) or done status. The hooks run contour agent report --agent <claude-code|codex> , which turns the agent's hook payload into pane.reportStatus or pane.clearStatus on the daemon hosting the pane. It prints nothing, always exits 0, gives up after two seconds (reading the payload included), ignores a payload larger than 1 MiB, and does nothing outside a pane of a Contour daemon (no $CONTOUR_DAEMON or $CONTOUR_PANE ; a window running its sessions in process does not pass those on to its own shells). The contour binary is written into the hooks by its absolute path (under an AppImage, the AppImage's), so rerun contour agent setup after moving it. Agent Hook file What is installed claude-code (Claude Code) ~/.claude/settings.json , or beneath $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR one hook group for each of UserPromptSubmit , PreToolUse , PermissionRequest , Notification , Elicitation , PostToolUse , PostToolUseFailure , Stop , StopFailure and SessionEnd codex (Codex) ~/.codex/hooks.json , or beneath $CODEX_HOME (which must already exist) one hook group for each of UserPromptSubmit , PreToolUse , PermissionRequest , PostToolUse , Stop , Interrupt and SessionEnd Your own hooks and settings are kept, and a file is replaced in one step (a symlinked one through its link, which stays). A hook of ours is one whose command is exactly the binary followed by agent report --agent <claude-code|codex> ; a command of yours that merely mentions it is left alone. A hook file that is not valid JSON is left alone and reported, and so is a $CODEX_HOME that names a directory that does not exist (it is not created). Codex runs only hooks you have reviewed: after contour agent setup , open Codex once and trust the new hooks (its hooks review), or they never run and the pane shows no status. contour agent setup --uninstall removes exactly these hooks (and leaves the skill file as it is), and the groups and event arrays that held only them; --dry-run reports what would change. Limits: Both agents show working (prompt, tool use), needs-you (a permission request; for Claude also a question) and done. Claude also shows an error ( StopFailure ); Codex shows idle after an interrupt. Claude's "idle, waiting for your input" notification is ignored. The event names and payload fields were checked against the agents' hook documentation on 2026-11-11; a renamed event shows up as a pane that never changes status. The hooks need the daemon. In in-process mode there is no control socket, and the hooks do nothing.
docs.title: Status hooks

docs.text: contour mcp serves the control API to coding agents that speak the Model Context Protocol (MCP): it reads JSON-RPC requests, one per line, on standard input and writes the replies, one per line, on standard output. Nothing else is ever written to standard output; diagnostics go to standard error. Register it once: claude mcp add contour -- contour mcp An agent started in a Contour pane inherits $CONTOUR_PANE , which is its own pane. The server offers these tools (an agent sees only those the daemon's grants permit, see daemon.info ): Tool Does Needs workspace_list Lists workspaces, tabs and panes, marking your own read daemon_info Reports the daemon and the connection's grants read pane_capture Reads a pane's screen screen block_list , block_read Lists and reads command blocks screen pane_run Runs a command in a pane and waits for its result input , screen pane_type Types into a pane input pane_split , tab_create Opens a split or a tab write pane_close , tab_close , object_rename Closes or names write pane_run needs OSC 133 shell integration in the pane. It types one command line (join several with && or ; ), waits, and returns the exit code and the last 64 KiB of output ( maxOutputBytes changes that). A result of timedOut means the command is still running; fetch its output later with block_read . It refuses the agent's own pane, as does pane_type : use pane_split to get a shell pane. By default the agent acts only on the panes of its own tab: an action aimed at another tab is refused, and a name or id suffix is matched within the own tab only. workspace_list still lists every tab, so the agent can tell you what exists; scoping limits what it may do, not what it can see. Without $CONTOUR_PANE the server refuses to start (exit status 2) unless you pass --allow-all-tabs , which lets the agent act on every tab and enables tab_create and tab_close . --read-only leaves out the tools that type or change the workspace. --daemon , --token-file and --tls-ca work as for every verb. The scoping is a guardrail against an agent wandering into the wrong tab, not a sandbox: an agent that can run shell commands can run contour itself, with the same connection. The real boundary is what the daemon's token grants ( contour daemon --access-file ); give an agent a token that can do no more than you want it to.
docs.title: MCP

docs.text:
Status-line extensions # Experimental Status-line extensions are new, and the interface they are written against, the terminal-extensions:statusline@0.1.0 world, may still change before it is declared stable. A status-line extension is a small WebAssembly module that draws part of the indicator status line, or all of it. It is told what happens in its pane (the working directory changed, a program set a user variable, the pane gained the focus, ...), and it answers with the text, colours and, when it owns the whole line, images to show. Extensions run sandboxed. A module sees no files, no network and no environment; it gets the time and the pane's state from Contour, and it can run only the commands it declared up front, and only once you said it may. Every call into an extension has a time limit, and its memory a cap. Extensions run on a small pool of worker threads shared by every pane -- as many as the machine has cores, four at most -- and never on the threads that read the terminal's output, parse it or draw it. Each extension is handed one of the workers, in turn. A slow, frozen or crashing extension therefore never slows the terminal down: it keeps reading, parsing and drawing at full speed (see Performance ). It can delay the other extensions on its worker, though, by up to its time limit per call, until it fails often enough to be disabled. Configuring extensions # Extensions are configured per profile. Each entry under extensions: is one extension; its key is the name the status line refers to it by. profiles : main : extensions : clock : {} git : { run_command : ask } plasma : { config : { text : "{mode} {title}" , speed : "2" } } mine : { path : ~/wasm/mine.wasm , run_command : deny } Key Meaning path The module to load; a leading ~ is the home directory, and a relative path is taken relative to the directory of the configuration file that declares it. Without a path the key selects the bundled extension of that name. config Text values the extension reads by key; what each extension understands is listed with it. run_command Whether the extension may run the commands its manifest declares: allow , deny or ask . Default: ask . See Permissions . An extension shows up where the status line names it. There are two ways: As a segment. {Extension:<name>} in one of the indicator status line's templates is replaced by the extension's text, with its colours and attributes. Every other placeholder keeps working beside it. The long form takes the usual formatting styles: {Extension:Name=git,Left= ,Right= } . profiles : main : status_line : indicator : left : " {InputMode:Bold}{Extension:git}" right : "{Extension:clock}" Taking the line over. status_line.extension names one extension that draws the whole indicator status line instead of its templates. Only an extension that takes the line over may draw images (Sixel or the kitty graphics protocol); as a segment an extension draws text only. profiles : main : status_line : display : indicator extension : plasma A name that is not one of the profile's extensions is reported in the log, and the templates are used. Every pane runs its own instance of each of its profile's extensions. Changing extensions: and reloading the configuration (or switching the profile) restarts them; an unchanged set keeps running. When an extension fails (it traps, exceeds its time limit or its memory, or writes too much output), it is restarted after a short back-off. Three failures within a minute disable it, and its place shows ⚠ <name> disabled: <reason> instead. A module that cannot be found or loaded shows the same notice right away. Bundled extensions # Contour ships these extensions. Name one under extensions: without a path to use it. Name Shows Settings clock The local time of day, HH:MM , daylight saving included. Wakes once a minute. none git The branch of the git repository the pane's working directory is in, with * when the working tree has changes. Runs git , so it asks first. Refreshes when the directory or the foreground process changes (the latter on Linux and macOS) and when the pane gains the focus. refresh-ms : also refresh this often while focused (default 0 , never) sysload The system's load: the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages from uptime , or the processor load on Windows. Runs a command, so it asks first. refresh-ms : how often, while focused (default 5000 ) agent-status A badge for the state a coding agent reports in a user variable ( working , waiting , done ), and the progress it reports (OSC 9;4). variable : the user variable to follow (default agent_status ) plasma An animated plasma drawn with Sixel across the whole line, with text on top. Meant to take the line over; animates only while the pane is focused. text : drawn on top, where {mode} , {title} and {tabs} are filled in; speed : how fast the colours cycle (default 1 ) A coding agent, or a hook it runs, sets the variable agent-status follows like this: printf '\e]1337;SetUserVar=agent_status=%s\a' " $( printf working | base64 ) " Permissions # An extension can run a program only if its module declares the command in its manifest , and only as declared: the program and its arguments are fixed, and the extension fills in only the placeholders the declaration names. No shell is involved. What run_command says decides the rest: deny : no command runs. allow : every declared command runs, without asking. ask (the default): the first time the extension tries to run a command, Contour asks you. The question names the extension, the module it was loaded from, and every command it declares, exactly as it would run. Allow lets it run its declared commands from now on. Deny refuses them from now on. Closing the question answers nothing: the extension's commands keep failing, and you are asked again once the extension starts anew, in a new pane or after a configuration reload restarts it. The call that triggered the question fails at once; nothing waits for your answer. Once you allowed it, the extension's next attempt succeeds. Your answer is remembered for that installation of the extension and for that exact manifest: an extension configured under another name or loaded from another path, or one whose manifest changed in any way (an update that adds a command, say), is asked about again. Answers are kept beside the configuration file: extension-grants.txt for the GUI; extension-grants.daemon.txt for contour daemon , named after the socket it serves, so that daemons sharing a configuration directory, and the GUI, keep their answers apart: extension-grants.daemon.<name>.txt for a daemon of another name than the default one (every character of the name but letters, digits, . , - and _ spelled _ ); extension-grants.daemon[.<name>].<hash>.txt for a daemon given a socket path other than its name's own, where <hash> is eight hex digits computed from that path. A daemon's answers govern commands that run on the daemon's machine. To take an answer back, delete its line from the file, or the whole file. In daemon sessions # A session hosted by contour daemon runs its extensions in the daemon, where the session's terminal lives, and its clients show what they draw. The profile the daemon loads decides which extensions run; a client's own profile only decides whether the status line is shown. Mirrored panes run no extensions of their own. A question about an extension's commands is asked in the attached client, and remembered in the daemon's grants file. This works with some limits for now: No font events. The daemon draws in no font, so extensions in daemon sessions are not told the font's size or the cell size, and an image an extension draws is sized for a default cell. A dismissed question waits for a reattach. If you close the question instead of answering it, it is asked again only when a client attaches to the session again. No tab events. The daemon does not tell its extensions about the client's tabs. Writing an extension # An extension is a WebAssembly core module built for wasm32-wasip1 that implements the terminal-extensions:statusline world. The world, at wit/statusline/ , is the contract, and its README spells out what the WIT text cannot: when the host calls what, what it guarantees, and how the contract is carried in the binary. Any language with a wit-bindgen generator works; the bundled extensions are written in Rust, and so is this walkthrough. The world in short # The host calls three functions of the module: load(config) : once, first, with the extension's config: values. It returns the event kinds the extension wants to hear about, any of title , cwd , foreground-process , input-mode , tabs , user-var , progress , focus and font . foreground-process is reported on Linux and macOS only; on Windows no such event arrives. It is always told when its own surface is resized, when a frame it asked for is due, and the terminal's replies to queries in its output. update(event) : once per event, in order. It answers render when what the extension shows has changed, none otherwise. render(cols, rows) : after load , and after an update that answered render . It returns the bytes that draw the status line on a terminal of that many cells: text, SGR colours and attributes, cursor movement and, when the extension takes the line over, images. And the module may call four functions of the host: state() : the pane's current state (working directory, title, focus, user variables, the time and the time zone's offset, the font, ...); request-frame(ms) : asks for a timer event; this is how an extension animates, or wakes at the next minute. It never sleeps; run-command(name, args) : runs a command its manifest declares, if allowed; log(level, message) : writes to Contour's log. A Rust crate # # Cargo.toml [package] name = "hello" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2021" [lib] crate-type = [ "cdylib" ] [dependencies] wit-bindgen = { version = "0.63.0" , default-features = false , features = [ "macros" , "realloc" ] } [profile.release] opt-level = "s" lto = true panic = "abort" // src/lib.rs wit_bindgen :: generate ! ({ path : "wit/statusline" , // a copy of Contour's wit/statusline directory world : "statusline" , }); struct Hello ; impl Guest for Hello { fn load ( _config : Vec < ( String , String ) > ) -> EventKinds { EventKinds :: CWD } fn update ( _event : Event ) -> RenderRequest { RenderRequest :: Render } fn render ( _cols : u32 , _rows : u32 ) -> Vec < u8 > { let cwd = terminal_extensions :: statusline :: host :: state (). cwd ; format! ( " \x1b [1m{cwd} \x1b [m" ). into_bytes () } } export ! ( Hello ); Build it with the wasm32-wasip1 target, and point a profile at the module: rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # target/wasm32-wasip1/release/hello.wasm profiles : main : extensions : hello : { path : ~/src/hello/target/wasm32-wasip1/release/hello.wasm } status_line : indicator : right : "{Extension:hello}" The module stays a plain core module: do not componentize it. The bundled extensions under extensions/bundled/ are complete examples; clock is the smallest. Keep the limits in mind: each call ( load included) has a deadline (50 ms for update and render ), the module's memory is capped at 32 MiB, one render may return at most 1 MiB, and renders are at least 16 ms apart. Events are coalesced under load, so an extension sees the latest working directory rather than every one in between. The manifest # A module that runs commands declares them in a custom section named terminal-extension-manifest , which Contour reads before it runs any of the module's code: name = git version = 1 command status = git --no-optional-locks -C {cwd} status --porcelain=v2 --branch run-command("status", [("cwd", "/home/me/src")]) then runs exactly that argv, the whole value of cwd as one argument. In Rust, the manifest crate under extensions/manifest emits the section: manifest :: declare_manifest ! ( "name = git 
 version = 1 
 command status = git --no-optional-locks -C {cwd} status --porcelain=v2 --branch 
 " ); A module without a manifest loads and runs; every command it tries fails. The manifest's full grammar, and the rules for the values filled into a command, are in the world's README . Performance # Extensions run on a small pool of worker threads, never on the threads that read the terminal's output, parse it or draw it, and nothing on those threads ever waits for an extension: an event an extension's queue cannot take is dropped, not waited for. A profile without extensions starts none of their machinery: no WebAssembly runtime, no worker thread, no timer. Throughput # Measured on a 32-thread Linux machine with bench-headless throughput , a release build, 16 MiB per workload fed from memory, the indicator status line shown and the terminal focused. Each cell is the faster of two rounds, run interleaved (one configuration after the other, twice), each round the fastest of 5 runs. The misbehaving guest spins until its time limit stops it, on every call, for the whole run (the benchmark restarts it at once and never disables it): Workload (primary screen) No extensions configured plasma animating + a guest spinning to its time limit Four such guests, every worker busy ascii 238 MiB/s 238 MiB/s 239 MiB/s colored 161 MiB/s 160 MiB/s 160 MiB/s sgr 95 MiB/s 95 MiB/s 94 MiB/s utf8 36 MiB/s 36 MiB/s 36 MiB/s tui 261 MiB/s 262 MiB/s 261 MiB/s The one dip that repeated is on the alternate screen, which the table does not show: with four guests keeping every worker busy, sgr there ran about 4 % slower in both rounds (98 against 94 MiB/s). Memory # Each extension runs as its own instance in every pane: its WebAssembly memory, and a small private terminal its output is drawn on. Measured with bench-headless memory (a release build on Linux, each pane 120×40 with 1000 lines of scrollback, the indicator shown and focused, refreshed at 60 Hz for 5 s, the process's resident set before and after): Panes No extensions All five bundled extensions ( plasma taking the line over and animating) Cost of the extensions 1 4.5 MiB 13.2 MiB 8.7 MiB 10 21.0 MiB 104.2 MiB 8.3 MiB per pane One extension costs about 1.6 MiB per pane, plasma about 2.3 MiB (its image is drawn on its surface, and again in the pane's status line). An empty module costs 1.4 MiB per pane too: most of an extension's cost is the private terminal and the runtime's per-instance state every extension has, not what it does. Shared by all panes, once, are the runtime and its workers: well under 1 MiB. Without extensions # A build without extensions compiled in runs within the same few percent: its parser executes the same number of instructions (Callgrind) as one with them. An idle Contour with no extensions configured wakes up exactly as often as one built without them (measured on Qt's offscreen platform). The WebAssembly runtime # Extensions run on WAMR 's fast interpreter, but nothing in Contour that hosts them names it. They are loaded, instantiated and called through a runtime-neutral interface ( src/vtextension/wasm/WasmRuntime.hpp ), and the runtime behind it is a backend chosen when Contour is built: the CMake cache variable CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME (today its one value is wamr ) selects the target vtextension_<runtime> . Only what composes a program links that backend, through vtextension_runtime , and creates it with vtextension::wasm::makeDefaultBackend() : the GUI, contour daemon , bench-headless and the test suites. The extension engine and the daemon's session host see only the interface. The check_wasm_runtime_containment lint gate ( ctest -L lint ) holds them to it: it fails when a file under src/ outside the backend directory includes WAMR's C headers or the backend's own headers, or when the vtextension or vthost library links WAMR. Bringing in another runtime is adding a backend directory beside src/vtextension/wasm/wamr/ and a value of CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME ; the behaviour an extension sees is pinned by the backend contract tests every backend must pass. Adding a backend # A backend for a runtime <runtime> is the directory src/vtextension/wasm/<runtime>/ , and it must provide all of the following; src/vtextension/wasm/wamr/ is the one to copy from. A CMakeLists.txt defining the target vtextension_<runtime> , which links vtextension publicly and the runtime itself privately. src/vtextension/CMakeLists.txt adds the directory named by CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME and links its target into vtextension_runtime ; nothing else may link the runtime. A value of CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME : <runtime> added to _CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIMES in the top-level CMakeLists.txt , which refuses any value not on that list. vtextension::wasm::makeDefaultBackend() (declared in src/vtextension/wasm/DefaultBackend.hpp ), defined in the backend's target and returning its IWasmBackend (WAMR: DefaultBackend.cpp ). vtextension::wasm::testing::preparedGeneration() (declared in src/vtextension/wasm/testing/PreparedGeneration.hpp ), defined in a PreparedGeneration.cpp added to vtextension_test only: the runtime generation the calling thread was prepared for, 0 if none. The contract suite, instantiated in vtextension_test : a *_test.cpp the directory adds to vtextension_test , holding a traits struct whose make() returns a new backend and the line CONTOUR_WASM_BACKEND_CONTRACT(Traits) (from src/vtextension/wasm/testing/BackendContract.hpp ). Every case tagged [wasm-contract] must pass, among them the two rules no backend is exempt from: the runtime generation increases on each bring-up, and entering a thread guard fails RuntimeUnavailable while no runtime is up. A passing containment gate : ctest -L lint ( check_wasm_runtime_containment ) must pass. The gate knows WAMR's C headers, backend directory and link target by name ( scripts/check-wasm-runtime-containment.py ); teach it the new runtime's alongside, so that they too stay inside the backend directory.

docs.text: Extensions are configured per profile. Each entry under extensions: is one extension; its key is the name the status line refers to it by. profiles : main : extensions : clock : {} git : { run_command : ask } plasma : { config : { text : "{mode} {title}" , speed : "2" } } mine : { path : ~/wasm/mine.wasm , run_command : deny } Key Meaning path The module to load; a leading ~ is the home directory, and a relative path is taken relative to the directory of the configuration file that declares it. Without a path the key selects the bundled extension of that name. config Text values the extension reads by key; what each extension understands is listed with it. run_command Whether the extension may run the commands its manifest declares: allow , deny or ask . Default: ask . See Permissions . An extension shows up where the status line names it. There are two ways: As a segment. {Extension:<name>} in one of the indicator status line's templates is replaced by the extension's text, with its colours and attributes. Every other placeholder keeps working beside it. The long form takes the usual formatting styles: {Extension:Name=git,Left= ,Right= } . profiles : main : status_line : indicator : left : " {InputMode:Bold}{Extension:git}" right : "{Extension:clock}" Taking the line over. status_line.extension names one extension that draws the whole indicator status line instead of its templates. Only an extension that takes the line over may draw images (Sixel or the kitty graphics protocol); as a segment an extension draws text only. profiles : main : status_line : display : indicator extension : plasma A name that is not one of the profile's extensions is reported in the log, and the templates are used. Every pane runs its own instance of each of its profile's extensions. Changing extensions: and reloading the configuration (or switching the profile) restarts them; an unchanged set keeps running. When an extension fails (it traps, exceeds its time limit or its memory, or writes too much output), it is restarted after a short back-off. Three failures within a minute disable it, and its place shows ⚠ <name> disabled: <reason> instead. A module that cannot be found or loaded shows the same notice right away.
docs.title: Configuring extensions

docs.text: Contour ships these extensions. Name one under extensions: without a path to use it. Name Shows Settings clock The local time of day, HH:MM , daylight saving included. Wakes once a minute. none git The branch of the git repository the pane's working directory is in, with * when the working tree has changes. Runs git , so it asks first. Refreshes when the directory or the foreground process changes (the latter on Linux and macOS) and when the pane gains the focus. refresh-ms : also refresh this often while focused (default 0 , never) sysload The system's load: the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages from uptime , or the processor load on Windows. Runs a command, so it asks first. refresh-ms : how often, while focused (default 5000 ) agent-status A badge for the state a coding agent reports in a user variable ( working , waiting , done ), and the progress it reports (OSC 9;4). variable : the user variable to follow (default agent_status ) plasma An animated plasma drawn with Sixel across the whole line, with text on top. Meant to take the line over; animates only while the pane is focused. text : drawn on top, where {mode} , {title} and {tabs} are filled in; speed : how fast the colours cycle (default 1 ) A coding agent, or a hook it runs, sets the variable agent-status follows like this: printf '\e]1337;SetUserVar=agent_status=%s\a' " $( printf working | base64 ) "
docs.title: Bundled extensions

docs.text: An extension can run a program only if its module declares the command in its manifest , and only as declared: the program and its arguments are fixed, and the extension fills in only the placeholders the declaration names. No shell is involved. What run_command says decides the rest: deny : no command runs. allow : every declared command runs, without asking. ask (the default): the first time the extension tries to run a command, Contour asks you. The question names the extension, the module it was loaded from, and every command it declares, exactly as it would run. Allow lets it run its declared commands from now on. Deny refuses them from now on. Closing the question answers nothing: the extension's commands keep failing, and you are asked again once the extension starts anew, in a new pane or after a configuration reload restarts it. The call that triggered the question fails at once; nothing waits for your answer. Once you allowed it, the extension's next attempt succeeds. Your answer is remembered for that installation of the extension and for that exact manifest: an extension configured under another name or loaded from another path, or one whose manifest changed in any way (an update that adds a command, say), is asked about again. Answers are kept beside the configuration file: extension-grants.txt for the GUI; extension-grants.daemon.txt for contour daemon , named after the socket it serves, so that daemons sharing a configuration directory, and the GUI, keep their answers apart: extension-grants.daemon.<name>.txt for a daemon of another name than the default one (every character of the name but letters, digits, . , - and _ spelled _ ); extension-grants.daemon[.<name>].<hash>.txt for a daemon given a socket path other than its name's own, where <hash> is eight hex digits computed from that path. A daemon's answers govern commands that run on the daemon's machine. To take an answer back, delete its line from the file, or the whole file.
docs.title: Permissions

docs.text: A session hosted by contour daemon runs its extensions in the daemon, where the session's terminal lives, and its clients show what they draw. The profile the daemon loads decides which extensions run; a client's own profile only decides whether the status line is shown. Mirrored panes run no extensions of their own. A question about an extension's commands is asked in the attached client, and remembered in the daemon's grants file. This works with some limits for now: No font events. The daemon draws in no font, so extensions in daemon sessions are not told the font's size or the cell size, and an image an extension draws is sized for a default cell. A dismissed question waits for a reattach. If you close the question instead of answering it, it is asked again only when a client attaches to the session again. No tab events. The daemon does not tell its extensions about the client's tabs.
docs.title: In daemon sessions

docs.text: An extension is a WebAssembly core module built for wasm32-wasip1 that implements the terminal-extensions:statusline world. The world, at wit/statusline/ , is the contract, and its README spells out what the WIT text cannot: when the host calls what, what it guarantees, and how the contract is carried in the binary. Any language with a wit-bindgen generator works; the bundled extensions are written in Rust, and so is this walkthrough.
docs.title: Writing an extension

docs.text: The host calls three functions of the module: load(config) : once, first, with the extension's config: values. It returns the event kinds the extension wants to hear about, any of title , cwd , foreground-process , input-mode , tabs , user-var , progress , focus and font . foreground-process is reported on Linux and macOS only; on Windows no such event arrives. It is always told when its own surface is resized, when a frame it asked for is due, and the terminal's replies to queries in its output. update(event) : once per event, in order. It answers render when what the extension shows has changed, none otherwise. render(cols, rows) : after load , and after an update that answered render . It returns the bytes that draw the status line on a terminal of that many cells: text, SGR colours and attributes, cursor movement and, when the extension takes the line over, images. And the module may call four functions of the host: state() : the pane's current state (working directory, title, focus, user variables, the time and the time zone's offset, the font, ...); request-frame(ms) : asks for a timer event; this is how an extension animates, or wakes at the next minute. It never sleeps; run-command(name, args) : runs a command its manifest declares, if allowed; log(level, message) : writes to Contour's log.
docs.title: The world in short

docs.text: # Cargo.toml [package] name = "hello" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2021" [lib] crate-type = [ "cdylib" ] [dependencies] wit-bindgen = { version = "0.63.0" , default-features = false , features = [ "macros" , "realloc" ] } [profile.release] opt-level = "s" lto = true panic = "abort" // src/lib.rs wit_bindgen :: generate ! ({ path : "wit/statusline" , // a copy of Contour's wit/statusline directory world : "statusline" , }); struct Hello ; impl Guest for Hello { fn load ( _config : Vec < ( String , String ) > ) -> EventKinds { EventKinds :: CWD } fn update ( _event : Event ) -> RenderRequest { RenderRequest :: Render } fn render ( _cols : u32 , _rows : u32 ) -> Vec < u8 > { let cwd = terminal_extensions :: statusline :: host :: state (). cwd ; format! ( " \x1b [1m{cwd} \x1b [m" ). into_bytes () } } export ! ( Hello ); Build it with the wasm32-wasip1 target, and point a profile at the module: rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # target/wasm32-wasip1/release/hello.wasm profiles : main : extensions : hello : { path : ~/src/hello/target/wasm32-wasip1/release/hello.wasm } status_line : indicator : right : "{Extension:hello}" The module stays a plain core module: do not componentize it. The bundled extensions under extensions/bundled/ are complete examples; clock is the smallest. Keep the limits in mind: each call ( load included) has a deadline (50 ms for update and render ), the module's memory is capped at 32 MiB, one render may return at most 1 MiB, and renders are at least 16 ms apart. Events are coalesced under load, so an extension sees the latest working directory rather than every one in between.
docs.title: A Rust crate

docs.text:
A module that runs commands declares them in a custom section named terminal-extension-manifest , which Contour reads before it runs any of the module's code: name = git version = 1 command status = git --no-optional-locks -C {cwd} status --porcelain=v2 --branch run-command("status", [("cwd", "/home/me/src")]) then runs exactly that argv, the whole value of cwd as one argument. In Rust, the manifest crate under extensions/manifest emits the section: manifest :: declare_manifest ! ( "name = git 
 version = 1 
 command status = git --no-optional-locks -C {cwd} status --porcelain=v2 --branch 
 " ); A module without a manifest loads and runs; every command it tries fails. The manifest's full grammar, and the rules for the values filled into a command, are in the world's README .
docs.title: The manifest

docs.text: Extensions run on a small pool of worker threads, never on the threads that read the terminal's output, parse it or draw it, and nothing on those threads ever waits for an extension: an event an extension's queue cannot take is dropped, not waited for. A profile without extensions starts none of their machinery: no WebAssembly runtime, no worker thread, no timer.
docs.title: Performance

docs.text: Measured on a 32-thread Linux machine with bench-headless throughput , a release build, 16 MiB per workload fed from memory, the indicator status line shown and the terminal focused. Each cell is the faster of two rounds, run interleaved (one configuration after the other, twice), each round the fastest of 5 runs. The misbehaving guest spins until its time limit stops it, on every call, for the whole run (the benchmark restarts it at once and never disables it): Workload (primary screen) No extensions configured plasma animating + a guest spinning to its time limit Four such guests, every worker busy ascii 238 MiB/s 238 MiB/s 239 MiB/s colored 161 MiB/s 160 MiB/s 160 MiB/s sgr 95 MiB/s 95 MiB/s 94 MiB/s utf8 36 MiB/s 36 MiB/s 36 MiB/s tui 261 MiB/s 262 MiB/s 261 MiB/s The one dip that repeated is on the alternate screen, which the table does not show: with four guests keeping every worker busy, sgr there ran about 4 % slower in both rounds (98 against 94 MiB/s).
docs.title: Throughput

docs.text: Each extension runs as its own instance in every pane: its WebAssembly memory, and a small private terminal its output is drawn on. Measured with bench-headless memory (a release build on Linux, each pane 120×40 with 1000 lines of scrollback, the indicator shown and focused, refreshed at 60 Hz for 5 s, the process's resident set before and after): Panes No extensions All five bundled extensions ( plasma taking the line over and animating) Cost of the extensions 1 4.5 MiB 13.2 MiB 8.7 MiB 10 21.0 MiB 104.2 MiB 8.3 MiB per pane One extension costs about 1.6 MiB per pane, plasma about 2.3 MiB (its image is drawn on its surface, and again in the pane's status line). An empty module costs 1.4 MiB per pane too: most of an extension's cost is the private terminal and the runtime's per-instance state every extension has, not what it does. Shared by all panes, once, are the runtime and its workers: well under 1 MiB.
docs.title: Memory

docs.text: A build without extensions compiled in runs within the same few percent: its parser executes the same number of instructions (Callgrind) as one with them. An idle Contour with no extensions configured wakes up exactly as often as one built without them (measured on Qt's offscreen platform).
docs.title: Without extensions

docs.text: Extensions run on WAMR 's fast interpreter, but nothing in Contour that hosts them names it. They are loaded, instantiated and called through a runtime-neutral interface ( src/vtextension/wasm/WasmRuntime.hpp ), and the runtime behind it is a backend chosen when Contour is built: the CMake cache variable CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME (today its one value is wamr ) selects the target vtextension_<runtime> . Only what composes a program links that backend, through vtextension_runtime , and creates it with vtextension::wasm::makeDefaultBackend() : the GUI, contour daemon , bench-headless and the test suites. The extension engine and the daemon's session host see only the interface. The check_wasm_runtime_containment lint gate ( ctest -L lint ) holds them to it: it fails when a file under src/ outside the backend directory includes WAMR's C headers or the backend's own headers, or when the vtextension or vthost library links WAMR. Bringing in another runtime is adding a backend directory beside src/vtextension/wasm/wamr/ and a value of CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME ; the behaviour an extension sees is pinned by the backend contract tests every backend must pass.
docs.title: The WebAssembly runtime

docs.text: A backend for a runtime <runtime> is the directory src/vtextension/wasm/<runtime>/ , and it must provide all of the following; src/vtextension/wasm/wamr/ is the one to copy from. A CMakeLists.txt defining the target vtextension_<runtime> , which links vtextension publicly and the runtime itself privately. src/vtextension/CMakeLists.txt adds the directory named by CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME and links its target into vtextension_runtime ; nothing else may link the runtime. A value of CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIME : <runtime> added to _CONTOUR_WASM_RUNTIMES in the top-level CMakeLists.txt , which refuses any value not on that list. vtextension::wasm::makeDefaultBackend() (declared in src/vtextension/wasm/DefaultBackend.hpp ), defined in the backend's target and returning its IWasmBackend (WAMR: DefaultBackend.cpp ). vtextension::wasm::testing::preparedGeneration() (declared in src/vtextension/wasm/testing/PreparedGeneration.hpp ), defined in a PreparedGeneration.cpp added to vtextension_test only: the runtime generation the calling thread was prepared for, 0 if none. The contract suite, instantiated in vtextension_test : a *_test.cpp the directory adds to vtextension_test , holding a traits struct whose make() returns a new backend and the line CONTOUR_WASM_BACKEND_CONTRACT(Traits) (from src/vtextension/wasm/testing/BackendContract.hpp ). Every case tagged [wasm-contract] must pass, among them the two rules no backend is exempt from: the runtime generation increases on each bring-up, and entering a thread guard fails RuntimeUnavailable while no runtime is up. A passing containment gate : ctest -L lint ( check_wasm_runtime_containment ) must pass. The gate knows WAMR's C headers, backend directory and link target by name ( scripts/check-wasm-runtime-containment.py ); teach it the new runtime's alongside, so that they too stay inside the backend directory.
docs.title: Adding a backend

docs.text: Features # Everything Contour does, grouped by what you do with it. A card with a link opens its guide. Window and sessions # Persistent sessions Daemon mode: sessions survive the window, reattach locally or over the network, and interoperate with tmux in both directions. Workspace sidebar Workspaces, tabs and panes as a tree. Remote hosts Attach to sessions on another machine. Quick terminal A global hotkey slides a terminal down from the top of the screen. Tabs and split panes Colored tabs, tab badges and drag-and-drop rearranging of panes and tabs. Layouts Named sets of tabs and panes that open together. Drag and drop Drop a tab on a pane edge to split it, or files to type their escaped paths. Native window chrome Windows 11, macOS and Linux, in light and dark, with a Settings window, a command palette and a character-cell Terminal style. Cross-platform Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and Windows. GPU-accelerated and high-DPI GPU-accelerated rendering with high-DPI support. Find bar A live match count, floating over the pane being searched. Runtime configuration reload Change the configuration and see it without a restart. Key binding customization Color schemes and profiles A profile groups a color scheme, a login shell and related behaviors. Transparent background Blurred behind the window on Windows 10 and on KDE; a blurrable background image is supported too. Read-only mode Protects the running application from accidental input, such as Ctrl + C . Text and graphics # Font ligatures Rendered out of the box, when your font has them. Unicode Colored emoji, including ZWJ, VS15 and VS16 sequences, and grapheme clusters: 🌈 💝 😛 👪 Bold and italic fonts Nerd Font glyphs Powerline, Font Awesome, Material Design, Devicons and more, with whichever font you choose: a symbols font is bundled. 256-color and Truecolor Images Sixel, kitty graphics and ReGIS vector graphics. Input method editor Emoji and pinyin input through ibus. Size indicator The terminal size appears while you resize the window. Status line VT320 host-programmable and indicator status line. Text reflow Lines re-wrap when the window resizes; configurable via SM ? 2028 / RM ? 2028 . Synchronized rendering SM ? 2026 / RM ? 2026 . Progress bar A built-in Fira Code inspired progress bar . Clickable links URLs, file paths and your own patterns in whatever a program prints, opened with Ctrl +click; hyperlinks via OSC 8 . See links . Clipboard Set the clipboard and primary selection via OSC 52, advertised as the Clipboard Extension ( DA1 52 ). Working in the scrollback # Command blocks Exit-status gutter, line numbers, per-line timestamps, folding, scrollbar marks and a sticky command header. Restored sessions History comes back above a "Restored" divider, with one toast saying what was restored. Finish notifications Know when a long-running command finishes in a tab you are not looking at. Shell integration For bash, zsh, fish, tcsh and PowerShell; Contour offers to install it for bash, zsh and fish, showing the one line it adds, also in Settings. Vi-like input modes Navigation, selection, copy and paste from the keyboard. Hint mode Keyboard-driven selection of URLs, file paths, git hashes and more. Line marks Vertical markers: jump quickly between marks in your history. Buffer capture A VT extension to quickly extract the terminal page's contents. Automation # Control API contour ls , new , split , send , pane capture and block script the daemon's workspaces, tabs, panes and command blocks. MCP server contour mcp lets coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex split panes, run commands and read their output in their own tab. Status-line extensions Sandboxed WebAssembly extensions that draw in the status line. Font ligatures # Contour renders your font ligatures out of the box. If your font supports them, Contour will render them. Images # Contour implements first-class Sixel image support, as well as the kitty graphics protocol and ReGIS vector graphics . The kitty graphics protocol includes Unicode placeholders and file media , which is what Claude Code draws its pictures, such as Mermaid diagrams, with. Most notably supporting libraries, are notcurses and libsixel . Also, libsixel does provide a CLI to convert well known image formats (like PNG) to Sixel format and have them printed to the terminal. Input method editor # An input method (or input method editor, commonly abbreviated IME) is an operating system component or program that enables users to generate characters not natively available on their input devices by using sequences of characters (or mouse operations) that are available to them. Using an input method is usually necessary for languages that have more graphemes than there are keys on the keyboard. More info can be found on wikipedia and with more info how to setup it and use here wiki.archlinux Example of emoji input using ibus # List of emoji from unicode You can insert any unicode character using ibus IME by pressing Ctrl+Shift+u (default) and then insert unicode code for the emoji or other character. Example of input using pinyin via ibus # Size indicator # On resize window with current terminal size will appear

docs.text: Input Modes # Normally, a terminal emulator only knows about one input mode, so there is no need of distinction. Inspired by Vi/Vim, the Termite terminal emulator started to introduce so called Vim-modes, where the user can use the keyboard only to screen text selection, amongst other things. So users can press Ctrl+Shift+Space to enter the vim mode. You can then move the cursor using vim motion keys and then start selecting. Contour introduces multiple Vim-like input modes: # insert mode : This is the default input mode. Everything is forwarded to the application. normal mode : Use motion keys to move the cursor and operators to act visual mode : Linear selection, use motion keys to alter the selection. visual line mode : Line based selection, use motion keys to alter the selection. visual block mode : Block based selection, use motion keys to alter the selection. hint mode : Overlay alphabetic labels on detected patterns (URLs, file paths, etc.) and type a label to act on it. Supported operators (Normal Mode) # Normal: [count] p (paste primary clipboard count times) Normal: yy (yank current line to primary clipboard) Normal: y {motion} (yank given motion to primary clipboard) Normal: y {TextObject} (yank given textObject to primary clipboard, such as yiw , yaw , yip , yap , ...) Visual: y (yank current selection into primary clipboard) v enables/disables visual mode V enables/disables visual line mode i activates insert mode Ctrl+v enables/disables visual block mode Normal: o {motion} (opens resource by given motion , this can be a URL or local file) Normal: o {TextObject} (opens resource by given textObject , such as oiw , oaw , oiW , ...) Visual: o (open current selection into primary clipboard) Normal: gh (enter hint mode — copy selected match to clipboard) Normal: gH (enter hint mode — open selected match) Normal: gx (opens the link under the cursor: a URL, a path, or a custom pattern) Normal: mm (set or clear a user mark on the cursor line) Normal: za / zo / zc (toggle / open / close the command block under the cursor) Normal: zM / zR (close / open every command block) Supported motions # Moving the cursor outside of the current view using a motion, will cause the terminal to scroll the view to make that target line visible. [count] h [count] j [count] k [count] l [count] w [count] b [count] e [count] | 0 $ gg G { & } [m & ]m (previous / next mark: a prompt or a user mark) [count] ]x (next link) [count] [x (previous link) Supported text objects # i< , a< - angle brackets enclosed text i{ , a{ - curly brackets enclosed text i" , a" - double quotes enclosed text ip , ap - backtick enclosed string i( , a( - round brackets enclosed string i' , a' - single quoted string i` , a` - backtick enclosed string i[ , a[ - square bracket enclosed string iw , aw - regular word iW , aW - space delimited word im , am - the lines between two marks, without / with the marked lines Opening local files and URLs # Contour finds URLs, file paths and patterns of your own in the output and underlines them (see Links in Terminal Output ). In normal mode, ]x and [x move the cursor from one link to the next, scanning beyond the screen when needed, and gx opens the link under the cursor as Ctrl+click would. A path counts once Contour has found that it exists. You can also open what is not detected as a link by moving the cursor onto a resource (URL or local file) and then pressing oiW (open in (space separated) word) or use any of the other supported text objects to denote what to open. You may as well type oo to open the URL under the current line. This works if no other information is on this current line, while spaces are trimmed left and right of the given URL in this line. Select and yank # This video shows how to get into normal mode (Ctrl+Shift+Space) and move to the text that is to be yanked ( y ) into the clipboard. Mind, the clipboard is pasted with newlines stripped off ( <Shift-p> ). Note how the status line at the bottom reflects the current input mode. Line marks # Ever wanted to jump quickly to the top of the previous prompt? With a little bit of shell integration, you can make the shell tell the terminal which lines in your screen and scrollback buffer to remember. Setting a line mark # This is what a shell integration would do, but you can simply mark lines yourself by trivially writing to stdout , as follows: printf "\033]133;A\033\\" This will tell the terminal to remember the line as a jump-target. Being a prompt mark, it also starts a new command block; to mark a line without that, see Bookmarking a line in Vi normal mode . OSC 133 ; A is the shell-integration sequence for "a new prompt starts here". Contour also accepted a dedicated SETMARK sequence ( CSI > M ) for this until 0.8.0, when it was removed in favour of this one. Jump via shortcut # Ensure you have a similar configuration set as follows to relatively jump up or down of your marked lines. input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : K , action : ScrollMarkUp , mode : "~Alt" } - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : J , action : ScrollMarkDown , mode : "~Alt" } Jump extension to Vi-like Normal Mode # Use [m and ]m to jump to the next line mark up and down when being in normal input mode. Bookmarking a line in Vi normal mode # In Vi-like normal mode, mm toggles a user mark on the line the cursor is on. A user mark is a bookmark, not a prompt: [m / ]m , the im / am text objects and ScrollMarkUp / ScrollMarkDown visit user marks and prompt marks alike, but a user mark never starts a command block, so it neither splits a fold nor decides where old output is dropped from the scrollback. A user mark is drawn as ◆ in the gutter and as a tick on the scrollbar; see Command blocks . Line marks as text objects # In Vi-like normal mode, you can span a text object in between two line marks, as follows: vim - visual select within two line marks (excluding marked lines) vam - visual select around two line marks (including marked line) yim - yank within two line marks (excluding marked lines) yam - yank around two line marks (including marked line)

docs.text: Normally, a terminal emulator only knows about one input mode, so there is no need of distinction. Inspired by Vi/Vim, the Termite terminal emulator started to introduce so called Vim-modes, where the user can use the keyboard only to screen text selection, amongst other things. So users can press Ctrl+Shift+Space to enter the vim mode. You can then move the cursor using vim motion keys and then start selecting.
docs.title: Input Modes

docs.text: insert mode : This is the default input mode. Everything is forwarded to the application. normal mode : Use motion keys to move the cursor and operators to act visual mode : Linear selection, use motion keys to alter the selection. visual line mode : Line based selection, use motion keys to alter the selection. visual block mode : Block based selection, use motion keys to alter the selection. hint mode : Overlay alphabetic labels on detected patterns (URLs, file paths, etc.) and type a label to act on it.
docs.title: Contour introduces multiple Vim-like input modes:

docs.text: Normal: [count] p (paste primary clipboard count times) Normal: yy (yank current line to primary clipboard) Normal: y {motion} (yank given motion to primary clipboard) Normal: y {TextObject} (yank given textObject to primary clipboard, such as yiw , yaw , yip , yap , ...) Visual: y (yank current selection into primary clipboard) v enables/disables visual mode V enables/disables visual line mode i activates insert mode Ctrl+v enables/disables visual block mode Normal: o {motion} (opens resource by given motion , this can be a URL or local file) Normal: o {TextObject} (opens resource by given textObject , such as oiw , oaw , oiW , ...) Visual: o (open current selection into primary clipboard) Normal: gh (enter hint mode — copy selected match to clipboard) Normal: gH (enter hint mode — open selected match) Normal: gx (opens the link under the cursor: a URL, a path, or a custom pattern) Normal: mm (set or clear a user mark on the cursor line) Normal: za / zo / zc (toggle / open / close the command block under the cursor) Normal: zM / zR (close / open every command block)
docs.title: Supported operators (Normal Mode)

[count] h [count] j [count] k [count] l [count] w [count] b [count] e [count] | 0 $ gg G { & } [m & ]m (previous / next mark: a prompt or a user mark) [count] ]x (next link) [count] [x (previous link)

docs.text: Contour finds URLs, file paths and patterns of your own in the output and underlines them (see Links in Terminal Output ). In normal mode, ]x and [x move the cursor from one link to the next, scanning beyond the screen when needed, and gx opens the link under the cursor as Ctrl+click would. A path counts once Contour has found that it exists. You can also open what is not detected as a link by moving the cursor onto a resource (URL or local file) and then pressing oiW (open in (space separated) word) or use any of the other supported text objects to denote what to open. You may as well type oo to open the URL under the current line. This works if no other information is on this current line, while spaces are trimmed left and right of the given URL in this line.

docs.text: Install # Contour is packaged for most systems; pick yours below, or take a build from the release page . Linux macOS Windows Source Fedora Linux # Use the official package . sudo dnf install contour-terminal Arch Linux # Use the official package . sudo pacman -S contour Ubuntu Linux # Download the .deb file for your Ubuntu version from the release page , then install it: sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/contour-0.3.12.262-UBUNTU_VERSION-ARCH.deb Flatpak # Contour is available at the Flathub store. AppImage # Every release also carries contour-VERSION-x86_64.AppImage , a single file that bundles Qt 6.11 (which Debian and Ubuntu do not ship) and everything else Contour needs but the C library. Make it executable and run it: chmod +x contour-VERSION-x86_64.AppImage ./contour-VERSION-x86_64.AppImage It runs on distributions with a glibc at least as new as Ubuntu 24.04's. Without FUSE, run it with --appimage-extract-and-run . Building the AppImage yourself To build it yourself, on the oldest distribution you want it to run on, install the build dependencies ( scripts/install-deps.sh ), Qt 6.11 with the qtmultimedia , qtshadertools and qtspeech modules (for instance through aqtinstall ), a C++23 compiler and scripts/install-rust-wasm.sh , then: QT_ROOT_DIR = /path/to/Qt/6.11.1/gcc_64 CXX = g++-15 VERSION_STRING = dev ./scripts/build-appimage.sh The script builds Contour, installs it into an AppDir and packs it with linuxdeploy and its Qt plugin, which scans the QML files for the modules to bundle. The result is contour-dev-x86_64.AppImage in the current directory. The Qt-free contour-daemon package for machines without a display is described in Contour daemon on a server . Homebrew # brew install contour Installers (Windows 10 or newer) # Download Contour for Windows from the release page and double click the installer (an .msi file). There are two installers, and you need one of them: Installer Installs for Default folder Needs contour-<version>-win64.msi everyone on the computer C:\Program Files\Contour\ an administrator's approval contour-<version>-win64-user.msi you only %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Contour\ nothing Pick the per-user installer when you cannot or do not want to elevate. Both add Contour to the Start menu and, unless you deselect their features in the installer, to your PATH and your desktop. There is also a contour-<version>-win64.zip that needs no installation at all: unpack it anywhere and run bin\contour.exe . With the Windows Package Manager: winget install --id contour-terminal.Contour --silent --scope machine winget install --id contour-terminal.Contour --silent --scope user Upgrades and running instances The two installers are separate products. Both can be installed on one computer, and neither ever upgrades or removes the other. When a command name is found in both, the per-machine PATH comes first. An installer upgrades in place. Run any later build over an earlier one, or over a release, without uninstalling first; an older build of the same release also installs over a newer one. An upgrade keeps the folder Contour is in, even a folder you chose; the one exception is an old release's folder with its version in the name ( Contour Terminal Emulator 0.8 ), which moves to a folder named Contour once. Installations of Contour 0.6.1 and earlier have to be uninstalled first. A running Contour is closed and opened again. Windows Installer closes the Contour window it finds running and starts it again, with the arguments it had, once the files are replaced. A window whose sessions run in its own process ( daemon.mode: in_process , or the fallback when no daemon could be started) loses them. Sessions a daemon hosts keep running: the installer moves a daemon started by hand out of the way first, and does not end one. What it leaves is described in Installing a new Contour on Windows . Unattended installation, installer properties and winget Run an installer without a dialog from a command prompt or a deployment tool: msiexec /i contour-<version>-win64.msi /qn /norestart /l*v contour-install.log Three properties change what it installs. Give them on the command line after the file name ( INSTALL_ROOT is older than the other two): Property Default Effect INSTALL_ROOT=<folder> the installer's default folder (table above); on an upgrade, the folder Contour is in where Contour goes. A folder given here wins over the installed one, which moves the installation. ADD_TO_PATH=0 1 does not add Contour's bin folder to PATH DESKTOP_SHORTCUT=0 1 does not put a shortcut on the desktop On an upgrade, ADD_TO_PATH=0 and DESKTOP_SHORTCUT=0 remove the entry or the shortcut the earlier installation made, and a later install with the default does not bring it back: name the feature again with ADDLOCAL=CM_C_contour_path (the PATH entry) or ADDLOCAL=ContourDesktopShortcutFeature (the shortcut). msiexec reports through its exit code: 0 success; 3010 success, but a restart is needed; 1602 the installation was cancelled; 1603 a fatal error (also what an installer says when a later version of Contour is already installed: "A later version of Contour is already installed"); 1618 another installation is already running; 1638 another build of the same product is already installed with the same product code: this happens only between builds made before Contour 0.9, which all builds of one release shared; uninstall it first. Builds of 0.9 and later each have a product code of their own, and upgrade each other. The log named by /l*v has the detail. With winget (commands above): --scope machine installs the per-machine installer, --scope user the per-user one. Without --scope , winget prefers the per-user installer unless your winget settings say otherwise ( installBehavior.preferences.scope ): a plain winget install contour-terminal.Contour needs no administrator and installs into your profile. Name --scope machine for an installation for every user. winget upgrade keeps the scope Contour was installed in. The portable package (the ZIP, without installer) is available as winget install --id contour-terminal.Contour --installer-type portable , and winget upgrade keeps an installation made that way portable. Installations of Contour 0.6.1 and earlier have to be uninstalled first, also when winget offers the upgrade. Installing as SYSTEM A deployment tool that installs as the SYSTEM account cannot reach your daemon. Contour is still installed, but a daemon that you started by hand keeps running from the old folder until it next restarts. Deployment tools pass --scope machine to winget install : without it winget prefers the per-user installer, which would install into the profile of the SYSTEM account. See Installing a new Contour on Windows . Installing from source # Contour is best installed from supported package managers, but you can build from source by following the instructions below. UNIX-like systems (Linux, FreeBSD, macOS) # Prerequisites # ./scripts/install-deps.sh This script might ask you for the administrator password if a package dependency can be installed via the system package manager. Compile # You can use cmake presets to compile contour. The full list of available presets can be seen using cmake --list-presets . To compile release build for linux clang-release or gcc-release , or appleclang-release on macOS accordingly. gcc-release , msvc-release and macos-package build as the packages are built (link-time optimization, so a slower link) and clang-release stays the fast developer build; -DCONTOUR_PRODUCTION_BUILD=ON turns the packages' flags on anywhere (see release builds ). cmake --preset clang-release cmake --build --preset clang-release # Optionally, if you want to install from source cmake --build --preset clang-release --target install Please note, if you want to install into a system root, e.g. /usr/local , you may need to prefix the install command with sudo . Also, ensure that the terminfo file is correctly resolved, as the terminfo library is very limited in locating the correct terminfo files (e.g. it does not search in /usr/local ), you can symlink into ~/.terminfo however. Windows 10 or newer # Prerequisites # For Windows, you must have Windows 10, 2018 Fall Creators Update, and Visual Studio 2019, installed. It will neither build nor run on any prior Windows OS, due to libterminal making use of ConPTY API . Set up vcpkg , preferably somewhere high up in the folder hierarchy, and add the folder to your PATH . cd C:\ git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git .\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat Install Visual Studio Build Tools (make sure to select the CLI tools for C++, which you might need to do in the separate components tab). Install Qt6 (i.e. to C:\Qt) Open the developer version of Powershell. In the contour source folder execute .\scripts\install-deps.ps1 . This step may take a very long time. Compile # In the developer version of Powershell: # change paths accordingly if you installed QT and vcpkg to somewhere else cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=C:\vcpkg\scripts\buildsystems\vcpkg.cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=C:\Qt\6.5.0\msvc2019_64\lib\cmake cmake --build build/ # Optionally, if you want to install from source cmake --build build/ --target install

docs.text: Persistent sessions (daemon mode) # Experimental Daemon mode is new in 0.7.0 and still settling. It is built into every Contour and covered by the test suite, but its command-line flags and its wire protocol may change between releases. Contour already gives you tabs and split panes inside one window. Daemon mode is different: it moves your sessions into a background process , so they survive the window that shows them. Close the window, reattach later, or attach from another machine — the shells keep running either way. Terms. The daemon is the background process. A workspace is what it holds: a set of tabs, each an arrangement of panes. A window is an operating-system window of the Contour GUI, which shows one workspace; closing the window leaves the workspace and its shells with the daemon. That buys you three things: A long build, a database migration or a training run keeps going after you close the window — deliberately or by accident. Work done over SSH survives the link dropping. Reconnect, reattach, carry on. The same sessions are reachable from a second machine, over an encrypted connection. If you have used tmux or screen , this is the same idea, with two differences: the sessions are rendered by a real Contour window (images, hyperlinks, sized text and all), and Contour can speak tmux's own protocol in both directions — so it interoperates with tmux rather than replacing it. Quick start # contour client That is the whole thing. contour client looks for a daemon, starts one if none is running , and opens a window showing its sessions. Close the window and the shells stay alive; run contour client again to pick them back up — with their scrollback, so you can scroll back through what the session did while nothing was watching. To manage the daemon yourself, start it first: contour daemon & # runs in the FOREGROUND; background it or use a service manager contour client # attaches to the daemon you started The distinction matters, because the two daemons have different lifetimes: How it started When it exits Auto-started by contour client 10 seconds after it has no sessions and no clients — it belongs to the clients that needed it, so nothing is left behind Started by you ( contour daemon ) Never on its own. It keeps serving with zero sessions, ready for the next client Started by the OS ( contour daemon-service ) Never on its own, see Starting the daemon at login Closing the last window therefore keeps your sessions: the auto-started daemon stays up as long as any session lives, and for 10 seconds after the last one is gone and the last client has disconnected. A client that attaches within those 10 seconds keeps the daemon alive. The policy is the daemon's --lifecycle option, and it rides on the daemon , not on the client that started it: --lifecycle The daemon ends persistent (default for contour daemon ) never on its own exit-with-last-session once its last hosted session is gone (tmux spells this exit-empty ) exit-when-idle (what contour client starts on demand) 10 seconds after it has no session and no client --exit-with-last-session is kept as an alias for --lifecycle=exit-with-last-session . Stating both is an error only when they differ. A status probe ( contour daemon status ) is not a client and never keeps an idle daemon alive. contour daemon does not detach by itself It runs in the foreground and logs to standard error, which is what you want under a service manager or in a container. Background it with & , or let contour client start it for you. Detaching versus ending a session # Because sessions outlive the window, "close" needs two answers — and Contour gives you both. Which one you get depends on what you close: What you close What happens to the shell The window (its close button, or quitting Contour) Detach. It keeps running; the next contour client shows it again A pane — Close Pane in the right-click menu, or the ClosePane action Ends. That session is closed on the daemon and does not come back A tab — its ✕, or the CloseTab action Ends , together with every pane in it Typing exit in the shell Ends , as always — the shell decided This is the same split tmux draws between detaching a client and kill-pane , and it works the same for a local session as for one hosted by a daemon: a pane you end is ended everywhere, including for any other client attached to that daemon. Neither ClosePane nor CloseTab ships with a default key binding — bind them yourself if you want one: input_mapping : - { mods : [ Ctrl , Shift ], key : 'W' , action : ClosePane } Ending a whole daemon's worth of sessions Closing panes one at a time is the fine-grained way. To end everything at once, stop the daemon — see Stopping a daemon . Running several daemons side by side # Daemons are told apart by a name , exactly as tmux's -L does: contour daemon --name work contour client --daemon work The name names a socket under your per-user runtime directory. Resolution order: --socket PATH — used verbatim. An explicitly given name, contour daemon --name NAME or contour client --daemon NAME (the value default included) — the name's own socket, exactly as tmux's -L beats $TMUX . $CONTOUR_MUX — used verbatim (analogous to tmux's $TMUX ). $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/<name> (the name default when none was given). <temp>/contour-<uid>/<name> when there is no runtime directory (tmux's /tmp/tmux-<uid>/<label> shape). A daemon exports $CONTOUR_MUX into every shell it hosts, so a command typed in one of its panes reaches that same daemon without a flag. That is why it ranks above the default name: a sandboxed (Flatpak) shell cannot derive where its daemon lives, and a plain contour client there still finds it. It ranks below an explicit name, so contour daemon --name work status from inside a pane asks the work daemon rather than the one hosting the pane. The daemon binds three endpoints, all derived from that one path: the control socket itself, <socket>-native for Contour's own clients, and <socket>-tmux for the tmux binary. The socket directory is created 0700 and checked on every bind: it must be a real directory, owned by you, and must not be world-accessible. Group access is permitted, matching tmux. Keep socket paths short A Unix socket path is limited to roughly 100 bytes by the operating system, not by Contour. A deeply nested --socket path will fail to bind. contour daemon options # Option What it does --socket PATH Path of the control socket file. Defaults to the configuration's daemon.socket , else $CONTOUR_MUX when no --name is given, else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/NAME . --name NAME The daemon's name, which tells daemon instances apart. Default default . Given, it beats $CONTOUR_MUX . Until 0.9.0, --label NAME still works, with a note on standard error. --config FILE Configuration file whose profile supplies the hosted sessions' terminal settings — including history.limit , which is how much scrollback a session keeps for clients that attach later. --profile NAME Which profile of that configuration to take them from. Defaults to the configuration's default profile. --lifecycle POLICY When the daemon ends on its own: persistent (the default), exit-with-last-session or exit-when-idle . See Quick start . --exit-with-last-session Alias for --lifecycle=exit-with-last-session . --size-policy POLICY Which attached client's size the shared grid takes when clients of different sizes are attached: latest , smallest or largest . Mirrors tmux's window-size . Defaults to the configuration's daemon.size_policy ( latest unless set). --background Relaunches the command detached and returns once the daemon accepts connections. Without --log-file the daemon logs beside its socket ( SOCKET.log ), since a detached process has no console. --stdio Relays the native protocol between standard input/output and this user's daemon, starting it if needed: what contour client --host runs over ssh.
