Honours --name , --socket , --config , --profile , --log , --log-file and --size-policy (forwarded to a daemon it starts); cannot be combined with --listen-tcp , --background or --tmux-compat-socket . --in-place Runs from the installed binary instead of a per-version copy. See After upgrading Contour . --tmux-compat-socket LABEL Additionally binds tmux's own discovery path /tmp/tmux-<uid>/<LABEL> , so a plain tmux -L LABEL -C attach-session finds this daemon. --listen-tcp HOST:PORT Also serve the native protocol over TCP. Opt-in; always TLS-encrypted, and clients sign in with an authorized key or a token. The daemon's TLS fingerprint is logged and shown by daemon status . Port 0 lets the system pick a free port, which the log names. See Remote access . --authorized-keys FILE SSH public keys, in authorized_keys format, that may log in to the TCP listener by signing a challenge. Defaults to authorized_keys in the configuration directory; a missing file is no keys. Needs --listen-tcp . --auth any\|keys How TCP clients authenticate: any (the default) accepts a token, an access-file entry or an authorized key; keys accepts authorized keys alone and refuses --token , --token-file and --access-file . Needs --listen-tcp . --token TOKEN Preshared token a TCP client may present. With --listen-tcp , one of a token or an authorized key is required. Visible to other local users through the process list — prefer --token-file . --token-file FILE Reads the token from FILE instead, so the secret is protected by that file's permissions. Trailing newlines are ignored. --access-file FILE Further TCP tokens with narrower grants, one per line. Needs --listen-tcp . See Narrower tokens . --tls-cert FILE , --tls-key FILE PEM certificate and matching private key for the TCP listener. Omit both to have the daemon generate an ephemeral self-signed certificate. --log TAGS Enable logging for a comma-separated list of tags, or all . See Diagnostics . --log-file FILE Append log output to FILE instead of standard error; - means standard error explicitly. Hosting from a plain contour # The thin client is the default: a plain contour shows sessions that a daemon hosts, starting that daemon when none runs. contour client always attaches; a plain contour decides by daemon.mode in the configuration, or by --daemon-mode on its command line: Mode Where the sessions run auto (the default) In the daemon, started if none runs; when none can be had, in the window's process, with a bar saying why — those shells end when the window closes in_process In the window's own process, as before daemon mode existed required In the daemon, or not at all: the launch ends with the reason before any window opens daemon : mode : auto # auto, in_process or required socket : "" # the daemon's socket path; empty selects the default size_policy : latest # whose size wins when clients disagree: latest, smallest or largest default_cell_pixel_size : { width : 10 , height : 20 } # cell size images use until a client reports one history_limit : 1000 # scrollback lines per session, -1 for unlimited; unset follows the profile contour --daemon-mode in_process # this launch only: keep the sessions in this window contour --daemon-mode required # this launch only: fail rather than fall back What a launch opens # A launch opens one window. So does New Window (a second launch of contour , NewTerminal on Cmd+N or Ctrl+Shift+N ). A new window never shows a workspace another window shows, on this computer or any other client attached to the daemon: it takes the hidden workspace that was left most recently — the one whose window you closed or switched away from last — and when there is none it gets a new workspace with one tab. So closing a window by mistake and opening a new one brings it straight back, and each further launch picks up the hidden workspace left before that. Workspaces no window has left since the daemon started, such as those a restarted daemon restores, are taken in the order the sidebar lists them. A fresh daemon gets its first tab in the first window, as before. The same rule moves a window whose workspace ends (its last tab closes). It moves on to the hidden workspace holding a tab that a new window would take, and never to one another window shows. When every other workspace is shown by some window, it has nowhere to go and the window closes, as closing the last tab of a window does; the other windows stay as they were. A launch that names a program ( -e , or a command after the options) runs it in the window's own process under auto ; under required it ends before any window, since a daemon session runs the host's profile. When the connection is lost # A window attached to a daemon keeps its panes when the connection drops. They show "Reconnecting…" while the window reconnects with backoff (250 ms doubling to 5 s) and picks its workspaces up again. A connection gone half-open — a laptop that changed networks — is noticed by a heartbeat within about 15 s instead of whenever TCP gives up. Input typed while disconnected is dropped rather than replayed into whatever shell answers next. A launch that falls back to in_process has no connection to lose. Switching a window # A window shows one workspace of one daemon, over a connection of its own: each window has exactly one connection, so a window on a remote host does not tie up, or depend on, the other windows. You can point a window somewhere else without closing it, and its panes are swapped in place: To another workspace of the same daemon , with SwitchToWorkspace or CycleWorkspace ( Ctrl+Alt+PageDown / PageUp , ⌃⌘↓ / ⌃⌘↑ on macOS, for the next / previous one). To another daemon : a local one by its name ( contour daemon --name ), or a saved host , with SwitchToDaemon or CycleDaemon . The window lands on that daemon's only workspace, on a new one when it has none, and asks which when it has several. A workspace that holds no tab -- a daemon no window has attached to yet keeps one -- counts as none: there is nothing in it to show. From the switcher ( ShowSwitcher , Ctrl+Shift+R , ⇧⌘R on macOS), a popup in the command palette's family, drawn over the window. See The switcher below. By mouse : click the location chip ( local › billing ▾ ) in the title band of a window on a daemon (Space or Return when it has keyboard focus) to open the same switcher below it, as ShowSwitcher does; its tooltip names that chord, and Escape closes the popup. With the sidebar shown, the daemon at the head of the sidebar does the same. Or pick Switch To Daemon or Daemon & Workspace Switcher… from the Window submenu of the main menu (☰). Switch To Daemon lists the same daemons as the command palette's Switch to daemon rows. The chip's connection state. The chip shows the daemon's connection too: a dot for a remote daemon that is connected, and the dot with Reconnecting… or Disconnected while the link is not up. In a narrow band the state text goes first, then the daemon name, then the workspace name, which keeps at least 6 characters. From a shell , with contour switch , which also works from a pane of the window being switched. The window asks first (see below). The Open… variants ( OpenWorkspace , OpenDaemon ) open a new window on the destination instead. If a window already shows the destination workspace, that window is focused and nothing else changes. The actions and their palette rows are listed in Key Mapping ; of them, only ShowSwitcher is bound to a key by default. A window stays on one connection while it moves between a daemon's workspaces, so switching, creating ( NewWorkspace ) and cycling are immediate and open no window. A window attached to a daemon that predates this is refused, with a hint to run contour daemon upgrade or to pick Upgrade daemon in the command palette. Bells and desktop notifications come from one window only: the most recently focused one. A command that finishes in a workspace no window shows is noticed once, by that window. A program's clipboard write (OSC 52) reaches only a window that shows its pane. A switch that cannot finish leaves the window as it was and says why in a notice: the destination is not reachable, it has no such workspace, or it did not show the workspace within 10 seconds. A switch asked for through the control API ( contour switch , or any program calling workspace.switch ) is a program pointing your window somewhere, so the window asks before it switches: a prompt in the window names the destination in full, the daemon by name or host and the workspace, and offers Deny or Switch. Ticking Don't ask again keeps the answer, Deny or Switch, for every later switch between the same two daemons (from the daemon the window is on to the destination's), whatever the workspace, until Contour exits; it is never written down. A remembered Deny answers refused without asking. A destination named by URL ( ssh://… ) asks every time and offers nothing to remember, since allowing it runs ssh with your credentials. The switches you make yourself, by key, palette or the switcher popup, never ask. The GUI cannot tell a script outside any pane from you typing contour switch , so that asks too. Note Windows of the in-process mode have no daemon behind them and cannot switch. The switcher # The switcher lists the workspaces of the daemon this window is on first, under Workspaces on ‹daemon› , with the status glyph the sidebar shows, the branch, and the tab count; the current one wears a Current pill. Under Other daemons come the other local daemons and the saved hosts, each with its workspace count and the most urgent status among its workspaces; a saved host also shows how it is reached ( SSH , TLS ). Actions end the list: New Workspace , and New Daemon… . Type to filter. What you type finds workspaces on every local daemon at once, each match with a pill naming its daemon. A saved host is searched only once you open it, since connecting may ask for a password. When nothing matches, the switcher says so and offers New Workspace “what you typed” . Return switches this window to the selected workspace; Shift+Return opens it in a new window, as does the button on the selected row and on the row under the pointer. Hovering a row does not move the selection: the arrow keys own it. → , or Return on a daemon, opens that daemon: its workspaces alone, with New Workspace on it. Backspace in an empty field, or Escape, goes back. A saved host shows Connecting… while it connects; you can type, or back out, meanwhile. A daemon that cannot be listed says why on its row, and everything else keeps working. New Daemon… asks for a name. As you type it says whether the name is available, already running (Return then switches to that daemon), or not a valid name, and shows the equivalent contour daemon --name command. Return starts the daemon and switches this window to it; Shift+Return opens it in a new window. Right-click a workspace of this window's daemon, or press the Menu key or Shift+F10, for the menu its sidebar row has. Another daemon's workspace offers switching and opening in a new window. Escape clears what you typed, then closes; a click elsewhere closes. Either changes nothing, and a daemon a New Daemon… start was still bringing up is not switched to. A workspace of another daemon shows a done or failed status as unseen for as long as it stands: this window never saw that pane, and a daemon keeps no record of who did. Shown and hidden workspaces # Every window selects exactly one workspace of the daemon, and the daemon keeps one of two states per workspace: State Meaning shown Some window selects it right now. hidden No window selects it. Closing a window, or losing its connection, leaves its workspace hidden ; it keeps running and keeps its state, so reopening Contour finds your sessions where you left them. The same holds across a daemon restart and a live upgrade . Select a hidden workspace from a window to show it again ( contour ls --json reports each workspace's state as visibility , see the control API ). contour client options # Option What it does --daemon PATH\|HOST:PORT\|URL\|NAME Which daemon to attach to, as every control verb reads it: a socket path, a TCP daemon, an ssh:// URL, or a name, which is a local daemon's, else a saved host's ( name:NAME picks a local daemon and host:NAME a saved host; a number after them that names no such daemon or host is a port, so host:2222 reaches a machine called host ; a bare name both have is refused). A local daemon resolves as above, daemon.socket of the client's configuration included. Not together with --socket , --host or --connect-tcp . Until 0.9.0, --label NAME still works, as --daemon name:NAME . --socket PATH The control socket of the daemon to attach to. --workspace WORKSPACE Show only that daemon workspace instead of what a launch brings back, named as every control verb names one: its id or an id suffix (as contour ls prints it), its name, or its 1-based position. Fails, saying why, when it names no workspace or several. It also works with --host . --size-policy POLICY The policy a daemon this client auto-starts runs with; defaults to daemon.size_policy . --tmux Attach to a real tmux server instead of a Contour daemon. See tmux interoperability . --tmux-socket PATH The tmux server socket (tmux's -S ) for --tmux . --profile NAME Config profile the window renders remote sessions with. --config FILE Configuration file to load. --host NAME\|URL Attach to a remote host: a name saved under hosts: , or an ad-hoc ssh://[USER@]HOST[:PORT] (or an ad-hoc tls://HOST:PORT , which signs in with your SSH agent's keys). The remote daemon is started there when none runs; the window title and the tab strip name the host. A host's profile: is used unless --profile names one. Cannot be combined with --socket , --connect-tcp , --token , --token-file , --tls-ca or --tmux . See Remote hosts . --connect-tcp HOST:PORT Connect to a remote daemon over TLS instead of a local socket. It signs in with a key of your SSH agent, or with the token. A daemon met for the first time is pinned once you trust its fingerprint in a dialog. --token TOKEN , --token-file FILE The preshared token to present, inline or read from a file. --tls-ca FILE PEM trust anchor the daemon's certificate is verified against. Omitted, the daemon is pinned on first use instead: you are asked to trust its fingerprint, which is kept in known_daemons , and a daemon that presents another one is refused. --daemon-fingerprint SHA256:... The fingerprint a --connect-tcp or --host daemon without a CA must present on first contact, as contour daemon status prints it on that machine. It is pinned without asking, and any other fingerprint is refused. --log TAGS , --log-file FILE As above — and passed on to a daemon this client auto-starts , which is otherwise the one instance nobody can configure. tmux interoperability # Contour speaks tmux's control-mode protocol in both directions, pinned to tmux 3.7b semantics. Attach tmux tooling to a Contour daemon # <socket>-tmux speaks the binary protocol the stock tmux client uses, so the real tmux binary can attach to a Contour daemon: tmux -S " $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR /contour/default-tmux" -C attach-session To let tmux find the daemon by a socket name alone, have the daemon bind tmux's own discovery path too: contour daemon --tmux-compat-socket mine tmux -L mine -C attach-session --tmux-compat-socket is opt-in for a reason That path is where tmux looks for its server. With the Contour daemon down, a new-session against it would silently start a real tmux server there instead. Control mode ( -C ) is supported; -CC is not — Contour never renders a full terminal client for tmux. Arbitrary startup commands are refused; the endpoint accepts attach- and new-session-shaped startup only. Show a real tmux server in a Contour window # The other direction: point Contour at a tmux server and mirror it. contour client --tmux # the default tmux server contour client --tmux --tmux-socket /tmp/x # a specific one tmux windows become Contour tabs, tmux panes become splits, and input travels back as send-keys . Content mirrors live. tmux replay carries text, not images Contour replays each pane's full history through capture-pane , so scrollback survives a reattach on this path too. Images do not, and that is a tmux limitation rather than Contour's: capture-pane serialises text and colour, never image data. Images drawn while you are attached display normally; images drawn before you attached cannot be recovered. Contour's own native protocol has no such gap — it transfers images by id. Remote access over TCP # By default a daemon is reachable only through its Unix socket, where the filesystem permissions are the access control. --listen-tcp additionally exposes the native protocol over the network. It serves one user per daemon : whoever signs in gets that user's sessions and everything they can do. To serve several users, give each their own daemon, reached over ssh, which is what separates them by account; see Remote hosts . # On the host running the sessions: authorize a key, then listen for keys alone. cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.config/contour/authorized_keys contour daemon --listen-tcp 127 .0.0.1:9090 --auth keys # On the machine you are sitting at (its SSH agent signs in; the first contact asks you to compare the # daemon's fingerprint, which `contour daemon status` prints on the host): contour client --connect-tcp server.example.com:9090 A token still works, and is the way for a script: --token-file FILE on the daemon (the default --auth any accepts both) and --token-file FILE on the client. Properties worth knowing before you open a port: TLS is not optional. The TCP endpoint is always encrypted; there is no plaintext mode. A credential is required. TCP has no filesystem gate to fall back on, so --listen-tcp with neither an authorized key nor --token / --token-file refuses to start rather than serving anonymously. A key signs in over the TLS connection itself, so a daemon never learns a secret it could replay. Prefer --token-file . A token passed as --token is readable by every other user on the machine through the process list; a file carries permissions. Without --tls-cert / --tls-key the daemon keeps a self-signed identity of its own , made on first start in <state-dir>/tls/<name>.pem and presented ever after. The daemon refuses that file unless it is yours and readable by you alone (mode 0600), so a copy with looser permissions needs a chmod 600 . The client pins it on first use, as ssh pins a host key: it asks you to compare the fingerprint, remembers it in known_daemons , and refuses the daemon for good if it ever presents another ( contour daemon forget-pin HOST:PORT after a reinstall). For a certificate verified the way a browser does, pass one on the daemon and name its CA with --tls-ca on the client — the certificate must then also be issued for the host you connect to , not merely signed by that CA. See Remote hosts . Bind deliberately. 127.0.0.1 reaches only the local machine; 0.0.0.0 reaches everyone who can route to you. Prefer forwarding the loopback port over SSH to exposing it directly. Control requests need a trusted daemon. A client of the control API sends nothing over a TLS connection whose daemon is neither verified by --tls-ca nor pinned: it asks you to trust the fingerprint first, or is given --daemon-fingerprint . With the control API a token types into and reads every pane, so it must not be handed to whoever answers. Narrower tokens for scripts # --token grants everything. A script that only needs to read a pane can be given a token of its own that grants less, through --access-file FILE , one entry per line: # grants token (to the end of the line) read,screen ci-reader s3cret all admin-token A line is a grant list — all , or a comma list of read (look at the workspaces), screen (read what is on screen and in command blocks), input (type into a pane) and write (change the workspaces, stop the daemon) — one space, then the token, which may contain spaces. Carriage returns and trailing whitespace are dropped, as for --token-file ; blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. An unknown grant, an empty token or a token that appears twice stops the daemon from starting, naming the line. The file adds tokens beside --token / --token-file , never instead of them: a hello may present either, and the --token keeps granting everything, so moving everyone to the access file means removing --token as well. A line that repeats the --token stops the daemon from starting too, since its narrower grants would silently read as everything. Running a program is typing it: tab.create and pane.split with a command need input as well as write , so a token granted read,screen,write can open shells and rearrange the workspaces but cannot run a program of its choosing in it. Events follow the same grants: block.finished carries the command line and needs screen , so a subscription of a read token is handed every other kind but that one, and a subscribe naming only kinds the token may not see is answered forbidden . A call outside a token's grants is answered forbidden and the connection stays open. Viewing the sessions needs every grant, so a contour client with a narrower token is refused exactly as with a wrong one. To attach over ssh instead, with no port to open, to save hosts by name, or to reach a home PC from the office over Tailscale, see Remote hosts . Starting the daemon at login # Instead of letting contour client start a daemon when it is needed, you can have the operating system start one for you when you log in: contour daemon-service install # register it (and start it with your next login) contour daemon-service status # registered? running? what does it run? contour daemon-service start # start it now contour daemon-service stop # stop it, leaving it registered contour daemon-service restart contour daemon-service uninstall # stop it and remove the registration Each verb takes --name NAME (default default ; --label NAME still works until 0.9.0). install additionally takes --socket , --config , --profile , --size-policy , --log and --log-file , which are recorded in the registration. A socket path is made absolute at install time, because the registration outlives the shell that wrote it. Unless you give --log-file the daemon logs to SOCKET.log . OS What is registered Runs as Linux the systemd user unit contour-daemon.service ( contour-daemon-NAME.service for other names), written to ~/.config/systemd/user and enabled you, no elevation macOS the LaunchAgent org.contourterminal.contour-daemon in ~/Library/LaunchAgents you, no elevation Windows a Scheduled Task triggered by your logon you, no elevation Packages for Linux also ship a contour-daemon.service unit file. It is not enabled by the package; contour daemon-service install writes your own copy, which takes precedence. daemon-service status and uninstall count the service as installed only once you registered it with install ; the packaged unit alone does not. A vendor unit enabled directly with systemctl --user enable or --global enable is likewise not seen by daemon-service or the client's auto-start; use daemon-service install instead. On Linux, a user's daemon stops when their last login session ends, unless lingering is on for that user. When loginctl reports lingering as off, contour daemon-service install prints a one-line note naming the command to run: loginctl enable-linger Contour never enables lingering itself. To install the daemon alone on a server, see Contour daemon on a server . A service-managed daemon runs with --lifecycle=persistent : it never exits on its own , not even with zero sessions and zero clients. contour client finds the registration and starts it before it falls back to spawning a daemon on demand. A registration made by an older release under another name is found as well. --start boot and --start manual (a Windows service) are not implemented yet. Contour daemon on a server # contour-daemon is the Qt-free package for machines that only host persistent sessions and have no display, such as a server you reach over SSH. It ships the contour command-line tool without the GUI stack (no Qt, no QML; the text shaper's Cairo dependency still pulls in the X11 client libraries). Packages are attached to each release (they are not served from a package repository): .deb for Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 (amd64), named contour-daemon-<version>-ubuntu<release>-amd64.deb .rpm for Fedora 44 (x86_64), named contour-daemon-<version>-fedora44-x86_64.rpm sudo apt install ./contour-daemon- [ 0 -9 ] *-ubuntu24.04-amd64.deb # Ubuntu 24.04 (use ubuntu26.04 on 26.04) sudo dnf install ./contour-daemon- [ 0 -9 ] *-fedora44-x86_64.rpm # Fedora 44 CentOS and RHEL (EL9, EL10) packages are not provided yet. The RPM packages come without the bundled status-line extensions; the .deb ships them. contour-daemon and the GUI package contour conflict, and contour already includes the daemon, so a desktop installation needs nothing more. On Debian and Ubuntu, apt replaces one with the other; on Fedora, dnf install refuses, so swap them with dnf swap contour contour-daemon (or dnf install --allowerasing ). The package installs a systemd user unit but does not enable it. Each user registers and enables their own copy (it then starts with their next login; daemon-service start starts it now): contour daemon-service install See Starting the daemon at login . The packaged service opens no listening port (TCP is opt-in, see Remote access over TCP ); reach it over SSH, see Remote hosts . Stopping a daemon # Ask it to stop, from anywhere: contour daemon stop # asks first when the daemon hosts sessions contour daemon stop --yes # does not ask contour daemon status # is one running? version, uptime, socket, sessions, clients contour daemon logs # the last 100 lines of its log contour daemon logs --follow --lines 20 All of them accept --name and --socket , written before or after the verb. Giving the same option before and after the verb with different values is a usage error, so that stop never silently targets another daemon than the one you named. When no daemon answers, status and stop exit with status 4. stop asks for confirmation only when sessions exist; without a terminal it refuses unless you pass --yes . logs shows the file the daemon reports as its log; if none is running it falls back to the default SOCKET.log beside the socket, and says so. A daemon started from a terminal also stops on SIGINT or SIGTERM — Ctrl + C if it is in the foreground, or kill <pid> . On Windows, a console-control event does the same. A daemon that predates contour daemon stop answers that it does not support it; stop it where it runs, or end its process. For a service-managed daemon, prefer contour daemon-service stop , which lets the service manager know it was stopped on purpose rather than restarting it. Stopping the daemon ends its shells Stopping the daemon ends every shell it hosts. Shutdown is abrupt by design — attached clients see the connection close with no goodbye, exactly as a real tmux kill-server looks to them. A daemon crash is another matter on Linux and macOS: see Surviving a daemon crash . What comes back after a reboot are the workspaces — see Surviving reboots . Surviving a daemon crash # On Linux and macOS, contour daemon runs the daemon behind a small PTY keeper : the process you started becomes the keeper, and the daemon and every shell are its children. The keeper holds each shell's terminal and the daemon's sockets, reads no output, and starts a new daemon when the old one crashes, is killed, or stops answering for 30 seconds ( daemon.keeper.restart_hung ). contour daemon status names the keeper's process id beside the daemon's. What survives a crash: the shells , and every program running in them: nothing is restarted, and they never notice; their output after you reconnect : the window reconnects to the same socket on its own (see When the connection is lost ), and from then on shows what the programs write; each pane's working directory and foreground program name , which the new daemon reads from the shell itself, so a new tab still opens where you were and a tab title still names the running program; the ids : the new daemon is the same instance with the same session, tab and workspace ids, so every window keeps its tabs and panes, and what you type into a pane still reaches the program it showed before the crash. What does not: what the dead daemon had read but not yet shown is lost, and the screen of each pane comes back with the scrollback the last workspace snapshot held rather than as it was; a program redraws its screen, a shell its prompt. Input typed while the daemon was down is dropped. A daemon that crashes again within 30 seconds is restarted after a pause that doubles up to 30 seconds. After five crashes within five minutes the keeper stops restarting it and keeps the shells for two minutes more, then tries once again; if that fails too, it ends the shells and exits with a failure, so that a service manager's own restart limits apply. Stopping the daemon ( contour daemon stop , SIGTERM , SIGINT ) ends the keeper with it, and a keeper that goes away takes its daemon along. These numbers are the defaults of daemon.keeper , in whole seconds but the count: daemon : keeper : give_up_crashes : 5 # this many crashes ... give_up_window : 300 # ... within this many seconds give up backoff_start : 1 # the first pause after a crash soon after another backoff_cap : 30 # the longest pause startup_timeout : 30 # a start silent that long, before serving, is killed as hung stop_timeout : 60 # a stopping daemon that has not ended by then is killed contour daemon reads them as it starts; a running keeper keeps the numbers it started with. An out-of-memory kill under systemd still stops the unit Under the systemd user unit ( contour daemon-service install ), a kernel out-of-memory kill of the daemon still stops the whole unit, keeper and shells included, as before. Keeping the shells through that is planned, and needs a change to the unit and to how the daemon places itself. Windows runs the daemon without a keeper for now, and its shells end with it. Surviving reboots # A daemon keeps a snapshot of its workspaces, so that after a reboot, a crash or an upgrade the next daemon brings it back. The shells themselves cannot survive a reboot, nor a stopped daemon (a crashed one is another matter: see Surviving a daemon crash ); what returns is: every workspace, tab and split, with its ratios, the active tab and pane, and a zoomed pane; the names you gave workspaces, tabs and panes, the tab titles, and the tab colours you set; each pane's working directory and profile; the newest lines of each pane's scrollback, under a dim marker row such as ── restored · snapshot of 2026-10-24 09:15 ── , followed by a fresh shell. The snapshot is written every interval seconds while the workspaces change, at once when you close a pane or a tab, and once more as the daemon ends. It is restored when a daemon starts and finds one: after a reboot, a crash, a SIGTERM , an idle exit, or the restart the drift chip offers after an upgrade (see After upgrading Contour ). It is not restored after a plain contour daemon stop , which empties it, and panes and tabs you closed are not brought back. contour daemon stop # ends the shells and discards the workspaces contour daemon stop --keep-snapshot # ends the shells; the next daemon restores the workspaces With no daemon running, contour daemon stop still offers to empty the saved workspaces, so a daemon started later does not bring back what you meant to end. Since a crash may have left those workspaces as all you have, it asks first, unless --yes is given, and without a terminal to ask on it clears nothing and tells you to pass --yes . It exits with status 4 as before, whether it cleared the workspaces or you kept them; with nothing saved it says so and creates no file. A daemon from a release before this feature keeps no workspaces: --keep-snapshot then says so and stops it plainly. A program is never started again by itself. Only one you list in rerun_programs is run once more when its pane was running it, and only when its command line holds nothing a shell would expand. When the saved directory no longer exists, the pane opens in the shell's default directory and the daemon logs it. daemon : restore : scrollback : true # bring the scrollback back scrollback_lines : 1000 # the most lines kept per pane, 0 to 100000 rerun_programs : [] # e.g. [vim, htop]; nothing is re-run unless listed interval : 30 # seconds between writes of changed workspaces, at least 5 scrollback_lines bounds the snapshot only; how much scrollback a session holds while it runs stays daemon.history_limit . The snapshot is <state-dir>/sessions/<name>.snapshot (the state directory is listed under Platform notes ); a daemon started with --name work keeps work.snapshot . A daemon given a socket of its own, by --socket or $CONTOUR_MUX , keeps <name>@<hash>.snapshot instead, the hash naming its socket, so it never restores or overwrites the workspaces of the daemon its name runs; contour daemon stop --socket finds the same file. The file is your user's alone: mode 0600 in a 0700 directory on Linux, macOS and BSD, and a protected ACL granting only your account on Windows. It is replaced atomically and durably: each write is flushed to the disk before it replaces the previous snapshot, and the replacement is flushed in turn, so a daemon crash, a power loss or a kernel crash in the middle of a write leaves either the previous snapshot or the new one, whole. The snapshot may hold secrets Restored scrollback is whatever was on screen: a password echoed by mistake, a token printed by a tool. It is written to disk in the clear. Set scrollback: false to keep only the layout and the directories, or scrollback_lines: 0 for the same. A snapshot that cannot be read is renamed <name>.snapshot.corrupt and the daemon starts with its startup layout, logging why; one written by a newer release is left in place. A restore that brought nothing back is tried once more at the next start, then set aside as <name>.snapshot.failed . Diagnostics # The daemon logs through Contour's category system; contour list-debug-tags prints every tag. The vthost.* categories are the daemon's: Category Default What it records vthost.daemon on Endpoints bound, listeners started, signals, shutdown vthost.conn off Per-connection accept, handshake, disconnect vthost.session off Session spawn, resize, exit vthost.tmux off Control-mode and tmux-binary attach or rejection vthost.client off The client side of the native protocol vthost.trace.proto off One line per protocol message, both directions vthost.trace.tmux off Every control-mode line, both directions contour daemon --log 'vthost.conn,vthost.session' contour daemon --log 'vthost.*' --log-file /var/log/contour-daemon.log Three behaviours to know: * is a plain prefix match, so vthost.* sweeps in the verbose vthost.trace.* tier as well. Name vthost.trace.* to select the trace tier alone. A filter is a selection : it disables the categories it does not name. Real failures are exempt — asking for extra detail never takes error reporting away. --log-file appends and never writes colour escapes, so restarting a daemon against the same file does not erase why the previous run died. Traces report sizes, never payloads: a keystroke message shows a byte count, a screen update a line count, and a token only as present or absent. A trace of a busy session must not become a transcript of what you typed. Platform notes # Contour keeps what outlives a daemon in a per-user state directory , separate from the runtime directory the sockets live in: OS State directory Linux, macOS, BSD $XDG_STATE_HOME/contour when set and absolute, otherwise ~/.local/state/contour Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\contour Without a usable home directory the fallback is <temp>/contour-state-<user> . That directory is shared ground, so a daemon never runs from a copy staged there: it runs in place instead. Daemon mode works on Linux, macOS, BSD and Windows 10 1803 or newer, over Unix domain sockets everywhere. On Windows, sessions are backed by ConPTY, the socket directory is governed by NTFS ACLs rather than POSIX permission bits, and the tmux-binary ( <socket>-tmux ) endpoint is absent — it needs file-descriptor passing, which Windows sockets do not have. After upgrading Contour # An upgrade never touches the running daemon. The daemon keeps serving, and the client you start next may be newer than the daemon it attaches to. Where an upgrade would disturb a running binary, the daemon does not run from the installed binary at all. On Windows (the installer replaces contour.exe , and Windows Installer moves the images a running copy holds aside rather than failing), on macOS (swapping the .app breaks the lazy loading of its frameworks) and for an AppImage (its mount vanishes when the AppImage process exits), a daemon runs from a copy of its own release under <state-dir>/bin/<version>-<id>/ . It is made the first time that release starts a daemon, and removed again once no daemon runs from it. What the copy costs A release contour binary is about 474 MB. On Windows the copy is the whole install folder, on macOS the whole .app , and one such copy exists per release that has a daemon running or about to start, until it is unused. Old copies are pruned automatically, never while a daemon runs from them. A packaged Linux install ( /usr/... , Flatpak /app/... ) runs in place, which a package upgrade cannot disturb. contour daemon --in-place opts out of the copy; a package upgrade may then replace the binary under the running daemon. A hand-started foreground contour daemon on Windows also runs from the installed binary. Installing a new Contour on Windows # A daemon started by hand runs from the folder an installer is about to replace. Windows Installer moves the files a running program holds aside, and that daemon would run on from its old images until it next restarts. So the installer asks the Contour it replaces to move your hand-started daemons first: each one is handed over to a copy of itself under %LOCALAPPDATA%\contour\bin\ , keeping its sessions and their programs, exactly as a live upgrade does. The installer then replaces the files. The same step is available as contour daemon relocate , which says for each daemon where it went ( moved the daemon at <socket> onto <executable> ) and which it left ( left the daemon at <socket>: <reason> ). A daemon that Contour starts for you already runs from such a copy, and needs none of this. What is not moved: A daemon started with --in-place , which asked to stay where it is. A silent install replaces the files under it all the same (Windows Installer moves the images it holds aside), and it keeps running from its old images until it next restarts. What an interactive install does with it has not been verified: Windows may list it in its files-in-use dialog, and what "close" does to its sessions is not known. To be safe, stop such a daemon ( contour daemon stop ) before installing. A daemon of an installation from before this change (0.8 and earlier, and earlier 0.9 development builds), which cannot be asked, and a daemon of another installation. A daemon whose socket is not in the default socket directory ( %TEMP%\contour-<user>\ ), such as one started with a --socket elsewhere. relocate looks only in that directory. Another user's daemon. The installer runs as the user who started it, so a UAC elevation as a different administrator account looks for that administrator's daemons, not yours; yours is left as it is. Any daemon, when a deployment tool installs as the SYSTEM account: SYSTEM has no daemon, so nothing is handed over, the install still succeeds, and your daemon keeps running from the old images until its next restart. Install as yourself to have it moved. Not moving a daemon never fails the install. After a move, the sessions' console host ( OpenConsole.exe ) keeps running from its old image, which Windows Installer moves aside and deletes at the next restart; the new files are in bin\ . The console host of a session cannot be replaced while the session runs. Keeping it elsewhere is not available yet. The installer also closes the running Contour window and opens it again with the arguments it had. That is Windows' Restart Manager, which closes and reopens a running Contour GUI. It does not end daemons: in a silent install it left a daemon, and its console host, running. The two negotiate a protocol version when they connect: each states the range of versions it speaks, and they agree on the newest one both know. Every release speaks the protocols of at least the previous two releases, so a client from a newer release attaches to an older daemon — and an older client to a newer daemon — as long as the two are within that window. Features the older side does not know are simply not used on that connection. When the daemon's release differs from the client's, the window shows a quiet chip, for instance daemon 0.8.1 is older than this client . For a local daemon that supports it, clicking it offers Upgrade daemon (keeps your programs running) ; see Live upgrade below. Otherwise it offers Restart daemon on the new version . The confirmation says what that costs: it ends every shell the daemon hosts , and a fresh one opens on the new daemon. A daemon that keeps its workspaces brings your workspaces, tabs, directories and scrollback back, and the confirmation says so (see Surviving reboots ). After the restart a new Contour window attaches to the new daemon, and this one closes. The chip is shown only for the local daemon: a remote one ( --connect-tcp ) is not yours to restart. The restart stops the daemon for an upgrade, then starts one the same way a client would: through the registered service when there is one, on demand otherwise. Live upgrade # The command palette's Upgrade daemon row (the UpgradeDaemon action, which can be bound to a key) starts a live upgrade (described below) at any time, drift chip or not, so a rebuilt binary of the same release can be picked up. It asks nothing, as the upgrade keeps every program running, and a refusal or failure is shown as a notice. A live upgrade replaces the daemon with the new release without ending anything it hosts . On Linux, macOS and the BSDs the daemon re-executes the new release's binary in its own process, so every shell and program keeps its process, its process ID, its parent and its terminal. Windows cannot replace a running process's binary: there the daemon starts the new release beside itself, hands it every session, and ends once the new release has taken over. The daemon's process ID changes; every shell's and program's does not, nor does its console. Each session's screens, scrollback, images, cursor and modes, and an escape sequence cut in half by the switch (up to a bound, below), come across as they were; so do your workspaces, tabs and splits. The windows show Upgrading daemon… for a moment and reconnect by themselves. Start it from the chip, or from a shell or script: contour daemon upgrade [ --name NAME | --socket PATH ] It exits 0 once the new release serves, 4 when no daemon runs, and 5 with the reason on standard error when the daemon declines or the switch fails; the daemon then serves on as before. When the daemon says nothing conclusive within 15 seconds, the outcome is unknown and the exit status is 1; check contour daemon status , whose upgrades line counts the live upgrades the daemon has been through and whose last upgrade line names the last one that failed. What the daemon declines on: The daemon declines when Because it runs in a Flatpak sandbox the sandbox cannot reach the new release's binary; update the Flatpak and use the restart the new release cannot read the state it would hand over, or load its configuration the check runs the new binary first; the restart is the way across a gap wider than two releases a session runs on an SSH or channel connection nothing could adopt it after the switch a program is in the middle of an escape sequence longer than the handover carries, or its sessions' state is too large the handover has a fixed bound a session is still starting, or the new release's image is not in the daemon's store try again in a moment; the next upgrade stages the image anew another upgrade is under way, or the clients and sessions do not settle in time try again in a moment on Windows, a session runs on Windows' own console host rather than the conpty.dll Contour ships only Contour's can be handed to the new daemon; it is missing only where conpty.dll is not beside contour.exe Most of these are checked before anything is stopped. A few show only after the daemon has told its clients it is upgrading and disconnected them: the clients and sessions not settling in time, a session that keeps starting, a program caught in an overlong escape sequence, state too large to hand over, and the new binary failing to start. The daemon then resumes; the windows reconnect to it a moment later, and the chip and contour daemon upgrade (exit 5) name the reason. On Windows the new release that does not say it is ready within 8 seconds is ended, and the old daemon resumes the same way. A refusal never costs a program, and neither does a failure after it: if the new binary cannot start, the old daemon resumes and says so. A few things to know: The chip offers the upgrade only for a daemon on this machine that announced it supports it and is not newer than the client (a newer one is offered the restart, as an upgrade would be a downgrade). A remote daemon ( --connect-tcp , --host ) is not yours to upgrade, and the chip offers nothing for it. It is available on Linux, macOS, the BSDs and Windows. Flatpak: a running sandbox keeps the old /app mounted, so the daemon cannot reach the new release. Update the Flatpak, then restart the daemon from the chip (this ends its shells). The first release that has it can be upgraded from, not to. The readiness check needs code in the old daemon, so a daemon from before live upgrade is restarted once, and every daemon after that is upgraded live. Extensions that a status line runs in the daemon are started again by the new daemon; the programs in your panes are never restarted. The daemon keeps its workspace snapshot current, as always; it is the safety net if everything else fails. Outside the window, or against a daemon from Contour 0.7.0 or another release before version negotiation, the client is refused, and it tells you both sides' versions: the daemon speaks protocol 3, from a release before version negotiation; this client speaks 4-4 A wrong token is reported as such instead ( wrong token or insufficient rights ): the refusal names the daemon's versions either way, so a probe learns nothing more from it. To move past a version refusal, stop the daemon and let it start again: contour daemon stop contour client # starts a matching daemon Remember that this ends the sessions it was hosting. An auto-started daemon rarely has the problem, since it exits 10 seconds after its last session and client are gone. Current limitations # contour client opens a window. There is no terminal-only client at present; if you need one, attach with tmux -C through the compatibility endpoint described above. You get the scrollback the daemon still holds, and no more. Attaching replays a session's history, but the daemon keeps only history.limit lines of it per session — 1000 unless the profile it was started with says otherwise. Lines that scrolled past that are gone, and there is no way to ask for them back. A session sitting on the alternate screen has no scrollback to show. Attach while vim , less or htop is running and you get that program's screen, which never has history of its own; the shell's scrollback appears when the program exits. The daemon keeps one cell size. Images (Sixel, kitty, Contour's own) are laid out on the cell size in pixels the attached client last reported, remembered after it detaches, and on daemon.default_cell_pixel_size until one reports. With a per-pane font zoom, or windows on monitors of different DPI, every pane other than the last-reporting one lays its images out for that pane's cell, so they come out larger or smaller than its own cells would make them. Shells end when the daemon is stopped (see Stopping a daemon ), and on Windows when it crashes; the workspaces come back without them (see Surviving reboots ). On Linux and macOS a crashed daemon is replaced and the shells live on (see Surviving a daemon crash ). ssh attach needs key or agent authentication. Contour never answers an ssh prompt — a password, a key passphrase, a second factor or an unknown host key — so run ssh USER@HOST once in a terminal first (see Remote hosts ). Images are not recoverable through tmux-mode replay (see the note under tmux interoperability ). For the architecture behind all of this — the two protocols, the delta transport, the stable row identity in the grid — see the internals page .
docs.title: persistent sessions

docs.text: Experimental Daemon mode is new in 0.7.0 and still settling. It is built into every Contour and covered by the test suite, but its command-line flags and its wire protocol may change between releases. Contour already gives you tabs and split panes inside one window. Daemon mode is different: it moves your sessions into a background process , so they survive the window that shows them. Close the window, reattach later, or attach from another machine — the shells keep running either way. Terms. The daemon is the background process. A workspace is what it holds: a set of tabs, each an arrangement of panes. A window is an operating-system window of the Contour GUI, which shows one workspace; closing the window leaves the workspace and its shells with the daemon. That buys you three things: A long build, a database migration or a training run keeps going after you close the window — deliberately or by accident. Work done over SSH survives the link dropping. Reconnect, reattach, carry on. The same sessions are reachable from a second machine, over an encrypted connection. If you have used tmux or screen , this is the same idea, with two differences: the sessions are rendered by a real Contour window (images, hyperlinks, sized text and all), and Contour can speak tmux's own protocol in both directions — so it interoperates with tmux rather than replacing it.
docs.title: Persistent sessions (daemon mode)

docs.text: contour client That is the whole thing. contour client looks for a daemon, starts one if none is running , and opens a window showing its sessions. Close the window and the shells stay alive; run contour client again to pick them back up — with their scrollback, so you can scroll back through what the session did while nothing was watching. To manage the daemon yourself, start it first: contour daemon & # runs in the FOREGROUND; background it or use a service manager contour client # attaches to the daemon you started The distinction matters, because the two daemons have different lifetimes: How it started When it exits Auto-started by contour client 10 seconds after it has no sessions and no clients — it belongs to the clients that needed it, so nothing is left behind Started by you ( contour daemon ) Never on its own. It keeps serving with zero sessions, ready for the next client Started by the OS ( contour daemon-service ) Never on its own, see Starting the daemon at login Closing the last window therefore keeps your sessions: the auto-started daemon stays up as long as any session lives, and for 10 seconds after the last one is gone and the last client has disconnected. A client that attaches within those 10 seconds keeps the daemon alive. The policy is the daemon's --lifecycle option, and it rides on the daemon , not on the client that started it: --lifecycle The daemon ends persistent (default for contour daemon ) never on its own exit-with-last-session once its last hosted session is gone (tmux spells this exit-empty ) exit-when-idle (what contour client starts on demand) 10 seconds after it has no session and no client --exit-with-last-session is kept as an alias for --lifecycle=exit-with-last-session . Stating both is an error only when they differ. A status probe ( contour daemon status ) is not a client and never keeps an idle daemon alive. contour daemon does not detach by itself It runs in the foreground and logs to standard error, which is what you want under a service manager or in a container. Background it with & , or let contour client start it for you.
docs.title: Quick start

docs.text: Because sessions outlive the window, "close" needs two answers — and Contour gives you both. Which one you get depends on what you close: What you close What happens to the shell The window (its close button, or quitting Contour) Detach. It keeps running; the next contour client shows it again A pane — Close Pane in the right-click menu, or the ClosePane action Ends. That session is closed on the daemon and does not come back A tab — its ✕, or the CloseTab action Ends , together with every pane in it Typing exit in the shell Ends , as always — the shell decided This is the same split tmux draws between detaching a client and kill-pane , and it works the same for a local session as for one hosted by a daemon: a pane you end is ended everywhere, including for any other client attached to that daemon. Neither ClosePane nor CloseTab ships with a default key binding — bind them yourself if you want one: input_mapping : - { mods : [ Ctrl , Shift ], key : 'W' , action : ClosePane } Ending a whole daemon's worth of sessions Closing panes one at a time is the fine-grained way. To end everything at once, stop the daemon — see Stopping a daemon .
docs.title: Detaching versus ending a session

docs.text: Daemons are told apart by a name , exactly as tmux's -L does: contour daemon --name work contour client --daemon work The name names a socket under your per-user runtime directory. Resolution order: --socket PATH — used verbatim. An explicitly given name, contour daemon --name NAME or contour client --daemon NAME (the value default included) — the name's own socket, exactly as tmux's -L beats $TMUX . $CONTOUR_MUX — used verbatim (analogous to tmux's $TMUX ). $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/<name> (the name default when none was given). <temp>/contour-<uid>/<name> when there is no runtime directory (tmux's /tmp/tmux-<uid>/<label> shape). A daemon exports $CONTOUR_MUX into every shell it hosts, so a command typed in one of its panes reaches that same daemon without a flag. That is why it ranks above the default name: a sandboxed (Flatpak) shell cannot derive where its daemon lives, and a plain contour client there still finds it. It ranks below an explicit name, so contour daemon --name work status from inside a pane asks the work daemon rather than the one hosting the pane. The daemon binds three endpoints, all derived from that one path: the control socket itself, <socket>-native for Contour's own clients, and <socket>-tmux for the tmux binary. The socket directory is created 0700 and checked on every bind: it must be a real directory, owned by you, and must not be world-accessible. Group access is permitted, matching tmux. Keep socket paths short A Unix socket path is limited to roughly 100 bytes by the operating system, not by Contour. A deeply nested --socket path will fail to bind.
docs.title: Running several daemons side by side

docs.text: Option What it does --socket PATH Path of the control socket file. Defaults to the configuration's daemon.socket , else $CONTOUR_MUX when no --name is given, else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/contour/NAME . --name NAME The daemon's name, which tells daemon instances apart. Default default . Given, it beats $CONTOUR_MUX . Until 0.9.0, --label NAME still works, with a note on standard error. --config FILE Configuration file whose profile supplies the hosted sessions' terminal settings — including history.limit , which is how much scrollback a session keeps for clients that attach later. --profile NAME Which profile of that configuration to take them from. Defaults to the configuration's default profile. --lifecycle POLICY When the daemon ends on its own: persistent (the default), exit-with-last-session or exit-when-idle . See Quick start . --exit-with-last-session Alias for --lifecycle=exit-with-last-session . --size-policy POLICY Which attached client's size the shared grid takes when clients of different sizes are attached: latest , smallest or largest . Mirrors tmux's window-size . Defaults to the configuration's daemon.size_policy ( latest unless set). --background Relaunches the command detached and returns once the daemon accepts connections. Without --log-file the daemon logs beside its socket ( SOCKET.log ), since a detached process has no console. --stdio Relays the native protocol between standard input/output and this user's daemon, starting it if needed: what contour client --host runs over ssh. Honours --name , --socket , --config , --profile , --log , --log-file and --size-policy (forwarded to a daemon it starts); cannot be combined with --listen-tcp , --background or --tmux-compat-socket . --in-place Runs from the installed binary instead of a per-version copy. See After upgrading Contour . --tmux-compat-socket LABEL Additionally binds tmux's own discovery path /tmp/tmux-<uid>/<LABEL> , so a plain tmux -L LABEL -C attach-session finds this daemon. --listen-tcp HOST:PORT Also serve the native protocol over TCP. Opt-in; always TLS-encrypted, and clients sign in with an authorized key or a token. The daemon's TLS fingerprint is logged and shown by daemon status . Port 0 lets the system pick a free port, which the log names. See Remote access . --authorized-keys FILE SSH public keys, in authorized_keys format, that may log in to the TCP listener by signing a challenge. Defaults to authorized_keys in the configuration directory; a missing file is no keys. Needs --listen-tcp . --auth any\|keys How TCP clients authenticate: any (the default) accepts a token, an access-file entry or an authorized key; keys accepts authorized keys alone and refuses --token , --token-file and --access-file . Needs --listen-tcp . --token TOKEN Preshared token a TCP client may present. With --listen-tcp , one of a token or an authorized key is required. Visible to other local users through the process list — prefer --token-file . --token-file FILE Reads the token from FILE instead, so the secret is protected by that file's permissions. Trailing newlines are ignored. --access-file FILE Further TCP tokens with narrower grants, one per line. Needs --listen-tcp . See Narrower tokens . --tls-cert FILE , --tls-key FILE PEM certificate and matching private key for the TCP listener. Omit both to have the daemon generate an ephemeral self-signed certificate. --log TAGS Enable logging for a comma-separated list of tags, or all . See Diagnostics . --log-file FILE Append log output to FILE instead of standard error; - means standard error explicitly.
docs.title: contour daemon options

docs.text: The thin client is the default: a plain contour shows sessions that a daemon hosts, starting that daemon when none runs. contour client always attaches; a plain contour decides by daemon.mode in the configuration, or by --daemon-mode on its command line: Mode Where the sessions run auto (the default) In the daemon, started if none runs; when none can be had, in the window's process, with a bar saying why — those shells end when the window closes in_process In the window's own process, as before daemon mode existed required In the daemon, or not at all: the launch ends with the reason before any window opens daemon : mode : auto # auto, in_process or required socket : "" # the daemon's socket path; empty selects the default size_policy : latest # whose size wins when clients disagree: latest, smallest or largest default_cell_pixel_size : { width : 10 , height : 20 } # cell size images use until a client reports one history_limit : 1000 # scrollback lines per session, -1 for unlimited; unset follows the profile contour --daemon-mode in_process # this launch only: keep the sessions in this window contour --daemon-mode required # this launch only: fail rather than fall back
docs.title: Hosting from a plain contour

docs.text: A launch opens one window. So does New Window (a second launch of contour , NewTerminal on Cmd+N or Ctrl+Shift+N ). A new window never shows a workspace another window shows, on this computer or any other client attached to the daemon: it takes the hidden workspace that was left most recently — the one whose window you closed or switched away from last — and when there is none it gets a new workspace with one tab. So closing a window by mistake and opening a new one brings it straight back, and each further launch picks up the hidden workspace left before that. Workspaces no window has left since the daemon started, such as those a restarted daemon restores, are taken in the order the sidebar lists them. A fresh daemon gets its first tab in the first window, as before. The same rule moves a window whose workspace ends (its last tab closes). It moves on to the hidden workspace holding a tab that a new window would take, and never to one another window shows. When every other workspace is shown by some window, it has nowhere to go and the window closes, as closing the last tab of a window does; the other windows stay as they were. A launch that names a program ( -e , or a command after the options) runs it in the window's own process under auto ; under required it ends before any window, since a daemon session runs the host's profile.
docs.title: What a launch opens

docs.text: A window attached to a daemon keeps its panes when the connection drops. They show "Reconnecting…" while the window reconnects with backoff (250 ms doubling to 5 s) and picks its workspaces up again. A connection gone half-open — a laptop that changed networks — is noticed by a heartbeat within about 15 s instead of whenever TCP gives up. Input typed while disconnected is dropped rather than replayed into whatever shell answers next. A launch that falls back to in_process has no connection to lose.
docs.title: When the connection is lost

docs.text: A window shows one workspace of one daemon, over a connection of its own: each window has exactly one connection, so a window on a remote host does not tie up, or depend on, the other windows. You can point a window somewhere else without closing it, and its panes are swapped in place: To another workspace of the same daemon , with SwitchToWorkspace or CycleWorkspace ( Ctrl+Alt+PageDown / PageUp , ⌃⌘↓ / ⌃⌘↑ on macOS, for the next / previous one). To another daemon : a local one by its name ( contour daemon --name ), or a saved host , with SwitchToDaemon or CycleDaemon . The window lands on that daemon's only workspace, on a new one when it has none, and asks which when it has several. A workspace that holds no tab -- a daemon no window has attached to yet keeps one -- counts as none: there is nothing in it to show. From the switcher ( ShowSwitcher , Ctrl+Shift+R , ⇧⌘R on macOS), a popup in the command palette's family, drawn over the window. See The switcher below. By mouse : click the location chip ( local › billing ▾ ) in the title band of a window on a daemon (Space or Return when it has keyboard focus) to open the same switcher below it, as ShowSwitcher does; its tooltip names that chord, and Escape closes the popup. With the sidebar shown, the daemon at the head of the sidebar does the same. Or pick Switch To Daemon or Daemon & Workspace Switcher… from the Window submenu of the main menu (☰). Switch To Daemon lists the same daemons as the command palette's Switch to daemon rows. The chip's connection state. The chip shows the daemon's connection too: a dot for a remote daemon that is connected, and the dot with Reconnecting… or Disconnected while the link is not up. In a narrow band the state text goes first, then the daemon name, then the workspace name, which keeps at least 6 characters. From a shell , with contour switch , which also works from a pane of the window being switched. The window asks first (see below). The Open… variants ( OpenWorkspace , OpenDaemon ) open a new window on the destination instead. If a window already shows the destination workspace, that window is focused and nothing else changes. The actions and their palette rows are listed in Key Mapping ; of them, only ShowSwitcher is bound to a key by default. A window stays on one connection while it moves between a daemon's workspaces, so switching, creating ( NewWorkspace ) and cycling are immediate and open no window. A window attached to a daemon that predates this is refused, with a hint to run contour daemon upgrade or to pick Upgrade daemon in the command palette. Bells and desktop notifications come from one window only: the most recently focused one. A command that finishes in a workspace no window shows is noticed once, by that window. A program's clipboard write (OSC 52) reaches only a window that shows its pane. A switch that cannot finish leaves the window as it was and says why in a notice: the destination is not reachable, it has no such workspace, or it did not show the workspace within 10 seconds. A switch asked for through the control API ( contour switch , or any program calling workspace.switch ) is a program pointing your window somewhere, so the window asks before it switches: a prompt in the window names the destination in full, the daemon by name or host and the workspace, and offers Deny or Switch. Ticking Don't ask again keeps the answer, Deny or Switch, for every later switch between the same two daemons (from the daemon the window is on to the destination's), whatever the workspace, until Contour exits; it is never written down. A remembered Deny answers refused without asking. A destination named by URL ( ssh://… ) asks every time and offers nothing to remember, since allowing it runs ssh with your credentials. The switches you make yourself, by key, palette or the switcher popup, never ask. The GUI cannot tell a script outside any pane from you typing contour switch , so that asks too. Note Windows of the in-process mode have no daemon behind them and cannot switch.
docs.title: Switching a window

docs.text: The switcher lists the workspaces of the daemon this window is on first, under Workspaces on ‹daemon› , with the status glyph the sidebar shows, the branch, and the tab count; the current one wears a Current pill. Under Other daemons come the other local daemons and the saved hosts, each with its workspace count and the most urgent status among its workspaces; a saved host also shows how it is reached ( SSH , TLS ). Actions end the list: New Workspace , and New Daemon… . Type to filter. What you type finds workspaces on every local daemon at once, each match with a pill naming its daemon. A saved host is searched only once you open it, since connecting may ask for a password. When nothing matches, the switcher says so and offers New Workspace “what you typed” . Return switches this window to the selected workspace; Shift+Return opens it in a new window, as does the button on the selected row and on the row under the pointer. Hovering a row does not move the selection: the arrow keys own it. → , or Return on a daemon, opens that daemon: its workspaces alone, with New Workspace on it. Backspace in an empty field, or Escape, goes back. A saved host shows Connecting… while it connects; you can type, or back out, meanwhile. A daemon that cannot be listed says why on its row, and everything else keeps working. New Daemon… asks for a name. As you type it says whether the name is available, already running (Return then switches to that daemon), or not a valid name, and shows the equivalent contour daemon --name command. Return starts the daemon and switches this window to it; Shift+Return opens it in a new window. Right-click a workspace of this window's daemon, or press the Menu key or Shift+F10, for the menu its sidebar row has. Another daemon's workspace offers switching and opening in a new window. Escape clears what you typed, then closes; a click elsewhere closes. Either changes nothing, and a daemon a New Daemon… start was still bringing up is not switched to. A workspace of another daemon shows a done or failed status as unseen for as long as it stands: this window never saw that pane, and a daemon keeps no record of who did.
docs.title: The switcher

docs.text: Every window selects exactly one workspace of the daemon, and the daemon keeps one of two states per workspace: State Meaning shown Some window selects it right now. hidden No window selects it. Closing a window, or losing its connection, leaves its workspace hidden ; it keeps running and keeps its state, so reopening Contour finds your sessions where you left them. The same holds across a daemon restart and a live upgrade . Select a hidden workspace from a window to show it again ( contour ls --json reports each workspace's state as visibility , see the control API ).
docs.title: Shown and hidden workspaces

docs.text: Option What it does --daemon PATH\|HOST:PORT\|URL\|NAME Which daemon to attach to, as every control verb reads it: a socket path, a TCP daemon, an ssh:// URL, or a name, which is a local daemon's, else a saved host's ( name:NAME picks a local daemon and host:NAME a saved host; a number after them that names no such daemon or host is a port, so host:2222 reaches a machine called host ; a bare name both have is refused). A local daemon resolves as above, daemon.socket of the client's configuration included. Not together with --socket , --host or --connect-tcp . Until 0.9.0, --label NAME still works, as --daemon name:NAME . --socket PATH The control socket of the daemon to attach to. --workspace WORKSPACE Show only that daemon workspace instead of what a launch brings back, named as every control verb names one: its id or an id suffix (as contour ls prints it), its name, or its 1-based position. Fails, saying why, when it names no workspace or several. It also works with --host . --size-policy POLICY The policy a daemon this client auto-starts runs with; defaults to daemon.size_policy . --tmux Attach to a real tmux server instead of a Contour daemon. See tmux interoperability . --tmux-socket PATH The tmux server socket (tmux's -S ) for --tmux . --profile NAME Config profile the window renders remote sessions with. --config FILE Configuration file to load. --host NAME\|URL Attach to a remote host: a name saved under hosts: , or an ad-hoc ssh://[USER@]HOST[:PORT] (or an ad-hoc tls://HOST:PORT , which signs in with your SSH agent's keys). The remote daemon is started there when none runs; the window title and the tab strip name the host. A host's profile: is used unless --profile names one. Cannot be combined with --socket , --connect-tcp , --token , --token-file , --tls-ca or --tmux . See Remote hosts . --connect-tcp HOST:PORT Connect to a remote daemon over TLS instead of a local socket. It signs in with a key of your SSH agent, or with the token. A daemon met for the first time is pinned once you trust its fingerprint in a dialog. --token TOKEN , --token-file FILE The preshared token to present, inline or read from a file. --tls-ca FILE PEM trust anchor the daemon's certificate is verified against. Omitted, the daemon is pinned on first use instead: you are asked to trust its fingerprint, which is kept in known_daemons , and a daemon that presents another one is refused. --daemon-fingerprint SHA256:... The fingerprint a --connect-tcp or --host daemon without a CA must present on first contact, as contour daemon status prints it on that machine. It is pinned without asking, and any other fingerprint is refused. --log TAGS , --log-file FILE As above — and passed on to a daemon this client auto-starts , which is otherwise the one instance nobody can configure.
docs.title: contour client options

docs.text: Contour speaks tmux's control-mode protocol in both directions, pinned to tmux 3.7b semantics.
docs.title: tmux interoperability

docs.text: <socket>-tmux speaks the binary protocol the stock tmux client uses, so the real tmux binary can attach to a Contour daemon: tmux -S " $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR /contour/default-tmux" -C attach-session To let tmux find the daemon by a socket name alone, have the daemon bind tmux's own discovery path too: contour daemon --tmux-compat-socket mine tmux -L mine -C attach-session --tmux-compat-socket is opt-in for a reason That path is where tmux looks for its server. With the Contour daemon down, a new-session against it would silently start a real tmux server there instead. Control mode ( -C ) is supported; -CC is not — Contour never renders a full terminal client for tmux. Arbitrary startup commands are refused; the endpoint accepts attach- and new-session-shaped startup only.
docs.title: Attach tmux tooling to a Contour daemon

docs.text: The other direction: point Contour at a tmux server and mirror it. contour client --tmux # the default tmux server contour client --tmux --tmux-socket /tmp/x # a specific one tmux windows become Contour tabs, tmux panes become splits, and input travels back as send-keys . Content mirrors live. tmux replay carries text, not images Contour replays each pane's full history through capture-pane , so scrollback survives a reattach on this path too. Images do not, and that is a tmux limitation rather than Contour's: capture-pane serialises text and colour, never image data. Images drawn while you are attached display normally; images drawn before you attached cannot be recovered. Contour's own native protocol has no such gap — it transfers images by id.
docs.title: Show a real tmux server in a Contour window

docs.text: By default a daemon is reachable only through its Unix socket, where the filesystem permissions are the access control. --listen-tcp additionally exposes the native protocol over the network. It serves one user per daemon : whoever signs in gets that user's sessions and everything they can do. To serve several users, give each their own daemon, reached over ssh, which is what separates them by account; see Remote hosts . # On the host running the sessions: authorize a key, then listen for keys alone. cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.config/contour/authorized_keys contour daemon --listen-tcp 127 .0.0.1:9090 --auth keys # On the machine you are sitting at (its SSH agent signs in; the first contact asks you to compare the # daemon's fingerprint, which `contour daemon status` prints on the host): contour client --connect-tcp server.example.com:9090 A token still works, and is the way for a script: --token-file FILE on the daemon (the default --auth any accepts both) and --token-file FILE on the client. Properties worth knowing before you open a port: TLS is not optional. The TCP endpoint is always encrypted; there is no plaintext mode. A credential is required. TCP has no filesystem gate to fall back on, so --listen-tcp with neither an authorized key nor --token / --token-file refuses to start rather than serving anonymously. A key signs in over the TLS connection itself, so a daemon never learns a secret it could replay. Prefer --token-file . A token passed as --token is readable by every other user on the machine through the process list; a file carries permissions. Without --tls-cert / --tls-key the daemon keeps a self-signed identity of its own , made on first start in <state-dir>/tls/<name>.pem and presented ever after. The daemon refuses that file unless it is yours and readable by you alone (mode 0600), so a copy with looser permissions needs a chmod 600 . The client pins it on first use, as ssh pins a host key: it asks you to compare the fingerprint, remembers it in known_daemons , and refuses the daemon for good if it ever presents another ( contour daemon forget-pin HOST:PORT after a reinstall). For a certificate verified the way a browser does, pass one on the daemon and name its CA with --tls-ca on the client — the certificate must then also be issued for the host you connect to , not merely signed by that CA. See Remote hosts . Bind deliberately. 127.0.0.1 reaches only the local machine; 0.0.0.0 reaches everyone who can route to you. Prefer forwarding the loopback port over SSH to exposing it directly. Control requests need a trusted daemon. A client of the control API sends nothing over a TLS connection whose daemon is neither verified by --tls-ca nor pinned: it asks you to trust the fingerprint first, or is given --daemon-fingerprint . With the control API a token types into and reads every pane, so it must not be handed to whoever answers.
docs.title: Remote access over TCP

docs.text: --token grants everything. A script that only needs to read a pane can be given a token of its own that grants less, through --access-file FILE , one entry per line: # grants token (to the end of the line) read,screen ci-reader s3cret all admin-token A line is a grant list — all , or a comma list of read (look at the workspaces), screen (read what is on screen and in command blocks), input (type into a pane) and write (change the workspaces, stop the daemon) — one space, then the token, which may contain spaces. Carriage returns and trailing whitespace are dropped, as for --token-file ; blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. An unknown grant, an empty token or a token that appears twice stops the daemon from starting, naming the line. The file adds tokens beside --token / --token-file , never instead of them: a hello may present either, and the --token keeps granting everything, so moving everyone to the access file means removing --token as well. A line that repeats the --token stops the daemon from starting too, since its narrower grants would silently read as everything. Running a program is typing it: tab.create and pane.split with a command need input as well as write , so a token granted read,screen,write can open shells and rearrange the workspaces but cannot run a program of its choosing in it. Events follow the same grants: block.finished carries the command line and needs screen , so a subscription of a read token is handed every other kind but that one, and a subscribe naming only kinds the token may not see is answered forbidden . A call outside a token's grants is answered forbidden and the connection stays open. Viewing the sessions needs every grant, so a contour client with a narrower token is refused exactly as with a wrong one. To attach over ssh instead, with no port to open, to save hosts by name, or to reach a home PC from the office over Tailscale, see Remote hosts .
docs.title: Narrower tokens for scripts

docs.text: Instead of letting contour client start a daemon when it is needed, you can have the operating system start one for you when you log in: contour daemon-service install # register it (and start it with your next login) contour daemon-service status # registered? running? what does it run? contour daemon-service start # start it now contour daemon-service stop # stop it, leaving it registered contour daemon-service restart contour daemon-service uninstall # stop it and remove the registration Each verb takes --name NAME (default default ; --label NAME still works until 0.9.0). install additionally takes --socket , --config , --profile , --size-policy , --log and --log-file , which are recorded in the registration.
