A socket path is made absolute at install time, because the registration outlives the shell that wrote it. Unless you give --log-file the daemon logs to SOCKET.log . OS What is registered Runs as Linux the systemd user unit contour-daemon.service ( contour-daemon-NAME.service for other names), written to ~/.config/systemd/user and enabled you, no elevation macOS the LaunchAgent org.contourterminal.contour-daemon in ~/Library/LaunchAgents you, no elevation Windows a Scheduled Task triggered by your logon you, no elevation Packages for Linux also ship a contour-daemon.service unit file. It is not enabled by the package; contour daemon-service install writes your own copy, which takes precedence. daemon-service status and uninstall count the service as installed only once you registered it with install ; the packaged unit alone does not. A vendor unit enabled directly with systemctl --user enable or --global enable is likewise not seen by daemon-service or the client's auto-start; use daemon-service install instead. On Linux, a user's daemon stops when their last login session ends, unless lingering is on for that user. When loginctl reports lingering as off, contour daemon-service install prints a one-line note naming the command to run: loginctl enable-linger Contour never enables lingering itself. To install the daemon alone on a server, see Contour daemon on a server . A service-managed daemon runs with --lifecycle=persistent : it never exits on its own , not even with zero sessions and zero clients. contour client finds the registration and starts it before it falls back to spawning a daemon on demand. A registration made by an older release under another name is found as well. --start boot and --start manual (a Windows service) are not implemented yet.
docs.title: Starting the daemon at login

docs.text: contour-daemon is the Qt-free package for machines that only host persistent sessions and have no display, such as a server you reach over SSH. It ships the contour command-line tool without the GUI stack (no Qt, no QML; the text shaper's Cairo dependency still pulls in the X11 client libraries). Packages are attached to each release (they are not served from a package repository): .deb for Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 (amd64), named contour-daemon-<version>-ubuntu<release>-amd64.deb .rpm for Fedora 44 (x86_64), named contour-daemon-<version>-fedora44-x86_64.rpm sudo apt install ./contour-daemon- [ 0 -9 ] *-ubuntu24.04-amd64.deb # Ubuntu 24.04 (use ubuntu26.04 on 26.04) sudo dnf install ./contour-daemon- [ 0 -9 ] *-fedora44-x86_64.rpm # Fedora 44 CentOS and RHEL (EL9, EL10) packages are not provided yet. The RPM packages come without the bundled status-line extensions; the .deb ships them. contour-daemon and the GUI package contour conflict, and contour already includes the daemon, so a desktop installation needs nothing more. On Debian and Ubuntu, apt replaces one with the other; on Fedora, dnf install refuses, so swap them with dnf swap contour contour-daemon (or dnf install --allowerasing ). The package installs a systemd user unit but does not enable it. Each user registers and enables their own copy (it then starts with their next login; daemon-service start starts it now): contour daemon-service install See Starting the daemon at login . The packaged service opens no listening port (TCP is opt-in, see Remote access over TCP ); reach it over SSH, see Remote hosts .
docs.title: Contour daemon on a server

docs.text: Ask it to stop, from anywhere: contour daemon stop # asks first when the daemon hosts sessions contour daemon stop --yes # does not ask contour daemon status # is one running? version, uptime, socket, sessions, clients contour daemon logs # the last 100 lines of its log contour daemon logs --follow --lines 20 All of them accept --name and --socket , written before or after the verb. Giving the same option before and after the verb with different values is a usage error, so that stop never silently targets another daemon than the one you named. When no daemon answers, status and stop exit with status 4. stop asks for confirmation only when sessions exist; without a terminal it refuses unless you pass --yes . logs shows the file the daemon reports as its log; if none is running it falls back to the default SOCKET.log beside the socket, and says so. A daemon started from a terminal also stops on SIGINT or SIGTERM — Ctrl + C if it is in the foreground, or kill <pid> . On Windows, a console-control event does the same. A daemon that predates contour daemon stop answers that it does not support it; stop it where it runs, or end its process. For a service-managed daemon, prefer contour daemon-service stop , which lets the service manager know it was stopped on purpose rather than restarting it. Stopping the daemon ends its shells Stopping the daemon ends every shell it hosts. Shutdown is abrupt by design — attached clients see the connection close with no goodbye, exactly as a real tmux kill-server looks to them. A daemon crash is another matter on Linux and macOS: see Surviving a daemon crash . What comes back after a reboot are the workspaces — see Surviving reboots .
docs.title: Stopping a daemon

docs.text: On Linux and macOS, contour daemon runs the daemon behind a small PTY keeper : the process you started becomes the keeper, and the daemon and every shell are its children. The keeper holds each shell's terminal and the daemon's sockets, reads no output, and starts a new daemon when the old one crashes, is killed, or stops answering for 30 seconds ( daemon.keeper.restart_hung ). contour daemon status names the keeper's process id beside the daemon's. What survives a crash: the shells , and every program running in them: nothing is restarted, and they never notice; their output after you reconnect : the window reconnects to the same socket on its own (see When the connection is lost ), and from then on shows what the programs write; each pane's working directory and foreground program name , which the new daemon reads from the shell itself, so a new tab still opens where you were and a tab title still names the running program; the ids : the new daemon is the same instance with the same session, tab and workspace ids, so every window keeps its tabs and panes, and what you type into a pane still reaches the program it showed before the crash. What does not: what the dead daemon had read but not yet shown is lost, and the screen of each pane comes back with the scrollback the last workspace snapshot held rather than as it was; a program redraws its screen, a shell its prompt. Input typed while the daemon was down is dropped. A daemon that crashes again within 30 seconds is restarted after a pause that doubles up to 30 seconds. After five crashes within five minutes the keeper stops restarting it and keeps the shells for two minutes more, then tries once again; if that fails too, it ends the shells and exits with a failure, so that a service manager's own restart limits apply. Stopping the daemon ( contour daemon stop , SIGTERM , SIGINT ) ends the keeper with it, and a keeper that goes away takes its daemon along. These numbers are the defaults of daemon.keeper , in whole seconds but the count: daemon : keeper : give_up_crashes : 5 # this many crashes ... give_up_window : 300 # ... within this many seconds give up backoff_start : 1 # the first pause after a crash soon after another backoff_cap : 30 # the longest pause startup_timeout : 30 # a start silent that long, before serving, is killed as hung stop_timeout : 60 # a stopping daemon that has not ended by then is killed contour daemon reads them as it starts; a running keeper keeps the numbers it started with. An out-of-memory kill under systemd still stops the unit Under the systemd user unit ( contour daemon-service install ), a kernel out-of-memory kill of the daemon still stops the whole unit, keeper and shells included, as before. Keeping the shells through that is planned, and needs a change to the unit and to how the daemon places itself. Windows runs the daemon without a keeper for now, and its shells end with it.
docs.title: Surviving a daemon crash

docs.text: A daemon keeps a snapshot of its workspaces, so that after a reboot, a crash or an upgrade the next daemon brings it back. The shells themselves cannot survive a reboot, nor a stopped daemon (a crashed one is another matter: see Surviving a daemon crash ); what returns is: every workspace, tab and split, with its ratios, the active tab and pane, and a zoomed pane; the names you gave workspaces, tabs and panes, the tab titles, and the tab colours you set; each pane's working directory and profile; the newest lines of each pane's scrollback, under a dim marker row such as ── restored · snapshot of 2026-10-24 09:15 ── , followed by a fresh shell. The snapshot is written every interval seconds while the workspaces change, at once when you close a pane or a tab, and once more as the daemon ends. It is restored when a daemon starts and finds one: after a reboot, a crash, a SIGTERM , an idle exit, or the restart the drift chip offers after an upgrade (see After upgrading Contour ). It is not restored after a plain contour daemon stop , which empties it, and panes and tabs you closed are not brought back. contour daemon stop # ends the shells and discards the workspaces contour daemon stop --keep-snapshot # ends the shells; the next daemon restores the workspaces With no daemon running, contour daemon stop still offers to empty the saved workspaces, so a daemon started later does not bring back what you meant to end. Since a crash may have left those workspaces as all you have, it asks first, unless --yes is given, and without a terminal to ask on it clears nothing and tells you to pass --yes . It exits with status 4 as before, whether it cleared the workspaces or you kept them; with nothing saved it says so and creates no file. A daemon from a release before this feature keeps no workspaces: --keep-snapshot then says so and stops it plainly. A program is never started again by itself. Only one you list in rerun_programs is run once more when its pane was running it, and only when its command line holds nothing a shell would expand. When the saved directory no longer exists, the pane opens in the shell's default directory and the daemon logs it. daemon : restore : scrollback : true # bring the scrollback back scrollback_lines : 1000 # the most lines kept per pane, 0 to 100000 rerun_programs : [] # e.g. [vim, htop]; nothing is re-run unless listed interval : 30 # seconds between writes of changed workspaces, at least 5 scrollback_lines bounds the snapshot only; how much scrollback a session holds while it runs stays daemon.history_limit . The snapshot is <state-dir>/sessions/<name>.snapshot (the state directory is listed under Platform notes ); a daemon started with --name work keeps work.snapshot . A daemon given a socket of its own, by --socket or $CONTOUR_MUX , keeps <name>@<hash>.snapshot instead, the hash naming its socket, so it never restores or overwrites the workspaces of the daemon its name runs; contour daemon stop --socket finds the same file. The file is your user's alone: mode 0600 in a 0700 directory on Linux, macOS and BSD, and a protected ACL granting only your account on Windows. It is replaced atomically and durably: each write is flushed to the disk before it replaces the previous snapshot, and the replacement is flushed in turn, so a daemon crash, a power loss or a kernel crash in the middle of a write leaves either the previous snapshot or the new one, whole. The snapshot may hold secrets Restored scrollback is whatever was on screen: a password echoed by mistake, a token printed by a tool. It is written to disk in the clear. Set scrollback: false to keep only the layout and the directories, or scrollback_lines: 0 for the same. A snapshot that cannot be read is renamed <name>.snapshot.corrupt and the daemon starts with its startup layout, logging why; one written by a newer release is left in place. A restore that brought nothing back is tried once more at the next start, then set aside as <name>.snapshot.failed .
docs.title: Surviving reboots

docs.text: The daemon logs through Contour's category system; contour list-debug-tags prints every tag. The vthost.* categories are the daemon's: Category Default What it records vthost.daemon on Endpoints bound, listeners started, signals, shutdown vthost.conn off Per-connection accept, handshake, disconnect vthost.session off Session spawn, resize, exit vthost.tmux off Control-mode and tmux-binary attach or rejection vthost.client off The client side of the native protocol vthost.trace.proto off One line per protocol message, both directions vthost.trace.tmux off Every control-mode line, both directions contour daemon --log 'vthost.conn,vthost.session' contour daemon --log 'vthost.*' --log-file /var/log/contour-daemon.log Three behaviours to know: * is a plain prefix match, so vthost.* sweeps in the verbose vthost.trace.* tier as well. Name vthost.trace.* to select the trace tier alone. A filter is a selection : it disables the categories it does not name. Real failures are exempt — asking for extra detail never takes error reporting away. --log-file appends and never writes colour escapes, so restarting a daemon against the same file does not erase why the previous run died. Traces report sizes, never payloads: a keystroke message shows a byte count, a screen update a line count, and a token only as present or absent. A trace of a busy session must not become a transcript of what you typed.
docs.title: Diagnostics

docs.text: Contour keeps what outlives a daemon in a per-user state directory , separate from the runtime directory the sockets live in: OS State directory Linux, macOS, BSD $XDG_STATE_HOME/contour when set and absolute, otherwise ~/.local/state/contour Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\contour Without a usable home directory the fallback is <temp>/contour-state-<user> . That directory is shared ground, so a daemon never runs from a copy staged there: it runs in place instead. Daemon mode works on Linux, macOS, BSD and Windows 10 1803 or newer, over Unix domain sockets everywhere. On Windows, sessions are backed by ConPTY, the socket directory is governed by NTFS ACLs rather than POSIX permission bits, and the tmux-binary ( <socket>-tmux ) endpoint is absent — it needs file-descriptor passing, which Windows sockets do not have.
docs.title: Platform notes

docs.text: An upgrade never touches the running daemon. The daemon keeps serving, and the client you start next may be newer than the daemon it attaches to. Where an upgrade would disturb a running binary, the daemon does not run from the installed binary at all. On Windows (the installer replaces contour.exe , and Windows Installer moves the images a running copy holds aside rather than failing), on macOS (swapping the .app breaks the lazy loading of its frameworks) and for an AppImage (its mount vanishes when the AppImage process exits), a daemon runs from a copy of its own release under <state-dir>/bin/<version>-<id>/ . It is made the first time that release starts a daemon, and removed again once no daemon runs from it. What the copy costs A release contour binary is about 474 MB. On Windows the copy is the whole install folder, on macOS the whole .app , and one such copy exists per release that has a daemon running or about to start, until it is unused. Old copies are pruned automatically, never while a daemon runs from them. A packaged Linux install ( /usr/... , Flatpak /app/... ) runs in place, which a package upgrade cannot disturb. contour daemon --in-place opts out of the copy; a package upgrade may then replace the binary under the running daemon. A hand-started foreground contour daemon on Windows also runs from the installed binary.
docs.title: After upgrading Contour

docs.text: A daemon started by hand runs from the folder an installer is about to replace. Windows Installer moves the files a running program holds aside, and that daemon would run on from its old images until it next restarts. So the installer asks the Contour it replaces to move your hand-started daemons first: each one is handed over to a copy of itself under %LOCALAPPDATA%\contour\bin\ , keeping its sessions and their programs, exactly as a live upgrade does. The installer then replaces the files. The same step is available as contour daemon relocate , which says for each daemon where it went ( moved the daemon at <socket> onto <executable> ) and which it left ( left the daemon at <socket>: <reason> ). A daemon that Contour starts for you already runs from such a copy, and needs none of this. What is not moved: A daemon started with --in-place , which asked to stay where it is. A silent install replaces the files under it all the same (Windows Installer moves the images it holds aside), and it keeps running from its old images until it next restarts. What an interactive install does with it has not been verified: Windows may list it in its files-in-use dialog, and what "close" does to its sessions is not known. To be safe, stop such a daemon ( contour daemon stop ) before installing. A daemon of an installation from before this change (0.8 and earlier, and earlier 0.9 development builds), which cannot be asked, and a daemon of another installation. A daemon whose socket is not in the default socket directory ( %TEMP%\contour-<user>\ ), such as one started with a --socket elsewhere. relocate looks only in that directory. Another user's daemon. The installer runs as the user who started it, so a UAC elevation as a different administrator account looks for that administrator's daemons, not yours; yours is left as it is. Any daemon, when a deployment tool installs as the SYSTEM account: SYSTEM has no daemon, so nothing is handed over, the install still succeeds, and your daemon keeps running from the old images until its next restart. Install as yourself to have it moved. Not moving a daemon never fails the install. After a move, the sessions' console host ( OpenConsole.exe ) keeps running from its old image, which Windows Installer moves aside and deletes at the next restart; the new files are in bin\ . The console host of a session cannot be replaced while the session runs. Keeping it elsewhere is not available yet. The installer also closes the running Contour window and opens it again with the arguments it had. That is Windows' Restart Manager, which closes and reopens a running Contour GUI. It does not end daemons: in a silent install it left a daemon, and its console host, running. The two negotiate a protocol version when they connect: each states the range of versions it speaks, and they agree on the newest one both know. Every release speaks the protocols of at least the previous two releases, so a client from a newer release attaches to an older daemon — and an older client to a newer daemon — as long as the two are within that window. Features the older side does not know are simply not used on that connection. When the daemon's release differs from the client's, the window shows a quiet chip, for instance daemon 0.8.1 is older than this client . For a local daemon that supports it, clicking it offers Upgrade daemon (keeps your programs running) ; see Live upgrade below. Otherwise it offers Restart daemon on the new version . The confirmation says what that costs: it ends every shell the daemon hosts , and a fresh one opens on the new daemon. A daemon that keeps its workspaces brings your workspaces, tabs, directories and scrollback back, and the confirmation says so (see Surviving reboots ). After the restart a new Contour window attaches to the new daemon, and this one closes. The chip is shown only for the local daemon: a remote one ( --connect-tcp ) is not yours to restart. The restart stops the daemon for an upgrade, then starts one the same way a client would: through the registered service when there is one, on demand otherwise.
docs.title: Installing a new Contour on Windows

docs.text: The command palette's Upgrade daemon row (the UpgradeDaemon action, which can be bound to a key) starts a live upgrade (described below) at any time, drift chip or not, so a rebuilt binary of the same release can be picked up. It asks nothing, as the upgrade keeps every program running, and a refusal or failure is shown as a notice. A live upgrade replaces the daemon with the new release without ending anything it hosts . On Linux, macOS and the BSDs the daemon re-executes the new release's binary in its own process, so every shell and program keeps its process, its process ID, its parent and its terminal. Windows cannot replace a running process's binary: there the daemon starts the new release beside itself, hands it every session, and ends once the new release has taken over. The daemon's process ID changes; every shell's and program's does not, nor does its console. Each session's screens, scrollback, images, cursor and modes, and an escape sequence cut in half by the switch (up to a bound, below), come across as they were; so do your workspaces, tabs and splits. The windows show Upgrading daemon… for a moment and reconnect by themselves. Start it from the chip, or from a shell or script: contour daemon upgrade [ --name NAME | --socket PATH ] It exits 0 once the new release serves, 4 when no daemon runs, and 5 with the reason on standard error when the daemon declines or the switch fails; the daemon then serves on as before. When the daemon says nothing conclusive within 15 seconds, the outcome is unknown and the exit status is 1; check contour daemon status , whose upgrades line counts the live upgrades the daemon has been through and whose last upgrade line names the last one that failed. What the daemon declines on: The daemon declines when Because it runs in a Flatpak sandbox the sandbox cannot reach the new release's binary; update the Flatpak and use the restart the new release cannot read the state it would hand over, or load its configuration the check runs the new binary first; the restart is the way across a gap wider than two releases a session runs on an SSH or channel connection nothing could adopt it after the switch a program is in the middle of an escape sequence longer than the handover carries, or its sessions' state is too large the handover has a fixed bound a session is still starting, or the new release's image is not in the daemon's store try again in a moment; the next upgrade stages the image anew another upgrade is under way, or the clients and sessions do not settle in time try again in a moment on Windows, a session runs on Windows' own console host rather than the conpty.dll Contour ships only Contour's can be handed to the new daemon; it is missing only where conpty.dll is not beside contour.exe Most of these are checked before anything is stopped. A few show only after the daemon has told its clients it is upgrading and disconnected them: the clients and sessions not settling in time, a session that keeps starting, a program caught in an overlong escape sequence, state too large to hand over, and the new binary failing to start. The daemon then resumes; the windows reconnect to it a moment later, and the chip and contour daemon upgrade (exit 5) name the reason. On Windows the new release that does not say it is ready within 8 seconds is ended, and the old daemon resumes the same way. A refusal never costs a program, and neither does a failure after it: if the new binary cannot start, the old daemon resumes and says so. A few things to know: The chip offers the upgrade only for a daemon on this machine that announced it supports it and is not newer than the client (a newer one is offered the restart, as an upgrade would be a downgrade). A remote daemon ( --connect-tcp , --host ) is not yours to upgrade, and the chip offers nothing for it. It is available on Linux, macOS, the BSDs and Windows. Flatpak: a running sandbox keeps the old /app mounted, so the daemon cannot reach the new release. Update the Flatpak, then restart the daemon from the chip (this ends its shells). The first release that has it can be upgraded from, not to. The readiness check needs code in the old daemon, so a daemon from before live upgrade is restarted once, and every daemon after that is upgraded live. Extensions that a status line runs in the daemon are started again by the new daemon; the programs in your panes are never restarted. The daemon keeps its workspace snapshot current, as always; it is the safety net if everything else fails. Outside the window, or against a daemon from Contour 0.7.0 or another release before version negotiation, the client is refused, and it tells you both sides' versions: the daemon speaks protocol 3, from a release before version negotiation; this client speaks 4-4 A wrong token is reported as such instead ( wrong token or insufficient rights ): the refusal names the daemon's versions either way, so a probe learns nothing more from it. To move past a version refusal, stop the daemon and let it start again: contour daemon stop contour client # starts a matching daemon Remember that this ends the sessions it was hosting. An auto-started daemon rarely has the problem, since it exits 10 seconds after its last session and client are gone.
docs.title: Live upgrade

docs.text: contour client opens a window. There is no terminal-only client at present; if you need one, attach with tmux -C through the compatibility endpoint described above. You get the scrollback the daemon still holds, and no more. Attaching replays a session's history, but the daemon keeps only history.limit lines of it per session — 1000 unless the profile it was started with says otherwise. Lines that scrolled past that are gone, and there is no way to ask for them back. A session sitting on the alternate screen has no scrollback to show. Attach while vim , less or htop is running and you get that program's screen, which never has history of its own; the shell's scrollback appears when the program exits. The daemon keeps one cell size. Images (Sixel, kitty, Contour's own) are laid out on the cell size in pixels the attached client last reported, remembered after it detaches, and on daemon.default_cell_pixel_size until one reports. With a per-pane font zoom, or windows on monitors of different DPI, every pane other than the last-reporting one lays its images out for that pane's cell, so they come out larger or smaller than its own cells would make them. Shells end when the daemon is stopped (see Stopping a daemon ), and on Windows when it crashes; the workspaces come back without them (see Surviving reboots ). On Linux and macOS a crashed daemon is replaced and the shells live on (see Surviving a daemon crash ). ssh attach needs key or agent authentication. Contour never answers an ssh prompt — a password, a key passphrase, a second factor or an unknown host key — so run ssh USER@HOST once in a terminal first (see Remote hosts ). Images are not recoverable through tmux-mode replay (see the note under tmux interoperability ). For the architecture behind all of this — the two protocols, the delta transport, the stable row identity in the grid — see the internals page .
docs.title: Current limitations

docs.text: Quick terminal # A global hotkey slides a terminal down from the top of the screen, from whatever application you are in, and the same hotkey hides it again. It is full width and 40 % of the screen's height, on the screen the pointer is on, in the Minimal chrome density. It is off until you give it a hotkey: open Settings › General › Quick Terminal , press Record and press the chord you want. A chord needs at least one of Control, Alt and Super, and cannot be one the macOS menu bar keeps (such as Command-Q). Delete in the field removes it. The setting # quick_terminal : hotkey : { mods : [ Control ], key : '`' } hide_on_focus_loss : true Key Meaning hotkey The chord, spelled as an input mapping spells its chord. Unset by default. hide_on_focus_loss Hides the quick terminal when another window takes the focus. true by default; with false it stays until the hotkey is pressed again. Changing the hotkey takes effect at once, without a restart. Per platform # macOS: the window is a non-activating panel, so the application you came from stays frontmost and keeps its menu bar while you type into the quick terminal. Windows: the hotkey is registered with the system. Another application that holds the chord makes the registration fail, and Contour says so. Linux: the hotkey goes through the desktop's GlobalShortcuts portal, which may ask you to confirm it. A desktop without that portal has no global hotkeys. Under Wayland a window cannot place itself, so the quick terminal opens where the compositor puts it and fades in. With Reduce Motion on, the quick terminal fades in and out instead of sliding. So does it where another screen is stacked above the one it opens on, since sliding in from above would show it on that screen. The quick terminal never keeps Contour running while it is hidden: closing the last ordinary window leaves the process running only while the quick terminal is on screen, and hiding it then quits. Closing its last tab ends it, and the next press opens a new one. In daemon mode it is a window of this machine alone: its terminals run here and the daemon never hosts, saves or restores them.

docs.text: Releases # 0.9.0 (unreleased) # Contour is now daemon-first: a plain contour shows sessions a daemon hosts, starting it when none runs, so closing the window no longer ends your shells. Reopen Contour, or attach from another machine over ssh or TLS, and they are still there. Set daemon: { mode: in_process } to keep sessions in the window as before. Its window and Settings are redesigned to feel native on macOS, Windows 11 and Linux, with a Terminal style of their own, a command palette, command blocks, split panes with cards and a status line. # Adds kitty graphics Unicode placeholders (virtual placements with U=1 , placeholder cells, the a=q,e=T,U=1 feature query, and d=i/I , d=n/N and d=r/R for them) and image numbers ( I= ), so Claude Code shows its pictures, such as Mermaid diagrams, in Contour, in-process and attached to a daemon alike; until Contour is on Claude Code's list, set CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_TERMINAL_IMAGES=1 Adds kitty graphics file media ( t=f , t=t ) for sessions whose output comes from a local program, under a strict policy: only below the temp directories and images.kitty_file_allow_list (default ~/.claude/plugins/data ), no hidden components or symbolic links, regular files the user owns with a single link; refused over SSH, in tmux panes and for daemon replicas, and switched off with images.kitty_file_transmission: false . A t=t file is deleted once read only when its path carries tty-graphics-protocol , as in kitty. Shared memory ( t=s ) is not supported Adds kitty graphics file media on Windows, at parity with Linux and macOS: below %TMP% , %TEMP% , %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp and the allow-list (default %USERPROFILE%\.claude\plugins\data ), on fixed and RAM disks only; no junctions or symbolic links below a root, no hidden or system entries, alternate data streams, device names or short 8.3 aliases; a file owned by the user (or, elevated, by Administrators) with a single link, opened so nobody writes, renames or deletes it while it is read. A POSIX path from WSL or MSYS is refused, and wsl , plink and Hyper-V's hvc count as relays On Windows, a pane now knows the program running in front of its shell (the command it runs, as Linux reports its process-group leader), so the pane header names it, closing an idle shell no longer asks first, and dropped files are quoted for the program in front Calls what you name a workspace, tab, pane or daemon its name, everywhere: contour rename OBJECT NAME names or (with an empty NAME) clears it, contour daemon --name and the daemon-service verbs name a daemon, --daemon NAME picks one on the control verbs and contour client (a local daemon's name, else a saved host's; name: and host: say which), contour switch --to-name , the SwitchToDaemon / OpenDaemon key name: , a layout tab's name: , the action RenameTab , and in the control API the name fields, object.rename , the event object.renamed (now also for tabs and panes) and the MCP tool object_rename (experimental) Gives a tab one name: Rename… in the tab strip, the sidebar or the palette sets the same name contour rename does, so a tab you renamed by hand is addressable as tab:NAME ; the tab's title stays the one its program or the title template gives it, and a typed name is taken literally, without placeholders Keeps the old spellings working until 0.9.0, each with a deprecation note: --label , contour label , contour workspace rename , switch --to-label , the configuration's label: daemon key and a layout tab's title: , the action SetTabTitle , the MCP tool object_setLabel , and the control API's old spelling ( label , object.setLabel , workspace.rename , workspace.labelChanged ), which a daemon and its clients still speak to an older peer during an upgrade Redesigns the daemon and workspace switcher (experimental) as a popup in the command palette's family, drawn in the window: it shows each workspace's status, branch and last failed command as the sidebar does, also for other daemons; typing finds workspaces on every local daemon; a daemon opens into its own level; New Daemon… checks the name as you type; workspace rows have the sidebar's right-click menu and a new-window button; it opens with Ctrl+Shift+R ( ⇧⌘R on macOS). The workspace chip's dropdown is the same popup, scoped to the window's daemon, with All daemons… to widen it Fixes emoji sequences the system's emoji font is too old to know, such as the Emoji 17.0 skin-tone variants, being drawn as their pieces far into the cells to the right: Contour now bundles Noto Color Emoji and uses it when no system emoji font draws a sequence whole, fits a sequence no font knows into its own cells, and centres an emoji a font composes from several glyphs, such as Segoe UI Emoji's families, as a whole instead of glyph by glyph (#2381) Prevents short commands from flashing the tab and desktop progress bars by delaying running and busy OSC 9;4 progress by 500 ms by default, configurable under Settings → Appearance → Tab bar (#2342) Changes the label option of contour workspace new , contour new and contour split to --name : --daemon picks the daemon on every control verb, and on these --label named both the daemon to reach and the object to make (experimental) Fixes a tab's name from contour rename tab:… NAME not being shown: the sidebar, the tab strip and the switcher now name the tab by it, as they do a workspace by its name, and show its title again once it is cleared (experimental) Fixes the status line at the top ( status_line.position: top ) having the page's first row drawn over it, and a row moving a row down while it was selected Fixes the sidebar's tab rows of a window without a daemon showing "Terminal" instead of the title the shell set, until something else changed Shows a working directory beneath your home as ~/… in the sidebar, as the pane header does, for a directory on this machine only: a path an ssh session or another machine's daemon reports is shown in full Fixes Contour on Windows ending when a terminal is resized just as its program exits Fixes inline images drawn smaller than they were sent, such as the Mermaid diagrams Claude Code renders at twice their size, looking jagged: each pixel now averages the image pixels it covers instead of picking one of them, so text and thin lines in a picture stay smooth, and transparent edges keep their colour Fixes a kitty graphics delete ( a=d ) arriving during a chunked image transmission being taken for the transmission's last chunk: as in kitty, the transmission is now aborted and the delete carried out Fixes the kitty graphics delete a=d,d=A freeing every stored image, even one never placed: as in kitty, it now frees only the images whose placements it removed, so an image transmitted for a later a=p survives it Fixes kitty graphics commands that name no image (neither i= nor I= ) being answered when they fail, which the application, expecting no reply, read as typed input: as in kitty, such a command is never answered Fixes symbols such as U+23BF and U+23F5 , which Claude Code draws its interface with, being drawn as the replacement character on Windows with strict_spacing: true : a character no configured font has is now drawn with the font Windows names for it, even a proportional one Fixes data races when a pane of a daemon session is attached: the connection's thread read which display showed the pane, and which pane the session was, while the window changed them Fixes Contour on Windows failing to save settings, load its configuration or write files with a few tabs open: each tab's fonts held files open until the process reached the C runtime's default limit of 512, which Contour now raises to 8192 (#2405) Fixes Contour on macOS and FreeBSD crashing, or no longer reading a terminal, once a process has more than about a thousand files open, as a daemon hosting a hundred or more sessions does Fixes Contour exiting at start on a Windows system without Cascadia Mono or Consolas: a missing font family now falls back to another monospace font, then to any font, and a system without any usable font is refused with a message instead of a crash Fixes a client attaching to a daemon over stdio, or a local connection, waiting forever on a daemon that never answers: the client gives up with an error after a deadline, and the daemon closes a local connection that sends nothing within 20 seconds (experimental daemon) Adds a keeper process in front of the daemon on Linux and other POSIX systems: it holds every shell's terminal and the listening sockets, so a daemon that crashes or hangs is restarted while your shells keep running, and your tabs and panes come back with them. Configure it under daemon.keeper Adds a configurable terminal type for built-in SSH profiles and falls back to xterm-256color on Windows when no terminal type is set (#2315) Adds installing Contour's terminfo entry on the remote host when a built-in SSH profile connects, so the shell starts with TERM=contour where the remote has tic , and otherwise keeps the terminal type it would have used; turn it off per profile with ssh.install_terminfo: false Adds ssh.connect_timeout , a per-profile limit (30 seconds by default, 0 for none) on how long a built-in SSH connection may take to come up, not counting the time spent waiting for a host key confirmation, passphrase or password; a host that stops answering while the connection comes up now ends it with an error instead of hanging; SSH agent authentication has its own allowance of 2 minutes Restores per-profile environment variables for local shells and built-in SSH sessions, with a Settings editor that shows each variable's name and value (#2315) Adds tab_style ( shape , spacing , material , active_fill , inactive_fill , bar_fill , active_indicator , indicator_color , tab_color_mode , close_button , new_tab_button , tab_width , min_tab_width , max_tab_width ) to restyle the tabs: their shape (the interface style's own, pill, flat, underline or outlined), the gap between them, what the bar is made of (solid, frosted or glass: Mica and Acrylic on Windows, the title bar's own material and Liquid Glass on each tab (macOS 26) on macOS, and KWin's blur on KDE Plasma), the fill of the active tab, the other tabs and the bar itself (whose labels and buttons are inked for it), a line under or over the active one and its colour, whether a tab's own colour is its fill, a tint or that line, when tabs show their close button, whether there is a "+" button, and whether the tabs share the bar equally or fit their titles, within a minimum and maximum width; also on the Tab Bar page in Settings, applied live (#2346) Adds tab_style.preset ( classic , minimal , rounded , glass , outlined ): a named look that sets the tab shape, spacing, material and fills at once; any tab_style key changed from its default still wins; also on the Tab Bar page in Settings (#2346) Animates the tab bar: a new tab fades in, the tabs beside one opened or closed slide over, and the active tab's indicator line slides to the tab made active; nothing slides when the system asks for reduced motion (#2346) Adds what runs in a tab and how its last command ended (exit status and duration, with shell integration) to the tab's hover card, and to the hover card of its row in the sidebar (#2346) Adds the profile setting tab_icon : auto shows the running program's initial in the tab's icon while a program runs, none hides the icon, and a path shows that image (PNG, JPEG, BMP, GIF, ICO or SVG); the square stays visible on a tab filled with its own colour or the accent; unlike other profile keys it is not inherited from the default profile; the sidebar's rows show it too, for the tabs the window holds; also in Settings › Profiles (#2346) Stops a program that only rewrites the host-writable status line (DECSASD), such as a prompt's clock, from marking its tab with unseen output (#2346) Fixes a sidebar row that appeared while the rows around it moved being left half transparent (#2346) Fixes dragging a tab within its own tab bar offering a drop slot where the tab already is, and past the end of the bar when it is the last tab: neither moves it, so neither is offered (#2346) Changes the Windows tab strip, under the native2026 defaults, to draw the line between two inactive tabs twice as strongly and no longer beside the active tab; configurations on the classic defaults keep the previous line (#2346) Fixes tab_bar_visibility never and multiple having no effect on Windows: the title bar now shows the window's title in place of the hidden tabs (#2346) Fixes built-in SSH profiles ignoring keystrokes after a successful login when the connection is idle (#2286) Fixes connecting to a daemon on a busy machine waiting past its connect timeout before reporting that it timed out, and reporting a connection that came up at the last moment as timed out Fixes memory corruption and crashes that program output could cause: a kitty graphics image whose declared size overflows (#2294), a character printed in insert mode right of the right margin (#2295), ICH and DECIC under origin mode with a left margin (#2296), DECCRA copying from a page of another size after a resize (#2297) and DECRQCRA for a rectangle whose corners are reversed (#2298) Fixes a ReGIS macrograph that invokes itself several times freezing the terminal (#2299) Fixes the bundled status-line extensions failing to start when built with Rust 1.100 or newer Fixes contour client occasionally crashing on Linux at startup when attaching with --connect-tcp or --host Fixes a status-line extension whose initialization never finishes hanging instead of being stopped by its load time limit, and one that calls the host while it initializes failing to start. An extension exporting another function the WebAssembly runtime would run by itself while loading it ( __post_instantiate , __wasm_call_ctors ), where no time limit applies, is refused (#2330) Fixes PNG images sent over the kitty graphics protocol ( f=100 ) not being shown: they are now decoded when they arrive (#2303) Fixes PNG images (kitty graphics f=100 , the Good Image Protocol, iTerm2 inline images) being refused in sessions hosted by a contour daemon built without the GUI, such as the contour-daemon package for servers: PNG is now decoded with libpng, a new build dependency, in every build alike; other image formats still need the GUI build Fixes control sequence numbers being taken modulo their storage size: CSI 260 h no longer sets insert mode and CSI 258 h no longer locks the keyboard (#2305), and OSC 65588 is no longer read as OSC 52 (#2304) Fixes tab stops: clearing one no longer shifts the default stops a column to the left, setting one keeps the default stops, clearing all leaves none (also in the DECTABSR report), a stop set twice is cleared at once, HT finds its stop under origin mode, and CBT from a tab stop goes to the previous one. The default stops now also reach columns the window gains later (#2309) Fixes XTPUSHCOLORS without a parameter overwriting the top of the palette stack instead of pushing, which lost the outer palette of a nested push and pop (#2310) Fixes the Good Image Protocol leaving the cursor on the image's first row when a render names a source rectangle (#2313), and ignoring the last header of a message that ends in ; , such as a release by name (#2314) Fixes built-in SSH: a host key accepted on a port other than 22 is now stored for that port only, as OpenSSH stores it, where it was trusted on every port of the host (#2306), and a long connection message can no longer be written past the read buffer (#2302) Fixes Contour terminating when closing a file descriptor fails, for instance when a signal interrupts it (#2307) Fixes tmux control mode: a layout with zero, negative or oversized pane sizes is refused instead of crashing (#2300), and send-keys sends text after -- that spells one of its own options (#2312) Fixes a daemon's client accepting screen updates whose row numbers overflow (#2308) Fixes "switch to previous tab" choosing the wrong tab after a tab was moved into another window's tab strip (#2311) Fixes a new window, from launching Contour again, contour client or New Window ( ⌘N , Ctrl+Shift+N ), showing a workspace another window already shows: it now shows the workspace no window shows that a window left most recently, so closing a window by mistake and opening a new one brings it back, or a new one. A window that loses its connection keeps its workspace for as long as it may reconnect, and one closed on purpose frees it at once Fixes Enter on a row of the workspace sidebar keeping the keyboard in the sidebar: the terminal of the row's tab or pane now takes it, as after a click Fixes a window forgetting which tab and pane were active in a workspace once it switched to another workspace and back: it now returns to the tab and pane it left Fixes the workspace chip, the switcher ( Ctrl+Shift+R ), switching by number and cycling workspaces doing nothing in a window whose sessions run in-process ( daemon: { mode: in_process } ): they now switch between that window's workspaces Fixes Contour crashing on exit when the window's sessions live in a daemon, which on macOS also started the system crash reporter beside the next launch Fixes Contour crashing when a terminal is resized just as its shell exits, for example when a window opens onto a shell that exits at once Fixes dialogs whose default button is Cancel, No or Deny drawing Trust, Yes or Allow as the default: the button Enter takes is now the highlighted one, and a destructive button that is not the default, such as Close when closing a tab, is labelled in red. Every line entering the page is now resized to the page width Fixes an application that opens a DECSET 2026 synchronized update and then stalls or dies before closing it freezing the display — not a slow frame, no frames at all. Rendering now resumes once a block has outlived 150 ms, with the mode register untouched so DECRQM still reports what the application set; on notcurses-demo the frame rate more than doubles, from 13.6 to 29.7 fps Fixes a column change — eight or nine of which Contour negotiates at startup, and one per column step of a window drag — costing time proportional to the configured history.limit rather than to what the scrollback actually holds. Reflow is now skipped where nothing is wrapped, and the remaining work walks only the rows in use, taking startup column work from 34.58 ms to 0.02 ms Fixes the scrollback being scrambled whenever the history limit changed, which happens on every profile apply and config reload. Such an exit reaches the session from two directions — its exit watcher, and the display finding the device already closed — and only the paths below the notice were guarded against being run twice (#2102) Configuration, packaging and build # Changes the build to take the coroutine, networking and generic utility code from a verbatim copy of core-cpp, the library shared by the Contour Terminal projects, in vendor/core-cpp. It brings no new dependency, and with CONTOUR_USE_CPM=OFF it fetches nothing Changes the minimum libunicode version to 0.9.5, whose decoder and SIMD text scan accept well-formed UTF-8 only, and whose SIMD text scan no longer reads every block of text four times over and stops in front of ill-formed UTF-8, and whose grapheme check pays for flag bookkeeping only on flag letters Fixes configuration reloads: saving contour.yml with live_config, or ReloadConfig, reloaded one session only, and new tabs kept the old settings; a reload left a profile's changed colors, the status line's position and indicator, folding's auto_collapse_on_new_command and on_jump_into_fold, and the osc_context limits as they were; a full reset afterwards brought back the previous terminal_id's operating level, initial status line and cursor; and after ResetConfig no later reload read the user's file until Contour restarted Fixes status_line.sync_to_window_title and highlight_word_and_matches_on_double_click having no effect, and contour client starting every new daemon tab with the profile it had read at attach, even after a reload Fixes one configuration value of the wrong shape (a word where a section belongs, a list where a single value belongs) silently dropping everything read after it — other profiles, layouts and key bindings — or resetting its whole profile or color scheme. Now only that entry keeps its default, and the error log names it by its path, line and column, such as profiles.main.cursor. A color palette written as a list now loads Fixes a value of the wrong type inside contour.yml's renderer or folding section, such as enabled: maybe under folding, dropping everything read after it — profiles, layouts and key bindings. In settings.yml it dropped the renderer overrides read after it, the GPU choice among them. Now only that value keeps its default, and the error log names it by its key path, such as folding.enabled Fixes a configuration value holding an unterminated ${ loading with the text before it doubled: ab${x read as abab${x Fixes contour generate … to FILE writing Windows line endings on Windows, which broke a bash script in Git Bash, and printing nothing and exiting successfully when the file could not be written Fixes the build on Linux with Clang and libc++, which selected the broken . The guard excluded it by platform — Apple and FreeBSD — but the header belongs to libc++, not to those systems, so any libc++ build reached it; it is now excluded by _LIBCPP_VERSION instead (#2087) 0.7.0 (2026-08-17) # Contour 0.7.0 makes the window a workspace: native GUI tabs in the title bar, split panes, saved layouts, and an optional terminal-styled UI that draws the application's own chrome on the character grid. It adds an experimental daemon mode for sessions that outlive the window showing them, accessibility support across the terminal and its chrome, the kitty graphics, text-sizing and clipboard protocols, ReGIS vector graphics, and a large round of VT conformance work. Tabs, splits and layouts # Adds first-class GUI tabs presented in a custom window title bar, replacing the status-line tab list (the {Tabs} status-line directive remains supported for existing configs) Adds split panes — split the active pane vertically (Ctrl+Shift+E) or horizontally (Ctrl+Shift+O), close a pane (Ctrl+Shift+X), and move pane focus with Alt+Shift+Arrow Adds pane management actions: swap the active pane with a neighbor (Ctrl+Alt+Arrow), resize it (Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Arrow), flip a split's orientation (Ctrl+Shift+Backslash), and move a pane to a new position in the split tree (unbound by default) Adds pane zoom (TogglePaneZoom, Ctrl+Shift+Z): gives the active pane the whole tab area, hiding its siblings, and toggles back to the tiled layout. Moving pane focus while zoomed keeps the zoom and shows the newly focused pane; splitting, closing or rearranging panes returns to the tiled view. A zoomed tab is titled after the pane on screen and wears a Z badge Adds dragging tabs: reorder a tab within its strip, drag it into another window, or tear it out into a new window, with a live drop-position indicator showing where it will land; the running terminal survives the move (within the same process) Adds renaming a tab by double-clicking it, and a color-swatch picker in its context menu. The picker is keyboard-driven — the cursor keys and the vim motions h/j/k/l walk the swatches, Enter or Space picks the highlighted one, Escape dismisses — and opens on the color the tab already wears Adds the actions SetTabColor and ResetTabColor, so coloring a tab is no longer mouse-only: both appear in the command palette, and either can be bound in input_mapping. SetTabColor opens the tab's color picker, or applies a color outright when given one (for example { mods: [Shift,Control], key: 'R', action: SetTabColor, color: '#ff0000' } ) Adds configurable layouts: named sets of tabs with per-tab command, working directory, name, color, profile, and split panes; open at startup via default_layout, via --layout NAME , or the LaunchLayout action. SaveLayout writes the current window's tabs back into layouts.yml, prompting for a name when none was given — and is reachable from the command palette, so saving a layout needs no keybinding Adds the dim_unfocused profile option: dims a pane while it is not the focused one (an inactive pane of a split, or any pane of an unfocused window) by blending it toward its background color; 0.0 (default) disables dimming Adds the top-level options tab_bar_position (Top/Bottom) and tab_bar_visibility (Always/Never/Multiple), to place the GUI tab bar at the top or bottom of the window and to hide it entirely or show it only when more than one tab is open BREAKING: tab_bar_position and tab_bar_visibility belong to the top level of contour.yml, not to a profile — a window shows one tab bar whichever profiles its tabs run. If you tried them in a 0.7.0 prerelease, move these two keys out of your profiles: block; a profile-scoped copy is no longer read Adds Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+Shift+Tab and Ctrl+PageDown / Ctrl+PageUp as tab-switching shortcuts. They reach existing configurations too, and binding them yourself still wins. Note that Ctrl+Tab is now taken from applications that request it through the Kitty keyboard protocol Adds switching tabs with a horizontal mouse wheel tilt or a two-finger trackpad swipe, over the tab strip or the terminal, configurable via the new global tab_switch_on_horizontal_wheel option (default on); an application that requested mouse reporting keeps the horizontal wheel, and the bypass modifier (Shift) switches tabs even then. Also fixes a sideways swipe over the tab bar doing nothing at all on a trackpad Fixes the tab bar placement and visibility settings appearing to do nothing until Contour was restarted Window and desktop integration # Changes the window to use a custom client-side-decorated title bar (tab strip plus window controls) by default on all platforms; set show_title_bar: true to use the native server-side window decoration instead, in which case the tab strip is kept but its window controls defer to the OS frame Adds window_control_style, deciding how the window's minimize/maximize/close buttons are drawn and which side of the tab bar they sit on — until now always Windows-shaped and always on the right, which on macOS is the wrong corner. The default auto follows the host: macOS gets real traffic lights on the left, KDE Plasma gets Breeze's circular hover fills, everything else keeps today's buttons. Set windows , macos or plasma to pin one. Changing it from the settings page applies to every open window at once, without a restart Fixes the window losing its drop shadow on KDE Plasma. Contour's window is frameless by default so its own tab bar can be the title bar, and a frameless window gets no decoration from the system — which is what draws the shadow. The window now publishes a shadow of its own to KWin, on both X11 and Wayland, sized and shaped like Breeze's so it matches the rest of the desktop; window_shadow sets it to None , Small , Medium , Large or VeryLarge . Only KWin can act on this, so on other compositors and window managers it has no effect Fixes the same loss on Windows and macOS, where it also cost the window its rounded corners. Neither goes frameless any more: on Windows the frame is kept and made invisible, so the system draws the shadow and the rounded corners while the tab bar still covers the whole window; on macOS the window stays a normal one whose content simply extends into the title bar, so the shadow, the rounded corners, full-screen, window tabbing and double-click-to-zoom all keep working. On macOS the system's own traffic lights are now used instead of Contour's drawn copies Fixes background blur never turning off again on X11 once it had been switched on, and fixes the window border being drawn dark on Windows regardless of the theme setting Fixes multi-monitor handling: the window no longer re-pins itself to the widest screen on every frame, refresh-rate/DPI tracking follows the window's actual screen after a monitor move, and new windows open on the spawning window's screen Changes a display-scale change (moving to a monitor with a different scale, a late Wayland fractional-scale arrival) to preserve the terminal's columns and lines with a single corrective window resize Changes font zoom to keep the window and pane size fixed and adjust the terminal's columns and lines (and the child PTY size) instead of resizing the window Fixes window resize oscillation/flicker: the terminal no longer fights the window manager by resizing its own window from resize events; the grid floors to the given size (sub-cell remainder renders as padding) while X11/macOS keep WM-side cell snapping via size hints Fixes window spawn flicker: the window is sized from the real font metrics before it is first shown and opens directly in the profile's window state, instead of appearing at a default size and jumping Fixes window sizing on tiling Wayland compositors: a freshly-spawned terminal was mis-sized until a manual resize (#1955), and the window snapped back to the configured terminal_size after a screen or scale change (#1941) Fixes programmatic window resizes (CSI 8 t) shrinking the window by the title-bar height on every call, and CSI 4 t resizing the grid without the window; in split windows both now solve the pane layout so the requesting pane receives its exact grid Fixes the KDE forced-font-DPI override being read from the X11 key in Wayland sessions (now honors forceFontDPIWayland) and no longer re-reads the setting file on every frame Fixes the window padding being computed against the wrong scale when a forced font DPI is configured (KDE's "Force font DPI"), which fitted the grid to a width the window did not have and left the terminal's own idea of where the grid starts disagreeing with where it was drawn Command palette, settings and menus # Adds a command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P): a searchable popup listing every command with its documentation and key binding, making actions that have no binding reachable at all. Recently used commands are pinned on top and remembered across restarts; command_palette_recent_count sets how many (0 disables) Adds a GUI settings page for changing the configuration. Settings are grouped into collapsible sections with a search box over them, and the indicator status line is built visually — a preview of the finished line, one chip per placeholder, and a style sheet exposing every attribute a template can carry, with the raw template still editable as text Adds a right-click context menu to the terminal: copy, paste, select all, the hyperlink under the cursor, opening the current folder, splitting and closing panes, switching profile, and a soft or hard terminal reset. It opens exactly when a selection drag would have worked, so an application that asked for the mouse (vim, tmux) still receives its right-click; hold Shift to open the menu anyway. Bind OpenContextMenu in input_mapping to move it to another button Adds a window menu on right-clicking the empty part of the title bar or tab bar: open a tab (optionally under a named profile), close the current tab or all of them, and switch the tab bar between always visible, auto-hide and hidden Adds ui_style: terminal , which draws the application's own chrome — the tab bar and title bar, and the controls within menus, popups and the settings page — as fixed-size character cells in the terminal font, with square corners and box-drawing separators, so the window reads as one continuous TUI. Tabs keep every affordance they have today: drag to reorder, tear off into a new window, rename, close, context menu and color picker. It is the recommended way to get the terminal look now that a window can hold split panes, where the indicator status line's {Tabs} item draws one tab list per pane instead of one per window. Colors keep following the OS palette and the theme setting; optionally set ui_font_family and ui_font_size , or leave them unset to inherit the default profile's font. Takes effect on the next start Adds a drop shadow to menus, context menus and popups, so they read as floating above the terminal rather than pasted onto it. Under ui_style: terminal it is a hard-edged offset shadow that stays on the character grid Hyperlinks, file paths and hint mode # Adds a tooltip naming an OSC 8 hyperlink's target when it is hovered, so it can be read before it is followed. A local file:// target is shown as a plain path. Turn it off with hyperlink_hover_tooltip: false Adds Ctrl-click support for opening detected local filesystem paths under the mouse cursor (#1947) Fixes an OSC 8 file:// hyperlink failing to open when the application spelled the host name in full: programs build such a link from gethostname(2) , which reports the fully-qualified name on some machines and the short one on others, and Contour accepted only the short form — every other spelling was taken for another machine's file and handed to the desktop as a network location. The short name, the fully-qualified name, localhost and no host at all are now all recognized as this machine, whatever their case, and the host is stripped before the file is opened. A link to a file that carries no host now opens in your $EDITOR like any other, instead of being sent to the desktop Adds a scope parameter to the HintMode action: scope: Scrollback scans the scrollback history as well as the visible page, capped by the new hint_scrollback_lines profile option (default 1000). Its labels are assigned once and stay put, so you can activate hint mode, scroll to older output, and then type the label you see; scope: Visible remains the default Fixes hint mode missing any URL or path that the terminal broke across two rows because the window was too narrow: patterns are now matched against the whole logical line, so such a match is one hint whose highlight follows it across the line break and which yields the complete text rather than the fragment on one row Accessibility # Adds accessibility support: the terminal caret is reported to the operating system, so screen magnifiers (Windows Magnifier, KDE Plasma zoom) and screen readers can follow it; with OSC 133 shell integration the live shell prompt is additionally exposed as its own focusable region Adds a description of the window chrome for screen readers: the tab bar reads as a tab list whose tabs announce themselves as they are switched, the window and tab buttons say what they do instead of naming their glyph, and every settings field carries its own label Adds screen-reader announcements for the bell, desktop notifications and read-only mode, which have no other way to be noticed. Turn them off with accessibility_announcements: false Adds reading the selected text aloud through the operating system's speech synthesizer, from the context menu or with Ctrl+Shift+S. Needs Qt's TextToSpeech module and an installed voice; where either is missing the feature is simply not offered Daemon mode and remote sessions # EXPERIMENTAL: Contour gains a daemon mode. contour daemon hosts shell sessions in a background process so they survive the window showing them, and contour client connects to it as a full Contour window whose tabs mirror the daemon's sessions live — images, hyperlinks and sized text included — starting a daemon on demand if none is running. The daemon speaks tmux's control-mode protocol in both directions, so tmux-aware tooling and the stock tmux binary can attach to it, and contour client --tmux attaches Contour to a real tmux server. A daemon can also be reached over the network with --listen-tcp HOST:PORT , always TLS-encrypted and requiring a preshared token. Works on Linux, macOS and Windows (10 1803+). Built in by default, but experimental: its command-line flags and wire protocol may still change between releases Keyboard and mouse input # Adds Win32 Input Mode (DEC private mode 9001) for native ConPTY keyboard input encoding, fixing keyboard input for applications that request this mode on Windows Adds WheelLeft and WheelRight as bindable mouse buttons in input_mapping Smooths mouse-wheel scrolling: a wheel notch now glides to rest with inertia instead of jumping whole lines, giving the mouse wheel the same smooth feel as a touchpad. Active whenever smooth_scrolling is enabled Fixes mouse-wheel scrolling in alternate-screen pagers such as less, most and man: a wheel notch now scrolls them out of the box (via alternate-scroll, emitting cursor-key presses) even when the pager has not enabled a mouse protocol, matching the behavior of other terminals; DECSET ?1007 works accordingly (#1951) Fixes input_mapping rejecting Ctrl as a modifier name — the very spelling Contour shows in its own menus and command palette — so a binding written with it was silently discarded; Control and Ctrl are now interchangeable, Hyper is bindable at last, and the same names work in bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier and mouse_block_selection_modifier Fixes a single-character key binding only firing when its letter was written in the same case the keyboard happened to report, which left key: 'q' parsing cleanly and then never firing; on macOS this also revived five built-in Ctrl+Alt shortcuts that were dead unless CapsLock was on Fixes an input_mapping entry that fails to parse vanishing without a word — Contour now reports which entry was dropped and which of its fields was at fault Fixes cursor, navigation and function keys sending a bogus modifier parameter while CapsLock or NumLock is active (for example UpArrow emitting ESC[1;65A instead of ESC[A), which broke arrow keys and F-keys in most applications, and fixes XTerm modifyOtherKeys mode 2 reporting plain keys as modified in the same situation, so applications enabling that mode (such as vim) received ESC[27;65;97~ instead of a plain a (#1954) Fixes Vi mode being unusable while CapsLock or NumLock is active: arrows, Home, End, PageUp and PageDown now move the cursor, the search prompt accepts typed characters again, Escape leaves visual mode, and a [count] prefix is parsed. Also fixes DECUDK user-defined keys being suppressed, hint-mode label characters leaking into the running application, and numpad digits never working as a Vi [count] prefix (#1954) Fixes macOS reporting where a key sits on the keyboard where the Kitty keyboard protocol asks which character that key types, so fifteen keys reached the application as an entirely different key — in any program speaking that protocol, fish among them. Ctrl+U arrived as Ctrl+Space, which fish does not bind, so it inserted a space instead of clearing the line; Ctrl+I, Ctrl+P, Ctrl+L, Ctrl+J, Ctrl+K, Ctrl+N, Ctrl+M and the bracket, semicolon, backslash, comma, period, slash and backtick keys were mistranslated the same way. The character is now taken from the keyboard layout that is actually active, so it is also right on a layout other than US ANSI Fixes xterm's CSI > Pp ; Pv m (XTMODKEYS) being read with its resource number in place of its value, so an application asking for modifyOtherKeys level 2 selected level 4 and got nothing. Adds the matching CSI > Ps n for turning a resource back off Fixes the Vi search prompt treating a Meta-modified key as if it were unmodified, so that for example Meta+Backspace deleted a character instead of being ignored Fixes leaving Vi visual mode with Escape also sending that Escape on to the running application Fixes the input-method (IME) candidate window opening at the wrong position: the reported cursor rectangle now honors the configured window margin and the pane's position inside a split, and widens over double-width (CJK) characters Rendering, fonts and Unicode # Improves Unicode width measurement: a grapheme cluster is measured as a whole, so ZWJ sequences, skin-tone modifiers and Indic conjuncts occupy the columns they actually need instead of being sized from their first codepoint. Following terminal-unicode-core, VS16 promotes a cluster to the emoji presentation and may widen it to two columns, while VS15 selects the text presentation without changing the width — a cluster already on screen is never narrowed. Cluster measurement is on by default and can be turned off with DEC mode 2027, which returns width measurement to the classic per-codepoint wcwidth() model Improves font fallback: a character no font in the chain covers is now resolved by asking which installed font actually covers it, rather than giving up at the end of the chain Prefers a monospaced font when falling back, rather than taking whichever font in the chain happens to come first; a proportional font is still used where no monospaced one has the character, so nothing that renders today stops rendering. The strict_spacing setting now genuinely refuses non-monospaced fallbacks, which it previously did not (#1939) Fixes text falling back to the wrong font, and being drawn a cell too far to the left, whenever a run contained a single character the primary font was missing. A prompt such as Claude Code's, where an ornament and a non-breaking space precede the first word, had that whole first word re-shaped in a fallback font. Only the characters the primary font genuinely lacks now fall back, and a glyph can no longer advance the cursor by zero cells (#1939) Fixes a font's weight: and slant: being silently ignored unless spelled exactly one way. The names are now matched without regard to case or separator, so bold , Bold , extra_bold , extra bold and ExtraBold all work — including the CamelCase spellings that contour generate config itself writes, which previously did not load back. The alternate names each weight is also known by ( regular , ultralight , semilight , semibold , ultrabold , ultrablack ) are accepted too, and a value that still cannot be read is now reported instead of quietly leaving the default in place Deprecates slant: thin . It never named a slant — it reached the table as a copy of the weight list — and continues to mean normal , now with a warning Fixes the terminal reporting a bold-italic font to the application (OSC 50) as merely italic, dropping the weight from the pattern Fixes curly underlines being drawn almost as tall as a lowercase letter and running into the text above them on fonts that declare line spacing, such as the default "monospace" on many Linux systems (#1754), and fixes the other underline styles sitting one row too high, on the baseline itself — the upper stroke of a double underline could be drawn inside the letters, a dotted underline came out as dashes or vanished entirely, and a double underline's strokes were a pixel too thin at even thicknesses Fixes combining marks vanishing from uniformly styled lines: a character written in decomposed form, such as a Greek or Cyrillic letter followed by a combining accent, was drawn as its base letter alone, because the batched rendering path those lines take can only carry one codepoint per column Fixes selecting text changing how wide a glyph is drawn, so that emoji and other multi-codepoint characters no longer gain padding and push the rest of the line to the right when highlighted (#1752) Fixes a tall glyph — a Nerd Font icon, a powerline separator — overwriting a neighbouring glyph in the texture atlas, and no longer shifts such a glyph sideways off its own bearing Fixes characters rendering as other characters, or shrunken and unreadable, on a pane whose size has changed a lot: the glyph cache was built once for the original size, so a window maximized from small, or a pane given most of the tab, could need more slots than it held and glyphs began overwriting each other mid-frame. The cache is now resized along with the page, and splitting no longer builds each pane's cache at the wrong size only to rebuild it immediately (#2040) Fixes a pane rendering blank or partially after a font, font-size or DPI change that reached it while it was not on screen — minimized, occluded, or on another tab. The pane kept shaping text with fonts it had already discarded, and the frame was dropped instead of drawn Fixes the status line and non-displayed pages being drawn against whichever screen was current rather than the one being rendered, which took the cursor row and the cursor colour from the wrong page Fixes searching for text outside Latin-1: a needle such as "Привет" or an emoji drove the case handling through functions that are undefined for those codepoints, which could silently mismatch or abort the terminal. Case is now folded per the Unicode character database, so "smart case" and case-insensitive search work for non-Latin scripts as well Fixes Unicode characters sometimes being wrongly decoded during high-bandwidth output Images and graphics # Adds the kitty graphics protocol (APC G): transmitting, displaying, placing and deleting images, in PNG or raw RGB/RGBA, including chunked transmission Adds the iTerm2 OSC 1337 extensions: the capabilities report and inline images Adds ReGIS vector graphics (DCS p), DEC's VT330/VT340 graphics language: lines, circles, arcs, interpolated curves, filled polygons, shading, text, colour registers with HLS/RGB specs, position reports, the interactive locator, and macrographs. ReGIS is now advertised in the primary Device Attributes (feature 3) and answered by XTSMGRAPHICS EXPERIMENTAL: Adds the Good Image Protocol (GIP) — a DCS-based protocol for displaying raster images with named image pools, LRU eviction, three compositing layers (below/replace/above), configurable resize and alignment policies, Auto/PNG/RGB/RGBA format support with automatic format detection, and DA1 capability advertisement via code 90. The limit now follows the image canvas, so a larger screen makes full use of the range it can display, and a stated image height can no longer overshoot that canvas Shell integration # Adds OSC 133 prompt marks (A, C and D) to the bundled shell integration, so Contour can tell a prompt apart from a command's output. performance and startup # Fixes Contour taking minutes to open on a desktop whose notification daemon is installed but not running — the case when dunst is disabled, for instance. Each terminal session asked the desktop about notifications synchronously as it was created, and with nothing there to answer, every one of them waited out D-Bus's 25-second reply timeout before any window could appear; a window with several tabs paid it once per tab. Desktop notifications are now sent without ever waiting for a reply, so an absent or wedged notification daemon costs nothing at startup, and can no longer freeze the terminal for the same 25 seconds when a program raises a notification or rings the bell. A notification daemon that starts after Contour did is now picked up too Fixes multi-second shell startup stall when the shell (e.g. fish) queries terminal capabilities before the display is attached — queued replies are now flushed on display attach instead of waiting for the next focus/input event Fixes a hang and a crash on startup when probing the audio device, for profiles that cannot ring an audible bell Improves PTY throughput performance determinism by rewriting the internal grid cell storage Fixes crashes and heap corruption when rapidly changing the font or window size, caused by data races between the UI thread and the Qt Scene Graph render thread; geometry/font changes are now deferred and applied on the render thread (#1922, probably #1712, #408) Fixes Contour aborting when a pane was closed or a tab switched while a frame was being drawn: closing a split pane could take the whole window down, because the drawing thread was reading the session the closing pane had just given up. A tab switch could likewise draw one frame out of two different terminals Fixes a crash when closing a tab, window or split pane, in the moment between the shell exiting and the session being destroyed: the thread watching for that exit was asked to stop but never waited for, and destroying it while it still ran aborted the application Fixes a crash on Windows when opening a new tab, window or split pane while the shell could not be started there — most visibly from a WSL or SSH session, or with a shell such as nushell. Such a spawn now retries in Contour's own directory before falling back to the login shell, and if it still cannot start, the reason is shown in the pane and the pane closes on a key press, rather than taking the whole application down Fixes a crash on Windows when opening a new tab or split from a pane that had reported its working directory over OSC 7 — a remote directory from an SSH session that does not exist locally, or the raw file:// URL handed to CreateProcess() instead of the extracted path. A working directory is now only inherited when it exists on the local machine Fixes a crash, and a possible window freeze, under heavy output on Wayland: the input method's cursor-position queries were answered from the render thread without locking the grid, racing a concurrent resize or reflow Fixes a crash when entering Vi normal mode (Ctrl+Shift+Space) while an application was producing output, most reliably a remote tmux session over SSH. Showing the indicator status line resizes the page, and that reflowed the grid without locking it against the thread writing into it. The same lock was missing from the scroll, selection, search and paste actions Fixes Contour aborting when an application's font request (OSC 50) was approved after the pane it came from had gone away, or after the window had briefly lost its drawing surface — leaving the dialog open across a pane close, a tab switch or a screen change was enough. The approved font is now remembered as that session's own, so it also survives a configuration reload or a tab rebind instead of silently reverting to the profile's font Fixes the built-in SSH client corrupting its own connection when a key was pressed or the window resized during heavy output, which ended the session with "Decrypt failed" or "Out of boundary" and then filled the log with write errors. The connection is no longer driven from two threads at once, and a failed write ends the session instead of being retried forever. Opening two SSH sessions at the same moment also no longer races the SSH library's one-time initialization Fixes an error being logged on every normal shell exit: a pseudo-terminal master reports its
