Adds Vi-like input modes for improved selection and copy'n'paste experience. Adds contour executable to search path for spawned shell process on macOS and Windows. Adds customizability to dim colors (#664). Adds the profile configuration option: draw_bold_text_with_bright_colors . Fixes CSI K accidentally removing line flags, e.g. line marks (#658). Fixes wrong-spacing rendering bug on some lines. Fixes assertion on font resize when a (Sixel) image is currently being rendered (#642). Fixes assertion on too quick shell terminations (#647). Fixes fallback shell execution on UNIX-like systems when the requested shell cannot be spawned (#647). Fixes selection being wrongly rendered when viewport is scrolled (#641). Fixes full-line selection not properly injecting linefeeds between the lines. Changes behavior of full-line selection to include a trailing linefeed for the last line (#641). Changes behavior of bold text to by rendered using normal colors by default (was forced to bright before, and is now configurable via draw_bold_text_with_bright_colors ).

TLDR; Many thanks to all for the great support and feedback. This release marks a huge milestone for me especially with regards to VT backend performance(!), improved rendering architecture, and a more complete list of pixel perfect box drawings. Fixes installation from .deb (missing terminfo dependency) Fixes PTY write race condition. Fixes VT sequence DECFI . Fixes VT sequence ICH (#559). Fixes VT sequence OSC 4 's response. Fixes VT sequence OESC 4 to also support setting color via #RRGGBB . Fixes VT sequence extension: capture buffer (#493). Fixes DECRC with respect to DECSTBM enabled and DECOM being inverted interpreted. Fixes XTGETTCAP (#582). Fixes SU in combination with DECLRM (#593). Fixes an assertion in text renderer. Fixes wrongly advertising DEC locator mode (it is not supported). Improved VT backend performance (#342). Improved text selection behavior. Improved detection of runtime DPI changes for KDE (Plasma) desktop environment. Improves Window manipulation VT sequence for saving/restoring window title ( CSI 22 ; Ps t , CSI 23 ; Ps t ) Adds pixel-perfect box-drawing for U+EE00 .. U+EE05 for progress bar glyphs as first introduced by Fira Code (#521). Adds pixel-perfect box-drawing for U+E0B0, U+E0B2, U+E0BA (Triangle Powerline glyphs). Adds new configuration option renderer.tile_hashtable_slots to configure texture atlas hashtable capacity. Adds new configuration option renderer.tile_cache_count to configure texture atlas cache capacity. Adds new configuration option renderer.tile_direct_mapping to enable/disalbe texture atlas direct mapping. Adds new colorscheme setting background_image.path and background_image.opacity to optionally render a terminal background image. Adds stdout-fastpipe support on new shell file descriptor 3 and exposing availability via environment variable STDOUT_FASTPIPE (with value 3 ). When writing to this file descriptor rather than to stdout (file descriptor 1 ), the full performance of Contour can be explored. Adds new configuration option pty_buffer_size for tweaking the new size in bytes for the PTY buffer objects. Adds mock font locator (mostly interesting for advanced use for CI testing). Important: It is recommended to also use the latest contour termcap file if you are already using one from a previous release. Changes contour exit code to reflect the shell's exit code of the last closed window. Improves text cursor rendering and extends cursor configuration accordingly (#526). Adds support for font feature settings. This is currently only implemented for openshaper , not yet for dwrite (#520). Fixes input mapping containing Control modifier. Fixes input mapping mode Select being ignored. Fixes Modifier+Enter input mapping not being caught. Fixes slant detection for DirectWrite. Changes DECCOLM to only switch back to 80 when it was 132 before. Adds new config option spawn_new_process to define new terminal window behavior. Adds action CancelSelection to allow actively canceling selection via input mappings. Adds contour license CLI command to show project license but also an overview of all dependencies. Adds a proper CLI to bench-headless . Building the headless benchmark tool is not shipped by default.

If this option is false, it cannot be enabled programmatically either. Remote hosts # A Contour window can show the sessions of a daemon running on another machine : your home PC from the office, a build server, a workstation under your desk. The sessions keep running there; the window here is a client of that daemon, exactly as it is of a local one (see Persistent sessions ). There are two ways to reach a remote daemon: Transport What it needs Authentication ssh ( ssh:// ) An OpenSSH client here, Contour on the remote machine. Nothing listens on the network besides sshd. ssh's own: keys or an agent. TLS ( tls:// ) A daemon on the remote machine started with --listen-tcp . A token, over TLS. If you can already ssh to the machine, use ssh: it needs no open port, no token and no certificate. Saved hosts # Hosts you attach to often are saved in the configuration under hosts: , by name ( reference ): hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc" studio : url : "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297" token_file : "~/.config/contour/studio.token" tls_ca : "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem" Hosts can also be added in Settings › Hosts , without editing the file: each one is written to hosts/<name>.yml beside contour.yml , with the same keys as an entry of hosts: . Its page shows the SSH or TLS fields its address calls for, says under a field what would keep the host from loading, and saves nothing until it is fixed; Attach opens a window attached to it. Hosts written in contour.yml are listed there too, read-only, with Duplicate to Edit . Then attach in any of these ways: "Attach to Host" in the command palette lists the saved hosts; pick one. The same list is in the terminal's context menu and the title-bar menu . From a shell: contour client --host home # a saved host, by name contour client --host ssh://me@homepc:2222 # an ssh URL that is not saved An ad-hoc tls:// URL works the same way. The first time, a daemon without a CA is pinned after you trust its fingerprint in a dialog ; --daemon-fingerprint SHA256:… settles it beforehand. Attaching to a host works like launching Contour against that daemon: the window selects the first workspace of the daemon that no window shows, or a new one (see shown and hidden workspaces ). Attaching from a second machine never mirrors what a window shows already. To look at one particular workspace, name it: contour client --host home --workspace 018f3c2a # only that workspace of home Naming a workspace asks the daemon for its list first. If the daemon is met for the first time, the dialog that asks whether to trust its fingerprint appears once the window is up, and the list is asked once you have answered; declining ends the launch. A window can also move to another host, or back to a local daemon, without closing: see Switching a window . A window attached to a remote host says so in its chrome, so it is never mistaken for a local one: its title reads home — <session title> , and the tab strip starts with the host's name. Choosing where a window lives: the Connect picker # The Connect picker is one question before a window opens: where do its sessions live? It lists This computer : Persistent sessions , the local daemon, with its state ( running · 3 sessions , or not running · starts on connect ), and This window only , with no daemon: its shells end when the window closes ( daemon.mode: in_process ); Saved hosts : each host of hosts: , tagged SSH or TLS; and, while you type an ssh:// or tls:// address in the field, a leading Connect to ADDRESS row for it. The address is not saved. Open it from File › New Window to… ( Ctrl + Shift + K , ⇧⌘K on macOS; the NewWindowTo action), from contour connect with no target, from the launchers below, or at every plain start, with Ask every time Contour starts ( connect_picker_on_start , also in Settings › General). A launch with command-line arguments never shows it. The field has the focus. Type to filter by name or address; ↑ and ↓ move, Return connects and Esc cancels, which quits when no other window is open. Every row shows a key, Alt + 1 to 9 ( ⌘1 to ⌘9 on macOS), that connects to it at once; plain digits stay typable, for addresses and ports. Filtering renumbers the rows, so star then Alt + 1 reaches a host named starfive . Ctrl + L ( ⌘L ) puts the caret back in the field. The selection starts on the target you used last, which Contour remembers in gui-state.yml , not in contour.yml . A host that cannot be reached stays in the picker: the reason is shown under its row, in the words Attach to Host uses (an unknown host key, an authentication failure, Contour missing on the host, an unreachable host), with Retry and Edit Host… , which opens Settings › Hosts on it. Manage Hosts… opens Settings › Hosts. contour connect # contour connect # the picker contour connect daemon # this computer's daemon; daemon:NAME for another one contour connect local # this window only, no daemon contour connect starfive # a saved host, by name contour connect ssh://me@pi4.lan # an ssh:// or tls:// address contour connect --list [ --json ] # the targets the picker would show A target opens the window as contour client does ( --daemon , --host ), or contour terminal --daemon-mode in_process for local ; no target shows the picker. --config FILE names the configuration that holds the hosts. --list prints each target, as contour connect reads it, with its detail, or a JSON array with --json . An ad-hoc tls:// address is refused, as for contour client --host : a TLS host needs its token file, so save it first. From the launchers # Linux : the desktop entry has a Connect… action ( contour connect ) beside Open a New Window , and org.contourterminal.Contour.Connect.desktop is a launcher of its own, "Contour — Connect…", for menus that show no actions. macOS : the Dock menu has New Window to… and each saved host. Windows : the jump list has the task Connect… and one per saved host, and the installer adds a Contour (Connect…) Start menu shortcut. Over SSH # Contour runs, for every attach and every reconnect: ssh -T -o ConnectTimeout = 10 -o ServerAliveInterval = 15 -o ServerAliveCountMax = 3 \ [ -p PORT ] -- [ USER@ ] HOST contour daemon --stdio with SSH_ASKPASS set to Contour itself, so that anything ssh needs to ask you is asked in a dialog of the window you attach from. On the remote side, contour daemon --stdio reaches your daemon there — starting it if none runs, the same way a local contour client does — and relays the session between it and ssh. Requirements # An OpenSSH client on this machine ( ssh on PATH ). On Windows, the built-in OpenSSH client ("OpenSSH Client" optional feature) works. Contour on the remote machine , findable by a non-interactive login — which often has a shorter PATH than your interactive shell. Check with: ssh me@homepc contour version If that says command not found , give the full path in the saved host: hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc" remote_command : "/opt/contour/bin/contour daemon --stdio" OpenSSH 8.4 or newer , which is what lets ssh hand its questions to Contour. Every login method OpenSSH has then works: a key or the agent, a password, a key's passphrase, a second factor (keyboard-interactive), a security key's touch, and the first-time host-key question. Each one appears as a dialog in the window that started the attach (the first attach of contour client --host , which runs before its window opens, asks in a small window of its own); a password or passphrase is typed into a masked field, and a host key's fingerprint is shown exactly as ssh words it, with No as the default answer. Nothing you type is stored by Contour. Cancelling a dialog ends the attempt as "Cancelled". Windows 10's built-in OpenSSH is older than that (8.1): install the current Win32-OpenSSH release, or keep to a key without a passphrase, which also works there. Your ~/.ssh/config applies as usual: host aliases, User , Port , ProxyJump and IdentityFile all work, so url: "ssh://homepc" can rely on what that file says about homepc . When it does not connect # Contour reads what ssh reports and says what to do. The messages, and the fix for each: Message (abridged) Cause Fix The host key of ssh://me@homepc was not accepted: … You answered No to the host-key question, or dismissed it. Attach again, compare the fingerprint with the one the machine's owner gives you, and answer Yes only if it matches. ssh could not log in to ssh://me@homepc: … The login was refused: a wrong password, or no key, passphrase or second factor ssh accepted. ssh's own words follow. Attach again and answer the dialog; for a key login, check ssh-add -l and that the key is in the remote authorized_keys . The ssh login to ssh://me@homepc was cancelled. You dismissed a dialog of the login: the password, a question, a security key's notice. Attach again and answer it. ssh could not log in to ssh://me@homepc without a prompt … Contour can only ask for passwords with OpenSSH 8.4 or newer (found …) The ssh on this machine is older than 8.4, so Contour cannot answer its prompts and ssh runs in batch mode: only a key or the agent can log in. Upgrade OpenSSH (on Windows, install the current Win32-OpenSSH release), or load a key into the agent ( ssh-add ). The host key of ssh://me@homepc has changed … The remote machine's key differs from the one in ~/.ssh/known_hosts : a reinstalled machine, or someone in between. If you expected it, remove the old key with ssh-keygen -R homepc , attach again, and answer the host-key question. If you did not, do not connect. ssh could not reach ssh://me@homepc: … The name does not resolve, nothing answers on the port, or there is no route. ssh's own words follow. Check the name, the port and the network (VPN, Tailscale). Contour retries this on its own while a window waits. Contour was not found on ssh://me@homepc by a non-interactive ssh login … contour is not installed there, or not on the non-interactive PATH . Install it, or set remote_command: to its full path (see above). Contour on ssh://me@homepc is too old for ssh attach … The remote Contour has no contour daemon --stdio . Upgrade Contour on the remote machine. ssh://me@homepc: daemon did not start within 5 seconds. (or another reason) The remote relay ran, but could not reach or start the daemon there. Run ssh me@homepc contour daemon --stdio in a terminal and read what it says; check the daemon's log on that machine. ssh://me@homepc printed more than 64 KiB before Contour answered … A login script on the remote machine prints output on non-interactive logins. Make .bashrc / profile scripts quiet when not interactive (e.g. wrap output in [[ $- == *i* ]] && … ). A short banner is skipped; only a long one fails. ssh to ssh://me@homepc ended before Contour answered (exit code N): … ssh ended for a reason Contour does not recognize. Run ssh me@homepc contour daemon --stdio in a terminal to see the whole output. Contour retries this one too. ssh://me@homepc did not answer within 30 seconds The connection hangs (a firewall that drops packets, a stuck login). As for "could not reach". ssh was not found on PATH; install the OpenSSH client No ssh client on this machine. Install OpenSSH. A connection that drops mid-session — the laptop sleeps, the Wi-Fi changes — is reconnected with a fresh ssh, while the window shows that it is reconnecting. A reconnect always goes on, in the background: a host that logs in with a key or the agent needs nobody. If the login asks you something again (a password that is not in the agent) and the window that attached is not on screen -- minimised or hidden -- the question waits instead of being put to a window nobody sees, and the window says "Reconnecting needs your attention"; it is shown once the window is. Contour never raises or focuses a window by itself for this. A failure that retrying cannot fix (a refused login, a host key, a missing Contour) ends the attempt with its message instead of repeating it. Over TLS # The daemon on the remote machine listens on a TCP port itself. Every connection is TLS 1.3-encrypted with the daemon's own identity, a key and certificate it makes on first start and keeps, and clients sign in with an SSH key you authorize, as for ssh itself, or with a token. Keys: authorized_keys # On the remote machine, list the public keys that may log in in authorized_keys in Contour's configuration directory, in OpenSSH's format ( ssh-ed25519 , ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and their sk- variants; grants="LIST" is the only option read, and narrows what the key may do, as an access file does for a token), and start the daemon for keys alone. A line with any other option ( from= , no-pty , command= , ...) is skipped whole , with its number and the reason in the daemon's log, so lines copied from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys may need their options removed to work here: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.config/contour/authorized_keys contour daemon --background --listen-tcp 192 .0.2.10:7297 --auth keys --auth keys takes no token and refuses --token , --token-file and --access-file ; the default, --auth any , accepts a token as well. --authorized-keys FILE names another file. On the machine you sit at, save the host with nothing but its address: hosts : studio : url : "tls://studio.example.net:7297" The client signs the daemon's challenge with a key of your SSH agent, bound to this very TLS connection so that nobody in between can pass it on. To use one key file instead, name it: hosts : studio : url : "tls://studio.example.net:7297" identity_file : "~/.ssh/id_ed25519_studio" A key with a passphrase that is not in the agent is asked for when it is used, in a dialog of the window. Contour itself waits for your answer as long as the dialog is open, but the daemon gives a connection 20 seconds from when it connects to sign in: answer within that, or the daemon closes the connection and the passphrase is asked for again on a new one. Better, load the key into the agent first with ssh-add , which is what to recommend for any key that has a passphrase. The contour control commands cannot ask for a passphrase at all: load such a key with ssh-add . The first contact: pinning the daemon # Without a CA to check its certificate against, a daemon is trusted on first use, as ssh trusts a new host. The first time Contour meets a daemon it shows the daemon's address and its fingerprint, SHA256: and a base64 text, and asks whether to trust it. In a window that is a dialog, whose Cancel is the default, with the fingerprint selectable. For the contour control commands it is a question on the terminal, Trust this daemon? [y/N] , asked only when both standard input and standard error are a terminal (a console, on Windows); anything but y or yes declines. contour client --workspace asks in the dialog, once its window is up. Compare the fingerprint with what contour daemon status prints on that machine, which is also in its log, and trust it only when they are the same. The fingerprint is then kept in known_daemons , in Contour's configuration directory ( ~/.config/contour , %LOCALAPPDATA%\contour on Windows) beside contour.yml , one line per HOST:PORT (an IPv6 address in brackets, [::1]:7297 ). A known_daemons that cannot be read refuses every daemon until it is repaired or removed: a pin that cannot be checked is never taken for no pin. Where nobody can be asked (a script, or a command whose input is not a terminal), pass the fingerprint beforehand: --daemon-fingerprint SHA256:... pins it on first contact and refuses a daemon that presents any other. A daemon that presents another certificate than the pinned one is refused , with both fingerprints, and never asked about: that is a reinstalled daemon, or someone in between, and only you can tell which. After a reinstallation, forget the old pin and meet the daemon again: contour daemon forget-pin studio.example.net:7297 A certificate of your own: tls_ca # Pinning needs no certificate authority. To have the client verify the daemon the way a browser does instead, give the daemon a certificate issued by a CA of your own, for the name you connect to, and name that CA on the client: # Once, anywhere: a CA of your own. openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -days 3650 \ -subj "/CN=My Contour CA" -keyout ca.key -out ca.pem # For the remote machine: a certificate for the name the client connects to. openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes \ -subj "/CN=studio.example.net" -keyout daemon.key -out daemon.csr printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:studio.example.net\n' > daemon.ext openssl x509 -req -in daemon.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -days 825 \ -extfile daemon.ext -out daemon.pem Start the daemon with --tls-cert daemon.pem --tls-key daemon.key , copy ca.pem (never ca.key ) to the client, and add tls_ca: "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem" to the saved host. The certificate must name the host in the url : one merely signed by the CA, for another name, is refused. A daemon verified by tls_ca is never asked about, and the control commands accept it like any other. A token # A host with token_file signs in with a token instead of a key, and a daemon started with --token-file accepts one: umask 077 && openssl rand -base64 32 > ~/.config/contour/daemon.token contour daemon --background --listen-tcp 192 .0.2.10:7297 --token-file ~/.config/contour/daemon.token hosts : studio : url : "tls://studio.example.net:7297" token_file : "~/.config/contour/studio.token" Copy the token file to the machine you sit at (for example with scp ), keeping it private ( chmod 600 ). The daemon is pinned on first use here as well, and the token is sent only to a daemon that was trusted. Reaching a home PC from the office with Tailscale # Tailscale puts your machines on a private network (a tailnet ) wherever they are, without opening ports on your router. Contour does not bundle Tailscale or talk to it; it simply connects to an address on the tailnet like any other. Install Tailscale on both machines from https://tailscale.com/download and log in to the same tailnet on each. Find the home PC's tailnet address — on the home PC: tailscale ip -4 # e.g. 100.101.102.103 With MagicDNS on (the default), the machine is also reachable as <machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net , e.g. homepc.tail1234.ts.net ; the admin console shows the exact name. The simplest way is ssh over the tailnet. If the home PC runs sshd, nothing else is needed: hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc.tail1234.ts.net" Or listen with TLS on the tailnet address only — on the home PC: umask 077 && openssl rand -base64 32 > ~/.config/contour/daemon.token contour daemon --background --listen-tcp 100 .101.102.103:7297 \ --token-file ~/.config/contour/daemon.token Binding to the 100.x.y.z address, not to 0.0.0.0 , keeps the port off every other network the PC is on. contour daemon-service install does not record --listen-tcp , so start this listener yourself (or from your login scripts). Then, at the office, with the token file copied over: hosts : home : url : "tls://homepc.tail1234.ts.net:7297" token_file : "~/.config/contour/home.token" Tailscale already encrypts and authenticates the traffic between your machines, which is what makes unverified TLS a reasonable choice here. For the control commands, or for defense in depth, add tls_ca as above , with the certificate issued for homepc.tail1234.ts.net . Attach : "Attach to Host" → home , or contour client --host home . Foreign paths # The sessions of a remote host run on that machine, so the directories and files they report — the current directory a shell announces (OSC 7), a command block's working directory, a link to a file — are that machine's paths. A window attached to a remote host shows them, but never opens them here: it does not open such a file, start a program in such a directory, or offer "open folder" for it, since on this machine the path names nothing, or something else.
docs.title: remote hosts

docs.text: A Contour window can show the sessions of a daemon running on another machine : your home PC from the office, a build server, a workstation under your desk. The sessions keep running there; the window here is a client of that daemon, exactly as it is of a local one (see Persistent sessions ). There are two ways to reach a remote daemon: Transport What it needs Authentication ssh ( ssh:// ) An OpenSSH client here, Contour on the remote machine. Nothing listens on the network besides sshd. ssh's own: keys or an agent. TLS ( tls:// ) A daemon on the remote machine started with --listen-tcp . A token, over TLS. If you can already ssh to the machine, use ssh: it needs no open port, no token and no certificate.
docs.title: Remote hosts

docs.text: Hosts you attach to often are saved in the configuration under hosts: , by name ( reference ): hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc" studio : url : "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297" token_file : "~/.config/contour/studio.token" tls_ca : "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem" Hosts can also be added in Settings › Hosts , without editing the file: each one is written to hosts/<name>.yml beside contour.yml , with the same keys as an entry of hosts: . Its page shows the SSH or TLS fields its address calls for, says under a field what would keep the host from loading, and saves nothing until it is fixed; Attach opens a window attached to it. Hosts written in contour.yml are listed there too, read-only, with Duplicate to Edit . Then attach in any of these ways: "Attach to Host" in the command palette lists the saved hosts; pick one. The same list is in the terminal's context menu and the title-bar menu . From a shell: contour client --host home # a saved host, by name contour client --host ssh://me@homepc:2222 # an ssh URL that is not saved An ad-hoc tls:// URL works the same way. The first time, a daemon without a CA is pinned after you trust its fingerprint in a dialog ; --daemon-fingerprint SHA256:… settles it beforehand. Attaching to a host works like launching Contour against that daemon: the window selects the first workspace of the daemon that no window shows, or a new one (see shown and hidden workspaces ). Attaching from a second machine never mirrors what a window shows already. To look at one particular workspace, name it: contour client --host home --workspace 018f3c2a # only that workspace of home Naming a workspace asks the daemon for its list first. If the daemon is met for the first time, the dialog that asks whether to trust its fingerprint appears once the window is up, and the list is asked once you have answered; declining ends the launch. A window can also move to another host, or back to a local daemon, without closing: see Switching a window . A window attached to a remote host says so in its chrome, so it is never mistaken for a local one: its title reads home — <session title> , and the tab strip starts with the host's name.
docs.title: Saved hosts

docs.text: The Connect picker is one question before a window opens: where do its sessions live? It lists This computer : Persistent sessions , the local daemon, with its state ( running · 3 sessions , or not running · starts on connect ), and This window only , with no daemon: its shells end when the window closes ( daemon.mode: in_process ); Saved hosts : each host of hosts: , tagged SSH or TLS; and, while you type an ssh:// or tls:// address in the field, a leading Connect to ADDRESS row for it. The address is not saved. Open it from File › New Window to… ( Ctrl + Shift + K , ⇧⌘K on macOS; the NewWindowTo action), from contour connect with no target, from the launchers below, or at every plain start, with Ask every time Contour starts ( connect_picker_on_start , also in Settings › General). A launch with command-line arguments never shows it. The field has the focus. Type to filter by name or address; ↑ and ↓ move, Return connects and Esc cancels, which quits when no other window is open. Every row shows a key, Alt + 1 to 9 ( ⌘1 to ⌘9 on macOS), that connects to it at once; plain digits stay typable, for addresses and ports. Filtering renumbers the rows, so star then Alt + 1 reaches a host named starfive . Ctrl + L ( ⌘L ) puts the caret back in the field. The selection starts on the target you used last, which Contour remembers in gui-state.yml , not in contour.yml . A host that cannot be reached stays in the picker: the reason is shown under its row, in the words Attach to Host uses (an unknown host key, an authentication failure, Contour missing on the host, an unreachable host), with Retry and Edit Host… , which opens Settings › Hosts on it. Manage Hosts… opens Settings › Hosts.
docs.title: Choosing where a window lives: the Connect picker

docs.text: contour connect # the picker contour connect daemon # this computer's daemon; daemon:NAME for another one contour connect local # this window only, no daemon contour connect starfive # a saved host, by name contour connect ssh://me@pi4.lan # an ssh:// or tls:// address contour connect --list [ --json ] # the targets the picker would show A target opens the window as contour client does ( --daemon , --host ), or contour terminal --daemon-mode in_process for local ; no target shows the picker. --config FILE names the configuration that holds the hosts. --list prints each target, as contour connect reads it, with its detail, or a JSON array with --json . An ad-hoc tls:// address is refused, as for contour client --host : a TLS host needs its token file, so save it first.
docs.title: contour connect

docs.text: Linux : the desktop entry has a Connect… action ( contour connect ) beside Open a New Window , and org.contourterminal.Contour.Connect.desktop is a launcher of its own, "Contour — Connect…", for menus that show no actions. macOS : the Dock menu has New Window to… and each saved host. Windows : the jump list has the task Connect… and one per saved host, and the installer adds a Contour (Connect…) Start menu shortcut.
docs.title: From the launchers

docs.text: Contour runs, for every attach and every reconnect: ssh -T -o ConnectTimeout = 10 -o ServerAliveInterval = 15 -o ServerAliveCountMax = 3 \ [ -p PORT ] -- [ USER@ ] HOST contour daemon --stdio with SSH_ASKPASS set to Contour itself, so that anything ssh needs to ask you is asked in a dialog of the window you attach from. On the remote side, contour daemon --stdio reaches your daemon there — starting it if none runs, the same way a local contour client does — and relays the session between it and ssh.
docs.title: Over SSH

docs.text: An OpenSSH client on this machine ( ssh on PATH ). On Windows, the built-in OpenSSH client ("OpenSSH Client" optional feature) works. Contour on the remote machine , findable by a non-interactive login — which often has a shorter PATH than your interactive shell. Check with: ssh me@homepc contour version If that says command not found , give the full path in the saved host: hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc" remote_command : "/opt/contour/bin/contour daemon --stdio" OpenSSH 8.4 or newer , which is what lets ssh hand its questions to Contour. Every login method OpenSSH has then works: a key or the agent, a password, a key's passphrase, a second factor (keyboard-interactive), a security key's touch, and the first-time host-key question. Each one appears as a dialog in the window that started the attach (the first attach of contour client --host , which runs before its window opens, asks in a small window of its own); a password or passphrase is typed into a masked field, and a host key's fingerprint is shown exactly as ssh words it, with No as the default answer. Nothing you type is stored by Contour. Cancelling a dialog ends the attempt as "Cancelled". Windows 10's built-in OpenSSH is older than that (8.1): install the current Win32-OpenSSH release, or keep to a key without a passphrase, which also works there. Your ~/.ssh/config applies as usual: host aliases, User , Port , ProxyJump and IdentityFile all work, so url: "ssh://homepc" can rely on what that file says about homepc .
docs.title: Requirements

docs.text: Contour reads what ssh reports and says what to do. The messages, and the fix for each: Message (abridged) Cause Fix The host key of ssh://me@homepc was not accepted: … You answered No to the host-key question, or dismissed it. Attach again, compare the fingerprint with the one the machine's owner gives you, and answer Yes only if it matches. ssh could not log in to ssh://me@homepc: … The login was refused: a wrong password, or no key, passphrase or second factor ssh accepted. ssh's own words follow. Attach again and answer the dialog; for a key login, check ssh-add -l and that the key is in the remote authorized_keys . The ssh login to ssh://me@homepc was cancelled. You dismissed a dialog of the login: the password, a question, a security key's notice. Attach again and answer it. ssh could not log in to ssh://me@homepc without a prompt … Contour can only ask for passwords with OpenSSH 8.4 or newer (found …) The ssh on this machine is older than 8.4, so Contour cannot answer its prompts and ssh runs in batch mode: only a key or the agent can log in. Upgrade OpenSSH (on Windows, install the current Win32-OpenSSH release), or load a key into the agent ( ssh-add ). The host key of ssh://me@homepc has changed … The remote machine's key differs from the one in ~/.ssh/known_hosts : a reinstalled machine, or someone in between. If you expected it, remove the old key with ssh-keygen -R homepc , attach again, and answer the host-key question. If you did not, do not connect. ssh could not reach ssh://me@homepc: … The name does not resolve, nothing answers on the port, or there is no route. ssh's own words follow. Check the name, the port and the network (VPN, Tailscale). Contour retries this on its own while a window waits. Contour was not found on ssh://me@homepc by a non-interactive ssh login … contour is not installed there, or not on the non-interactive PATH . Install it, or set remote_command: to its full path (see above). Contour on ssh://me@homepc is too old for ssh attach … The remote Contour has no contour daemon --stdio . Upgrade Contour on the remote machine. ssh://me@homepc: daemon did not start within 5 seconds. (or another reason) The remote relay ran, but could not reach or start the daemon there. Run ssh me@homepc contour daemon --stdio in a terminal and read what it says; check the daemon's log on that machine. ssh://me@homepc printed more than 64 KiB before Contour answered … A login script on the remote machine prints output on non-interactive logins. Make .bashrc / profile scripts quiet when not interactive (e.g. wrap output in [[ $- == *i* ]] && … ). A short banner is skipped; only a long one fails. ssh to ssh://me@homepc ended before Contour answered (exit code N): … ssh ended for a reason Contour does not recognize. Run ssh me@homepc contour daemon --stdio in a terminal to see the whole output. Contour retries this one too. ssh://me@homepc did not answer within 30 seconds The connection hangs (a firewall that drops packets, a stuck login). As for "could not reach". ssh was not found on PATH; install the OpenSSH client No ssh client on this machine. Install OpenSSH. A connection that drops mid-session — the laptop sleeps, the Wi-Fi changes — is reconnected with a fresh ssh, while the window shows that it is reconnecting. A reconnect always goes on, in the background: a host that logs in with a key or the agent needs nobody. If the login asks you something again (a password that is not in the agent) and the window that attached is not on screen -- minimised or hidden -- the question waits instead of being put to a window nobody sees, and the window says "Reconnecting needs your attention"; it is shown once the window is. Contour never raises or focuses a window by itself for this. A failure that retrying cannot fix (a refused login, a host key, a missing Contour) ends the attempt with its message instead of repeating it.
docs.title: When it does not connect

docs.text: The daemon on the remote machine listens on a TCP port itself. Every connection is TLS 1.3-encrypted with the daemon's own identity, a key and certificate it makes on first start and keeps, and clients sign in with an SSH key you authorize, as for ssh itself, or with a token.

docs.text: On the remote machine, list the public keys that may log in in authorized_keys in Contour's configuration directory, in OpenSSH's format ( ssh-ed25519 , ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and their sk- variants; grants="LIST" is the only option read, and narrows what the key may do, as an access file does for a token), and start the daemon for keys alone. A line with any other option ( from= , no-pty , command= , ...) is skipped whole , with its number and the reason in the daemon's log, so lines copied from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys may need their options removed to work here: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.config/contour/authorized_keys contour daemon --background --listen-tcp 192 .0.2.10:7297 --auth keys --auth keys takes no token and refuses --token , --token-file and --access-file ; the default, --auth any , accepts a token as well. --authorized-keys FILE names another file. docs.text: Secure input # While a program in a pane hides what you type, as sudo and ssh do when they ask for a password, Contour shows a lock for that pane. On macOS it also turns on Secure Keyboard Entry for as long as that pane has focus, which keeps other applications from reading your keystrokes. The setting # secure_input : auto Value Meaning auto Lock and, on macOS, Secure Keyboard Entry while a pane asks for hidden input. off Never. false and no read as off . A new configuration ( defaults_edition: native2026 ) uses auto ; the Classic edition keeps off . Reloading the configuration applies the change at once: turning it off releases Secure Keyboard Entry immediately. What counts as a password prompt # A pane is locked when its terminal has echo off and canonical (line) mode on : the state sudo , readpassphrase(3) , ssh and read -s put it in. A program that clears echo for its own screen, such as an editor, htop , less or the line editor of your shell, also turns canonical mode off, so it shows no lock. Ghostty reads the same two flags ( password_input in its termio/Exec.zig ); xterm has no automatic detection and only a manual Secure Keyboard menu entry. What it cannot see # Contour looks at the terminal's flags and nothing else, so it misses a password reader that clears both echo and canonical mode. Those readers show no lock and turn nothing on: sudo with pwfeedback , and sudo-rs with its feedback option pinentry-curses sudo and similar asked over ssh , where the prompt runs on another machine's terminal panes whose program runs on a host Contour cannot read flags from (an SSH pane, a Windows ConPTY pane) For these, the lock is simply absent: a lock means the program hides the typing, and no lock means only that Contour could not tell. How quickly it notices # Contour re-reads the flags when output reaches the pane, before each key and paste is sent, and on focus. For two seconds after the pane's last output or key it also checks every 100 ms while the pane has focus, then stops: an idle pane wakes nothing. A program that turns echo off only after more than two quiet seconds is noticed at the first key you type. That key has already reached the system by then, so Secure Keyboard Entry protects the keys after it, not that one. The opposite case leans safe: a program that turns echo back on silently, more than two seconds after the last key or output, leaves the lock and Secure Keyboard Entry on until the next key or output. Panes hosted by a daemon report the same state over the native protocol, so the lock works under daemon.mode: auto as well. Where the lock shows # Wherever something showing the pane is on screen: in the pane's header, on its tab, in a chip in the title band, and, when none of those is on screen, in a small pill over the pane's blank cells at the top right. The pill avoids the prompt and yields to the link pill and the find bar; if a full-screen program leaves no blank place, it covers a few cells rather than disappear. The words beside the lock read Secure input on only for the pane the system's Secure Keyboard Entry protects: on macOS, the focused pane of the front application. Every other locked pane (an unfocused split, a background tab) and every other platform read Input hidden , which says only that the terminal hides what you type. Screen readers announce the same words.
docs.title: secure input

docs.text: While a program in a pane hides what you type, as sudo and ssh do when they ask for a password, Contour shows a lock for that pane. On macOS it also turns on Secure Keyboard Entry for as long as that pane has focus, which keeps other applications from reading your keystrokes.
docs.title: Secure input

docs.text: secure_input : auto Value Meaning auto Lock and, on macOS, Secure Keyboard Entry while a pane asks for hidden input. off Never. false and no read as off . A new configuration ( defaults_edition: native2026 ) uses auto ; the Classic edition keeps off . Reloading the configuration applies the change at once: turning it off releases Secure Keyboard Entry immediately.
docs.title: The setting

docs.text: A pane is locked when its terminal has echo off and canonical (line) mode on : the state sudo , readpassphrase(3) , ssh and read -s put it in. A program that clears echo for its own screen, such as an editor, htop , less or the line editor of your shell, also turns canonical mode off, so it shows no lock. Ghostty reads the same two flags ( password_input in its termio/Exec.zig ); xterm has no automatic detection and only a manual Secure Keyboard menu entry.
docs.title: What counts as a password prompt

docs.text: Contour looks at the terminal's flags and nothing else, so it misses a password reader that clears both echo and canonical mode. Those readers show no lock and turn nothing on: sudo with pwfeedback , and sudo-rs with its feedback option pinentry-curses sudo and similar asked over ssh , where the prompt runs on another machine's terminal panes whose program runs on a host Contour cannot read flags from (an SSH pane, a Windows ConPTY pane) For these, the lock is simply absent: a lock means the program hides the typing, and no lock means only that Contour could not tell.
docs.title: What it cannot see

docs.text: Contour re-reads the flags when output reaches the pane, before each key and paste is sent, and on focus. For two seconds after the pane's last output or key it also checks every 100 ms while the pane has focus, then stops: an idle pane wakes nothing. A program that turns echo off only after more than two quiet seconds is noticed at the first key you type. That key has already reached the system by then, so Secure Keyboard Entry protects the keys after it, not that one. The opposite case leans safe: a program that turns echo back on silently, more than two seconds after the last key or output, leaves the lock and Secure Keyboard Entry on until the next key or output. Panes hosted by a daemon report the same state over the native protocol, so the lock works under daemon.mode: auto as well.
docs.title: How quickly it notices

docs.text: Wherever something showing the pane is on screen: in the pane's header, on its tab, in a chip in the title band, and, when none of those is on screen, in a small pill over the pane's blank cells at the top right. The pill avoids the prompt and yields to the link pill and the find bar; if a full-screen program leaves no blank place, it covers a few cells rather than disappear. The words beside the lock read Secure input on only for the pane the system's Secure Keyboard Entry protects: on macOS, the focused pane of the front application. Every other locked pane (an unfocused split, a background tab) and every other platform read Input hidden , which says only that the terminal hides what you type. Screen readers announce the same words.
docs.title: Where the lock shows

docs.text: The workspace sidebar # The sidebar is a list down the left edge of a window. It shows every workspace of the daemon the window is attached to (or the window's own workspaces, when sessions run in-process) as a tree: a workspace , the tabs in it, and the panes of a tab that is split. It is also an inbox: it tells you which program is waiting for you, which finished while you were looking elsewhere, and takes you there with one key. Note The sidebar is part of the native2026 defaults. A new configuration shows it; a configuration written before the redesign ( defaults_edition: classic ) keeps its tab strip and hides it. See Defaults . What a row shows # A workspace row is one line. A tab or pane row is always two lines tall, so the list never jumps as a program starts or stops talking: a status glyph, a title and a time on the right, and beneath them a second line. The second line is the reason when the program has something to say, and otherwise the idle line : the folder the pane is in and the program running there, such as ~/src/billing · claude , either one left out when it is not known. Row Title Right-hand side Second line Workspace Its name, or the folder or repository it was started in The git branch with ↑ commits ahead and ↓ behind its upstream, such as feat/billing ↑2 ↓1 , then the status glyph of its most urgent pane None Tab Its name, or the title its program or the title template gives it Time in the current state What the program in it says it is doing; otherwise its folder and program Pane Shown only for a tab with more than one pane The same The same A tab's rows list in the order of the tab strip, and follow it when a tab is moved there. Status and reason. The status comes from agent hooks (see contour agent setup ), from a blocked program, from OSC 133 shell integration (a command that finished, with its exit code) and from the bell. The reason is that program's own words ( waiting for approval ), or how the command ended ( exit 1 · 18s ). A command a program asks permission to run ( Bash: psql $DEV_URL ), or the command line of a finished one ( exit 1 · make deploy ), is set in the monospace face; the words before it ( Permission · , exit 1 · ) stay in the proportional face, on the same baseline. Reason text is shown as plain text, one bounded line, whatever the program sent. Time. A running state counts up ( 4:12 ), a finished one counts since it ended ( 2m ago ), and a program that reports progress shows a percentage meter instead. The clock ticks once a second, and only while a visible row shows a live time. A finished command's exit status has no timestamp to measure from, so it has a reason but no time. Roll-up. A parent row shows its most urgent descendant: the glyph, reason and time of the pane that asks the most. A collapsed workspace therefore still tells you that something inside it needs you. Git. A workspace row shows the branch of its active pane's repository, with ↑ and ↓ once an upstream exists. A directory outside a repository, a detached HEAD and a branch without an upstream show only what is known. The daemon refreshes it when the active pane changes directory, when the active tab or pane changes, when a command finishes (OSC 133;D) and every 30 seconds, whether or not a window is attached, so another daemon's switcher rows show it too. A window without a daemon refreshes on the same events but has no 30-second timer. The probe never blocks the daemon or the window. Current tab. The tab this window displays is marked as selected, as the platform marks it: on macOS in the accent while the keyboard is in the sidebar and in a quiet grey while it is elsewhere, as a source list's selection is; on Linux a neutral fill, focused or not, with the accent focus ring on the row the keyboard is on; on Windows a subtle grey fill and a rounded accent pill at the leading edge, focused or not; on the Terminal style inverse video. When its workspace is folded, the workspace row carries the selection instead, until it is unfolded. Failed. A failed status is drawn as the red ❌ on the native rows, in the sidebar, the location chip and the tab strip's badge; the Terminal style keeps a single-cell red ✕, because ❌ is two cells wide. Urgency # One order ranks every status, in the sidebar, the tab strip, the taskbar and the location chip, most urgent first: Rank Urgency Meaning 1 Needs you A program is blocked waiting for you, or a pane rang the bell 2 Failed A command or agent failed and you have not seen it 3 Done, not seen Something finished and you have not seen the result 4 Working Something runs; it needs nothing yet 5 Unseen output Output arrived out of sight 6 Idle Nothing to show Each status has its own shape as well as its colour, so none relies on colour alone. Working uses the accent colour, and needs-you uses amber (on the Terminal style, as a glyph only). A done or failed result stays shown until you see its pane, which is the done, not seen state. Seen never hides a program that is still blocked. Jump to the next item that needs you # ⌘J (macOS) or Ctrl+Shift+J (Linux and Windows), the JumpToNextAttention action, shows the next pane that asks something of you. It visits needs-you panes first, then failed, then done-not-seen, each class in sidebar order, and wraps around. It never lands on a working or idle pane. Landing on a pane marks it seen. Mark Seen in a row's menu (the MarkSeen action) does that without going there. The footer shows the key, so you find it again. Showing, hiding and focusing # Action macOS Linux and Windows ToggleSidebar : show or hide ⌘\ Ctrl+Shift+B FocusSidebar : move keyboard focus into it, showing it first when hidden ⌘⇧E Ctrl+Shift+D JumpToNextAttention ⌘J Ctrl+Shift+J CycleWorkspace : show the next / previous workspace ⌃⌘↓ / ⌃⌘↑ Ctrl+Alt+PageDown / PageUp MoveWorkspaceDown / MoveWorkspaceUp : move the current workspace in the list ⌃⇧⌘↓ / ⌃⇧⌘↑ Ctrl+Shift+Alt+PageDown / PageUp NewWorkspace : create a workspace and show it ⇧⌘N Ctrl+Shift+Alt+N FilterWorkspaces : open the filter, showing the sidebar first when hidden none none These are bound in the native2026 defaults only, except CycleWorkspace , MoveWorkspaceDown / Up and NewWorkspace , which every defaults edition binds, one level up from the tab and window chords (Ctrl+PageUp/PageDown, Ctrl+Shift+PageUp/PageDown, Ctrl+Shift+N). FilterWorkspaces has no default chord; bind one in input_mapping . Each control's tooltip names the chord its action is bound to at the time, so a binding you add shows there at once. By pointer, the sidebar toggle at the start of the title band (beside the traffic lights on macOS, at the header bar's start on Linux, in the sidebar's own top row while a macOS sidebar is shown) hides and shows it, from the same spot both ways. The title bar's menu has Show Sidebar / Hide Sidebar , and so has the View menu on macOS. When no title band is on screen (full screen, or tab_bar: never with the title bar hidden) and the sidebar is hidden, the terminal's own right-click menu offers Show Sidebar , so the sidebar can always be brought back the way it went. The width you drag it to and whether you left it shown are remembered per user and win over the configured start state. Keyboard # With the focus in the sidebar ( ⌘⇧E or Ctrl+Shift+D ): Key Does ↑ / ↓ Move to the previous or next row Home / End Move to the first or last row ← Collapse the row; on a collapsed or leaf row, move to its parent → Expand the row; on an expanded row, move to its first child Return Show what the row names: the workspace, the tab, the pane F2 Rename the workspace or tab row Menu, Shift+F10 Open the row's menu, as a right click does Escape While a filter is typed, clear it; otherwise leave the sidebar and give the focus back to the terminal Any printable key Start filtering Type to filter. The filter button in the sidebar's top row (a funnel; in the header bar on Linux) opens the same field. Typing narrows the tree to rows whose title, reason or git text contains what you typed (case-insensitive for ASCII). Every parent of a match stays and is expanded while the filter is set. The filter is only a view: it never changes what a drag or a rename acts on. Mouse # Click a row to show it. Click the disclosure triangle to fold or unfold it. Double-click a workspace's or a tab's name to rename it, or press F2 on its row. Return commits, Escape cancels. A workspace's or a tab's name is shared: every window of the daemon and every object.renamed subscriber of the control API hears it, and contour rename addresses the object by it ( tab:logs ). Right-click for the row's menu: a workspace: Workspace Color , Rename…, Mark Seen, New Tab Here, Move Up, Move Down, Merge into Tab (a workspace of one tab only), Close Workspace… (the last workspace of an in-process window cannot be closed); a tab: the tab strip's menu (Tab Color, Rename…, and its close row reads Close Tab…), then Split Vertically and Split Horizontally , which split the tab's active pane, then Move to Workspace , Merge into Tab and Move to New Workspace ; a pane: Go to Pane, Mark Seen, Split Vertically , Split Horizontally , Move to Tab , Move to New Tab , Move to New Workspace , Close Pane…. Move to Tab and Merge into Tab list every other tab, under the name of its workspace; the pane, or the tab's panes, join that tab as splits, as a drop on its row does. Move to New Workspace makes a workspace named as any new one is, which an in-process window then shows. Move to New Workspace is greyed out for a workspace's only tab, which already is a workspace of its own. Workspace Color, Mark Seen, Rename…, Move Up, Move Down and the Move and Merge rows act on the row the menu was opened on and leave the window where it is. The rest (Go to Pane, New Tab Here, the Split rows and the tab strip's own commands) act on what the window shows, so the window shows that row first; a Split row then splits the pane the row names, or the tab's active pane. The three close rows (Close Workspace…, Close Tab…, Close Pane…) always ask first, in one confirmation that names what ends (the tabs and panes, and the running command where known). Cancel is the default button and Escape cancels; the answer closes the row the menu was opened on. - Drag to reorder or move. A row's upper and lower thirds are the gaps beside it, shown as a line where the drop lands; its middle is the row itself, shown highlighted. A drop the row refuses shows the refusal. - a workspace onto another workspace row: before it in the upper half, after it in the lower half; - a tab or a pane onto a tab row: in the upper or lower third, before or after that tab, as a tab (a pane becomes a tab of its own); in the middle, into that tab: the pane, or every pane of the tab, joins it as a split beside its active pane, on the side a drop on a tab of the tab strip takes, and becomes its active pane; - a workspace that holds one tab onto the middle of a tab row: its tab joins that tab, and the emptied workspace closes. A workspace of several tabs is refused there; - a tab or a pane onto a workspace row: to the end of it (the middle of the row), or to the start of it (the lower third), or to the end of the workspace above (the upper third); - a tab or a pane onto the tree's empty area below the last row, or onto a New Workspace button: a workspace of its own, named as any new workspace is. A workspace's only tab is refused there, as it already is one; - anything onto a pane row, or onto its own tab's middle, is refused. A pane that is its tab's only pane moves as that tab. Its sessions keep running wherever it goes: the shell, its scrollback and its status move with it, and nothing restarts. Drops resolve to the real positions in the daemon, so a filter or a folded row never moves where a drop lands. Moving the last pane out of a tab closes that tab, and moving the last tab out of a workspace closes that workspace, as their last pane or tab ending does. A window and a daemon keep their last workspace, so that one cannot be closed. - Drag the divider at the sidebar's right edge to resize it. The width snaps to whole cells on the Terminal style, stays within the style's bounds (160 to 480 px, 18 to 60 cells) and is saved when you let go. A new workspace # The ＋ button, and the NewWorkspace action (⇧⌘N, Ctrl+Shift+Alt+N), create a workspace and show it. The button stands where each platform keeps a sidebar's "add": in the sidebar's footer on macOS, Windows and the Terminal style, and as a "new folder" icon in the header bar on Linux, so it is never the title band's new-tab + . It is named after the folder the current pane is in, or, inside a git worktree, after the repository's root folder , and its first shell starts in that directory. A pane with no known directory leaves the name empty and the workspace shows as Workspace N . The name is written once at creation; renaming changes it from then on. workspace.create of the control API does the same, with an optional cwd and name . The hover card # Resting the pointer on a row opens a card with the full reason line, wrapped instead of cut off (up to 2000 characters, so a runaway one cannot flood it), and the program, the folder and the time, the folder shown to its end. It follows the pointer onto itself, so you can read it, and closes when the pointer leaves. The footer # The footer counts what asks for you across every workspace, folded or not: 2 need you · 3 working . It counts panes (the leaves under each workspace), not rolled-up rows, leaves out a count that is zero, and shows the jump key beside it. When the sidebar is hidden # With the sidebar away, a window on a daemon shows one location chip at the leading edge of its title band: local › billing ▾ , the daemon the window is on and the shown workspace. The default local daemon reads local , a named one its name ( work ), a remote one its host, and a daemon without a name daemon . A window with no daemon shows the workspace alone. The chip is marked when another workspace needs you, has failed, or has a result you have not seen (done-not-seen and up). Work that is only running, or unseen output, does not mark it: the chip is not a progress indicator. The tabs move into the title band behind the chip, following tab_bar_position . The daemon's connection shows in the chip too: a remote daemon that is connected has a green dot, a local one shows nothing. While the link is not up, any daemon shows a dot and its state, starfive Reconnecting… or local Disconnected . The dot keeps its shape, so colour is never the only cue, and the state is also in the chip's accessible description. When the band runs short, the chip gives way in this order, so the workspace name outlasts the daemon's: the state text goes (the dot stays), then the daemon name is shortened in the middle, then the daemon shrinks to its dot, and only then is the workspace name shortened, never below 6 characters and an ellipsis. The window cannot be made narrower than the chip at that last step, the buttons and one tab need. Clicking the chip, or pressing Space or Return on it, opens the switcher below it: the same popup ShowSwitcher opens ( Ctrl+Shift+R , ⇧⌘R on macOS), with the workspaces of this window's daemon first and typing filtering at once. The chip's tooltip, "Switch workspace or daemon", names whatever chord is bound. The chip stays highlighted while the popup is open, and clicking it again closes it; Escape closes the popup. With the sidebar shown, the band has no chip. The daemon heads the sidebar instead, local ▾ with the same dot for a remote daemon, and opens the same switcher below itself with the same tooltip. Type to filter the workspaces; Return switches this window to the selected one, Shift+Return opens it in a new window. The row under the pointer shows a button that does the same. New Workspace creates one on this daemon, named after what you typed, if anything. Below this daemon's workspaces the popup lists every other local daemon and saved host, as the ShowSwitcher popup does: the click and the chord open the same rows. Right-click a workspace (or press the Menu key, or Shift+F10) for the same menu its sidebar row has: colour, rename, mark seen, new tab, move, close. Escape, or a click elsewhere, closes it and changes nothing; Escape does not narrow it first. The switcher keeps the sidebar's times running while it is open, so a working workspace's time moves on even with the sidebar hidden. Tab placement # tab_placement chooses where the tabs of a window live: sidebar : tabs are rows of the sidebar under their workspace. While the sidebar is shown the tab strip is hidden and the title band shows the breadcrumb workspace › tab . While the sidebar is hidden, the tabs are in the title band as above. top : the tab strip, placed by tab_bar_position and shown by tab_bar_visibility , as before. The sidebar still lists the tabs. Configuration # sidebar : visible : true # start shown; what you last chose in a window wins over this width : 240 # logical pixels (cells under ui_style: terminal); omit for the style's own tab_color : tint # tint | bar | name workspace_color : tint # tint | group | swatch row_spacing : comfortable # comfortable | compact tab_placement : sidebar # sidebar | top tab_color picks how a coloured tab shows its colour on its rows, the tab's and its panes'; an uncoloured tab looks the same in all three, and workspace rows never carry a tab's colour. tint (the default): the row is filled with the colour, faded as the tab strip fades it, and its text turns black or white to stay legible. bar : a narrow bar in the colour runs the row's full height at its leading edge. name : the tab's name is drawn in the colour. workspace_color picks how a coloured workspace shows its colour in the sidebar, independently of tab_color ; an uncoloured workspace looks the same in all three, a folded workspace keeps its paint, and the colour is shown in the sidebar only. tint (the default): the workspace's row is filled with the colour, faded as the tab strip fades a coloured tab, and its text turns black or white to stay legible. group : a rail in the colour runs down the sidebar's leading edge beside the workspace's row and every row beneath it, over a faint wash of the colour; a coloured tab's own tint is drawn over the wash. swatch : a small square in the colour stands before the workspace's name. To colour a workspace, right-click its row and pick from Workspace Color : a swatch, Custom… for the colour picker, or Reset . The SetWorkspaceColor action without a colour opens the picker for the shown workspace. A workspace's colour belongs to the daemon, as its name does: every window of the daemon shows it, and it survives a restart and a live upgrade. Against a daemon that predates workspace colours, Workspace Color is greyed out, and the SetWorkspaceColor and ResetWorkspaceColor actions only say so in a notice. A tab is coloured from Tab Color in its menu, as on the tab strip. row_spacing picks how much room a tab's or a pane's two-line row takes; a workspace's row is one line in both, and under ui_style: terminal a two-line row is two cells in both. comfortable (the default): 40 px rows on macOS, Windows and Linux. The extra room goes between the rows, not between a row's two lines, so each row's lines read as one. compact : 36 px rows, so more of them fit. It is also in the Settings window, under Appearance › Tab bar . tab_color , workspace_color and row_spacing are read when a window opens: a window that is open when the configuration is reloaded keeps the styles it opened with, and a window opened after it uses the new ones. See Key mapping for the actions and their default chords. The default width is 220 px on macOS, 240 px on Fluent and ContourLinux, and 28 cells under ui_style: terminal . Defaults # defaults_edition: native2026 , which a newly generated configuration carries, shows the sidebar ( sidebar.visible: true ), places the tabs in it ( tab_placement: sidebar ) and binds the chords above. A configuration that does not set defaults_edition is classic : the sidebar is hidden, the tab strip stays on top and the sidebar chords are not bound. Set either key explicitly to override one decision. The Terminal style # Under ui_style: terminal the sidebar is a tree of whole cells, drawn with ├ └ │ . Its width is a whole number of cells, a one-cell │ divides it from the terminal at one fixed column, and urgency is a glyph only. Known limits # Ahead and behind are not shown on Windows. They come from running git , and the daemon's command runner does not support that there. The branch still shows. The sidebar has a solid background. macOS vibrancy and Windows Mica behind it are not done yet. Rows have no accessible expanded state , because Qt's accessibility has none. The state is part of the row's name instead; see Accessibility .

Typing narrows the tree to rows whose title, reason or git text contains what you typed (case-insensitive for ASCII). Every parent of a match stays and is expanded while the filter is set. The filter is only a view: it never changes what a drag or a rename acts on.
docs.title: Keyboard

docs.text: Click a row to show it. Click the disclosure triangle to fold or unfold it. Double-click a workspace's or a tab's name to rename it, or press F2 on its row. Return commits, Escape cancels. A workspace's or a tab's name is shared: every window of the daemon and every object.renamed subscriber of the control API hears it, and contour rename addresses the object by it ( tab:logs ). Right-click for the row's menu: a workspace: Workspace Color , Rename…, Mark Seen, New Tab Here, Move Up, Move Down, Merge into Tab (a workspace of one tab only), Close Workspace… (the last workspace of an in-process window cannot be closed); a tab: the tab strip's menu (Tab Color, Rename…, and its close row reads Close Tab…), then Split Vertically and Split Horizontally , which split the tab's active pane, then Move to Workspace , Merge into Tab and Move to New Workspace ; a pane: Go to Pane, Mark Seen, Split Vertically , Split Horizontally , Move to Tab , Move to New Tab , Move to New Workspace , Close Pane…. Move to Tab and Merge into Tab list every other tab, under the name of its workspace; the pane, or the tab's panes, join that tab as splits, as a drop on its row does. Move to New Workspace makes a workspace named as any new one is, which an in-process window then shows. Move to New Workspace is greyed out for a workspace's only tab, which already is a workspace of its own. Workspace Color, Mark Seen, Rename…, Move Up, Move Down and the Move and Merge rows act on the row the menu was opened on and leave the window where it is. The rest (Go to Pane, New Tab Here, the Split rows and the tab strip's own commands) act on what the window shows, so the window shows that row first; a Split row then splits the pane the row names, or the tab's active pane. The three close rows (Close Workspace…, Close Tab…, Close Pane…) always ask first, in one confirmation that names what ends (the tabs and panes, and the running command where known). Cancel is the default button and Escape cancels; the answer closes the row the menu was opened on. - Drag to reorder or move. A row's upper and lower thirds are the gaps beside it, shown as a line where the drop lands; its middle is the row itself, shown highlighted. A drop the row refuses shows the refusal. - a workspace onto another workspace row: before it in the upper half, after it in the lower half; - a tab or a pane onto a tab row: in the upper or lower third, before or after that tab, as a tab (a pane becomes a tab of its own); in the middle, into that tab: the pane, or every pane of the tab, joins it as a split beside its active pane, on the side a drop on a tab of the tab strip takes, and becomes its active pane; - a workspace that holds one tab onto the middle of a tab row: its tab joins that tab, and the emptied workspace closes. A workspace of several tabs is refused there; - a tab or a pane onto a workspace row: to the end of it (the middle of the row), or to the start of it (the lower third), or to the end of the workspace above (the upper third); - a tab or a pane onto the tree's empty area below the last row, or onto a New Workspace button: a workspace of its own, named as any new workspace is. A workspace's only tab is refused there, as it already is one; - anything onto a pane row, or onto its own tab's middle, is refused. A pane that is its tab's only pane moves as that tab. Its sessions keep running wherever it goes: the shell, its scrollback and its status move with it, and nothing restarts. Drops resolve to the real positions in the daemon, so a filter or a folded row never moves where a drop lands. Moving the last pane out of a tab closes that tab, and moving the last tab out of a workspace closes that workspace, as their last pane or tab ending does. A window and a daemon keep their last workspace, so that one cannot be closed. - Drag the divider at the sidebar's right edge to resize it. The width snaps to whole cells on the Terminal style, stays within the style's bounds (160 to 480 px, 18 to 60 cells) and is saved when you let go.
docs.title: Mouse

docs.text: The ＋ button, and the NewWorkspace action (⇧⌘N, Ctrl+Shift+Alt+N), create a workspace and show it. The button stands where each platform keeps a sidebar's "add": in the sidebar's footer on macOS, Windows and the Terminal style, and as a "new folder" icon in the header bar on Linux, so it is never the title band's new-tab + . It is named after the folder the current pane is in, or, inside a git worktree, after the repository's root folder , and its first shell starts in that directory. A pane with no known directory leaves the name empty and the workspace shows as Workspace N . The name is written once at creation; renaming changes it from then on. workspace.create of the control API does the same, with an optional cwd and name .
docs.title: A new workspace

docs.text: Resting the pointer on a row opens a card with the full reason line, wrapped instead of cut off (up to 2000 characters, so a runaway one cannot flood it), and the program, the folder and the time, the folder shown to its end. It follows the pointer onto itself, so you can read it, and closes when the pointer leaves.
docs.title: The hover card

docs.text: The footer counts what asks for you across every workspace, folded or not: 2 need you · 3 working . It counts panes (the leaves under each workspace), not rolled-up rows, leaves out a count that is zero, and shows the jump key beside it.
docs.title: The footer

docs.text: With the sidebar away, a window on a daemon shows one location chip at the leading edge of its title band: local › billing ▾ , the daemon the window is on and the shown workspace. The default local daemon reads local , a named one its name ( work ), a remote one its host, and a daemon without a name daemon . A window with no daemon shows the workspace alone. The chip is marked when another workspace needs you, has failed, or has a result you have not seen (done-not-seen and up). Work that is only running, or unseen output, does not mark it: the chip is not a progress indicator. The tabs move into the title band behind the chip, following tab_bar_position . The daemon's connection shows in the chip too: a remote daemon that is connected has a green dot, a local one shows nothing. While the link is not up, any daemon shows a dot and its state, starfive Reconnecting… or local Disconnected . The dot keeps its shape, so colour is never the only cue, and the state is also in the chip's accessible description. When the band runs short, the chip gives way in this order, so the workspace name outlasts the daemon's: the state text goes (the dot stays), then the daemon name is shortened in the middle, then the daemon shrinks to its dot, and only then is the workspace name shortened, never below 6 characters and an ellipsis. The window cannot be made narrower than the chip at that last step, the buttons and one tab need. Clicking the chip, or pressing Space or Return on it, opens the switcher below it: the same popup ShowSwitcher opens ( Ctrl+Shift+R , ⇧⌘R on macOS), with the workspaces of this window's daemon first and typing filtering at once. The chip's tooltip, "Switch workspace or daemon", names whatever chord is bound. The chip stays highlighted while the popup is open, and clicking it again closes it; Escape closes the popup. With the sidebar shown, the band has no chip. The daemon heads the sidebar instead, local ▾ with the same dot for a remote daemon, and opens the same switcher below itself with the same tooltip. Type to filter the workspaces; Return switches this window to the selected one, Shift+Return opens it in a new window. The row under the pointer shows a button that does the same. New Workspace creates one on this daemon, named after what you typed, if anything. Below this daemon's workspaces the popup lists every other local daemon and saved host, as the ShowSwitcher popup does: the click and the chord open the same rows. Right-click a workspace (or press the Menu key, or Shift+F10) for the same menu its sidebar row has: colour, rename, mark seen, new tab, move, close. Escape, or a click elsewhere, closes it and changes nothing; Escape does not narrow it first. The switcher keeps the sidebar's times running while it is open, so a working workspace's time moves on even with the sidebar hidden.
docs.title: When the sidebar is hidden

docs.text: tab_placement chooses where the tabs of a window live: sidebar : tabs are rows of the sidebar under their workspace. While the sidebar is shown the tab strip is hidden and the title band shows the breadcrumb workspace › tab . While the sidebar is hidden, the tabs are in the title band as above. top : the tab strip, placed by tab_bar_position and shown by tab_bar_visibility , as before. The sidebar still lists the tabs.
docs.title: Tab placement

docs.text: sidebar : visible : true # start shown; what you last chose in a window wins over this width : 240 # logical pixels (cells under ui_style: terminal); omit for the style's own tab_color : tint # tint | bar | name workspace_color : tint # tint | group | swatch row_spacing : comfortable # comfortable | compact tab_placement : sidebar # sidebar | top tab_color picks how a coloured tab shows its colour on its rows, the tab's and its panes'; an uncoloured tab looks the same in all three, and workspace rows never carry a tab's colour. tint (the default): the row is filled with the colour, faded as the tab strip fades it, and its text turns black or white to stay legible. bar : a narrow bar in the colour runs the row's full height at its leading edge. name : the tab's name is drawn in the colour. workspace_color picks how a coloured workspace shows its colour in the sidebar, independently of tab_color ; an uncoloured workspace looks the same in all three, a folded workspace keeps its paint, and the colour is shown in the sidebar only. tint (the default): the workspace's row is filled with the colour, faded as the tab strip fades a coloured tab, and its text turns black or white to stay legible. group : a rail in the colour runs down the sidebar's leading edge beside the workspace's row and every row beneath it, over a faint wash of the colour; a coloured tab's own tint is drawn over the wash. swatch : a small square in the colour stands before the workspace's name. To colour a workspace, right-click its row and pick from Workspace Color : a swatch, Custom… for the colour picker, or Reset . The SetWorkspaceColor action without a colour opens the picker for the shown workspace. A workspace's colour belongs to the daemon, as its name does: every window of the daemon shows it, and it survives a restart and a live upgrade. Against a daemon that predates workspace colours, Workspace Color is greyed out, and the SetWorkspaceColor and ResetWorkspaceColor actions only say so in a notice. A tab is coloured from Tab Color in its menu, as on the tab strip. row_spacing picks how much room a tab's or a pane's two-line row takes; a workspace's row is one line in both, and under ui_style: terminal a two-line row is two cells in both. comfortable (the default): 40 px rows on macOS, Windows and Linux. The extra room goes between the rows, not between a row's two lines, so each row's lines read as one. compact : 36 px rows, so more of them fit. It is also in the Settings window, under Appearance › Tab bar . tab_color , workspace_color and row_spacing are read when a window opens: a window that is open when the configuration is reloaded keeps the styles it opened with, and a window opened after it uses the new ones. See Key mapping for the actions and their default chords. The default width is 220 px on macOS, 240 px on Fluent and ContourLinux, and 28 cells under ui_style: terminal .
docs.title: Configuration

docs.text: defaults_edition: native2026 , which a newly generated configuration carries, shows the sidebar ( sidebar.visible: true ), places the tabs in it ( tab_placement: sidebar ) and binds the chords above. A configuration that does not set defaults_edition is classic : the sidebar is hidden, the tab strip stays on top and the sidebar chords are not bound. Set either key explicitly to override one decision.
docs.title: Defaults

docs.text: Under ui_style: terminal the sidebar is a tree of whole cells, drawn with ├ └ │ . Its width is a whole number of cells, a one-cell │ divides it from the terminal at one fixed column, and urgency is a glyph only.
docs.title: The Terminal style

docs.text: Ahead and behind are not shown on Windows. They come from running git , and the daemon's command runner does not support that there. The branch still shows. The sidebar has a solid background. macOS vibrancy and Windows Mica behind it are not done yet. Rows have no accessible expanded state , because Qt's accessibility has none. The state is part of the row's name instead; see Accessibility .
docs.title: Known limits

docs.text: Configuring Contour # Contour offers a wide range of configuration options that can be customized, including color scheme, shell, initial working directory, and more. The configuration options can be categorized into several groups: Global options: These settings determine the overall behavior of the terminal and apply to all profiles. Profiles: With profiles, you can configure the terminal more granularly and create multiple profiles that can be easily switched between. Color scheme: Contour allows you to define different color schemes for the terminal and choose which one to use for each of the profiles. On Unix systems, the main configuration file is located at ~/.config/contour/contour.yml and is both read from and auto-generated there. On Windows systems, the file is located at %LocalAppData%\contour\contour.yml . Please note that on Unix systems, the environment variable XDG_CONFIG_HOME (by default set to ~/.config ) is taken into account. By default, on Unix systems, Contour is executed with the following arguments contour config ~/.config/contour/contour.yml profile main . If the configuration file includes a default_profile variable, it will be used as the default profile. Otherwise, the first profile listed in the file will be the default one.
