docs.title: default_layout

docs.text: Saved remote hosts that "Attach to Host" lists.
docs.title: hosts

docs.text: Contour implements rendering of git branch characters used by e.g. vim-flog and gitgraph.nvim . Initially introduced to kitty , the symbol set was later expanded to support more commit options. The symbols use codepoints U+F5D0 ... U+F60D. Note: U+F5D2 ... U+F5D5 are supposed to be fading out symbols but currently are rendered as simple lines. The symbols may be customized via config options: branch_style controls the style of connecting branches. May be one of none , thin , thick , double . The default value is thin . arc_style controls the style of arcs. May be one of round , ellips . arc_style has effect only if branch_style is thin . The default value is round . merge_commit_style controls the style of merge commits. May be one of solid , bullet . The default value is bullet . git_drawings : branch_style : thin arc_style : round merge_commit_style : bullet
docs.title: git_drawings

docs.text: Controls how arcs in box drawing characters are drawn. May be one of round or ellips . The default value is round . box_arc_style : round
docs.title: box_arc_style

docs.text: Controls how Unicode Braille characters are rendered. May be one of font , solid , circle , circle_empty , square , square_empty , aa_square , aa_square_empty . The default value is circle . font disables special rendering and uses font characters. solid splits the character box into 8 rectangles without space between them. No antialiasing is used, some font sizes may result in differently sized "dots". circle<..> and <..>square<..> groups use circle and square "dots" respectively. <..>_empty draws non-filled "dots". square<..> does not use antialiasing, which may result in differently sized "dots". aa_square<..> uses antialiasing. braille_style : circle
docs.title: braille_style

docs.text: platform_plugin : auto renderer : backend : auto tile_hashtable_slots : 4096 tile_cache_count : 4000 tile_direct_mapping : true word_delimiters : " /\\()\"'-.,:;<>~!@#$%^&*+=[]{}~?|│" read_buffer_size : 65536 pty_buffer_size : 1048576 default_profile : main spawn_new_process : false reflow_on_resize : true bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier : Shift mouse_block_selection_modifier : Control on_mouse_select : CopyToSelectionClipboard live_config : false images : sixel_scrolling : true sixel_register_count : 4096 The default profile is automatically the top (first) defined profile in the configuration file, but can be explicitly set to an order-independent name using default_profile configuration key.
docs.title: Default global parameters

docs.text: Profiles is the main part of user specific customizations, you can create more than one profile and chose which you want to use during startup or define in configuration file. By default each profile inherites values from default_profile . This means that you can specify only values that you want to change in respect to default profile, for example you can create new profile to use bash as a shell preserving other configuration from main profile profiles: main: # default profile here bash: shell: "/usr/bin/bash" For the full list of options see generated configuration file on your system or Profiles section of documentation.
docs.title: Profiles

docs.text: In contour you can specify different colors inside terminal, for example text background and foreground, cursor properties, selection colors and plenty others. You can configure your color profiles, whereas a color can be expressed in standard web format, with a leading # followed by red/green/blue values, 7 characters in total. You may alternatively use 0x as prefix instead of #. For example 0x102030 is equal to '#102030'. Syntax for color schemes repeat the one of profiles. First color scheme inside configuration file must be named default , each other color schemes inherit values from default color scheme. Example of configuration for color_schemes color_schemes: default: # values for default color scheme different_selection: selection: background: '#fff0f0' For the full list of options see generated configuration file on your system or Colors section of documentation.
docs.title: Color Schemes

docs.text: Color scheme configure colors that are used inside terminal. To specify which color scheme you want to use you need to define the name of the scheme inside profile configuration or inline colors inside profile. Color scheme configuration # Color configuration is set under profiles with colors . Then the scheme is defined under color_schemes . default # section defines the default colors used in the terminal. color_schemes : default : default : background : '#1a1716' foreground : '#d0d0d0' bright_foreground : '#ffffff' dimmed_foreground : '#808080' - background determines the default background color of the terminal. - foreground option sets the default foreground text color of the terminal. - bright_foreground option sets the default foreground text color of the terminal when text text is instructed to be bold (/bright). This is only used if profile option draw_bold_text_with_bright_colors is set to true - dimmed_foreground option sets the default foreground text color of the terminal when text text is instructed to be dimmed. background_image # section in the configuration file allows you to control various aspects of the background image feature. color_schemes : default : background_image : path : '/path/to/image.png' opacity : 0.5 blur : false - path To specify the image file to use as the background, you need to provide the full path to the image. Both ~ (home directory) and ${VAR} (environment variable) expansion are supported — see Path Handling for details. By default, the path option is set to an empty string, indicating that background image support is disabled. - opacity option controls the opacity of the background image. It determines how transparent or intense the image appears. The default value is 0.5, which provides a moderately transparent background. You can adjust this value to make the image more or less prominent, depending on your preferences. - blur option applies a blur effect to the background image. This can help reduce distractions and keep the focus on the terminal contents. By default, the blur option is set to false, indicating that background image blurring is disabled. If you want to enable it, set the value to true. cursor # section in the configuration file let you customize the color of the cursor and optionally override the text color. color_schemes : default : cursor : default : CellForeground text : CellBackground - default option allows you to specify the color of the cursor shape. By default, the default value is set to CellForeground, which means the cursor color will be the same as the cell's foreground color. You can change this value to any valid RGB color or use the special options CellForeground or CellBackground. - text allows you to specify the color of the characters that would be covered by the cursor shape. This is useful for ensuring readability when the cursor overlaps with the text. By default, the text value is set to CellBackground, which means the overridden text color will be the same as the cell's background color. Similarly to the default option, you can specify any valid RGB color or use the CellForeground or CellBackground options. hyperlink_decoration # allows you to customize the colors used for hyperlink decoration when hovering over them. These colours apply to the links Contour detects in output as well as to OSC 8 hyperlinks. color_schemes : default : hyperlink_decoration : normal : '#f0f000' hover : '#ff0000' - normal defines the color to be used for hyperlink decoration in its normal state (not being hovered). - hover determines the color to be applied to hyperlink decoration when it is being hovered over. vi_mode_highlight # customize the colors used for highlighting in Vi mode. color_schemes : default : vi_mode_highlight : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#ffa500' background_alpha : 0.5 - foreground section specifies the color to be used for the foreground of the highlighted text. - foreground_alpha option determines the transparency level of the foreground color. It accepts a value between 0.0 (fully transparent) and 1.0 (fully opaque). This option allows you to control the visibility of the highlighted text. - background option in the vi_mode_highlight section defines the color to be used for the background of the highlighted text. - background_alpha option controls the transparency level of the background color. It accepts a value between 0.0 (fully transparent) and 1.0 (fully opaque). vi_mode_cursorline # customize the colors used for the cursor line in Vi mode. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight . color_schemes : default : vi_mode_cursorline : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#ffa500' background_alpha : 0.5 selection # section customize the colors used for text selection. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight . color_schemes : default : selection : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#4040f0' background_alpha : 0.5 search_highlight # section customize the colors used for search highlight. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight . color_schemes : default : search_highlight : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#4040f0' background_alpha : 0.5 search_highlight_focused # section customize the colors used for focused search highlight. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight . color_schemes : default : search_highlight_focused : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#4040f0' background_alpha : 0.5 word_highlight_current # Coloring for the word that is highlighted due to double-clicking it. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight . color_schemes : default : word_highlight_current : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#4040f0' background_alpha : 0.5 word_highlight_other # Coloring for the word that is highlighted due to double-clicking another word that matches this word. Options similar to vi_mode_highlight . color_schemes : default : word_highlight_other : foreground : CellForeground foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#4040f0' background_alpha : 0.5 indicator_statusline # Defines the colors to be used for the Indicator status line. Configuration entry consist of following sections, namely default , inactive , insert_mode , normal_mode , visual_mode . Each section have foreground and background options. You can specify only the sections you want to customize after configuring the default section. Minimal configuration looks like this: color_schemes : default : indicator_statusline : default : foreground : '#808080' background : '#000000' fold_marker # Defines the colors of the fold markers drawn in the gutter's block column, left of the grid, when output folding is enabled (see folding.show_markers ). Two independent sections, default and hover , each with foreground and background ; hover applies to the whole run of the fold the pointer is currently over, not just the row under it. Both are optional , and left unset by default. When a section is missing, its colors are derived from this scheme's own default foreground and background: at rest the glyph is faded partway toward the background so it stays quieter than the text beside it, and on hover it comes up to the full foreground. Only the glyph changes — the background stays the page's own in both states, so the gutter never paints over a transparent window. That is what lets a scheme which has never heard of folding still draw a legible, obviously-clickable column, in light and dark themes alike — so only set these if you actively want something else. color_schemes : default : fold_marker : default : foreground : '#7e7c7c' background : '#1a1716' hover : foreground : '#d0d0d0' background : '#1a1716' default Colors of the fold column at rest. Set the background to this scheme's own background to keep the gutter transparent along with the rest of the window. hover Colors of the fold run under the pointer — the whole run of the hovered fold, not just the row beneath it. block_status # Defines the colors of a command block's marks by how its command ended (see Command blocks ): what the gutter's block column draws beside it while gutter.exit_status is on (the default), and its tick on the scrollbar. Each is a single color, and all three are optional , left unset by default. A missing one is derived from this scheme, so a scheme that has never heard of them still shows them legibly: success — a command that exited with 0, or whose exit status is unknown. Derived from the fold marker's color, so a successful block looks exactly as the fold column always has. failure — a command that exited non-zero, or was killed. Derived from this scheme's normal red (normal color 1). running — a command that has not finished yet. Derived from this scheme's normal yellow (normal color 3). Under the pointer, failure and running — and a success set here — are lifted halfway toward the text color; an unset success comes up to full strength, as the fold column does. color_schemes : default : block_status : success : '#7E7C7C' failure : '#C63939' running : '#A0A000' The values shown are what the default scheme derives. gutter_text # The color of the gutter's line numbers and timestamps, and of the chip a collapsed fold carries ( 1,234 lines hidden ⌄ ), lifted where it would not read on the chip's band. Optional , and unset by default: it is then this scheme's foreground faded toward its background, as the resting fold markers are, so the numbers stay quieter than the text beside them. color_schemes : default : gutter_text : '#7E7C7C' sticky_header # Defines the colors of the sticky command header (see the profile key sticky_header ): the band pinned over the top row while you read a command's output with the command itself scrolled out of view, and the one-pixel line along its bottom edge. Both are optional , and unset by default. A missing one is derived from this scheme's own default colors: the band is the background lifted a tenth of the way toward the foreground, the line about a third of the way — quiet in every theme, yet distinct from the page. color_schemes : default : sticky_header : background : '#2C2928' separator : '#595757' background The band's color. The command copied into it keeps its own colors; only the cells the shell left on the default background take this one. separator The one-pixel line along the band's bottom edge. docs.text: Hosts # A saved host is a remote machine whose daemon Contour can attach to by name: "Attach to Host" lists them, and contour client --host NAME attaches to one. How remote attach works, and how to set the far side up (including over Tailscale), is described in Remote hosts . Configuration # A profile's ssh: block instead opens a remote login shell through Contour's built-in SSH client; it does not require Contour on the server. Contour chooses the first nonempty value from the profile's environment.TERM , the top-level ssh_default_term , and the Contour process's TERM environment variable. If none is set, Windows uses xterm-256color . Other platforms send an empty terminal type. Choose a terminal type whose terminfo entry is installed on the server. In Settings, edit Default SSH terminal type under General → Advanced and Environment variables under the profile's Shell group. Settings can edit profiles it manages. For a profile defined in contour.yml , edit the file or duplicate the profile in Settings. ssh_default_term : xterm-256color profiles : remote-shell : ssh : host : homepc user : me environment : TERM : contour COLORTERM : truecolor The profile's environment: values go to the shell the profile opens. A local shell receives them directly. For built-in SSH, TERM travels in the PTY request. Other entries, such as COLORTERM , are sent as SSH environment requests and may require server permission (for example, OpenSSH's AcceptEnv ). Review values in existing profiles before using them with a remote host. Connect timeout # ssh.connect_timeout limits, in seconds, how long a built-in SSH connection may take to come up: from the TCP connect through the handshake, authentication and the terminfo installation below to the started shell. Time spent waiting for you (confirming a new host key, typing a key's passphrase or a password) does not count. It defaults to 30 ; 0 means no limit, and more than 86400 (24 hours) is taken as 86400 . A connection that runs out of time ends with an error naming the step it was in, the host and ssh.connect_timeout . Once the shell runs, no limit applies. Resolving the host name is left to the system resolver and its own timeouts. Authenticating through an SSH agent does not count toward ssh.connect_timeout either: an agent may ask you to approve each use of a key (1Password, Secretive, ssh-add -c , a FIDO key waiting for a touch, gpg-agent asking for its PIN), and Contour cannot tell that wait apart from the host's. The agent step has its own allowance of 2 minutes (or connect_timeout , if that is longer), for all of the agent's keys together; when it runs out, the connection ends with an error saying the agent did not finish in time. On Linux, macOS and other Unix systems this also cuts off an agent that never answers, or an approval left pending. On Windows it does not: there the allowance takes effect only once the agent has answered, so an agent that never replies, or an approval left pending, is not cut off. With connect_timeout: 0 the agent step has no limit either. profiles : remote-shell : ssh : host : homepc connect_timeout : 10 Terminfo installation # When a built-in SSH profile connects, Contour first runs a one-off command on a second SSH channel that compiles Contour's terminfo entry with the remote tic and installs it into the remote user's ~/.terminfo ( c/contour , or 63/contour where the remote's tic uses hex-named directories, as on macOS). The entry stays there; every later connect reinstalls it, which also updates it after a Contour upgrade. When the install succeeds, the shell starts with TERM=contour . If the remote has no tic (for example Alpine without ncurses, or BusyBox), the home directory is not writable, or anything else fails, the connection proceeds with the terminal type chosen above; the details go to the SSH log only. The step is bounded by 3 seconds, and never by more than what is left of ssh.connect_timeout . When it times out and the connection is still usable, one line is shown in the terminal and the shell starts. When the install leaves the connection unable to open the shell's channel (the host stopped answering while the install channel was being opened, or while a request was still being sent), the connection ends with an error that names ssh.install_terminfo: false . A host whose install failed, timed out or ended the connection is skipped for the rest of that Contour run, so connecting again works. A profile environment.TERM set to anything other than contour skips the install. To turn it off for a profile, set install_terminfo: false (default true ); the error message names it as ssh.install_terminfo: false : profiles : remote-shell : ssh : host : homepc install_terminfo : false Two kinds of hosts need care: Hosts that allow only one session per connection, or that drop the connection after a command, can fail to open the shell after the attempt. The error message then says to set ssh.install_terminfo: false . Hosts with a forced command ( ForceCommand , or command= in authorized_keys ) run that command once more on the first connect of a Contour run instead of the install; the install then fails and the host is skipped from then on. If that forced command prompts (for example for MFA), turn the option off for that profile. The installed file is a regular terminfo entry; removing ~/.terminfo/*/contour on the remote undoes it. Saved hosts # Hosts are configured under the top-level hosts entry, a map of host name to its settings. Listings are sorted by name. hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc" remote_command : "/opt/contour/bin/contour daemon --stdio" profile : "remote" studio : url : "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297" token_file : "~/.config/contour/studio.token" tls_ca : "~/.config/contour/studio-ca.pem" Key Meaning url Where the host is: ssh://[user@]host[:port] or tls://host:port . Required. token_file The file holding the remote daemon's token ( tls:// ). Not needed when an SSH key signs in. tls_ca A CA certificate to verify the daemon's TLS certificate against ( tls:// ). Without it the daemon is pinned on first use, as ssh does for a host: its certificate's fingerprint is kept in known_daemons , and a daemon that presents another one is refused. identity_file The SSH private key that signs in to a tls:// daemon, instead of the keys of your SSH agent. remote_command Replaces the whole command run on the remote side of ssh:// (default: contour daemon --stdio ). Use it when contour is not on the remote non-interactive PATH . It reaches the remote shell verbatim, so quote a path with spaces inside the YAML string yourself ( "'/opt/my apps/contour' daemon --stdio" ). profile The profile the remote sessions are created with; empty selects the default one. Paths in token_file , tls_ca and identity_file expand ~ and ${VAR} , as every path in the configuration does. Key binding # The AttachToHost action opens a new window attached to the saved host its name names, as the "Attach to Host" entries do; a binding without name is skipped. input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : H , action : AttachToHost , name : home } A host is attached like a launch against its daemon: one window, which shows the first workspace of the daemon no window shows (else a new one) and switches between the daemon's other workspaces in place. contour client --host NAME --workspace W shows the workspace W first. A window that is already open can move to a saved host with the SwitchToDaemon and OpenDaemon actions, which take host: NAME ; see Key Mapping . ssh:// # hosts : home : url : "ssh://me@homepc:2222" Contour runs ssh <target> contour daemon --stdio ; ssh does the authentication, with keys or an agent only (no password or host-key prompt is answered from the GUI). The user and the port are optional; ssh's own configuration ( ~/.ssh/config ) applies as usual. A host or user that begins with - is refused. tls:// # hosts : studio : url : "tls://studio.tailnet.ts.net:7297" token_file : "~/.config/contour/studio.token" A tls:// host needs nothing beyond its url : it signs in with the keys of your SSH agent, or with its identity_file (best loaded into the agent with ssh-add when it has a passphrase, as the daemon waits only 20 seconds for the sign-in), when the daemon authorizes keys, and with its token_file otherwise. The first time a daemon without a tls_ca is met, a dialog (a question on the terminal, for the control commands) shows its fingerprint to compare with what contour daemon status prints on that machine, and asks whether to trust it; where nobody can be asked, it is refused unless the fingerprint is given ( --daemon-fingerprint ). A trusted daemon is pinned, and one that later presents another certificate is refused, never asked about. After a daemon was reinstalled, contour daemon forget-pin HOST:PORT forgets the old pin. docs.text: A saved host is a remote machine whose daemon Contour can attach to by name: "Attach to Host" lists them, and contour client --host NAME attaches to one. How remote attach works, and how to set the far side up (including over Tailscale), is described in Remote hosts .

docs.text: A profile's ssh: block instead opens a remote login shell through Contour's built-in SSH client; it does not require Contour on the server. Contour chooses the first nonempty value from the profile's environment.TERM , the top-level ssh_default_term , and the Contour process's TERM environment variable. If none is set, Windows uses xterm-256color . Other platforms send an empty terminal type. Choose a terminal type whose terminfo entry is installed on the server. In Settings, edit Default SSH terminal type under General → Advanced and Environment variables under the profile's Shell group. Settings can edit profiles it manages. For a profile defined in contour.yml , edit the file or duplicate the profile in Settings. ssh_default_term : xterm-256color profiles : remote-shell : ssh : host : homepc user : me environment : TERM : contour COLORTERM : truecolor The profile's environment: values go to the shell the profile opens. A local shell receives them directly. For built-in SSH, TERM travels in the PTY request. Other entries, such as COLORTERM , are sent as SSH environment requests and may require server permission (for example, OpenSSH's AcceptEnv ). Review values in existing profiles before using them with a remote host.
docs.title: Configuration

docs.text: ssh.connect_timeout limits, in seconds, how long a built-in SSH connection may take to come up: from the TCP connect through the handshake, authentication and the terminfo installation below to the started shell. Time spent waiting for you (confirming a new host key, typing a key's passphrase or a password) does not count. It defaults to 30 ; 0 means no limit, and more than 86400 (24 hours) is taken as 86400 . A connection that runs out of time ends with an error naming the step it was in, the host and ssh.connect_timeout . Once the shell runs, no limit applies. Resolving the host name is left to the system resolver and its own timeouts. Authenticating through an SSH agent does not count toward ssh.connect_timeout either: an agent may ask you to approve each use of a key (1Password, Secretive, ssh-add -c , a FIDO key waiting for a touch, gpg-agent asking for its PIN), and Contour cannot tell that wait apart from the host's. The agent step has its own allowance of 2 minutes (or connect_timeout , if that is longer), for all of the agent's keys together; when it runs out, the connection ends with an error saying the agent did not finish in time. On Linux, macOS and other Unix systems this also cuts off an agent that never answers, or an approval left pending. On Windows it does not: there the allowance takes effect only once the agent has answered, so an agent that never replies, or an approval left pending, is not cut off. With connect_timeout: 0 the agent step has no limit either. profiles : remote-shell : ssh : host : homepc connect_timeout : 10
docs.title: Connect timeout

docs.text: When a built-in SSH profile connects, Contour first runs a one-off command on a second SSH channel that compiles Contour's terminfo entry with the remote tic and installs it into the remote user's ~/.terminfo ( c/contour , or 63/contour where the remote's tic uses hex-named directories, as on macOS). The entry stays there; every later connect reinstalls it, which also updates it after a Contour upgrade. When the install succeeds, the shell starts with TERM=contour . If the remote has no tic (for example Alpine without ncurses, or BusyBox), the home directory is not writable, or anything else fails, the connection proceeds with the terminal type chosen above; the details go to the SSH log only. The step is bounded by 3 seconds, and never by more than what is left of ssh.connect_timeout . When it times out and the connection is still usable, one line is shown in the terminal and the shell starts. When the install leaves the connection unable to open the shell's channel (the host stopped answering while the install channel was being opened, or while a request was still being sent), the connection ends with an error that names ssh.install_terminfo: false . A host whose install failed, timed out or ended the connection is skipped for the rest of that Contour run, so connecting again works. A profile environment.TERM set to anything other than contour skips the install. To turn it off for a profile, set install_terminfo: false (default true ); the error message names it as ssh.install_terminfo: false : profiles : remote-shell : ssh : host : homepc install_terminfo : false Two kinds of hosts need care: Hosts that allow only one session per connection, or that drop the connection after a command, can fail to open the shell after the attempt. The error message then says to set ssh.install_terminfo: false . Hosts with a forced command ( ForceCommand , or command= in authorized_keys ) run that command once more on the first connect of a Contour run instead of the install; the install then fails and the host is skipped from then on. If that forced command prompts (for example for MFA), turn the option off for that profile. The installed file is a regular terminfo entry; removing ~/.terminfo/*/contour on the remote undoes it.

docs.text: Indicator Statusline # The indicator statusline used to be a feature, from the old DEC VT level 4 terminals. Contour revives this feature to prominently show the terminal status. Configuration # profiles: your_profile: status_line: indicator: left: "{InputMode:Bold,Left= ,Right= ,Chip,Hide=Insert}{Context:Left= }{Cwd:Color=success,Left= }{Git:Left= }" middle: "{LastCommand}{Selection:Left= }{SearchPrompt:Color=warning,Left= }" right: "{Progress:Color=accent,Right= }{Scroll:Right= }{Clock:Faint,Right= }" This is the default of a configuration with defaults_edition: native2026 : the vi mode as a chip (hidden while typing), the directory and Git branch, how the last command went, the selection and search, and the scroll position and clock. Its colours are roles, so it follows the color scheme. A configuration with defaults_edition: classic (one written before the redesign) keeps the earlier default, with the tabs, the title and fixed colors: profiles: your_profile: status_line: indicator: left: " {InputMode:Bold,Color=#FFFF00}{TraceMode:Bold,Color=#FFFF00,Left= │ }{Tabs:ActiveColor=#FFFF00,Left= │ }{ProtectedMode:Bold,Left= │ }{Context:Left= │ }" middle: "« {Title} »" right: "{HistoryLineCount:Faint,Color=#c0c0c0} │ {Clock:Bold}" Each segment, left , middle , and right may contain text to be displayed in the left, middle, or right segment of the indicator statusline. This text may contain placeholders to be replaced by their respective dynamic content. Variables # Variable Description {Clock} current clock in HH:MM format {Cwd} the working directory the shell reports, with the home directory as ~ when it is on this machine; at most MaxWidth= columns (default 40 ), eliding the middle directories ( /…/d59 ) {Command} yields the output of the given command, as specified via parameter Program=... (or the {Command:<command>} shorthand), re-run every Interval=... seconds {Extension} what the status-line extension named by parameter Name=... (or the {Extension:<name>} shorthand) draws {UserVar} the value a program last set for the user variable named by parameter Name=... (or the {UserVar:<name>} shorthand) with OSC 1337 ; SetUserVar=<name>=<base64 value> , as iTerm2 and WezTerm do; empty while it is unset. At most 64 variables of at most 4096 bytes each are kept per session, and they survive a terminal reset {Git} the branch of the Git repository the shell's directory is in (a ref outside refs/heads/ as remotes/origin/x , a detached HEAD as its first 7 hex digits in parentheses, (a1b2c3d) ), read from .git/HEAD or a worktree's .git file; empty outside a repository or in a directory on another machine. It is looked up in the background, so it shows a moment after the directory does, and again only after a command ends or the shell reports its directory, never per frame. As git does by default, the search for the repository stops at a filesystem boundary. The directory is walked as the shell reports it: in a symlink to a directory inside a repository, no branch shows. A repository using the reftable ref backend ( git init --ref-format=reftable ) shows no branch for now. {HistoryLineCount} number of lines in history (only available in primary screen) {Hyperlink} reveals the hyperlink at the given mouse location {LastCommand} how the last command went, from the shell integration's command blocks (OSC 133): ✓ make · 4ms after a success, ✗ exit 8 ctest · 12s after a failure; the status drawn in the success or danger role and the duration in muted , unless the item names a Color= of its own. Empty while a command runs, and when a newer prompt ended one that reported no exit status. A multi-line command's line breaks and tabs read as spaces. The command text is at most MaxWidth= columns (default 32 ), cut at its end with … {InputMode} current input mode (e.g. INSERT, NORMAL, VISUAL); see Hide= and Chip below {ProtectedMode} indicates protected mode, if currently enabled {Scroll} how far the view is scrolled back into the history, out of how far it can be: ↑ 1 240 / 10 000 , thousands grouped by a space. Empty at the bottom, and while the view cannot scroll (the alternate screen) {SearchMode} indicates search highlight mode, if currently active {SearchPrompt} the active search pattern, if any (read-only; search is typed into the find bar) {Selection} how much the selection holds, as y would copy it: 12 lines · 418 chars , thousands grouped by a space ( 1 240 ). Empty without a selection. The characters are those a copy yields: each row up to its last non-blank cell, the spaces between words included, a wide character once. They are counted only while the selection spans fewer than 10 000 cells (its rows at the page's width, or at a rectangle's own width); a larger one shows its lines alone, 1 240 lines {Tabs} indicates active tabs {Text} given text (makes only sense when customized with flags) {Title} current window title {VTType} currently active VT emulation type Formatting Styles # Each Variable, as specified above, can be parametrized for customizing the look of it. The common syntax to these variables and their parameters looks as follows: {VariableName:SomeFlag,SomeKey=SomeValue} So parameters can be specified after a colon ( : ) as a comma separated list of flags and key/value pairs. A key/value pair is further split by equal sign ( = ). The following list of formatting styles are supported: Parameter Description Left=TEXT text to show on the left side, if the variable is to be shown Right=TEXT text to show on the right side, if the variable is to be shown Color=COLOR text color: #RRGGBB , or one of the roles accent , success , danger , warning , muted BackgroundColor=COLOR background color: #RRGGBB , or one of the roles accent , success , danger , warning , muted Bold text in bold font face Italic text in italic font face Underline underline text (only one underline style can be active) CurlyUnderline curly underline text (only one underline style can be active) DoubleUnderline double underline text (only one underline style can be active) DottedUnderline dotted underline text (only one underline style can be active) DashedUnderline dashed underline text (only one underline style can be active) Blinking blinking text RapidBlinking rapid blinking text Overline overline text Inverse inversed text/background coloring These parameters apply to all variables above. {Cwd} , {Context} , {LastCommand} and {UserVar} additionally take this attribute: Parameter Description MaxWidth=N the widest the item may draw, in columns; beyond it the middle is elided and both ends kept. Default 40 for {Cwd} , 32 for {Context} and for {LastCommand} 's command text, which is cut at its end instead, as is {UserVar} 's value (default 40 ); a value that is not a number > 0 keeps the default. A role names a color by what it means rather than by its value, and takes it from the active color scheme when the line is drawn, so it follows a scheme change: accent is palette color 4 (blue), success 2 (green), danger 1 (red), warning 3 (yellow) and muted 8 (bright black). The scheme is the configured one: a program changing the palette (OSC 4) recolours its own text, not the status line. Where a role's color would not read on the bar it is drawn on (at 4.5:1; muted , secondary text, at 3:1), the role's text takes the bar's legible ink instead -- the scheme's foreground or background, bright white, then black or white -- so it stays readable in every input mode and scheme; a #RRGGBB color is drawn as written. Roles are read in any case and written lowercase. A value that is neither a role nor a color leaves the color unset. The same values are accepted by the Tabs attributes ActiveColor and ActiveBackground . The InputMode variable additionally takes these attributes: Parameter Description Hide=<mode> shows nothing, Left= / Right= included, while the terminal is in that mode: Normal , Insert , Visual , VisualLine , VisualBlock or Hint , read in any case. An unknown mode hides the item in none. Chip draws the item, Left= and Right= included, as a chip filled with its mode's colors ( indicatorStatusLine*Mode of the color scheme), while the rest of the line keeps the idle (Insert) colors in every mode. The chip's text takes the fill's legible ink where the scheme's own would not read at 4.5:1. Only the focused pane's chip is colored, and an item naming Color= or BackgroundColor= takes those instead. Without Chip , the whole line takes the mode's colors. They are written after the other attributes: {InputMode:Bold,Left= ,Right= ,Chip,Hide=Insert} The Command variable additionally takes these attributes: Parameter Description Program the command to execute (required, unless the shorthand below is used) Interval seconds between runs; default 10 . An invalid value or one <= 0 selects the default. {Command:Program=git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD,Interval=30,Bold} Shorthand. {Command:<command>} takes everything after Command: verbatim as the command, so it may contain commas and = , but no styling and no Interval= : {Command:git log -1 --format=%h,%s} . A template naming Program= or Interval= is read in the attribute form instead; anything else is the shorthand, so {Command:Bold} runs a program named Bold (a style flag needs Program= ). A command cannot contain } . Execution. Commands run asynchronously in the background, so they never slow down rendering and, on Windows, never open a console window. The item shows the output of the previous run until a new one arrives, and is empty before the first run completes. A command that is still running after 5 seconds (or after its Interval , if that is shorter) is killed together with its child processes, and the previous output is kept. Only the first line of the command's standard output is shown. Standard error and the exit status are ignored, and a command that cannot be started shows the operating system's error message. Unlike popen , background processes a command leaves behind are killed as soon as the command finishes, even when it succeeds (the process group on Unix, the job object on Windows): a command like start notepad starts nothing that outlives it. Tabs formatting extensions # The Tabs key allows additional styling through the following attributes: Parameter Description ActiveColor color of the active tab ActiveBackground background color of the active tab {Tabs} versus the GUI tab bar The indicator status line belongs to a pane , so with split panes a window draws one {Tabs} list per pane rather than one per window — several tab lists side by side, each describing the same tabs. If what you want is the terminal look rather than the placement, set the global ui_style to terminal . That keeps the single window-level tab bar and every one of its affordances (drag to reorder, tear off, rename, close, context menu) but draws it cell-quantized, in the terminal font, with square corners and box-drawing separators. {Tabs} remains fully supported, and the two can be used together. Host-programmable status line # The status line in Contour is an implementation of the DEC VT320 status line feature . Besides the indicator status line described on this page, a second one can be displayed alternatively, which can be written to and fully controlled like the main display. There are not many applications yet doing so, but any application that has fast output but a rarely updating status line, maybe even tmux or screen, could make use of it to trivialize the common use-case. If you consider playing around with it, have a look at the VT sequences DECSASD - Select Active Status Display DECSSDT - Select Status Display (Line) Type The indicator status line itself can be toggled via configuration, e.g.: input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : '.' , action : ToggleStatusLine }
