docs.title: Default chords

docs.text: GNOME Shell takes both pane chords before any window sees them: its default switch-to-workspace-* shortcuts are Ctrl+Alt+Arrow and its move-to-workspace-* shortcuts are Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Arrow . So on GNOME, focusing and swapping panes with the defaults never reaches Contour. Either free the chords in GNOME's Settings › Keyboard › Keyboard Shortcuts › Navigation, or give the pane commands chords of their own in input_mapping , for example on Alt+Arrow and Alt+Shift+Arrow : input_mapping : - { mods : [ Alt ], key : LeftArrow , action : FocusPaneLeft } - { mods : [ Alt ], key : RightArrow , action : FocusPaneRight } - { mods : [ Alt ], key : UpArrow , action : FocusPaneUp } - { mods : [ Alt ], key : DownArrow , action : FocusPaneDown } - { mods : [ Alt , Shift ], key : LeftArrow , action : SwapPaneLeft } - { mods : [ Alt , Shift ], key : RightArrow , action : SwapPaneRight } - { mods : [ Alt , Shift ], key : UpArrow , action : SwapPaneUp } - { mods : [ Alt , Shift ], key : DownArrow , action : SwapPaneDown } Alt+Arrow then no longer reaches the program in the pane, so a shell's word motion on Alt+Left / Right is gone. Alt+Shift+Arrow is the default resize chord: input_mapping is matched in the order it lists its rows, so change the mods of the ResizePane rows a generated configuration writes on [Alt, Shift] , or remove them, for the swap rows to fire.
docs.title: Pane chords on GNOME

docs.text: The menu bar provides ⌘Q (Quit) and ⌘, (Settings…), and ⌘H , ⌥⌘H and ⌘M ; Contour binds none of them by default, so they never reach input_mapping . Ctrl+Shift+letter reaches the program in the terminal, and a ⌘ chord nothing is bound to is consumed rather than typed as its letter. ⌘K clears to the prompt ( ClearToPrompt ) on the primary screen; in the alternate screen it is consumed, so a running vim or tmux is never reset. ClearHistoryAndReset has no macOS default. Font size is on ⌘0 , ⌘- and ⌘+ only; Ctrl+0 reaches the program. ⌘X and ⌘S are deliberately unbound (a terminal cannot cut, and there is nothing to save). The defaults that hang on Ctrl+Alt plus a character answer to ⌃⌘ on macOS instead, because Option composes characters there (see below). ⌥← / ⌥→ move by word ( ESC b / ESC f ) outside the alternate screen, and ⌘← / ⌘→ / ⌘⌫ edit the line, so these shell conventions work out of the box. Inside the alternate screen ⌥← reaches the program as the Alt+Left it is ( CSI 1;3D ).
docs.title: macOS defaults

docs.text: Option has two jobs on a Mac: composing characters ( ⌥E then E gives é) and acting as Alt. The profile setting option_as_alt chooses which Option keys are Alt: off , left , right or both ( true and false are still read as both and off ). One rule applies everywhere: An Option key that option_as_alt names is Alt, for every key: ⌥B sends ESC b , and an Alt+B binding fires. An Option key it does not name composes on any key that has a composed character ( ⌥E , ⌥1 gives ¡) and is Alt only on keys that type nothing (arrows, Return, Backspace, the function keys), so ⌥← and Option+Enter keep working with option_as_alt: off . Because of the second half, a binding of Alt plus a character cannot fire on an Option key that composes. Contour says so when it loads such a binding with option_as_alt set to off or to one side; bind the chord to Primary or Control instead, or name that side in option_as_alt .
docs.title: Option as Alt

docs.text: Each element in the input_mapping represents one key binding, whereas mods represents an array of keyboard modifiers that must be pressed - as well as the key or mouse - in order to activate the corresponding action. Additionally one can filter input mappings based on special terminal modes using the mode option: Alt : The terminal is currently in alternate screen buffer, otherwise it is in primary screen buffer. AppCursor : The application key cursor mode is enabled (otherwise it's normal cursor mode). AppKeypad : The application keypad mode is enabled (otherwise it's the numeric keypad mode). Select : The terminal has currently an active grid cell selection (such as selected text). Insert : The Insert input mode is active, that is the default and one way to test that the input mode is not in normal mode or any of the visual select modes. Search : A search term is currently set. It outlives the find bar, so this stays true for as long as the matches are still highlighted; an open bar with nothing typed into it does not match. Trace : The terminal is currently in trace-mode, i.e., each VT sequence can be interactively single-step executed using custom actions. See TraceEnter/TraceStep/TraceLeave actions. Every condition separated by | must match. Prefix a condition with ~ to require that mode to be inactive. For example, Insert|Select requires both Insert mode and a terminal selection. Omit mode to match regardless of the active modes. To make Ctrl+V paste from the clipboard in Insert mode, including at a prompt with no selection, use the following entry under input_mapping . - { mods : [ Control ], key : V , action : PasteClipboard , mode : Insert } key represents keys on your keyboard, and mouse represents buttons as well as the scroll wheel. Modifiers, which are case-insensitive ( Control , control and CONTROL are the same modifier): Shift Alt Control — may also be written Ctrl Super — may also be written Meta . This is the Windows key on Windows, the Command key on macOS, and the Super key on anything else. Hyper Note Meta is a synonym for Super for historical reasons: contour.yml has spelled the Windows/Command key Meta since before a separate Meta modifier existed. There is currently no configuration spelling for the distinct Meta modifier that the extended CSI u keyboard protocol reports. Primary — the chord an application's own commands hang on: Command ( Super ) on macOS, Control + Shift everywhere else. One row mods: [Primary], key: C, action: CopySelection is therefore Ctrl+Shift+C on Linux and Windows and ⌘C on macOS, and Contour's built-in defaults are written that way. Primary can be combined with further modifiers ( [Primary, Shift] ), and the generated contour.yml spells it Primary wherever a default row uses it, so one file works on every machine you share it between. An entry naming a modifier that is not in this list is rejected as a whole — the binding is dropped rather than bound with a partial chord — and the reason is reported on startup. Keys can be expressed case-insensitively symbolic: APOSTROPHE, ADD, BACKSLASH, COMMA, DECIMAL, DIVIDE, EQUAL, LEFT_BRACKET, MINUS, MULTIPLY, PERIOD, RIGHT_BRACKET, SEMICOLON, SLASH, SUBTRACT, SPACE Enter, Backspace, Tab, Escape, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, DownArrow, LeftArrow, RightArrow, UpArrow, Insert, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, Numpad_Divide, Numpad_Multiply, Numpad_Subtract, Numpad_Add, Numpad_Decimal, Numpad_Enter, Numpad_Equal, Numpad_0, Numpad_1, Numpad_2, Numpad_3, Numpad_4, Numpad_5, Numpad_6, Numpad_7, Numpad_8, Numpad_9 or in case of standard characters, just the character. A single-character key also matches case-insensitively: key: 'q' and key: 'Q' bind the same chord. Shift is carried by mods , not by the letter's case, so writing an uppercase letter does not mean "with Shift" — use mods: [Shift] for that. Mouse buttons can be one of the following self-explanatory ones: Left, Middle, Right, WheelUp, WheelDown, WheelLeft, WheelRight A mouse binding may also name a click count with clicks (1 to 4). Such a binding fires on that click of a multi-click sequence only, and it is consulted before Contour's own double-, triple- and quadruple-click selection, so it replaces that selection for the chord it names: input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control ], mouse : Left , clicks : 3 , action : SelectCommandBlock , target : pointer , part : output } A binding without clicks fires on every press that no clicks binding claimed. Like the selection it replaces, a clicks binding never takes a click that an application asked for, unless the bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier is held. clicks applies to the Left , Middle and Right buttons only: a wheel step is never more than a first click. An entry that gives it to a key or a wheel, or a count other than 1 to 4, is dropped and the reason is reported on startup.
docs.title: Writing bindings

docs.text: These actions re-point the window they fire in at another workspace or daemon (see Switching a window ). Two of them are bound by default. CycleWorkspace is Ctrl+Alt+PageDown / PageUp (Linux, Windows) and ⌃⌘↓ / ⌃⌘↑ (macOS): it shows the next / previous workspace, one level up from the tab chords. MoveWorkspaceDown / MoveWorkspaceUp are the same chords with Shift: they move the current workspace down / up the list. The command palette lists them all under Daemons . They need a window that shows a daemon. Action Key What it does SwitchToWorkspace index: (1-based, required) Shows the Nth workspace of this window's daemon here. NewWorkspace none Creates a workspace and shows it in this window; for a window attached to a daemon, the workspace is created on that daemon. OpenWorkspace index: (1-based, required) Shows it in a new window. CycleWorkspace direction: next\|previous (default next ) Shows the next or previous workspace of this window's daemon here, hidden and left ones included, in their position order. CycleDaemon direction: next\|previous (default next ) Shows the next or previous daemon here: the local daemons running, by name, then the saved hosts a window here shows. SwitchToDaemon name: or host: (exactly one) Shows the named local daemon, or saved host, here. OpenDaemon name: or host: (exactly one) Shows it in a new window. input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : '2' , action : SwitchToWorkspace , index : 2 } - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : PageDown , action : CycleWorkspace , direction : next } - { mods : [ Control , Alt , Shift ], key : RightArrow , action : CycleDaemon , direction : next } - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : A , action : SwitchToDaemon , name : admin } - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : H , action : OpenDaemon , host : home } The cycling actions never wait on a daemon: they step through what was last looked up, and look again in the background for the next press, so the first press after a change (or right after start-up) may still see the earlier list. A binding that gives no index (or 0), an unknown direction , or neither or both of name and host is dropped, and the reason is reported on startup. Until 0.9.0 a binding's label: still loads as name: , with a configuration warning naming the new key. Landing on a daemon with several workspaces opens the switcher popup on that daemon's workspaces, to pick one; Esc there cancels the switch and changes nothing. Action What it does ShowSwitcher Opens the daemon and workspace switcher popup over this window. NewDaemon Asks for a name, starts a local daemon under it, and opens a new window on it. UpgradeDaemon Upgrades this window's local daemon in place, keeping every program running (palette: Upgrade daemon ). The switcher popup lists the daemons under This computer (the local daemons running, by name) and Saved hosts . This window's daemon is expanded; Right expands any other one to its workspaces, each with its tab count and whether it is shown in this window , shown elsewhere , hidden or not shown , plus "+ new workspace on …". A saved host not connected yet says so, and is connected to when it is expanded or chosen. Typing filters the list, Return switches this window to the selected row, Shift+Return opens it in a new window, and Esc closes the popup without changing anything. NewDaemon (also the popup's New daemon… row) refuses a name a socket cannot be named after (letters, digits, - , _ and . only, not starting with a dot, at most 64 characters) right under the field; a name that is already running is offered as "Switch to daemon …" instead of starting a second one. The daemon it starts keeps running when its last window closes, like one started with contour daemon --name . UpgradeDaemon (the palette's Upgrade daemon row) starts a live upgrade of the window's daemon at any time, without the daemon-drift chip: it also upgrades a daemon that runs the same release, to pick up a rebuilt binary. It asks nothing, as an upgrade keeps every program running. It is for the local daemon this client launched on (one started with New daemon… is not); for a remote daemon, one a switch reached, a daemon too old to upgrade in place, or one newer than this client it does nothing but tell you why in a notice. It is not bound to a key by default.
docs.title: Switching daemons and workspaces

docs.text: The workspace sidebar is shown and started by the native2026 defaults ( defaults_edition ), which also bind its chords. A configuration with defaults_edition: classic binds none of them but MoveWorkspaceUp / Down , which every edition binds beside CycleWorkspace . A native2026 configuration written before the sidebar existed still gets them, unless it binds the same chord itself. Action Default (Linux / Windows) Default (macOS) What it does ToggleSidebar Ctrl+Shift+B ⌘\ Shows the sidebar when hidden, hides it when shown. FocusSidebar Ctrl+Shift+D ⇧⌘E Moves keyboard focus into the sidebar, showing it first when hidden. FilterWorkspaces none none Opens the sidebar's filter with the keyboard in it, showing the sidebar first when hidden. JumpToNextAttention Ctrl+Shift+J ⌘J Shows the next pane that needs you: blocked or bell first, then failed, then done and not seen. MarkSeen none none Marks the active pane's output as seen. RenameWorkspace none none Renames the current workspace inline. SetWorkspaceColor none none Colours the current workspace: color: '#RRGGBB' applies that colour; without it, opens the colour picker on the workspace's row in the sidebar. ResetWorkspaceColor none none Takes the current workspace's colour away. MoveWorkspaceUp , MoveWorkspaceDown Ctrl+Shift+Alt+PageUp / PageDown ⌃⇧⌘↑ / ⌃⇧⌘↓ Moves the current workspace one place in the sidebar's list. CloseWorkspace none none Closes the current workspace and everything in it, after asking. The last workspace of an in-process window cannot be closed. GoToPane none none Shows the pane a sidebar row names; a row of the pane menu. MoveTabToWorkspace index: (1-based, required) Moves the current tab into the Nth workspace. NewWorkspace is listed under Switching daemons and workspaces ; the sidebar's ＋ button runs it. The settings are sidebar: { visible, width, tab_color, workspace_color, row_spacing } and tab_placement: sidebar | top ; see the sidebar guide . List of supported actions for key mappings. Action Description CancelSelection Cancels currently active selection, if any. ChangeProfile Changes the profile to the given profile name . ClearHistoryAndReset Clears the history, performs a terminal hard reset and attempts to force a redraw of the currently running application. CopyPreviousMarkRange Copies the most recent range that is delimited by vertical line marks into clipboard. CopySelection Copies the current selection into the clipboard buffer. With fallback: last_command_output and nothing selected, copies what the last command printed instead (requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks). CreateDebugDump Create dump for debug purposes CreateSelection Creates selection with custom delimiters configured via delimiters member. DecreaseFontSize Decreases the font size by 1 pixel. DecreaseOpacity Decreases the default-background opacity by 5%. FocusNextSearchMatch Focuses the next search match (if any). FocusPreviousSearchMatch Focuses the next previous match (if any). FollowHyperlink Follows the hyperlink that is exposed via OSC 8 under the current cursor position. HintMode Activates hint mode: scans the terminal for regex-matched patterns (URLs, file paths, git hashes, etc.), renders short alphabetic labels on each match, and lets the user type a label to act on that match (copy, open, paste). Parameter patterns selects which pattern set to use, hint_action specifies the action (Copy, Open, Paste, CopyAndPaste, Select), and scope selects how much to scan: Visible (the default, the current viewport) or Scrollback (the viewport plus up to hint_scrollback_lines rows of history, whose labels stay put while you scroll to reach them). A pattern that wraps across a line break is matched as one hint. IncreaseFontSize Increases the font size by 1 pixel. IncreaseOpacity Increases the default-background opacity by 5%. NewTerminal Spawns a new terminal at the current terminals current working directory. NewWindowTo Opens the Connect picker as a sheet: choose where the new window's sessions live (this computer's daemon, this window only, a saved host, or a typed ssh:// or tls:// address), then the window opens attached there. NoSearchHighlight Disables current search highlighting, if anything is still highlighted due to a prior search. OpenCommandPalette Opens the command palette: a searchable popup listing every runnable command with its description and key binding. Recently used commands are listed first, then all commands alphabetically. OpenConfiguration Opens the Settings window (profiles, color schemes, global settings). Set in_editor: true on the binding to instead open the configuration file in an external editor. OpenFileManager Opens the current working directory in a system file manager. OpenSelection Open the current terminal selection with the default system application (eg; xdg-open) PasteClipboard Pastes clipboard to standard input. Pass boolean parameter 'strip' to indicate whether or not to strip repetitive whitespaces down to one and newlines to whitespaces. PasteSelection Pastes current selection to standard input.Option evaluate_in_shell specify if pasted text must be appended with linefeed and used as an input for the running shell Quit Quits the application. ReloadConfig Forces a configuration reload. ResetConfig Overwrites current configuration with builtin default configuration and loads it. Attention, all your current configuration will be lost due to overwrite! ResetFontSize Resets font size to what is configured in the config file. ScreenshotVT Takes a screenshot in form of VT escape sequences. SaveScreenshot Takes a screenshot and saves it into a file. CopyScreenshot takes a screenshot and puts it into the system clipboard CollapseAllFolds Collapses every finished command, hiding all of their output (requires shell integration) CollapseLastFold Collapses the most recently finished command, hiding its output ExpandAllFolds Expands every collapsed command again ScrollDown Scrolls down by the multiplier factor. ScrollMarkDown Scrolls one mark down (if none present, bottom of the screen) ScrollMarkUp Scrolls one mark up ScrollOneDown Scrolls down by exactly one line. ScrollOneUp Scrolls up by exactly one line. ScrollPageDown Scrolls a page down. ScrollPageUp Scrolls a page up. ScrollToBottom Scrolls to the bottom of the screen buffer. ScrollToTop Scrolls to the top of the screen buffer. ToggleFold Collapses or expands the command block the cursor is in ToggleFoldAt Collapses or expands the command block covering a given grid line (used by the context menu) ToggleLastFold Collapses or expands the most recently finished command FocusPreviousCommand Focuses the command block before the focused one (else the last one in view), scrolls it into view and announces how it went. FocusNextCommand Focuses the command block after the focused one (else the first one in view), scrolls it into view and announces how it went. SelectPreviousCommandOutput Focuses the previous command block, as FocusPreviousCommand does, and selects its output. SelectNextCommandOutput Focuses the next command block, as FocusNextCommand does, and selects its output. OpenBlockMenu Opens the menu of the focused command block. Bind it with the BlockFocus mode, so the key keeps reaching the application otherwise. ClearCommandBlockFocus Takes the keyboard focus off the command block. Bind it with the BlockFocus mode, so the key keeps reaching the application otherwise. ScrollUp Scrolls up by the multiplier factor. SearchReverse Opens the find bar, searching upwards from the current cursor position. SearchSelection Searches for the selected text: its first line becomes the find bar's pattern, escaped when the bar searches by regular expression. SendChars Writes given characters in chars member to the applications input. ToggleAllKeyMaps Disables/enables responding to all keybinds (this keybind will be preserved when disabling all others). ToggleFullscreen Enables/disables full screen mode. ToggleInputMethodHandling Enables/disables IME (input method editor) handling. ToggleInputProtection Enables/disables terminal input protection. ToggleMouseForwarding Blocks/forwards mouse events to applications that track the mouse, until a profile switch or a configuration reload re-imposes the profile's mouse_forwarding. ToggleStatusLine Shows/hides the VT320 compatible Indicator status line. ToggleTitleBar Shows/Hides titlebar TraceBreakAtEmptyQueue Executes any pending VT sequence from the VT sequence buffer in trace mode, then waits. TraceEnter Enables trace mode, suspending execution until explicitly requested to continue (See TraceLeave and TraceStep). TraceLeave Disables trace mode. Any pending VT sequence will be flushed out and normal execution will be resumed. TraceStep Executes a single VT sequence that is to be executed next. ViNormalMode Enters/Leaves Vi-like normal mode. The cursor can then be moved via h/j/k/l movements in normal mode and text can be selected via v , yanked via y , and clipboard pasted via p . WriteScreen Writes VT sequence in chars member to the screen (bypassing the application). CreateNewTab Creates a new tab in the terminal emulator. CloseTab Closes current tab. MoveTabTo Moves current tab to the given position (starting at number 1). MoveTabToLeft Moves current tab to the left. MoveTabToRight Moves current tab to the right. SwitchToTab Switch to absolute tab position (starting at number 1) SwitchToPreviousTab Switch to the previously focused tab SwitchToTabLeft Switch to tab to the left SwitchToTabRight Switch to tab to the right RenameTab Rename the current tab inline (opens the tab's name editor). Its old name SetTabTitle still loads until 0.9.0. SplitVertical Splits the active pane into two side-by-side panes (a vertical divider). SplitHorizontal Splits the active pane into two stacked panes (a horizontal divider). ClosePane Closes the active pane (or the tab if it is the last pane). FocusPaneLeft Moves pane focus to the left. FocusPaneRight Moves pane focus to the right. FocusPaneUp Moves pane focus up. FocusPaneDown Moves pane focus down. SwapPaneLeft Swaps the active pane with its left neighbor. SwapPaneRight Swaps the active pane with its right neighbor. SwapPaneUp Swaps the active pane with its upper neighbor. SwapPaneDown Swaps the active pane with its lower neighbor. MovePaneLeft Moves the active pane past its left neighbor. MovePaneRight Moves the active pane past its right neighbor. MovePaneUp Moves the active pane past its upper neighbor. MovePaneDown Moves the active pane past its lower neighbor. ToggleSplitOrientation Flips the orientation of the active pane's split (horizontal <-> vertical). TogglePaneZoom Zooms the active pane so it alone fills the tab, hiding its siblings; toggles back to the tiled layout. While zoomed, moving pane focus keeps the zoom and shows the newly focused pane. NewWorkspace Creates a workspace and shows it in this window; the one shown before keeps running, hidden. On a window attached to a daemon the daemon creates it; a window attached to a tmux server refuses. ResizePane Grows or shrinks the active pane in the given direction (by an optional percent). LaunchLayout Opens a named layout, appending its tabs to the current window. SaveLayout Saves the current window's tabs as a named layout in layouts.yml. Without a name it opens a prompt to type one in (which is how the command palette offers it). AttachToHost Opens a new window attached to the saved host name (see hosts: ). OpenContextMenu Opens the terminal pane's context menu. Bound to the right mouse button by default, and only fired when the running application has not asked for the mouse itself (hold Shift to open it anyway). SelectAll Selects everything the terminal holds: the whole scrollback and the whole screen. SoftReset Performs a terminal soft reset (DECSTR): resets modes, rendition and cursor state, while keeping the screen contents and the scrollback. CopyLastCommandPrompt Copies the prompt line(s) of the most recently finished command into the clipboard. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks (see Contour's shell integration). CopyLastCommandOutput Copies what the most recently finished command printed into the clipboard. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks (see Contour's shell integration). CopyLastCommandBlock Copies both the prompt and the output of the most recently finished command into the clipboard. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks (see Contour's shell integration). CopyHyperlink Copies the URI of the hyperlink under the mouse cursor into the clipboard. SetTabColor Colorize the current tab. Without a color, this opens the tab's color picker; with one (e.g. color: '#ff0000') it applies that color right away. ResetTabColor Removes the color you gave the current tab, restoring its default look (or the color the running application assigned, if it assigned one). CloseAllTabs Closes every tab in this window. With only one window open, that closes Contour. SetTabBarVisibility Sets when this window's tab bar is shown (mode: always, never or multiple). Applies to this window until it is closed; the settings page is where the choice is made permanent. SetTabBarPosition Places this window's tab bar above or below the terminal (position: top or bottom). Applies to this window until it is closed; the settings page is where the choice is made permanent. SpeakSelection Reads the selected text aloud through the operating system's speech synthesizer. Available only where a speech engine and a voice are installed. StopSpeaking Stops reading aloud. SelectCommandBlock Selects one part of a command block as whole lines (target: pointer, cursor or last; part: output, input or all). Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. CopyCommandBlock Copies one part of a command block into the clipboard as plain text (target: pointer, cursor or last; part: output, input or all). Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. CopyCommandLine Copies the command line of a command block into the clipboard, with the control characters that would be unsafe to paste removed (target: pointer, cursor or last). Requires a shell that reports its command lines (OSC 133;C cmdline_url). RerunCommand Runs the command line of a command block again: typed at the shell's prompt and entered, once the command it would run has been shown and confirmed (target: pointer, cursor or last). Requires a shell that marks its prompts (OSC 133) and reports or shows its command lines; refused while a command is running, and for a command line that cannot be typed as it is. ToggleCommandFold Collapses or expands a command block's output (target: pointer, cursor or last). Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks, and folding to be enabled. ClearToPrompt Clears the scrollback and the screen above the current prompt. A prompt on the screen moves to its top, with a running command's output; one in the scrollback becomes the oldest line kept. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. OpenCommandOutput Opens a command's output in a pager (target: pointer, cursor or last; program: the pager, read as command_blocks.pager is, which it replaces when given; placement: split, tab or detached; format: sgr or plain, by default command_blocks.pager_format for the configured pager and sgr for a named program). Detached pipes plain text into the program's standard input instead of opening a pane, and is the one placement a daemon-attached session offers. Requires a shell that emits OSC 133 marks. CloseOtherTabs Closes every tab in this window except the current one. CloseTabsToRight Closes every tab to the right of the current one. MoveTabToNewWindow Moves the current tab into a new window of its own. Does nothing with a single tab. ShowAbout Shows the version of Contour. MinimizeWindow Minimizes this window. ZoomWindow Maximizes this window, or restores it when it is maximized (the macOS Zoom). FocusNextArea Moves keyboard focus to the next area of the window: terminal, tabs, toolbar, and back. FocusPreviousArea Moves keyboard focus to the previous area of the window: terminal, toolbar, tabs, and back. FocusToolbar Moves keyboard focus to the window's toolbar. ToggleSidebar Shows the workspace sidebar when it is hidden, and hides it when it is shown. FocusSidebar Moves keyboard focus into the workspace sidebar, showing it first when it is hidden. FilterWorkspaces Opens the workspace sidebar's filter with the keyboard in it, showing the sidebar first when it is hidden. JumpToNextAttention Shows the next pane that needs you: one that waits for input, or whose command failed. MarkSeen Marks the output of the active pane as seen. RenameWorkspace Renames the current workspace inline. MoveWorkspaceUp Moves the current workspace one place up in the sidebar's list. MoveWorkspaceDown Moves the current workspace one place down in the sidebar's list. CloseWorkspace Closes the current workspace and everything in it, after asking. The last workspace of a window that runs its sessions in-process cannot be closed. SetWorkspaceColor Colorize the current workspace. Without a color, this opens the workspace's color picker; with one (e.g. color: '#c2548f') it applies that color right away. ResetWorkspaceColor Removes the color you gave the current workspace, restoring its default look. GoToPane Shows the pane a sidebar row names and focuses it. MoveTabToWorkspace Moves the current tab into the workspace at the 1-based position index of this window's list. MoveToTab Moves the current pane into another tab, as a split beside its active pane: the tab at the 1-based position tab of the workspace at the 1-based position workspace of this window's list. MoveToNewTab Moves the current pane into a tab of its own, at the end of its workspace. MoveToNewWorkspace Moves the current pane into a workspace of its own, named as a new workspace is. SwitchToWorkspace Shows the workspace at the 1-based position index of this window's daemon in this window. Hidden workspaces are not counted. Does nothing for a window that runs its sessions in-process. OpenWorkspace Shows the workspace at the 1-based position index of this window's daemon in a new window. Does nothing for a window that runs its sessions in-process. CycleWorkspace Shows the next ( direction: next , the default) or previous ( direction: previous ) workspace of this window's daemon in this window, wrapping around. CycleDaemon Shows the next ( direction: next , the default) or previous ( direction: previous ) daemon in this window: the local daemons by name, then the saved hosts some window shows; wrapping around. SwitchToDaemon Shows the daemon named by name (a local daemon) or host (a saved host, see hosts: ) in this window. A binding that names neither, or both, is dropped. OpenDaemon Shows the daemon named by name (a local daemon) or host (a saved host, see hosts: ) in a new window. A binding that names neither, or both, is dropped. ShowSwitcher Opens the popup to switch this window to another daemon or workspace, or to open one in a new window. NewDaemon Asks for a name, starts a new local daemon of that name and shows it in this window. UpgradeDaemon Upgrades this window's local daemon in place, keeping every program running, even when the daemon already runs this release (to pick up a rebuilt binary). Refused for a remote daemon, or one this client did not start or launch on. docs.text: Layouts # A layout is a named set of tabs that are opened together. Each tab can change into a directory, run a specific command instead of your shell, carry a name and a color, and optionally be split into a tree of panes. Layouts let you reproduce a working set of tabs — for example an editor, a chat/agent tool, and a couple of monitoring panes — with a single action instead of opening and arranging them by hand every time. Configuration # Layouts are configured under the top-level layouts entry, a map of layout name to its list of tabs . An optional top-level default_layout names a layout to open automatically at startup instead of the usual single default tab. layouts : work : tabs : - name : "editor" color : "#d75f00" directory : "~/proj/foo" command : "nvim" arguments : [ "." ] profile : "dark-big" - name : "claude" color : "#00af5f" directory : "~/proj/foo" command : "claude" - name : "servers" split : orientation : vertical panes : - { command : "npm run dev" , directory : "~/proj/foo" , ratio : 0.6 } - split : orientation : horizontal panes : - { command : "htop" } - { command : "journalctl -f" } dev : tabs : - name : "shell" directory : "~/proj/bar" default_layout : work Tab options # Each entry under tabs describes either a single-pane tab (leaf fields) or a split tab (a split node). A tab uses leaf fields or split , not both. Option Description name Optional. The tab's name, as Rename… sets it. Until 0.9.0 the older key title is read as name , with a warning. color Optional. Hex in '#RRGGBB' form (e.g. '#d75f00' ); sets the tab's user color. directory Optional working directory for the tab. Falls back to the profile's configured directory when omitted. command Optional. Replaces the shell — the program to run in the pane. May be a full command line (see Command lines below). When omitted, the effective profile's shell is used. arguments Optional list of extra arguments, appended after any arguments already given in command . profile Optional per-tab profile override (see Per-tab profile below). split Optional. Turns the tab into a split node instead of a single pane; see Split panes . Command lines # command may be written as a full command line. It is kept as written and read when the pane starts, the way a profile's shell is read: when it names a program to run — a file at that path, or a name found on PATH — it runs as it is, spaces and all; otherwise its first word is the program and the rest are its arguments. So both of these are equivalent: - command : "emacs -nw" # is the same as - command : "emacs" arguments : [ "-nw" ] How the words are read depends on the platform: On Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, as a POSIX shell reads them: whitespace separates words; double quotes ( "..." , allowing \" and \\ ) or single quotes ( '...' , literal) keep spaces inside one word; a backslash outside quotes escapes the next character. On Windows, as CreateProcess reads a command line: the program runs up to the first space at which what precedes it names a program — so C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe --login runs bash.exe — or up to its closing double quote, and a backslash separates directories. What follows the program is handed to it as written, for it to split itself: cmd.exe /s /c ""C:\Tools x\app.exe" --flag" reaches cmd.exe unchanged. A program path with spaces in it that names no file is split like any other command line; quote it to keep it whole — e.g. command: '"/opt/My App/bin/foo" --flag' . In the Flatpak build, where a pane runs on the host, Contour cannot see the host's files: a command holding whitespace is always read as a command line there, so quote a program path with spaces in it. Any entries in a separate arguments: list are passed after the words of command . ${NAME} inside command or arguments expands to the environment variable NAME . To pass a literal ${...} through to the program (e.g. for template tooling), escape it as $${...} . SaveLayout (below) writes command: back as the pane was started with it, and arguments: after it — escaping any literal ${ — so everything round-trips. Split panes # A split node replaces the leaf fields ( command , directory , ...) with: Option Description orientation vertical or horizontal (case-insensitive). vertical arranges panes side by side; horizontal stacks them. panes A list of child panes. Each child is either a leaf (with command , directory , arguments , profile , ratio ) or another split node, nested recursively. ratio Optional, set on a child pane/split. The fraction of the parent split's space (between 0 and 1) that child occupies; children without a ratio share the remaining space equally. In the example above, ratio: 0.6 gives the first pane 60% and leaves 40% for its unspecified sibling. Splits can be nested arbitrarily deep, as shown in the servers tab of the example above: a vertical split whose second pane is itself a horizontal split. Per-tab profile # A tab (or an individual pane) may set profile to use a different profile than the window's own profile for that tab/pane. The override is terminal-level only — it affects things like the shell, fonts, colors, and scrollback of that pane. Window-level settings (window size, decorations, and similar) always come from the profile that launched the window itself. Opening a layout # There are four ways to open a layout: At startup # Set default_layout to a layout name; it opens automatically when Contour starts, replacing the usual single default tab. default_layout : work From the command line # Pass --layout NAME to open a layout in the newly launched window: contour terminal --layout work From a keybinding # Bind the LaunchLayout action to a key, passing the layout's name : input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : L , action : LaunchLayout , name : work } Unlike the startup and CLI cases, LaunchLayout appends the layout's tabs to the current window rather than opening a new one. From the command palette # Open the command palette ( Ctrl+Shift+P by default) and pick the Launch Layout: name entry — one is listed for every saved layout, so no keybinding is required. Picking one appends that layout's tabs to the current window, exactly like the LaunchLayout action. Saving the current window as a layout # The SaveLayout action captures the active window's current tabs and panes — their directories, the command each pane was started with, names, colors, and split structure — and writes them out as a named layout. input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : S , action : SaveLayout , name : work } SaveLayout never modifies your hand-written configuration file. Instead it writes a machine-managed layouts.yml file next to your main configuration file, in the same directory. Layouts from layouts.yml are merged with any layouts defined inline in your main configuration; if a name exists in both, the layouts.yml version wins, since it reflects the most recently saved state. You don't need a keybinding to save: open the command palette ( Ctrl+Shift+P ) and pick Save Layout . Because saving needs a name, that entry opens a small prompt for you to type one in, then saves exactly as the SaveLayout action does. A key bound to SaveLayout with no name opens the same prompt. Tab colors # A tab's color is what makes it findable in a long tab bar. A new tab takes the tab_color of the profile it starts with: profiles : main : tab_color : '#2E3440' Like a layout's color , tab_color is a hex '#RRGGBB' value; null , the default, means no color. A color from a layout, one an application sets for its own tab, or one you pick from the tab's context menu takes precedence over the profile's, and clearing it brings the profile's color back. A split tab keeps the color of the profile that created it.

Because saving needs a name, that entry opens a small prompt for you to type one in, then saves exactly as the SaveLayout action does. A key bound to SaveLayout with no name opens the same prompt.

docs.text: A tab's color is what makes it findable in a long tab bar. A new tab takes the tab_color of the profile it starts with: profiles : main : tab_color : '#2E3440' Like a layout's color , tab_color is a hex '#RRGGBB' value; null , the default, means no color. A color from a layout, one an application sets for its own tab, or one you pick from the tab's context menu takes precedence over the profile's, and clearing it brings the profile's color back. A split tab keeps the color of the profile that created it.
docs.title: Tab colors

docs.text: Links in Terminal Output # Contour underlines URLs, file paths and patterns you define in the output of your programs, the way it shows OSC 8 hyperlinks , about 100 ms after the output goes quiet. Ctrl +click opens them. profiles : main : hyperlink_decoration : mode : always # always | hover | modifier | never normal : dotted-underline hover : underline link_detection : primary_screen : { urls : true , file_paths : true } other_screens : { urls : true , file_paths : false } file_opener : command : 'code --goto {path}:{line}:{column}' placement : detached # detached | split | tab hint_patterns : - name : url clickable : false # stops underlining URLs: a built-in, changed by its name alone - name : jira regex : '\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+\b' clickable : true url : 'https://jira.example.com/browse/{0}' Everything here has a default, so a configuration without any of these keys detects links as described below. What is detected # URLs with the schemes http , https , ftp , file and mailto . Trailing punctuation is left out of the link, so the full stop after a URL at the end of a sentence is not part of it; a closing bracket the URL opened itself is kept, as in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_(bar) . A file:// URL is the file it names, and is a path in all that follows: underlined only once it is found on this machine, and opened as a file is. Contour never runs it; without a file_opener it goes to the application your system associates with it, which on Windows and macOS may run a program. File paths : absolute ( /usr/include/stdio.h , C:\Users\me\notes.txt ), relative ( src/main.cpp , ../build/log.txt ), home-relative ( ~/notes.md ), and bare file names ( Makefile , main.cpp ). A location printed after a path, :line[:column] or (line[,column]) as compilers print them, is kept and passed on when the file is opened. Patterns of your own , see below . A path is underlined only once Contour has checked that it exists on this machine. A relative path is resolved against the directory of the command that printed it, which the shell reports through shell integration (OSC 133 and OSC 7), so a cd since then does not change what an earlier command's output names. A path printed by a command that ran on another machine, over ssh or in a container, names a file there and is never underlined, once Contour can tell: the remote shell reports the directory it runs in, with its host, through its own shell integration (OSC 7). Without that, everything an ssh session prints belongs to the local ssh command, and its paths are looked up on this machine. Where links are detected # link_detection switches the automatic detection per screen. OSC 8 hyperlinks are always links, and hint mode always offers everything; only the underlining of text found by scanning is affected. Key Default Meaning primary_screen.urls true URLs and your own patterns on the shell screen primary_screen.file_paths true file paths on the shell screen other_screens.urls true URLs and patterns on the alternate screen other_screens.file_paths false file paths on the alternate screen other_screens covers the alternate screen (vim, less, htop, ...) and every further page. A key you leave out keeps its default, or the value it inherits from a parent profile. Your own patterns follow the urls switch, unless they open a file: URL, which follows the file_paths switch. When links are shown # hyperlink_decoration decides when links are decorated, for OSC 8 hyperlinks and detected links alike: mode Links are decorated always always (the default) hover only the one under the mouse pointer modifier all of them while the modifier of Ctrl+click is held never never; Ctrl+click still opens them normal is the decoration of a link at rest and hover the one of the link under the pointer. Each is one of underline , dotted-underline , double-underline , curly-underline , dashed-underline , overline , crossed-out , framed and encircle . The colours of both live in the colour scheme, see hyperlink_decoration . Opening links # Ctrl+click : the FollowHyperlink mouse binding. Inside an application that uses the mouse itself, such as vim or tmux with mouse support, add the global bypass_mouse_protocol_modifier (Shift by default): Shift+Ctrl+click. The context menu : right-click a link for Open Link and Copy Link Address . Vi normal mode : gx opens the link under the cursor, and ]x / [x move the cursor to the next / previous link (see Input Modes ). Hint mode : gH in vi normal mode, or a HintMode binding with hint_action: Open (see Hint Mode ). A web URL opens in your browser. A path, or a file:// URL, opens as what it names: a directory in your file manager, and a file with file_opener , or with the application your system associates with it. That application is the system's choice: on Windows and macOS, a program it is handed may run. file_opener # file_opener says how a detected file opens. The string form is the command alone; the map form adds where it runs: profiles : main : file_opener : 'code --goto {path}:{line}:{column}' profiles : main : file_opener : command : 'nvim +{line} {path}' placement : split # detached (the default), split or tab {path} is the file's absolute path, {line} and {column} the location printed after it, 1 where none was printed. No shell is involved: the command line is split into arguments once, and each placeholder is filled in inside its own argument, so a file name with spaces or quotes in it stays one argument and cannot run anything. placement: detached starts the command as a program of its own; split and tab run it in a new Contour pane, in the directory a relative path was resolved against or, for an absolute path, the file's own directory. A directory always opens in the file manager. Without file_opener , a file opens with the system's default application. Write the program out, without a placeholder. A program path with a space in it is read as one program where that path exists on this machine; where it does not, or under flatpak with escape_sandbox , it is split at the space. Use a wrapper script on a path without spaces in that case. On Windows, name an .exe as the program. A .cmd or .bat file is run by cmd.exe , which parses its command line again, so a file name could change what it runs. Your own clickable patterns # The patterns of hint mode , hint_patterns , are detected in output too when you say so: profiles : main : hint_patterns : - name : jira regex : '\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+\b' clickable : true url : 'https://jira.example.com/browse/{0}' - name : commit regex : '\b[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b' clickable : true url : 'https://github.com/contour-terminal/contour/commit/{0}' clickable: true detects the pattern in output, decorates it and opens it with Ctrl+click. Your own patterns are hint-mode-only unless they say so. url is what is opened: {0} is the whole match, {1} to {9} its capture groups. Without it, the match is opened as printed. A url naming a group the regex does not have is reported when the configuration is loaded and disables the pattern. Where the printed text chooses the scheme, there is a link only for a scheme Contour opens in URLs it finds itself: http , https , ftp , mailto or file . That is so without a url , and with a url that does not start with a scheme of its own, such as {0} or {1}:{2} . Printed text cannot open a smb: share or a ms-msdt: handler. A url that writes its scheme itself, as https://jira.example.com/browse/{0} does, may open any scheme: you chose it. Hint mode still offers such a match, to copy, and opens nothing. A group is percent-encoded only where a URL cannot hold a character: spaces, control characters and "#<>[\]^`{|} . / ? & = + @ : % pass through, so a group placed in a query can add parameters, and one placed before the host can change it. Write the scheme and the host in the template, groups after them. An entry named like a built-in ( url , filepath , githash , ipv4 , ipv6 ) changes only the keys it gives, and may leave out its regex . A built-in takes no url ; a url given to one is reported and ignored. profiles : main : hint_patterns : - name : filepath clickable : false # stop underlining paths; hint mode still offers them A regex that overrides filepath names the path with capture group 1, and its location with groups 2 and 3 ( :line[:column] ) and 4 and 5 ( (line[,column]) ). Patterns are ECMAScript regular expressions, with these limits: Back-references ( \1 to \9 ) are not supported: a pattern using one is reported when the configuration is loaded and disabled, on every platform. A non-ASCII character inside […] matches byte by byte, not as one character; such a pattern is reported with a warning. On Linux, Contour is built with libstdc++, whose matcher runs breadth-first: where one alternative's match is a prefix of another's at the same place, as in foo|foobar , it takes the longer one, and lazy quantifiers may stop elsewhere, where macOS (libc++) and Windows take the first alternative ECMAScript names. Write patterns whose result does not depend on which alternative or which repetition count wins. A clickable pattern must not match the empty string; one that can is disabled. The settings page # Under Profiles , the Links group holds Show links ( hyperlink_decoration.mode ), Normal style , Hover style , Open files with ( file_opener.command ) and Open in ( file_opener.placement ). The Links: opening and patterns section names the gesture that opens links and lists the patterns: the built-ins, whose Clickable switch you can change, and the profile's own, which you can add, edit and remove. Below the list, a sample text shows what the selected pattern finds, checked and matched as the terminal does; a problem with a pattern is shown under it. Performance # Detection stays off the path the terminal reads output on: The output is scanned once it has gone quiet, at most once a second under continuous output, on a background thread. The parser never runs a pattern. Whether a path exists is checked on a thread of its own, so a slow network mount delays the underlines and nothing else.

docs.text: Path Handling in Configuration # Contour supports special syntax in configuration file paths to make configs portable across machines and platforms. Tilde Expansion # Use ~ at the start of a path to refer to the user's home directory: profiles : main : shell : initial_working_directory : ~/workspace On Linux/macOS this expands to e.g. /home/user/workspace , on Windows to C:\Users\user\workspace . Environment Variable Expansion # Use ${VAR_NAME} to reference environment variables: color_schemes : default : background_image : path : '${HOME}/Pictures/terminal-bg.png' This resolves ${HOME} to its value at config load time. Multiple Variables # You can use several variables in the same value: profiles : main : shell : program : '${MY_SHELL_DIR}/${MY_SHELL_NAME}' Combining with Tilde # Environment variables are expanded before tilde resolution, so both syntaxes compose correctly: profiles : main : shell : initial_working_directory : '~/${PROJECT_DIR}' This first resolves ${PROJECT_DIR} (e.g. to workspace ), then resolves ~ to the home directory, yielding /home/user/workspace . Where Expansion Applies # The following configuration values support both ~ and ${VAR} expansion: Configuration value Example background_image.path '${HOME}/Pictures/bg.png' shell.program '${MY_SHELL}' shell.arguments (each entry) '--config=${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/shell.conf' shell.initial_working_directory '~/${PROJECT_DIR}' Any std::filesystem::path config entry General file path values Cross-Platform Configuration # A primary motivation for environment variable expansion is writing configs that work on multiple operating systems without modification: # Works on both Linux and Windows — no hardcoded paths color_schemes : default : background_image : path : '${HOME}/Pictures/terminal-bg.png' profiles : main : shell : initial_working_directory : '${HOME}/projects' Edge Cases # Undefined variables expand to an empty string and a warning is logged. Malformed markers like ${UNCLOSED (missing closing } ) pass through the string unchanged — no partial substitution occurs. No markers — strings without any ${...} syntax are passed through unchanged.
