docs.text: The Settings Window # Settings opens in a window of its own, one per application, from Settings… in the Contour menu ( ⌘ + , on macOS, Ctrl + Shift + , elsewhere), from the command palette, or with the OpenConfiguration binding. Asking for it again brings the open window forward, and it reopens on the page it was left on. The sidebar lists five sections, then your profiles, then Edit contour.yml… , which opens the file in your editor. A search field above them finds a row by its label, then its help text, then its key, in any case. Section What it holds General Windows, the command palette, and the advanced global options such as the rendering GPU. Appearance Window chrome, the tab bar, and whether tabs sit in it or in the workspace sidebar. Keyboard Key bindings, as a list. Shell Integration What shell integration draws: the gutter, command blocks and folding. Profiles One page per profile: colors, window, text, scrolling, behaviour, cursor, bell, background, links, status line and more. A profile's page has a live preview at its top: a small terminal that shows the profile's font, size and colors, and follows every change before it is written. Colors , Links and Status Line open as pages of their own from the profile, and the Status Line fields are on both the profile's page and the Status Line page. Every change applies at once # There is no Apply or Save button. A change takes effect in every terminal that uses the profile, in every window, and is written to disk within about 300 ms of the last edit. Revert Changes , at the top right, undoes everything changed since the window opened, and is disabled until something has. Settings writes only the files it owns: settings.yml for the global options, profiles/<name>.yml for each profile it edits, and colorschemes/<name>.yml for each color scheme. It never writes contour.yml . Each write replaces the whole file at once, so a crash never leaves half of one. A file you edited meanwhile is never overwritten. If an editor saves a profile while Settings has it open, Settings writes nothing, shows the version on disk, and says which file changed. That includes a file saved in a state that does not parse: it stays as you left it until you fix it. Profiles and color schemes defined in contour.yml are read-only. The page says "Defined in contour.yml" and offers Duplicate to Edit , which makes a copy Settings can change. With gui_config_locked: true every control is disabled and nothing is written; a banner says why. A change that cannot be applied (a value the loader would reject, or a folder you cannot write to) is refused with the reason, and the control goes on showing the value in effect. Names for new profiles and color schemes follow the rules of every system the configuration may travel to, so they cannot contain path separators or .. and, because a configuration directory may be copied to Windows, may not be one of its reserved device names such as con , aux or nul . A profiles/aux.yml or nul.yml you already have on Linux still loads, can be edited and deleted. Colors # The Colors page picks the color scheme (one for both appearances, or one for light and one for dark) from a gallery of every scheme with its eight ANSI colors. New scheme and Duplicate to Edit create a scheme; a scheme made in Settings can be renamed and deleted. Renaming moves every profile that draws with it. A scheme a profile defined in contour.yml draws with cannot be renamed or deleted here, and neither can one that is still in use. Every color well shows its contrast against the background and says whether it passes, so a scheme whose ink does not read is found while you make it. A scheme file that does not parse is never renamed over: open it and fix it first. Links and Status Line # The Links page edits hint_patterns with a preview line that shows what each pattern underlines, as described in Links . The Status Line page edits the indicator status line's segments with a preview of the bar, as described in the indicator status line . Option as Alt on macOS # option_as_alt takes off , left , right or both , so that one Option key can type accents (é, ü) while the other acts as Alt. In Settings it is the Use Option as Meta row on the Keyboard group of a profile. true and false in an existing file are still read, as both and off .

docs.text: Command blocks # With shell integration installed, every command you run becomes a command block : the prompt you typed it at and the output it printed. For each block Contour remembers the command line, how it ended, when it started, how long it took and the directory it ran in — for the last 1000 commands by default ( command_blocks.max_records ), even after their output has scrolled out of the history. Most of this page is built on those records. Without shell integration — and without OSC 3008 , which systemd 258 and later send on their own — there are no command blocks: no block marks in the gutter or on the scrollbar, no sticky header and no finish notifications. Line numbers, timestamps and user marks work either way. The gutter # The strip left of the grid holds up to three columns, each switched on by configuration. Its width depends only on the configuration, never on what is on screen — a gutter that grew would resize the page mid-command. On the alternate screen of a full-screen program such as vim, less or htop it keeps its width and stays empty. Column Shows Configured by Default Timestamps when each line was first reached gutter.timestamps , gutter.timestamp_format off Line numbers absolute, relative or hybrid numbers gutter.line_numbers , gutter.line_number_width off Block column fold controls, exit status, user marks folding.show_markers , gutter.exit_status , gutter.user_marks on gutter : exit_status : true user_marks : true line_numbers : hybrid line_number_width : 6 timestamps : true timestamp_format : "%H:%M:%S" The block column # One cell per line, beside the grid, showing the first of these that applies: Mark Where Meaning boxed minus / boxed plus a prompt line the block's output is shown / collapsed; click to toggle ◆ any other line a user mark ( mm in Vi normal mode) │ , ┕ the output the extent of the block ▸ a prompt line the command is still running ● a prompt line the command finished without output to fold — or, with folding.show_markers: false , finished at all A block's marks take the color of how its command ended, from the color scheme's block_status colors: neutral for success, red for a failure, yellow while it runs. With gutter.exit_status: false the column keeps the plain fold-marker color and draws neither ▸ nor ●; with gutter.user_marks: false it draws no ◆. The column is there while any of the three is on. Hover the block column to see the block's exit code (and the signal that ended it, named by OSC 3008 or by a 128 + n exit status), its duration, start time, directory and command line. Line numbers # gutter.line_numbers works like vim's number and relativenumber : Value vim Cursor line Other lines off nonu nornu — — absolute nu its number their numbers relative rnu 0 distance from the cursor line hybrid nu rnu its number distance from the cursor line An absolute number counts rows from the first row of the session, including rows that have since left the history, so a row keeps its number while the history scrolls away. Resizing the window re-wraps the lines and renumbers the rows below the top. A relative distance counts the rows you see: a collapsed block counts as one row, exactly as j and k do, so 12k lands on the row labeled 12. The cursor is the Vi-mode cursor while Vi mode is on, and the terminal's cursor otherwise. gutter.line_number_width (3 to 10, default 6) is the column count; a longer number shows its last digits after … . Timestamps # gutter.timestamps: true shows beside each line the local time output first reached it. gutter.timestamp_format is a std::format chrono format such as %H:%M:%S (the default) or %H:%M . It must begin with a % conversion, and every character it spells must take exactly one column; a format that cannot be used is reported when the configuration loads, and the default is kept. A line shows its time only where it differs from the line above, so a burst of output does not repeat the same second all the way down. Recording the time costs no memory per line. Folding # A finished command's output can be collapsed to its prompt line (see folding ): click its fold control in the block column, or use the ToggleFold , ToggleLastFold , CollapseLastFold , CollapseAllFolds and ExpandAllFolds actions. A collapsed block says how much it hides — 1,234 lines hidden ⌄ — after its prompt; that chip is drawn over the page and is never selected or copied. In Vi normal mode, vim's fold keys work: Key Action za toggle the block under the cursor zo open it zc close it zM close every block zR open every block Unlike vim's, these know one fold level only, take no count, and work in normal mode alone; zn , zN and zi do not exist. With folding.enabled: false , za , zc and zM do nothing, while zo and zR still open what is collapsed. The rail, the chip and the block menu # On the native chrome styles each block gets a rail : a thin strip after the line numbers and timestamps, beside the block's rows. It is neutral for a success (a ✓ appears while the pointer is over the block), red with a ✗ for a failure, and the accent colour with a ▸ while the command runs. The strip has a fixed width, so the page never changes size when a block starts or ends. The ui_style: terminal row keeps the block column described above. The chip. Right of a finished command's prompt, in cells that are blank, a small pill says how it went — Failed · exit 1 · 0.0 s — and a running command's pill ticks. The pill is placed only where it covers nothing: a prompt with an RPROMPT keeps it, and a prompt filling the whole row shows the rail's mark alone, with the details in the block menu and read out by screen readers. A folded block's chip says 80 lines hidden ⌄ ; clicking it expands the block. The menu. A ⋯ button beside the block, or a right-click on it, opens a native menu whose header names the command and how it ended, above Copy Output , Copy Command , Rerun , Open in Pager and Collapse Output . The block's tooltip is gone; the header carries what it said. Keyboard. Cmd+Up and Cmd+Down (macOS) step through the blocks and announce each one; Shift+Cmd+Up and Shift+Cmd+Down also select its output. Ctrl+Enter or Shift+F10 opens the focused block's menu, Enter toggles its fold, Escape leaves the block, and typing reaches the shell again. The actions are FocusPreviousCommand , FocusNextCommand , SelectPreviousCommandOutput , SelectNextCommandOutput , OpenBlockMenu , ClearCommandBlockFocus and ToggleCommandFold , and the keys are free to rebind; while a block holds the focus the input mode BlockFocus is on. Ending a session with a command still running closes its block as abandoned: no ▸, no tick and no finish notification stay behind, and a restarted pane starts with no blocks. Scrollbar marks # The scrollbar marks where commands are, so a failure far up the history is one glance — and one click — away. Clicking a mark scrolls its line to the top, opening its block if that was collapsed. Marks that fall on the same pixel merge, the most important winning: a failure, then a running command, then a user mark, then any other command. A failure is a solid tick, a running command a hollow one, and a search match ( search_matches ) a yellow one. A command's mark takes its block_status color. profiles : main : scrollbar : marks : [ failures , commands , user_marks , running , search_matches ] # [] turns the marks off The scrollbar is shown on the right by default, so the marks are there from the start. It floats over the edge of the terminal without taking a column away, and appears only once there is history to scroll through. That default applies to new configurations. Contour writes out its full default configuration on first run, so a contour.yml written by an earlier version still says position: Hidden and shows neither the scrollbar nor its marks. Set position: Right to see them, or pick right for Scrollbar position on the settings page: profiles : main : scrollbar : position : Right # Left | Right (the default) | Hidden The marks hide whenever the scrollbar does: on the alternate screen ( hide_in_alt_screen , on by default), and with position: Hidden , or hidden on the settings page. Sticky command header # Scrolled back into a long output, the command that produced it stays pinned above it — in the pane header of a split, in the title band of a single pane, and in the grid's own band under show_title_bar: true — with its exit status and duration — or running 12s while it runs. Click the header to jump to the command. profiles : main : sticky_header : mode : scrolled # never | scrolled | always show_evicted : true scrolled (the default) shows the header only while you are scrolled back into the history; always also shows it while following live output, so a running make stays labeled above its own output; never turns it off. It never shows on the alternate screen. The header needs prompt marks ( OSC 133 ; A ): a shell that marks only where its commands run gets none. When a command's own line has already been evicted from the history, the header names the command instead — ⋯ make -j8 — earlier output evicted — so its remaining output still says where it came from. It does so wherever the header would show, and at the very top of the history even with mode: never ; show_evicted: false turns it off. The header is drawn over the page: selection, copying and screen readers see only the page. Its colors: sticky_header . Acting on a block # To Use select a command's output Ctrl + triple-click on it, or SelectCommandBlock copy part of a command block — its output, its input line, or both — as plain text CopyCommandBlock copy a command line, safe to paste CopyCommandLine open the last command's output in a pager Ctrl + Shift + G , or OpenCommandOutput select, copy or page the block under the pointer the context menu clear everything above the current prompt ClearToPrompt copy the last command's output when nothing is selected CopySelection with fallback: last_command_output input_mapping : # Ctrl+triple-click: select the clicked command's output (built in; a row like this replaces it) - { mods : [ Control ], mouse : Left , clicks : 3 , action : SelectCommandBlock , part : output , target : pointer } # Ctrl+Shift+G: the last command's output in the pager (built in; command_blocks.pager) - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : G , action : OpenCommandOutput , target : last } # Copy the last command's output, or its command line, without selecting anything - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : C , action : CopyCommandBlock , target : last , part : output } - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : P , action : CopyCommandLine , target : last } # Copy the selection -- or, with nothing selected, the last command's output - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : C , action : CopySelection , fallback : last_command_output } SelectCommandBlock takes part — output , input (the prompt with the command typed at it) or all — and target : pointer (the block under the mouse), cursor (the block holding the cursor, the Vi-mode cursor in Vi mode) or last (the newest finished one). CopyCommandBlock takes the same part and target as SelectCommandBlock and copies that part into the clipboard as plain text. CopyCommandLine takes a target and copies that block's command line with the control characters that would be unsafe to paste removed, so an embedded end-of-paste sequence cannot make a shell run the rest. OpenCommandOutput takes the same target , plus a program that defaults to command_blocks.pager ( less -R , or more on Windows). Its placement is split (a new pane below, the default), tab , or detached , which pipes the output into the program as plain text and opens no pane; for a pane, the output goes to a private file that is deleted when the pane closes. Its format is sgr , which keeps the colors, or plain , which drops them; without one, the configured pager gets command_blocks.pager_format ( sgr by default) and a program the binding names gets sgr . CopySelection 's fallback is off unless you ask for it, so copying with nothing selected never replaces your clipboard with a build log by accident. The context menu's Select Output , Copy Output , Copy Command and Open Output in Pager act on the block under the pointer. Relative file paths in a command's output — Ctrl +clicked, or picked in hint mode — resolve against the directory that command ran in, not the shell's current one. Paths from a command that ran in a container or over ssh are not opened locally. New bindings and an existing input_mapping Defining input_mapping replaces the default bindings (see Key mapping ). That costs you nothing here: Ctrl +triple-click and Ctrl + Shift + G are built-in fallbacks, not defaults, so they work whatever your input_mapping says — unless it binds the same chord itself, in which case your binding wins. CopyCommandBlock , CopyCommandLine and ClearToPrompt have no chord at all: add the bindings you want to your input_mapping . Finish notifications # When a command that took a while finishes somewhere you are not looking, Contour posts a desktop notification — ✓ make finished , ✗ make failed (exit 2) or ✗ make killed (SIGSEGV) — with how long it took, where it ran and which tab it is in. Clicking it brings that pane forward where the desktop reports clicks, and a newer notification from the same pane replaces the older one. profiles : main : notify_on_command_finish : when : unfocused # never | unfocused | hidden | always min_duration : 10 # seconds; quicker commands never notify outcome : any # any | failure action : notify # notify | bell | notify_bell clear_on : focus # focus | next | never Key Meaning when unfocused : unless the pane is the focused one of the active window (the default); hidden : only while the pane is off screen (another tab, a zoomed sibling, a minimized window); always ; never min_duration commands quicker than this many seconds never notify (default 10) outcome notify for any command, or only for a failure (a non-zero exit or a signal) action a desktop notification ( notify ), the profile's bell ( bell ), or both ( notify_bell ) clear_on withdraw the notification when you focus the pane ( focus ), when the next command there starts ( next ), or never . Only a desktop notification can be withdrawn (Linux); a tray message elsewhere stays until it times out It is on by default because the case it serves — a build in a background tab — is exactly when nobody thinks to turn it on; the 10-second floor keeps ordinary commands quiet. User marks # mm in Vi normal mode marks the cursor line, and clears the mark again. A user mark is drawn as ◆ in the gutter and as a tick on the scrollbar, and [m / ]m jump between marks of both kinds. Unlike a prompt, it never starts a command block: folding and block-wise history eviction ignore it. See Line marks . Daemon sessions # All of this works in a contour client session attached to a daemon: the daemon sends the block records along with the screen. Reattaching does not replay notifications for commands that finished while you were away. OpenCommandOutput opens no pane there — the pane would run on the daemon's side, which never sees the file — so bind it with placement: detached instead. Restored sessions # When the daemon brings a workspace back after a restart, each pane's history comes back above a dimmed "Restored · session ended hh:mm" row, which names the day too when it is not today. A command that was still running when the snapshot was taken is shown as abandoned: its chip stops counting, since the program it belonged to is gone. The first window to attach also shows one toast, such as "Restored 2 windows, 7 tabs". Installing shell integration # Contour offers to turn shell integration on when a bash, zsh or fish session needs it. After you have entered three commands in a pane whose shell writes no prompt marks, a card appears in the pane's bottom rows: Turn on command blocks , with Install and Not Now . Install shows the one line it would add to the shell's startup file ( ~/.zshrc , ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile on macOS, or ~/.config/fish/config.fish ) and nothing is written yet. Add Line appends it and says so in a toast; new sessions of that shell then show command blocks. Cancel hides the card for this run, and Not Now is remembered for that shell, in gui-state.yml beside contour.yml . The line runs contour generate integration shell <shell> from the binary that is running, and only in a shell Contour started ( TERM_PROGRAM is contour ). Contour only ever appends: it never rewrites or replaces the file, a file that is a symlink is appended through, and the line is not added twice. It adds nothing when Contour runs as root, when the file changed while it was being read, or when an earlier append was cut short and left half a Contour line at the end of the file: delete that line, then install again. The card is not offered in a window attached to another host. Shell Integration on the settings page starts with an Install group: one row per shell, saying Installed in ~/.zshrc , Not installed or why the file cannot be read. Install… asks the same question, with the same line, and adds it the same way, also for a shell you declined at the card. A row whose file ends in a cut-short Contour line shows that exact line to delete. Settings page # Every setting above but the key bindings can also be changed on the settings page: Global settings has the rows named Gutter: … , Command blocks: … and Folding: … ( configuration ). Each saves the one key it edits to settings.yml , and the rest of its section keeps what contour.yml says. Command blocks: pager format picks sgr or plain . Command blocks: pager cannot be left blank; Reset goes back to the pager contour.yml names. A profile's page has a Command blocks group ( profiles ): the three Scrollbar marks: … rows, Sticky command header , Name evicted commands , Notify on finish and the Notify: … rows. Scrollbar position is under History & scrollbar . A profile defined in contour.yml is read-only there; Save As makes an editable copy. A color scheme's page has the swatches Block status: success , failure and running , Gutter text , and Sticky header: background and separator ( colors ). A swatch the scheme leaves unset says that it follows the scheme's other colors, and shows the color they give it. Typing a new color pins the swatch, and so does Enter in its field, which keeps the color it shows now; tabbing through the field pins nothing. Each of these swatches that the scheme sets has a ↺ button, which makes it follow the other colors again. Keybindings lists the bindings without editing them: the input_mapping of contour.yml , then the built-in bindings none of its rows takes, such as Ctrl +triple-click and Ctrl + Shift + G , marked built-in . A binding that runs several actions names them all. When the page refuses a value, a message above the rows says why, and screen readers announce it. The message goes away with the next change that goes through, or when you open another page. Configuration reference # Global: gutter , command_blocks , folding Profile: scrollbar , sticky_header , notify_on_command_finish Color scheme: block_status , gutter_text , sticky_header Actions and bindings: Key mapping

Its width depends only on the configuration, never on what is on screen — a gutter that grew would resize the page mid-command. On the alternate screen of a full-screen program such as vim, less or htop it keeps its width and stays empty. Column Shows Configured by Default Timestamps when each line was first reached gutter.timestamps , gutter.timestamp_format off Line numbers absolute, relative or hybrid numbers gutter.line_numbers , gutter.line_number_width off Block column fold controls, exit status, user marks folding.show_markers , gutter.exit_status , gutter.user_marks on gutter : exit_status : true user_marks : true line_numbers : hybrid line_number_width : 6 timestamps : true timestamp_format : "%H:%M:%S"
docs.title: The gutter

docs.text: One cell per line, beside the grid, showing the first of these that applies: Mark Where Meaning boxed minus / boxed plus a prompt line the block's output is shown / collapsed; click to toggle ◆ any other line a user mark ( mm in Vi normal mode) │ , ┕ the output the extent of the block ▸ a prompt line the command is still running ● a prompt line the command finished without output to fold — or, with folding.show_markers: false , finished at all A block's marks take the color of how its command ended, from the color scheme's block_status colors: neutral for success, red for a failure, yellow while it runs. With gutter.exit_status: false the column keeps the plain fold-marker color and draws neither ▸ nor ●; with gutter.user_marks: false it draws no ◆. The column is there while any of the three is on. Hover the block column to see the block's exit code (and the signal that ended it, named by OSC 3008 or by a 128 + n exit status), its duration, start time, directory and command line.
docs.title: The block column

docs.text: gutter.line_numbers works like vim's number and relativenumber : Value vim Cursor line Other lines off nonu nornu — — absolute nu its number their numbers relative rnu 0 distance from the cursor line hybrid nu rnu its number distance from the cursor line An absolute number counts rows from the first row of the session, including rows that have since left the history, so a row keeps its number while the history scrolls away. Resizing the window re-wraps the lines and renumbers the rows below the top. A relative distance counts the rows you see: a collapsed block counts as one row, exactly as j and k do, so 12k lands on the row labeled 12. The cursor is the Vi-mode cursor while Vi mode is on, and the terminal's cursor otherwise. gutter.line_number_width (3 to 10, default 6) is the column count; a longer number shows its last digits after … .
docs.title: Line numbers

docs.text: gutter.timestamps: true shows beside each line the local time output first reached it. gutter.timestamp_format is a std::format chrono format such as %H:%M:%S (the default) or %H:%M . It must begin with a % conversion, and every character it spells must take exactly one column; a format that cannot be used is reported when the configuration loads, and the default is kept. A line shows its time only where it differs from the line above, so a burst of output does not repeat the same second all the way down. Recording the time costs no memory per line.
docs.title: Timestamps

docs.text: A finished command's output can be collapsed to its prompt line (see folding ): click its fold control in the block column, or use the ToggleFold , ToggleLastFold , CollapseLastFold , CollapseAllFolds and ExpandAllFolds actions. A collapsed block says how much it hides — 1,234 lines hidden ⌄ — after its prompt; that chip is drawn over the page and is never selected or copied. In Vi normal mode, vim's fold keys work: Key Action za toggle the block under the cursor zo open it zc close it zM close every block zR open every block Unlike vim's, these know one fold level only, take no count, and work in normal mode alone; zn , zN and zi do not exist. With folding.enabled: false , za , zc and zM do nothing, while zo and zR still open what is collapsed.
docs.title: Folding

docs.text: On the native chrome styles each block gets a rail : a thin strip after the line numbers and timestamps, beside the block's rows. It is neutral for a success (a ✓ appears while the pointer is over the block), red with a ✗ for a failure, and the accent colour with a ▸ while the command runs. The strip has a fixed width, so the page never changes size when a block starts or ends. The ui_style: terminal row keeps the block column described above. The chip. Right of a finished command's prompt, in cells that are blank, a small pill says how it went — Failed · exit 1 · 0.0 s — and a running command's pill ticks. The pill is placed only where it covers nothing: a prompt with an RPROMPT keeps it, and a prompt filling the whole row shows the rail's mark alone, with the details in the block menu and read out by screen readers. A folded block's chip says 80 lines hidden ⌄ ; clicking it expands the block. The menu. A ⋯ button beside the block, or a right-click on it, opens a native menu whose header names the command and how it ended, above Copy Output , Copy Command , Rerun , Open in Pager and Collapse Output . The block's tooltip is gone; the header carries what it said. Keyboard. Cmd+Up and Cmd+Down (macOS) step through the blocks and announce each one; Shift+Cmd+Up and Shift+Cmd+Down also select its output. Ctrl+Enter or Shift+F10 opens the focused block's menu, Enter toggles its fold, Escape leaves the block, and typing reaches the shell again. The actions are FocusPreviousCommand , FocusNextCommand , SelectPreviousCommandOutput , SelectNextCommandOutput , OpenBlockMenu , ClearCommandBlockFocus and ToggleCommandFold , and the keys are free to rebind; while a block holds the focus the input mode BlockFocus is on. Ending a session with a command still running closes its block as abandoned: no ▸, no tick and no finish notification stay behind, and a restarted pane starts with no blocks.
docs.title: The rail, the chip and the block menu

docs.text: The scrollbar marks where commands are, so a failure far up the history is one glance — and one click — away. Clicking a mark scrolls its line to the top, opening its block if that was collapsed. Marks that fall on the same pixel merge, the most important winning: a failure, then a running command, then a user mark, then any other command. A failure is a solid tick, a running command a hollow one, and a search match ( search_matches ) a yellow one. A command's mark takes its block_status color. profiles : main : scrollbar : marks : [ failures , commands , user_marks , running , search_matches ] # [] turns the marks off The scrollbar is shown on the right by default, so the marks are there from the start. It floats over the edge of the terminal without taking a column away, and appears only once there is history to scroll through. That default applies to new configurations. Contour writes out its full default configuration on first run, so a contour.yml written by an earlier version still says position: Hidden and shows neither the scrollbar nor its marks. Set position: Right to see them, or pick right for Scrollbar position on the settings page: profiles : main : scrollbar : position : Right # Left | Right (the default) | Hidden The marks hide whenever the scrollbar does: on the alternate screen ( hide_in_alt_screen , on by default), and with position: Hidden , or hidden on the settings page.
docs.title: Scrollbar marks

docs.text: Scrolled back into a long output, the command that produced it stays pinned above it — in the pane header of a split, in the title band of a single pane, and in the grid's own band under show_title_bar: true — with its exit status and duration — or running 12s while it runs. Click the header to jump to the command. profiles : main : sticky_header : mode : scrolled # never | scrolled | always show_evicted : true scrolled (the default) shows the header only while you are scrolled back into the history; always also shows it while following live output, so a running make stays labeled above its own output; never turns it off. It never shows on the alternate screen. The header needs prompt marks ( OSC 133 ; A ): a shell that marks only where its commands run gets none. When a command's own line has already been evicted from the history, the header names the command instead — ⋯ make -j8 — earlier output evicted — so its remaining output still says where it came from. It does so wherever the header would show, and at the very top of the history even with mode: never ; show_evicted: false turns it off. The header is drawn over the page: selection, copying and screen readers see only the page. Its colors: sticky_header .
docs.title: Sticky command header

docs.text: To Use select a command's output Ctrl + triple-click on it, or SelectCommandBlock copy part of a command block — its output, its input line, or both — as plain text CopyCommandBlock copy a command line, safe to paste CopyCommandLine open the last command's output in a pager Ctrl + Shift + G , or OpenCommandOutput select, copy or page the block under the pointer the context menu clear everything above the current prompt ClearToPrompt copy the last command's output when nothing is selected CopySelection with fallback: last_command_output input_mapping : # Ctrl+triple-click: select the clicked command's output (built in; a row like this replaces it) - { mods : [ Control ], mouse : Left , clicks : 3 , action : SelectCommandBlock , part : output , target : pointer } # Ctrl+Shift+G: the last command's output in the pager (built in; command_blocks.pager) - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : G , action : OpenCommandOutput , target : last } # Copy the last command's output, or its command line, without selecting anything - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : C , action : CopyCommandBlock , target : last , part : output } - { mods : [ Control , Alt ], key : P , action : CopyCommandLine , target : last } # Copy the selection -- or, with nothing selected, the last command's output - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : C , action : CopySelection , fallback : last_command_output } SelectCommandBlock takes part — output , input (the prompt with the command typed at it) or all — and target : pointer (the block under the mouse), cursor (the block holding the cursor, the Vi-mode cursor in Vi mode) or last (the newest finished one). CopyCommandBlock takes the same part and target as SelectCommandBlock and copies that part into the clipboard as plain text. CopyCommandLine takes a target and copies that block's command line with the control characters that would be unsafe to paste removed, so an embedded end-of-paste sequence cannot make a shell run the rest. OpenCommandOutput takes the same target , plus a program that defaults to command_blocks.pager ( less -R , or more on Windows). Its placement is split (a new pane below, the default), tab , or detached , which pipes the output into the program as plain text and opens no pane; for a pane, the output goes to a private file that is deleted when the pane closes. Its format is sgr , which keeps the colors, or plain , which drops them; without one, the configured pager gets command_blocks.pager_format ( sgr by default) and a program the binding names gets sgr . CopySelection 's fallback is off unless you ask for it, so copying with nothing selected never replaces your clipboard with a build log by accident. The context menu's Select Output , Copy Output , Copy Command and Open Output in Pager act on the block under the pointer. Relative file paths in a command's output — Ctrl +clicked, or picked in hint mode — resolve against the directory that command ran in, not the shell's current one. Paths from a command that ran in a container or over ssh are not opened locally. New bindings and an existing input_mapping Defining input_mapping replaces the default bindings (see Key mapping ). That costs you nothing here: Ctrl +triple-click and Ctrl + Shift + G are built-in fallbacks, not defaults, so they work whatever your input_mapping says — unless it binds the same chord itself, in which case your binding wins. CopyCommandBlock , CopyCommandLine and ClearToPrompt have no chord at all: add the bindings you want to your input_mapping .
docs.title: Acting on a block

docs.text: When a command that took a while finishes somewhere you are not looking, Contour posts a desktop notification — ✓ make finished , ✗ make failed (exit 2) or ✗ make killed (SIGSEGV) — with how long it took, where it ran and which tab it is in. Clicking it brings that pane forward where the desktop reports clicks, and a newer notification from the same pane replaces the older one. profiles : main : notify_on_command_finish : when : unfocused # never | unfocused | hidden | always min_duration : 10 # seconds; quicker commands never notify outcome : any # any | failure action : notify # notify | bell | notify_bell clear_on : focus # focus | next | never Key Meaning when unfocused : unless the pane is the focused one of the active window (the default); hidden : only while the pane is off screen (another tab, a zoomed sibling, a minimized window); always ; never min_duration commands quicker than this many seconds never notify (default 10) outcome notify for any command, or only for a failure (a non-zero exit or a signal) action a desktop notification ( notify ), the profile's bell ( bell ), or both ( notify_bell ) clear_on withdraw the notification when you focus the pane ( focus ), when the next command there starts ( next ), or never . Only a desktop notification can be withdrawn (Linux); a tray message elsewhere stays until it times out It is on by default because the case it serves — a build in a background tab — is exactly when nobody thinks to turn it on; the 10-second floor keeps ordinary commands quiet.
docs.title: Finish notifications

docs.text: mm in Vi normal mode marks the cursor line, and clears the mark again. A user mark is drawn as ◆ in the gutter and as a tick on the scrollbar, and [m / ]m jump between marks of both kinds. Unlike a prompt, it never starts a command block: folding and block-wise history eviction ignore it. See Line marks .
docs.title: User marks

docs.text: All of this works in a contour client session attached to a daemon: the daemon sends the block records along with the screen. Reattaching does not replay notifications for commands that finished while you were away. OpenCommandOutput opens no pane there — the pane would run on the daemon's side, which never sees the file — so bind it with placement: detached instead.
docs.title: Daemon sessions

docs.text: When the daemon brings a workspace back after a restart, each pane's history comes back above a dimmed "Restored · session ended hh:mm" row, which names the day too when it is not today. A command that was still running when the snapshot was taken is shown as abandoned: its chip stops counting, since the program it belonged to is gone. The first window to attach also shows one toast, such as "Restored 2 windows, 7 tabs".
docs.title: Restored sessions

docs.text: Contour offers to turn shell integration on when a bash, zsh or fish session needs it. After you have entered three commands in a pane whose shell writes no prompt marks, a card appears in the pane's bottom rows: Turn on command blocks , with Install and Not Now . Install shows the one line it would add to the shell's startup file ( ~/.zshrc , ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile on macOS, or ~/.config/fish/config.fish ) and nothing is written yet. Add Line appends it and says so in a toast; new sessions of that shell then show command blocks. Cancel hides the card for this run, and Not Now is remembered for that shell, in gui-state.yml beside contour.yml . The line runs contour generate integration shell <shell> from the binary that is running, and only in a shell Contour started ( TERM_PROGRAM is contour ). Contour only ever appends: it never rewrites or replaces the file, a file that is a symlink is appended through, and the line is not added twice. It adds nothing when Contour runs as root, when the file changed while it was being read, or when an earlier append was cut short and left half a Contour line at the end of the file: delete that line, then install again. The card is not offered in a window attached to another host. Shell Integration on the settings page starts with an Install group: one row per shell, saying Installed in ~/.zshrc , Not installed or why the file cannot be read. Install… asks the same question, with the same line, and adds it the same way, also for a shell you declined at the card. A row whose file ends in a cut-short Contour line shows that exact line to delete.
docs.title: Installing shell integration

docs.text: Every setting above but the key bindings can also be changed on the settings page: Global settings has the rows named Gutter: … , Command blocks: … and Folding: … ( configuration ). Each saves the one key it edits to settings.yml , and the rest of its section keeps what contour.yml says. Command blocks: pager format picks sgr or plain . Command blocks: pager cannot be left blank; Reset goes back to the pager contour.yml names. A profile's page has a Command blocks group ( profiles ): the three Scrollbar marks: … rows, Sticky command header , Name evicted commands , Notify on finish and the Notify: … rows. Scrollbar position is under History & scrollbar . A profile defined in contour.yml is read-only there; Save As makes an editable copy. A color scheme's page has the swatches Block status: success , failure and running , Gutter text , and Sticky header: background and separator ( colors ). A swatch the scheme leaves unset says that it follows the scheme's other colors, and shows the color they give it. Typing a new color pins the swatch, and so does Enter in its field, which keeps the color it shows now; tabbing through the field pins nothing. Each of these swatches that the scheme sets has a ↺ button, which makes it follow the other colors again. Keybindings lists the bindings without editing them: the input_mapping of contour.yml , then the built-in bindings none of its rows takes, such as Ctrl +triple-click and Ctrl + Shift + G , marked built-in . A binding that runs several actions names them all. When the page refuses a value, a message above the rows says why, and screen readers announce it. The message goes away with the next change that goes through, or when you open another page.
docs.title: Settings page

docs.text: Global: gutter , command_blocks , folding Profile: scrollbar , sticky_header , notify_on_command_finish Color scheme: block_status , gutter_text , sticky_header Actions and bindings: Key mapping
docs.title: Configuration reference

docs.text: Drag and drop # Contour accepts drops on a pane. What happens depends on what you drag: a pane or a tab moves, files and text are typed into the pane's shell ( below ). Moving panes and tabs # You can pick up any pane, or any tab, and put it anywhere a terminal can live: elsewhere in its tab, in another tab, in another window, in a tab of its own, or in a window of its own. The shells inside keep running through the move. Nothing is restarted and nothing is lost: scrollback, the running program, the cursor, the selection and any search move with the pane, and output keeps arriving while you drag. The two handles # You pick up By a pane its header (the buttons on its right keep their click). The header is shown inline in Comfortable density; in Minimal density it is shown while you hold the reveal modifier. a tab the tab itself, in any window's tab bar. A tab with a single pane is that pane: dragging it behaves exactly as dragging the pane does, including the swap below. A pane whose header is hidden because the pane is too short to spare the row has no handle of its own; drag its tab instead. While you drag a pane, a translucent card (its header, with a grip and the pane's name, and its last few lines) follows the pointer, and the pane's place shows a dashed outline reading " name 's place", so you can see what will close up behind it. Dragging a tab keeps the tab's own drag image. Where you can drop # Every target works for both handles, unless the table says otherwise. # Release on What happens T1 the edge band of a pane (the outer 20 % of each side) the dragged pane or tab splits beside, above or below that pane, taking half of it. The same tab, another tab, or another window. T2 the middle of a pane, with a single pane dragged the two panes swap places. T3 the middle of a pane, with a tab of several panes dragged nothing: a whole layout cannot trade places with one pane. No ghost is drawn. T4 hovering a tab in any tab bar for 600 ms that tab becomes the visible tab of its window, with the drag still in your hand, so T1 and T2 then apply to its panes. T5 a tab , released on it (its middle, clear of the gaps) the dragged pane or tab is added to that tab, as a split to the right of the tab's active pane. T6 a gap of a tab bar: between two tabs, before the first, after the last, or in the empty bar the dragged pane or tab becomes a new tab at that place. For a tab this is the reorder, or the move into another window's tab bar. T7 outside every Contour window a new window with the dragged pane or tab as its only tab. What you will get is drawn before you let go: Over a pane, a ring in the accent colour marks the pane, and a ghost shows the part of it the dragged node would take: the half beside the edge you are nearest (a corner goes to the edge you are proportionally nearer to; a tie goes to left or right), or the whole pane for a swap. A label on the ghost says what happens: Pane → split left , Pane → split right , Pane → split up , Pane → split down or Swap with <pane name> . A dragged tab of several panes says Tab → split left and so on. Over a tab, the tab is outlined in the accent. If hovering would open it, a bar fills along the tab's foot during the 600 ms, and it stays full once the tab has opened. In a gap, a dashed, tab-shaped slot named for what you carry shows where the new tab will stand. Between two tabs, the tabs after the gap move aside to make room for it. Dropping a pane on itself , or on the empty place it left, does nothing, and nothing is drawn. Dropping a pane on the only other pane of its own tab is a legal swap or re-dock. Dropping a tab onto a pane of its own tab does nothing either. Hover-to-open never moves the wrong thing. It opens only another tab: never the tab you are dragging, never the tab the drag came from, and never a tab of a window that would refuse the drop. Gaps versus tabs. Each boundary between tabs counts as a gap for 10 px to either side (at most a quarter of a narrow tab), so a gap is easy to aim at and a tab keeps a middle to rest on. The tab strip does not reorder by where you drop along it any more; you reorder by dropping in the gap you want. Out to a new window # Release outside every Contour window (T7) and the pane or tab opens as a window of its own, at the cursor position when you let go, on the screen you released on. On Wayland, which does not tell an application where the pointer is outside its windows, the window opens at the last position the drag was seen inside a Contour window, on that window's screen, and the compositor places it as it places every Wayland window. The platform cannot draw outside Contour's windows, so the drag image alone shows what is happening until you let go. A tab of several panes behaves as it always has: it tears off into a new window. A pane dragged out of a tab of several panes now does the same, and leaves its place to its sibling. Press Escape during a drag to cancel it: nothing moves and no window opens, even when the pointer is inside Contour. The same goes for a release inside one of Contour's windows that no target takes. What a move does # The new split divides the target pane in half, exactly as the ghost showed. In the tab the pane left, its sibling takes over the space. A swap trades the two places, and each place keeps its size. Focus follows the moved pane into its new tab and window, and that window is raised. Zoom is cleared on both the tab it left and the tab it entered. A tab left empty closes, and so does a window left empty, without asking : a move loses no session, and the question exists to protect running sessions. Moving the last pane of the last tab of a window out closes that window; the moved shell keeps running, and Contour does not quit. A screen reader announces the move ("Pane moved", "Pane moved to new tab", "Pane moved to window name ", "Panes swapped", "Pane moved to new window"). Daemon-hosted layouts are saved as they are after the move, so restoring a workspace brings the new arrangement back. If the shell in the pane you carry exits before you let go, the drop does nothing. Between windows # Where the windows are Moving a pane or tab between them two windows of the same Contour process works, every target above two windows hosted by the same daemon , even when different Contour processes show them (see Persistent sessions ) works, every target above a window of another Contour process that shares no daemon with this one refused a window whose daemon is older than this one's pane-move support refused for panes; see below a tmux window ( contour client --tmux ) refused A refused target is not silent. The ring turns amber, and a note on the pane says why and names what to do instead. Releasing there does nothing at all: it is accepted as a no-op, so it never tears off a window by accident, and everything stays where it was. The three notes, under the title Can't move a pane here : another process: This window belongs to another Contour process. Run Contour in daemon mode to move panes between any windows. an older daemon: This window's daemon is too old to move panes. Update Contour on the daemon side. tmux: Panes can't be moved into a tmux window yet. Older daemons. A daemon that predates pane moves keeps serving what it always did: reordering tabs, moving a tab to another window's tab bar, tearing a tab off into a new window, and dropping a tab on a pane of its own window to split it. Dragging a pane, and every tab target that needs more than those, shows the second note above. Nothing is ever half done: a move happens completely or not at all. Dragging files onto a pane # Drop files from your file manager onto a pane, and their paths are typed at the cursor, escaped for the program in the foreground, and not run. A trailing space lets you keep typing. Foreground program Quoting a known POSIX shell (bash, zsh, fish, sh, dash, ksh, ...) each special character, and spaces, escaped with a backslash PowerShell ( pwsh , powershell ) single quotes, ' doubled cmd double quotes anything else: Windows, a pane hosted by the daemon, a multiplexer ( tmux , screen , zellij ), a transport ( ssh , mosh , docker exec , su , sudo , wsl ), nushell, elvish, vim double quotes, and a name holding any character one of those shells reads as syntax is refused The text arrives as a paste, so an application that enabled bracketed paste receives it wrapped. Web links are typed the same way as file names, each one a quoted word, so a link a web page chose cannot run anything. Dropping plain text pastes it as text, as Ctrl+V does, except that text with a line break is refused where the program has not enabled bracketed paste: without it each line would run as it arrives, and the page that started the drag chose the text, not you. Quoting assumes the drop starts a new word. If you have an open quote at the prompt (a " or ' you typed and have not closed), a dropped name can close it, and what follows runs as syntax. Contour cannot see the state of your shell's line editor, so finish or clear the line before you drop a file onto it. What is refused # A file name holding a control character (a newline, an escape, and the like) or a character that makes the typed text look other than it runs (a text-direction control such as U+200E or U+202E, U+2028, U+2029) refuses the whole drop with "Not inserted: a file name holds a control or text-direction character.", because such a name could run as a command in the shell. Under cmd , a name holding % , " or ! cannot be quoted safely and is refused too. Where the shell is not known, a name holding any of $ ` ; & | < > ( ) ' " \ ! % ^ is refused, and the window says its shell is not known. A name or link starting with - would be read as an option: a local file is typed as ./-name , and a link (which has no path to put ./ in front of) is refused except for a POSIX shell, which gets ./ too. A pane whose program has ended ignores drops.

The tab strip does not reorder by where you drop along it any more; you reorder by dropping in the gap you want.
docs.title: Where you can drop

docs.text: Release outside every Contour window (T7) and the pane or tab opens as a window of its own, at the cursor position when you let go, on the screen you released on. On Wayland, which does not tell an application where the pointer is outside its windows, the window opens at the last position the drag was seen inside a Contour window, on that window's screen, and the compositor places it as it places every Wayland window. The platform cannot draw outside Contour's windows, so the drag image alone shows what is happening until you let go. A tab of several panes behaves as it always has: it tears off into a new window. A pane dragged out of a tab of several panes now does the same, and leaves its place to its sibling. Press Escape during a drag to cancel it: nothing moves and no window opens, even when the pointer is inside Contour. The same goes for a release inside one of Contour's windows that no target takes.
docs.title: Out to a new window

docs.text: The new split divides the target pane in half, exactly as the ghost showed. In the tab the pane left, its sibling takes over the space. A swap trades the two places, and each place keeps its size. Focus follows the moved pane into its new tab and window, and that window is raised. Zoom is cleared on both the tab it left and the tab it entered. A tab left empty closes, and so does a window left empty, without asking : a move loses no session, and the question exists to protect running sessions. Moving the last pane of the last tab of a window out closes that window; the moved shell keeps running, and Contour does not quit. A screen reader announces the move ("Pane moved", "Pane moved to new tab", "Pane moved to window name ", "Panes swapped", "Pane moved to new window"). Daemon-hosted layouts are saved as they are after the move, so restoring a workspace brings the new arrangement back. If the shell in the pane you carry exits before you let go, the drop does nothing.
docs.title: What a move does

docs.text: Where the windows are Moving a pane or tab between them two windows of the same Contour process works, every target above two windows hosted by the same daemon , even when different Contour processes show them (see Persistent sessions ) works, every target above a window of another Contour process that shares no daemon with this one refused a window whose daemon is older than this one's pane-move support refused for panes; see below a tmux window ( contour client --tmux ) refused A refused target is not silent. The ring turns amber, and a note on the pane says why and names what to do instead. Releasing there does nothing at all: it is accepted as a no-op, so it never tears off a window by accident, and everything stays where it was. The three notes, under the title Can't move a pane here : another process: This window belongs to another Contour process. Run Contour in daemon mode to move panes between any windows. an older daemon: This window's daemon is too old to move panes. Update Contour on the daemon side. tmux: Panes can't be moved into a tmux window yet. Older daemons. A daemon that predates pane moves keeps serving what it always did: reordering tabs, moving a tab to another window's tab bar, tearing a tab off into a new window, and dropping a tab on a pane of its own window to split it. Dragging a pane, and every tab target that needs more than those, shows the second note above. Nothing is ever half done: a move happens completely or not at all.
docs.title: Between windows

docs.text: Drop files from your file manager onto a pane, and their paths are typed at the cursor, escaped for the program in the foreground, and not run. A trailing space lets you keep typing. Foreground program Quoting a known POSIX shell (bash, zsh, fish, sh, dash, ksh, ...) each special character, and spaces, escaped with a backslash PowerShell ( pwsh , powershell ) single quotes, ' doubled cmd double quotes anything else: Windows, a pane hosted by the daemon, a multiplexer ( tmux , screen , zellij ), a transport ( ssh , mosh , docker exec , su , sudo , wsl ), nushell, elvish, vim double quotes, and a name holding any character one of those shells reads as syntax is refused The text arrives as a paste, so an application that enabled bracketed paste receives it wrapped. Web links are typed the same way as file names, each one a quoted word, so a link a web page chose cannot run anything. Dropping plain text pastes it as text, as Ctrl+V does, except that text with a line break is refused where the program has not enabled bracketed paste: without it each line would run as it arrives, and the page that started the drag chose the text, not you. Quoting assumes the drop starts a new word. If you have an open quote at the prompt (a " or ' you typed and have not closed), a dropped name can close it, and what follows runs as syntax. Contour cannot see the state of your shell's line editor, so finish or clear the line before you drop a file onto it.
docs.title: Dragging files onto a pane

docs.text: A file name holding a control character (a newline, an escape, and the like) or a character that makes the typed text look other than it runs (a text-direction control such as U+200E or U+202E, U+2028, U+2029) refuses the whole drop with "Not inserted: a file name holds a control or text-direction character.", because such a name could run as a command in the shell. Under cmd , a name holding % , " or ! cannot be quoted safely and is refused too. Where the shell is not known, a name holding any of $ ` ; & | < > ( ) ' " \ ! % ^ is refused, and the window says its shell is not known. A name or link starting with - would be read as an option: a local file is typed as ./-name , and a link (which has no path to put ./ in front of) is refused except for a POSIX shell, which gets ./ too. A pane whose program has ended ignores drops.
docs.title: What is refused

docs.text: Hint Mode # Hint mode lets you quickly act on clickable elements visible in the terminal — URLs, file paths, git commit hashes, IP addresses — using only the keyboard. When activated, Contour scans the visible screen for recognized patterns, overlays a short alphabetic label on each match, and waits for you to type a label to perform an action on that match. Think of it like Vimium for your terminal. Activating Hint Mode # There are two ways to enter hint mode: Via Key Binding (from any mode) # The default key binding activates hint mode for URLs: input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : U , action : HintMode , patterns : url , hint_action : Open } Press Ctrl + Shift + U to scan for URLs and open the selected one in your browser. Via Vi Normal Mode # When in normal mode , you can use: gh — activate hint mode with Copy action (yank the match to clipboard) gH — activate hint mode with Open action (open the match, e.g. URL in browser) These commands scan with the profile's patterns: the builtins (URLs, file paths, git hashes, IPs) and your own hint_patterns . Using Hint Mode # Once hint mode is active: Labels appear — Each detected match gets a short label ( a , b , ..., z ; or two-character labels aa , ab , ... for more than 26 matches). Type the label — Type the label characters to select a match. Labels are case-insensitive. Auto-select — As soon as your typed characters uniquely identify a match, the action is performed automatically. Cancel — Press Escape to exit hint mode without selecting anything. Backspace — Press Backspace to undo the last typed label character. Recognized Patterns # Contour ships with the following builtin pattern detectors: Pattern Examples Description url https://example.com , http://localhost:8080 http , https , ftp , file and mailto URLs filepath /home/user/file.txt , ./src/main.cpp , src/main.cpp:12:5 , C:\Users\me\notes.txt , Makefile Absolute, relative, home-relative ( ~/... ) and Windows paths, and bare file names; a :line[:column] or (line[,column]) after one is kept as its location githash a1b2c3d , abc1234567890def1234567890abcdef12345678 7–40 character hex strings (git commit SHAs) ipv4 192.168.1.1 , 10.0.0.1:8080 IPv4 addresses, optionally with port ipv6 ::1 , fe80::1 , 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 IPv6 addresses Smart File Path Detection # Hint mode and the links Contour underlines in output share one path grammar, which takes bare names and a location printed after a path ( main.cpp:42:10 ). When the terminal knows the current working directory, or the directory a command ran in (via shell integration ), file path detection also matches: Bare filenames with extensions — main.cpp , README.md Extensionless files — Makefile , LICENSE , Dockerfile , CHANGELOG Directory names — src , build , docs These bare names are validated against the filesystem: only entries that actually exist in that directory are shown as hints. This means you can look at ls output, compiler errors, or git status and jump directly to the referenced files. Actions # The hint_action parameter controls what happens when you select a match: Action Description Copy Copy the matched text to the system clipboard (default); a path, resolved to its absolute form Open Open the match as Ctrl+click opens it — web URLs in the browser, directories in the file manager, and files (a file:// URL among them) with file_opener at the line they were printed with Paste Paste the matched text into the terminal input CopyAndPaste Copy to clipboard and paste into the terminal Select Enter vi visual mode with the match range pre-selected for manual adjustment Configuration # Key Bindings # You can create multiple hint mode bindings for different pattern sets and actions: input_mapping : # Open URLs in browser - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : U , action : HintMode , patterns : url , hint_action : Open } # Copy file paths to clipboard - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : F , action : HintMode , patterns : filepath , hint_action : Copy } # Copy git hashes to clipboard - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : G , action : HintMode , patterns : githash , hint_action : Copy } # Scan for all patterns and copy - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : H , action : HintMode , patterns : all , hint_action : Copy } The patterns parameter accepts: A single pattern name: url , filepath , githash , ipv4 , ipv6 Multiple pattern names separated by | : filepath|githash all or empty: scan for all builtin patterns at once Scope: Reaching Into Scrollback # By default hint mode scans only what is on screen. The scope parameter widens that to the scrollback history: input_mapping : # Scan the visible page (the default — may be omitted) - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : U , action : HintMode , patterns : url , hint_action : Open , scope : Visible } # Scan the visible page *and* scrollback history - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : Y , action : HintMode , patterns : url , hint_action : Open , scope : Scrollback } Under scope: Scrollback , labels are assigned once when hint mode is activated and then stay put : scrolling reveals the labels on other rows rather than renaming the ones you have already read. So the workflow is: activate, scroll to the output you want, then type its label. A label acts on its match even while it is off screen. scope: Visible behaves the other way round, because its scan region is the viewport: scrolling re-scans and re-labels. How much history a Scrollback activation reads is capped per profile, so a very large scrollback does not turn one keystroke into a long scan: profiles : main : # Maximum scrollback rows a `scope: Scrollback` activation scans (default: 1000). hint_scrollback_lines : 1000 Wrapped Lines # A pattern is matched against the logical line, so a URL that the terminal broke across two or more rows because the window was too narrow is still found as a single hint, and selecting it yields the whole URL rather than the fragment on one row. The label sits at the start of the match, and the highlight follows the match across the line break. A hint is only offered where its label can be drawn. A match that begins above the scanned region — so that its label would be invisible — is not offered, since a label you cannot see is a label you cannot type. A match that begins inside the region and runs past its end is offered, and still yields its complete text. Colors # Hint mode label and match colors are configured in the color scheme section of your configuration: color_schemes : default : # Colors for the short alphabetic labels overlaid on matches. hint_label : foreground : '#000000' foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#E5C07B' background_alpha : 1.0 # Colors for the matched text behind the labels. hint_match : foreground : '#ABB2BF' foreground_alpha : 1.0 background : '#3E4452' background_alpha : 0.8 Custom Patterns # You can define your own hint patterns in the profile configuration. Each pattern needs a name (used to reference it in key bindings) and a regex ( ECMAScript syntax ): profiles : main : hint_patterns : - name : uuid regex : '\b[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}\b' - name : docker_id regex : '\b[0-9a-f]{12,64}\b' Custom patterns with the same name as a builtin override the builtin definition. You can then reference custom patterns in key bindings just like builtins: input_mapping : - { mods : [ Control , Shift ], key : I , action : HintMode , patterns : uuid , hint_action : Copy } Back-references ( \1 to \9 ) are not supported; a pattern using one is reported when the configuration is loaded and disabled. Clickable Patterns # Links in Terminal Output describes the links Contour finds in output, and how they open, in full. A pattern can also be found in the terminal's output without entering hint mode: with clickable: true its matches are decorated as links are (see hyperlink_decoration ) and opened with Ctrl+click. url says what is opened, with {0} standing for the whole match and {1} to {9} for its capture groups. Without url , the match is opened as printed. Where the printed text chooses the scheme (no url , or a url that does not start with a scheme of its own, such as {0} ), a match opens only with a scheme Contour opens in URLs it finds itself: http , https , ftp , mailto or file . Any other is no link: it is not underlined, and hint mode offers it to copy and opens nothing. A url that writes its scheme itself may open any. Only what a URL cannot hold is percent-encoded as a group is put in: spaces, control characters and "#<>[\]^`{|} . Characters such as / ? & = + @ : % pass through, so a group placed in a query can add parameters, and one placed before the host can change it. Write the scheme and the host in the template itself, as the examples below do, and put groups after them. profiles : main : hint_patterns : - name : jira regex : '\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+\b' clickable : true url : 'https://jira.example.com/browse/{0}' - name : github_issue regex : '\b([\w.-]+)/([\w.-]+)#(\d+)\b' clickable : true url : 'https://github.com/{1}/{2}/issues/{3}' - name : commit regex : '\b[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b' clickable : true url : 'https://github.com/contour-terminal/contour/commit/{0}' The builtins url and filepath are clickable, and githash , ipv4 and ipv6 are offered in hint mode only. An entry named like a builtin changes only the keys it gives, so it may leave out its regex : hint_patterns : - name : filepath clickable : false # stop underlining paths; hint mode still offers them A url template applies to your own patterns only: a builtin opens what it finds, and a url given to one is reported and ignored. So clickable: true on githash , ipv4 or ipv6 alone makes no link, as a bare hash or address names no scheme; to link commits to their page, write a pattern of your own with a url , as commit above does. A url that names a capture group the regex does not have, such as {2} for a regex with one group, is reported when the configuration is loaded and disables the pattern. A regex that overrides filepath must say which part of its match is the path: capture group 1 is the path, groups 2 and 3 a :line[:column] printed after it, and groups 4 and 5 a (line[,column]) . An override of filepath without a capture group is reported and disabled. Every other pattern's link is its whole match, {0} . Path Resolution # When copying or opening file paths, Contour resolves relative paths to absolute using the directory the command that printed them ran in, as shell integration recorded it, so a cd since then does not change what an earlier command's output names. Outside any command's output, the terminal's current working directory is used. For example, copying a hint for src/main.cpp gives you /home/user/project/src/main.cpp in the clipboard, and opening it passes the full path to your editor or file manager. Ctrl+clicking a path resolves it the same way. A command that changes directory itself, such as cd build && make , prints paths relative to where it went. The shell reports that directory only at the next prompt, so a path not found where the command started is looked up there too. Paths printed by a command that ran on another machine (over ssh, in a container) name files there, so they are neither offered as hints nor opened here. That includes the output of an ssh session whose remote shell reports its directory but marks no commands of its own: everything it printed belongs to the local ssh command, and stays refused after you return to the local prompt. Home-relative paths ( ~/... ) are expanded using the HOME environment variable. Tips and Tricks # Shell integration matters — Ensure your shell reports the current working directory via OSC 133 for the best file path detection. Without it, only paths containing a / separator are matched. Combine with Vi mode — In normal mode, gh (copy) and gH (open) are quick ways to enter hint mode without reaching for modifier keys. Works with scrollback — Hint mode scans the currently visible viewport. Scroll to the area of interest first, then activate hint mode. Compiler errors — When viewing build output with file paths like src/main.cpp:42:10: error: ... , hint mode detects the file path portion, making it easy to copy or open the referenced file. docs.text: ReGIS Vector Graphics # Contour implements ReGIS (Remote Graphics Instruction Set), DEC's vector-graphics language introduced with the VT330/VT340 terminals. Where Sixel transmits a raster (a grid of pixels), ReGIS transmits drawing instructions — lines, circles, arcs, curves, filled polygons and text — which the terminal rasterises. This makes ReGIS compact and resolution-independent: a circle is a few bytes, not a bitmap. This page is a practical reference for people who script and program terminals. It matches Contour's implementation; where Contour deviates from the VT340 it is called out explicitly. Authoritative reference The behaviour here follows the VT330/VT340 Programmer Reference Manual, Volume 2: Graphics Programming . That manual is the ground truth for ReGIS semantics. Entering and leaving ReGIS # ReGIS is carried inside a DCS (Device Control String): ESC P p <ReGIS commands> ESC \ ESC P (0x1B 0x50) is the DCS introducer, the letter p selects ReGIS, and ESC \ (String Terminator) ends it. An optional numeric parameter before p controls state carry-over: Introducer Meaning ESC P p or ESC P 0 p Resume: position, colours, write controls and the addressing window carry over from the previous ReGIS string. ESC P 1 p / ESC P 3 p Reset the graphics state and clear the canvas before drawing. From a shell you can emit ReGIS with printf : # Draw a diagonal line from the top-left toward the middle of the screen. printf '\033PpP[100,100]V[400,300]\033\\' Detecting ReGIS support # ReGIS-capable terminals advertise feature 3 in their primary Device Attributes reply. Send CSI c ( ESC [ c ) and look for ;3 in the response: printf '\033[c' # Contour replies e.g. ESC [ ? 65 ; ... ; 3 ; 4 ; ... c (3 = ReGIS, 4 = Sixel) You can also query the ReGIS graphics geometry with XTSMGRAPHICS ( CSI ? 3 ; 1 S ); Contour reports the fixed VT340 addressing area of 800 x 480 . The coordinate system # ReGIS addresses an 800 × 480 pixel screen. The origin [0,0] is the top-left corner and Y increases downward , so [799,479] is the bottom-right. Contour rasterises the ReGIS canvas and scales it across the terminal window, drawing it above the text so that painted pixels overlay the cells and untouched areas remain transparent. Coordinates are written in brackets, [x,y] . Each axis is independent and may be: Form Meaning [100,50] Absolute position. [+30,-10] Relative to the current position (signed). [100] X only; Y unchanged. [,50] Y only; X unchanged. [] The current position (used by V to plot a dot). Pixel vectors # Outside brackets, a run of the digits 0–7 moves in one of eight compass directions, each step scaled by the pixel-vector multiplier W(M...) : 3 2 1 \ | / 4 -- + -- 0 / | \ 5 6 7 0 = right, 2 = up, 4 = left, 6 = down, and the odd digits are the diagonals. For example V0000 draws a line four pixels to the right. Commands # Every ReGIS command is a single, case-insensitive letter, optionally followed by parenthesised options ( ... ) , bracketed coordinates [ ... ] , pixel-vector digits, and quoted strings. A ; ends a command. Whitespace is ignored between tokens. P — Position # Moves the graphics cursor without drawing. printf '\033PpP[400,240]\033\\' # move to the centre [x,y] or pixel-vector digits move the cursor. (B) / (S) begin a bounded / unbounded position stack, (E) ends it. (W...) applies temporary write controls (see W ). V — Vector # Draws straight lines from the current position, honouring the current colour, line pattern and width. printf '\033PpP[100,100]V[400,100]V[400,300]V[100,300]V[100,100]\033\\' # a rectangle [x,y] draws a line to that point and moves there. [] plots a single dot at the current position. Pixel-vector digits draw along each step. C — Curve # Circles, arcs and interpolated curves. printf '\033PpP[400,240]C[500,240]\033\\' # circle of radius 100, centred at the cursor C[x,y] — a circle whose centre is the current position and whose radius reaches [x,y] . C(C)[x,y] — the bracket is the centre ; the current position lies on the circumference. C(A<degrees>)[x,y] — an arc ; a positive angle sweeps counter-clockwise, negative clockwise. C(S)[...]...(E) — an open interpolated curve through the listed points. C(B)[...]...(E) — a closed interpolated curve (the cursor returns to the start). W — Write controls # Sets the state that governs all drawing. Options combine inside one W( ... ) . Option Effect I<n> / I(<spec>) Foreground colour: a register index, or a colour spec (see Colour ). V R C E Writing mode: V overlay (default), R replace, C complement, E erase. P<n> Line pattern 0–9 (see Patterns ); P(M<n>) sets the pattern multiplier. M<n> Pixel-vector multiplier (pixels per PV step). L<n> Line width in pixels. N<0/1> Invert (negate) the line pattern. S... Shading (see Shading ). When written inside another command as (W...) , the controls apply only to that command. T — Text # Draws text with anti-aliased glyphs. In the GUI, ReGIS text is shaped by the same font engine as normal terminal text; the terminal engine itself ships a self-contained bitmap font as a fallback (headless use, or before a font is configured). An injected interface keeps the terminal engine free of any font-stack dependency. printf "\033PpP[100,100]T(S2)'Hello, ReGIS'\033\\" 'text' or "text" — the string to draw at the current position. (S<0-16>) — a standard cell size (0 = 9×10, up to 16 = 144×240); (S[w,h]) a custom cell. (M[wf,hf]) — width/height multipliers; (H<n>) a height multiplier. (D<degrees>) — writing direction in 45° steps (0 = rightward, 90 = up). (I<degrees>) — italic slant. S — Screen # Screen-wide operations. Option Effect (E) Erase the canvas to the background. (A[ul][lr]) Set the addressing window (defaults to [0,0][799,479] ). (I<n>) / (I(<spec>)) Background colour. (M<i>(<spec>)...) Program colour registers (the colour map). printf '\033PpS(E)S(A[0,0][799,479])\033\\' # clear and reset the coordinate window Page selection, scrolling, output scaling, hardcopy and time-delay sub-options are accepted but have no effect in Contour (they describe hardware Contour does not emulate). F — Polygon fill # Fills the region enclosed by a set of vectors or a curve. printf '\033PpP[300,100]F(V[500,100][400,280])\033\\' # a filled triangle F(V...) fills the polygon traced by the vector operations (the current position is the first vertex). F(C...) fills a curved region. R — Report # Queries state and sends a reply to the host application. Request Reply R(P) The graphics cursor position, as [x,y] . R(P(I)) The interactive locator (mouse) position, as <button>[x,y] . Contour reports it immediately rather than blocking. R(E) The last error code ( 0 = none). R(L) The current alphabet. @ — Macrographs # Stores and replays command strings. # Define macro A as a box, then invoke it twice at different positions. printf '\033Pp@:AV[+100,0]V[0,+100]V[-100,0]V[0,-100]@;P[100,100]@AP[300,100]@A\033\\' @:X ... @; defines macro X . @X invokes macro X (expanded recursively; Contour bounds the depth and output size). @. clears all macros. L — Load character set # Down-loadable custom character sets are recognised but not rendered in Contour (as in several other ReGIS implementations); text uses the built-in font. Colour # Contour keeps 16 colour registers, initialised to the VT340 default palette. A colour is named in three ways: Register index — W(I5) selects register 5. Named colour — W(I(R)) , where D =dark, R =red, G =green, B =blue, C =cyan, Y =yellow, M =magenta, W =white. HLS or RGB spec — W(I(H<0-360>L<0-100>S<0-100>)) for hue/lightness/saturation, or W(I(R<0-100>G<0-100>B<0-100>)) . On the DEC hue wheel 0° is blue, 120° red, 180° yellow, 240° green. Registers are reprogrammed with S(M<index>(<spec>)) , e.g. S(M1(H240L50S100)) makes register 1 green. Patterns # W(P<n>) selects one of ten standard line patterns: n Pattern n Pattern 0 (none) 5 dash-dot-dot 1 solid (default) 6 sparse dot 2 dash 7 asymmetric sparse dot 3 dash-dot 8 sparse dash-dot 4 dot 9 sparse dot-dash A custom pattern is a bit string, e.g. W(P11110000) . Shading # Shading fills the area between a drawn primitive and a reference line: W(S1) turns shading on (reference defaults to the cursor's current Y); W(S0) turns it off. W(S[,Y]) sets a horizontal reference at Y ; W(S(X)[X]) a vertical reference at X . # Shade the area under a line down to y=300. printf '\033PpW(S[,300])P[100,100]V[400,200]\033\\' Example programs # Contour ships four ReGIS demos under examples/ : regis-primitives.cpp — a static showcase of every primitive (lines, circles, arcs, curves, fills, patterns, colours and text). A good visual conformance check. regis-plot2d.cpp — a labelled 2D plot of a mathematical function with axes and a grid. regis-animation.cpp — an animated analog clock, redrawing each frame with S(E) + redraw. regis-plot3d.cpp — an interactive 3D plot of the complex function |z² − 1| ; drag with the mouse to rotate it (horizontal = yaw, vertical = pitch), press q to quit. Build them with the test build enabled and run them inside Contour: cmake --build --preset clang-release --target regis-primitives regis-plot3d ./out/clang-release/examples/regis-primitives ./out/clang-release/examples/regis-plot3d # then drag with the mouse
