docs.text: Buffer Capture # The screen's text buffer can be captured via VT sequence suitable for shell integration, such as fzf . Request Syntax # CSI > Pl ; Pr , t The , intermediate is required. The bare CSI > Pl ; Pr t this sequence originally used is xterm's XTSMTITLE opcode — a genuine collision, which XTSMTITLE now owns. Pl is 1 if the lines are to be counted logically and 0 if the lines are to be counted visually. A logical line is may be a wrapped line that spans more than one visual line, whereas a visual line always maps to exactly one line on the screen. The parameter Pr is the number of lines to be captured. Response Syntax # PM 314 ; <data> ST The response is may span multiple PM sequences. The reply will always end with a PM message with an empty <data> block, denoting the end of the reply. Each <data> chunk will be UTF-8 encoded of the text lines to be captured. Each line will be delimited by a newline escape sequenced ( LF ). Permission # Capturing the buffer is guarded by the permissions.capture_buffer profile setting ( allow , deny or ask ). A request that is refused — by configuration, by the user, or because it was addressed to a background pane that has no window to ask in — is answered with the terminating empty <data> chunk and nothing else. A refusal is therefore indistinguishable from capturing an empty screen, which is deliberate: the sequence has no way to report "no reply is coming", so a client that reads until the terminator is never left waiting. A pane hosted by contour daemon refuses every capture the same way: the daemon has nobody to ask and no configuration to answer with, so it replies with the terminating chunk alone rather than leaving the request unanswered.

docs.text: Dark and Light Mode detection # Most modern operating systems and desktop environments do support Dark and Light themes, this includes at least MacOS, Windows, KDE Plasma, Gnome, and probably others. Some even support switching from dark to light and light to dark mode based on sun rise / sun set. In order to not make the terminal emulator look bad after such switch, we must enable the applications inside the terminal to detect when the terminal has updated the color palette. This may happen either due to the operating system having changed the current theme or simply because the user has explicitly requested to reconfigure the currently used theme (e.g. because the user requested to change the terminal profile, also containing a different color scheme). Ideally we are getting CLI tools like delta to query the theme mode before sending out RGB values to the terminal to make the output look more in line with the rest of the desktop. But also TUIs like vim should be able to reflect dark/light mode changes as soon as the desktop has changed to light/dark mode or the user has changed the terminal profile. Query the current theme mode? # Send CSI ? 996 n to the terminal to explicitly request the current color preference (dark mode or light mode) by the operating system. The terminal will reply back in either of the two ways: VT sequence description CSI ? 997 ; 1 n DSR reply to indicate dark mode CSI ? 997 ; 2 n DSR reply to indicate light mode Request unsolicited DSR on color palette updates # Send CSI ? 2031 h to the terminal to enable unsolicited DSR (device status report) messages for color palette updates and CSI ? 2031 l respectively to disable it again. The sent out DSR looks equivalent to the already above mentioned. This notification is not just sent when dark/light mode has been changed by the operating system / desktop, but also if the user explicitly changed color scheme, e.g. by configuration. When to send out the DSR? # A terminal emulator should only send out the DSR when the palette has been updated due to a change in the terminal emulator's color palette, e.g. because the user has changed the terminal profile directly or indirectly by changing the operating system theme. Example source code # Please have a look at our example C++ source code in order to see how to implement this in your own application. docs.text: Query or Change Font Settings # This VT extension can be used to query the current font settings of the connected terminal or to change them. docs.text: Kitty graphics: Unicode placeholders and file media # Contour speaks the kitty graphics protocol : images transmitted with APC G … ST , placed at the cursor, animated, and deleted again. This page describes the two parts of it that let a program draw a picture as text : Unicode placeholders , and the file media such programs send their pictures with. Together they are what Claude Code needs to show a Mermaid diagram as a picture rather than as source. Unicode placeholders # A normal kitty placement draws an image at the cursor, and the image then lives beside the text rather than in it. A placeholder placement turns that around: the program prints ordinary characters, and the terminal draws a piece of the image in each of their cells. Because the picture is text, it scrolls, wraps, clears and survives an application that only knows how to print — which is why tmux-aware programs and full-screen UIs prefer it. A virtual placement # ESC _G a=T,U=1,i=<id>,c=<columns>,r=<rows>,f=100;<payload> ESC \ U=1 on a=T (transmit and place) or a=p (place) creates a virtual placement : it writes no cell and leaves the cursor where it was. It names the image ( i= ), an optional placement id ( p= ), and the span in cells ( c= , r= ; without them, the image's size in cells, rounded up). An image may have several virtual placements. A virtual placement can have no parent: U=1 with P= is refused with EINVAL , as in kitty. The refusal changes nothing: unlike kitty, an a=T refused so does not store its image either, and the placement the same i= / p= names stays. As in kitty, a virtual placement always fits the whole image into its span, keeping its aspect ratio and centring it; the source rectangle keys x= , y= , w= and h= are ignored. Where the image does not fill the span, the cell's own background shows. The placeholder cells # Each cell of the picture is the character U+10EEEE , followed by combining marks from kitty's row/column diacritic table : What Says foreground colour the image id: an indexed colour 38;5;<n> is id n , a true colour 38;2;r;g;b is r<<16 \| g<<8 \| b , the default colour is id 0 first diacritic the row of the image this cell shows second diacritic the column third diacritic the image id's most significant byte (for ids above 2²⁴) underline colour the placement id; absent or 0 means the image's first virtual placement Diacritics may be left out, and Contour infers them as kitty does: a cell without a column continues its left neighbour's row and column, and one without a row takes its left neighbour's row. A placeholder cell is always one column wide. # A 2x4 image 42 drawn at the cursor: one virtual placement, then two rows of placeholder cells. printf '\033_Ga=T,U=1,i=42,c=4,r=2,f=100,q=2;%s\033\\' " $( base64 -w0 picture.png ) " printf '\033[38;5;42m\U10EEEE̅̅\U10EEEE̅̍\U10EEEE̅̎\U10EEEE̅̐\033[m\n' printf '\033[38;5;42m\U10EEEE̍̅\U10EEEE̍̍\U10EEEE̍̎\U10EEEE̍̐\033[m\n' The cells are resolved at the end of each read from the program, a whole line at a time, so a cell whose diacritics arrive in a later read still shows its piece; a cell printed before its image or placement exists is resolved once they arrive. A cell that names no image shows nothing. The U+10EEEE characters are never drawn as glyphs, while the grid keeps them as received: copying, reflow and DECRQCRA see what the program wrote. Writing over a placeholder cell removes its piece of the picture. A rectangular copy ( DECCRA ) of placeholder cells shows the picture where it lands, as printing the cells there would; on another page it shows that page's placement of the image. Deleting # Delete Reaches virtual placements d=i / d=I with i= (and p= ) yes: the image's placements of both kinds; upper case frees the image once none remains d=n / d=N with I= (image number) yes, as d=i / d=I for the newest image of that number d=r / d=R with x= , y= (an id range) yes, as d=i / d=I for every id in the range d=a / d=A no: placeholder cells stay; d=A frees only the images whose placements it removed, and none a virtual placement still holds positional targets ( c , p , q , x , y , z ) not supported ( ENOTSUP ) Image numbers ( I= ) are supported: transmitting with I= and no i= picks a free id and replies i=<id>,I=<number> . A put, frame, playback or composition command ( a=p , a=f , a=a , a=c ) with I= reaches the newest image of that number, and a re-transmission with i= alone takes the replaced image's number away, as in kitty. Querying support # kitty's feature query tells a program whether placeholders are understood: ESC _G a=q,i=31,e=T,U=1 ESC \ → ESC _G i=31,e=T,U=1;OK ESC \ The reply echoes the keys Contour supports for the queried action ( e= ), so one that is missing is one Contour does not support. A query without i= gets no reply, as in kitty. File media # Besides direct transmission ( t=d , the payload in the sequence itself), a program may name a file for the terminal to read: Medium t=d direct always t=f a file read under the policy below t=t a temporary file as t=f , and deleted after it is read when its full path contains tty-graphics-protocol , as kitty requires t=s POSIX shared memory not supported : it would let any program writing to the terminal unlink any shared memory object the user owns A file is read, and a t=t file deleted, only when every one of these holds: it lies below one of the roots : the temp directories ( $TMPDIR and /tmp on Linux; $TMPDIR , /private/tmp and the per-user temp directory on macOS; /dev/shm too, for t=t only, on Linux; %TMP% , %TEMP% and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp on Windows, each as spelled -- often in short 8.3 names -- and in long names), or a directory of images.kitty_file_allow_list . Only temporary files are deleted, only below a temp directory, and only when their path carries the tty-graphics-protocol marker; one without it is read and kept; no component of the path below that root is hidden (starts with . ), and no symbolic link below the root is followed; it is a regular file, owned by the user Contour runs as, with a single link (so that a hard link cannot reach a file elsewhere), and no larger than one direct transmission may be; it is not below /proc , /sys or /dev (except /dev/shm as above); its path is at most 4095 bytes long. On Windows, besides: the path is drive-absolute ( C:\... or C:/... ), on a fixed or RAM disk. A share ( \\server\... ), the device and NT namespaces ( \\?\ , \\.\ , \??\ ), a network, removable or optical drive are refused, and so is a POSIX path a WSL or MSYS program names ( /tmp/... , /mnt/c/... ): it is not mapped to a Windows one; no component is one Windows reads as something else: an alternate data stream ( a.png:x ), a device name ( CON , NUL , COM1 , ... with any extension), . or .. , a wildcard, or a trailing dot or space; no reparse point below the root is followed -- a junction no more than a symbolic link -- and no entry below the root is hidden or system by its attributes, nor offline or fetched on access (a cloud placeholder); the file is opened shared for reading only, so nobody writes, renames or deletes it while it is read, and the path Windows reports for it must be the one walked: a short 8.3 alias of a long name is refused; its owner is the user Contour runs as or, for an elevated Contour, the Administrators group that owns what it creates; who else may write it (its ACL) is not judged, as POSIX judges no mode bits; a t=t file is deleted through the handle it was read with; one whose directory forbids deleting is read and kept. Root and path are compared ignoring the case of ASCII letters. Every refusal, whatever its reason — missing, outside the roots, the wrong kind of file, too large, undecodable, or a medium not supported — is the same reply, so that a program learns nothing about a file it may not read: ESC _G i=<id>;EBADF:file not readable ESC \ Who may read # A file is read where the program that named it runs, so file media are granted only to output that comes from a local program. They are refused: in a session started from an SSH profile; in a tmux control-mode pane; in a daemon's replica of a session, and for bytes a client injects into a session; while the terminal's context (OSC 3008) says the output comes from another host; while the foreground process relays output from elsewhere: a remote shell client ( ssh , mosh , et , telnet , PuTTY's plink and the like), a terminal multiplexer's client ( tmux , screen , zellij ), or a container's or a VM's front end ( docker , podman , kubectl , incus , lxc , distrobox-enter , toolbox , vagrant , multipass , wsl , wslhost , Hyper-V's hvc ); or while the terminal cannot tell which process that is. On Windows ssh.exe , SSH.EXE and ssh are all ssh . This last rule is a list of known programs, so a relay it does not name passes as local. What such a program could then learn is limited to whether a decodable image exists at a path it names inside the roots, and a t=t name it gives could delete one of the user's own temporary files carrying the tty-graphics-protocol marker. Turn images.kitty_file_transmission off where that matters. The foreground process is looked at when the command is parsed, so a relay that exits right after sending one can race the check; and only the process-group leader is named, so sudo ssh … passes as local. A Windows console has no process group: the command the shell runs stands in for its leader -- below the session's shell, and any shell it starts in turn, the newest child that is not itself a shell -- so an ssh running a ProxyCommand is still ssh . A relay that is not a process of the session at all -- PowerShell remoting ( Enter-PSSession ), which runs in the shell's own process -- is not seen: its output passes as local. With contour daemon , the daemon reads the files: its own configuration decides, and a client can neither widen nor narrow what a daemon reads. A daemon on another machine reads that machine's files, which is where a program running there wrote them. On the BSDs, file media are refused for now: a file is judged by the path its open descriptor names, which only Linux, macOS and Windows report (issue #2423). Configuration # images : # Whether kitty graphics may read files a local program names (t=f, t=t). kitty_file_transmission : true # Directories, besides the temp directories, that t=f may read files below. A leading ~/ is your # home directory; a directory that would open all of it (/, ~ or above), a relative one and a ~name # one are ignored. kitty_file_allow_list : [ '~/.claude/plugins/data' ] The default allow-list is where Claude Code's plugins keep what they render ( %USERPROFILE%\.claude\plugins\data on Windows). The window reads its configuration as each session starts, so an edit reaches the sessions opened after it; a daemon reads its configuration once, when it starts. Claude Code # Claude Code shows pictures — Mermaid diagrams via the rich-terminal plugin, and anything a plugin draws with its <Image> element — in terminals it knows to speak placeholders. Until Contour is on its list, set CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_TERMINAL_IMAGES=1 in the environment of the session. Not yet supported # tmux control mode. Placeholders reach a tmux pane through tmux's passthrough, and a file named there would be read on the machine running Contour while the tmux server may be elsewhere; such panes refuse file media until this is designed. S= and O= for file media. A file is always read whole; a raw image at an offset inside a larger file is refused. Reading off the parser thread. A file is read while the terminal holds its state lock, so a file on a slow filesystem (NFS, FUSE) inside an allow-listed directory stalls drawing until it is read.

docs.text: Line Reflow Reconfiguration # On resize, overly long lines, that would otherwise be cut off, are usually reflowed to the next line on modern terminals. This extension allows toggling reflow for the current line and subsequent lines using a DEC mode ( 2028 ). Feature detection # Use DECRQM ( CSI ? 2028 $ p ) to detect support for line reflow reconfiguration. Using the feature # Use CSI ? 2028 h to enable text reflow on the current line and the following lines. Use CSI ? 2028 l to disable text reflow on the current line and the following lines.

docs.text: OSC 133 - Shell Integration # This documentation describes the OSC 133 sequence used for shell integration, inspired by FinalTerm. Installing Contour's shell integration # Contour ships a script for bash, zsh, fish, tcsh and PowerShell. Write it out once with contour generate integration shell <SHELL> to <FILE> , then load it from your shell's start-up file: Shell Write the script Load it bash contour generate integration shell bash to ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.bash at the end of ~/.bashrc : source ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.bash zsh contour generate integration shell zsh to ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.zsh in ~/.zshrc : source ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.zsh fish contour generate integration shell fish to ~/.config/fish/conf.d/contour.fish nothing to do: fish reads conf.d/ by itself tcsh contour generate integration shell tcsh to ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.tcsh in ~/.tcshrc , after setting prompt : source ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.tcsh PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1 contour generate integration shell pwsh to "$(Split-Path $PROFILE)/contour-integration.ps1" in your $PROFILE , after anything that sets up the prompt: . "$(Split-Path $PROFILE)/contour-integration.ps1" The same pwsh script serves both PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1; there is no separate powershell name. Contour can also install it for you: see Installing PowerShell's integration from Contour . Every script marks the start of the prompt ( A ), its end ( B ), the start of the command's output ( C ) and the end of the command with its exit status ( D ), and reports the working directory with OSC 7. What differs is the command line: Shell Command line bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell sent with C as cmdline_url tcsh not sent, as no tcsh hook sees it: Contour reads it off the screen instead (see C ) bash: the script carries its own copy of bash-preexec , which installs itself by appending to PROMPT_COMMAND . A later PROMPT_COMMAND=... throws that away, and then no marks are sent at all, without an error: that is why the script belongs at the end of ~/.bashrc , after anything that sets PROMPT_COMMAND . bash hands over a command line only once its history has recorded it, so a command kept out of the history ( HISTIGNORE , HISTCONTROL , set +o history ) is read off the screen instead. tcsh: the script extends prompt once, so it is sourced after prompt is set. PowerShell: the script runs in PowerShell 7 and in Windows PowerShell 5.1, and needs PSReadLine. Like VS Code's integration, it wraps PSConsoleHostReadLine , so the command line is reported when PSReadLine hands it back — after the newline, before the command runs — rather than from a key handler. Without PSReadLine there is no C , and so no D either. Installing PowerShell's integration from Contour # Instead of editing your profile by hand, install it from Settings › Shell Integration (the rows "PowerShell", and on Windows "Windows PowerShell"), or from the pane's "Turn on command blocks" card, which appears after three commands without prompt marks. The confirm step shows the exact line and the profile file before anything is written. The line is if ( $env:TERM_PROGRAM -eq 'contour' ) { . ( [scriptblock] :: Create ((& '<contour binary>' generate integration shell pwsh to - | Out-String ))) } # Contour shell integration It runs only inside Contour, and regenerates the script from the running Contour at every start. A manual install that dot-sources contour-integration.ps1 , shell-integration.ps1 or shell-integration.pwsh counts as installed. Writing the script to a .ps1 and dot-sourcing it, as in the table above, stays an alternative. The line goes into the profile of the shell: Shell Profile PowerShell 7, Windows <Documents>\PowerShell\Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 Windows PowerShell 5.1 <Documents>\WindowsPowerShell\Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 PowerShell 7, Linux and macOS $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/powershell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 , else ~/.config/powershell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 <Documents> is the Documents known folder, so a OneDrive-redirected Documents is followed. Encoding: a profile in UTF-8 (with or without a BOM) or UTF-16LE, the encoding Windows PowerShell 5.1's > and Out-File write, is read and appended to in its own encoding. A new profile is created as UTF-8 with a BOM. A Contour path with non-ASCII characters is refused for a Windows PowerShell profile without a BOM, which 5.1 would misread; a UTF-16BE or UTF-32 profile is refused. Execution policy (Windows): Contour reads the policy each shell would apply, the way the shell does. Windows PowerShell 5.1: Group Policy (machine, then user), then the user's and the machine's ShellIds\Microsoft.PowerShell setting in the registry, else Restricted (RemoteSigned on Windows Server). A powershell.config.json that does not parse is never overwritten: the install is refused, and the profile stays as it was. If the line cannot be added after the policy was set, the policy stays set (you agreed to it), and trying again only adds the line. A policy enforced by Group Policy, or AllSigned, blocks the install, and the dialog says why. PowerShell 7's default, RemoteSigned, needs no change. Installed, but the policy stops it: a profile that already loads Contour under a policy that keeps it from running is listed in Settings as "Installed in …, but PowerShell's script policy stops it from running", with Install… offering "Allow Scripts": the same per-user fix, adding no line. Sequence Specification # Format: OSC 133 ; <Command> [; <Parameters>...] ST Where: OSC is \033] . ST (String Terminator) is \033\ (or BEL \007 ). <Command> is a single character identifier (A, N, B, I, P, C, D, L). Commands # A - Prompt Start # Sent before the shell prompt starts printing. Format: OSC 133 ; A [; <Key>=<Value>...] ST Parameters: click_events=1 : Optional. Accepted for compatibility and currently ignored: Contour does not yet move the cursor on a click inside the prompt. redraw=0 : Optional, as kitty reads it. The shell does not redraw this prompt when the window is resized, so Contour re-wraps it like any other text (see below). Each prompt says it for itself; any other value, or none, means the shell redraws it. k=<Kind> : Optional. i , or none, is the prompt itself. c and s start a further line of the prompt in progress — a continuation prompt such as bash's PS2 ; Nushell sends k=s before each — and r a right-hand prompt. Behavior: Marks the current line as a prompt line (conceptually similar to setting a "mark"). Notifies the terminal that the prompt is beginning. A command still running has ended. Does no fresh-line (see L ), though the semantic-prompts proposal asks for one: kitty, foot and Konsole do none either, and a line break the shell did not print would change what it drew. Re-wrapped under it as well, the prompt would span other rows than the shell counts, so Contour leaves the live prompt as the shell drew it, as kitty does and the semantic-prompts proposal recommends: The live prompt is the rows from the line the last A marked down to the bottom of the page, while the cursor stands in it and no C has followed. Each of those rows is cut at the new width or padded to it and stays a row of its own. The cursor keeps its row; the rows above re-wrap as ever. The columns B , D and P;k=r marked move with the cells they name, so the input is found where it stands until the shell's redraw marks it afresh. A prompt sent with redraw=0 is re-wrapped like any other text, and so is one that began above the page, or that shares its line with output that did not end in a newline. N - New Command # Format: OSC 133 ; N [; <Key>=<Value>...] ST Behavior: As A . The proposal's "may first end the command before" is what A does already. B - Prompt End # Sent after the shell prompt has finished printing and before user input begins. Format: OSC 133 ; B ST Behavior: Notifies the terminal that the prompt has ended. Marks the logical line the prompt ended on, together with the column the cursor stood at — the border between what the shell painted and what the user is about to type. This border cannot be recovered after the fact: once the user starts typing, the prompt and the input are one run of cells. It is what lets Contour tell an accessibility client where the prompt area is (see Accessibility ), and it is recorded whether or not DEC mode 2034 is enabled — the line marks are terminal memory, not part of the semantic-block reader protocol. The column is counted across the whole logical line, so a window resize that re-wraps the line into different physical rows does not move it. Contour's bundled integrations send ;B at the very end of the prompt. The border is also what lets Contour read a command line that was never reported off the screen (see C ). I - Prompt End, Input to the End of the Line # Format: OSC 133 ; I ST Behavior: As B , but the user's input ends with the line it begins on: a command line Contour reads off the screen (see C ) is that line's text alone. Where both B and I are sent on one line, the later counts. P - Prompt Part Start # Sent where a further part of the prompt in progress starts, such as a right-aligned prompt. Format: OSC 133 ; P [; k=<Kind>] ST Parameters: k=r : a right prompt, drawn beside the input (Nushell sends it). Other kinds ( i , c , s ) are accepted and change nothing. Behavior: Starts no new prompt and no command block. With k=r , Contour remembers where on its line the right prompt begins, so that the command line it reads off the screen when the shell does not report one (see C ) leaves the right prompt out. Should the command later be drawn over the right prompt, as zsh does once the command reaches it, the mark no longer counts. On a line B marked and no P;k=r did, a run of text that ends at the right margin, or one column short of it, and stands at least two blanks clear of the command is taken for a right prompt. C - Command Output Start # Sent after the user has finished typing the command (usually on Enter press) and before the command output begins. Format: OSC 133 ; C [; <Key>=<Value>...] ST Parameters: cmdline_url=<EncodedURL> : Optional. The command line being executed, percent-encoded (kitty's convention). Contour's bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell integrations send it. Its value runs to the end of the sequence, as kitty reads it: a ; in it belongs to the command, encoded or not. cmdline=<Quoted> : Optional. The command line quoted for a shell, as kitty's bash and zsh integrations send it ( printf %q ), and read as kitty reads it: the first word of the quoted text, with backslash escapes, single and double quotes, and $'...' ANSI-C quoting. Its value runs to the end of the sequence: a ; in it belongs to the command. Behavior: Notifies the terminal that command execution is starting and output will follow. The cmdline_url and cmdline parameters tell the terminal exactly what command is being run. The first of them in the sequence is the one read, and as its value runs to the end of the sequence, a parameter after it is part of the command line: OSC 133 ; C ; cmdline_url=;cmdline=ls ST reports the command line ;cmdline=ls . An empty one, or a cmdline= whose quoting is broken, counts as none. Contour records the command line with the command block : the gutter's block tooltip, finish notifications and the sticky header of a command whose prompt has left the history show it, and CopyCommandLine copies it. Without one — tcsh, Nushell, or a hand-written prompt — Contour reads it off the screen when the prompt's end was marked with B (or I ): from the ;B column to the start of the output, leaving a right prompt out. So ;B is worth sending even where the command line is not. A command line is untrusted input: anything that writes to the terminal can send one. Contour keeps at most 4 KiB of it, shows it with control and bidirectional-override characters replaced by a visible placeholder, and removes escape and other control characters (but tab and newline) from the copy CopyCommandLine puts on the clipboard. D - Command Finished # Sent after the command has finished executing and before the next prompt starts. Format: OSC 133 ; D [; <ExitCode>] ST Parameters: <ExitCode> : The integer exit code of the command (e.g., 0 for success). A missing or non-numeric one reads as 0 . Behavior: Notifies the terminal that the command has finished. Reports the exit code of the command. Contour records the exit status with the command block: it colors the block's marks in the gutter and on the scrollbar, labels the sticky header, and decides whether a finish notification set to outcome: failure is sent. L - Fresh Line # Format: OSC 133 ; L ST Behavior: Moves the cursor to the start of the next line, as \r\n does, unless it already stands at the start of a line -- where a carriage return would leave it. Example Flow # # Prompt Start printf "\033]133;A\033\\" # ... print prompt ... printf "user@host:~ $ " # Prompt End printf "\033]133;B\033\\" # ... user types command (e.g., 'ls') ... # Command Output Start printf "\033]133;C\033\\" # ... command output ... ls # Command Finished (exit code 0) printf "\033]133;D;0\033\\" Related Extensions # SETMARK ( CSI > M ) : a Contour-only extension that marked the current line, equivalent to OSC 133 ; A . Deprecated in favour of OSC 133 and removed in 0.8.0 — use OSC 133 ; A .

docs.text: Contour ships a script for bash, zsh, fish, tcsh and PowerShell. Write it out once with contour generate integration shell <SHELL> to <FILE> , then load it from your shell's start-up file: Shell Write the script Load it bash contour generate integration shell bash to ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.bash at the end of ~/.bashrc : source ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.bash zsh contour generate integration shell zsh to ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.zsh in ~/.zshrc : source ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.zsh fish contour generate integration shell fish to ~/.config/fish/conf.d/contour.fish nothing to do: fish reads conf.d/ by itself tcsh contour generate integration shell tcsh to ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.tcsh in ~/.tcshrc , after setting prompt : source ~/.config/contour/shell-integration.tcsh PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1 contour generate integration shell pwsh to "$(Split-Path $PROFILE)/contour-integration.ps1" in your $PROFILE , after anything that sets up the prompt: . "$(Split-Path $PROFILE)/contour-integration.ps1" The same pwsh script serves both PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1; there is no separate powershell name. Contour can also install it for you: see Installing PowerShell's integration from Contour . Every script marks the start of the prompt ( A ), its end ( B ), the start of the command's output ( C ) and the end of the command with its exit status ( D ), and reports the working directory with OSC 7. What differs is the command line: Shell Command line bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell sent with C as cmdline_url tcsh not sent, as no tcsh hook sees it: Contour reads it off the screen instead (see C ) bash: the script carries its own copy of bash-preexec , which installs itself by appending to PROMPT_COMMAND . A later PROMPT_COMMAND=... throws that away, and then no marks are sent at all, without an error: that is why the script belongs at the end of ~/.bashrc , after anything that sets PROMPT_COMMAND . bash hands over a command line only once its history has recorded it, so a command kept out of the history ( HISTIGNORE , HISTCONTROL , set +o history ) is read off the screen instead. tcsh: the script extends prompt once, so it is sourced after prompt is set. PowerShell: the script runs in PowerShell 7 and in Windows PowerShell 5.1, and needs PSReadLine. Like VS Code's integration, it wraps PSConsoleHostReadLine , so the command line is reported when PSReadLine hands it back — after the newline, before the command runs — rather than from a key handler. Without PSReadLine there is no C , and so no D either.

docs.text: OSC 3008 — Hierarchical Context Signalling # Contour consumes OSC 3008 , the UAPI.15 hierarchical context signalling specification . A terminal connects a user with programs, and control of the program side is passed around while the user works: a shell invokes a command, run0 acquires privileges, systemd-nspawn enters a container, ssh connects to another machine. OSC 3008 lets each of those components tell the terminal that a new context begins, and carry metadata describing it. The value is not that this is more metadata. It is that it arrives without any configuration : systemd 258 and later ship a shell snippet that emits these sequences around every interactive command, so on such a system Contour learns command boundaries, exit statuses and working directories with no shell integration installed at all. Sequences # OSC 3008 ; start= CTXID [ ; field=value ]... ST OSC 3008 ; end= CTXID [ ; field=value ]... ST start= initiates a context, updates one that already exists, or returns to one further up. end= terminates one. Contexts nest: the newest is active, and everything written while it is active belongs to it. Because ; separates fields, a literal semicolon in a value is written as the four characters \x3b , and a literal backslash as \x5c . Values are UTF-8 and are stored as sent. Fields on start= # Field Meaning type= service , session , shell , command , vm , container , elevate , chpriv , subcontext , remote , boot , app user= , hostname= , machineid= , bootid= , pid= , pidfdid= , comm= who and where the announcing process is cwd= the working directory ( shell , command ) cmdline= the command line ( command ) vm= , container= the VM or container being entered targetuser= , targethost= , sessionid= what is being connected or elevated to Fields on end= # exit= ( success , failure , crash , interrupt ), status= (numeric), and signal= (symbolic, e.g. SIGSEGV ). Note that crash , interrupt and signal= express things OSC 133 's numeric exit code structurally cannot. What Contour does with it # Tracks the ancestry , so every line of output is associated with the context that produced it. The association survives reflow and scrolling into history. Derives semantic marks when no shell integration is present, so prompt navigation, output folding and "copy last command output" work with no setup. See Interaction with OSC 133 below. Tints the page background under a boundary context, if the colour scheme opts in. Shows a breadcrumb in the indicator status line via the {Context} placeholder. Resolves the working directory for the tab tooltip and "Open Current Folder". Replicates all of it to daemon clients , so a contour attach pane behaves like a local one. Interaction with OSC 133 # Both protocols describe the same prompt cycle, so exactly one of them owns a session's semantic marks, and the rule is one-way: If OSC 133 speaks at any point , it owns the marks for the rest of the session. OSC 3008 then contributes metadata only — working directories, identity, and the richer exit information — and never a mark. If OSC 133 has said nothing, OSC 3008 stands in for it: a type=shell update marks the prompt, a type=command start marks where output begins, and its end= marks where output stopped. OSC 3008 can never take the marks back, which is what stops a session flapping between sources. There is one thing it cannot supply: OSC 133's ;B , the border between the prompt and what the user types. OSC 3008 has no event there, so a session driven by it alone reports the prompt's line span but not the column input begins at. Reset behaviour # RIS and DECSTR deliberately do not clear the context stack. The specification makes this a safety property: a program running down the ancestry must not be able to erase context a program above it established, and RIS is something any program can send. A shell that announced "you are inside container X" must still be able to say so after a program inside that container resets the terminal. The stack is destroyed when the session is. Limits # Configurable through the osc_context section: max_depth (default 16) bounds the ancestry, and max_retained_contexts (default 256) bounds how much history is kept for scrolled-back output. Per the specification, hitting the depth limit drops the newer contexts, so a program deep in the ancestry cannot push out the one above it. Field lengths are protocol constants and are not configurable. Security # Every field is a display hint. Nothing gates behaviour on one. Any program that can write to the terminal can emit type=elevate or user=root , so nothing Contour draws from these sequences is an assurance. Two consequences worth stating outright: The absence of an elevate context is not a statement that nothing is running as root. A program in a genuinely elevated shell can simply end= the context, and no terminal can detect that. This is why Contour ships no default tint and never decorates a context with a lock, a shield or a warning colour: doing so would teach users to read a spoofable signal as authority. A cwd= is not trusted for opening or spawning unless it is provably this machine's. A context carries no host authority, so a container's /app would otherwise pass every locality test and open the host's directory of the same name. Contour requires a matching machineid= (or failing that a matching hostname= ) and refuses when a container, VM or remote boundary is in force. A context that claims nothing at all is treated as unknown, not local — which matters because nothing emits a remote context for ssh today, so a remote host's own sequences look entirely local. A machineid= counts only as the 32 hexadecimal digits of machine-id(5); anything else, systemd's uninitialized placeholder included, is as if it were left out, and the hostname= decides. Host names are compared whole, ignoring case, and localhost proves nothing. On a machine that has no machine id of its own — Windows, a system without systemd — a context naming one is foreign: it comes from another installation, such as a shell in a WSL distribution beside a Windows terminal that shares its host name. To opt out of all of it: osc_context: { enabled: false } . Not implemented # Killing a context tree via pidfdid= . That field is a pidfd inode , not a handle, so it can only verify a pidfd_open(pid) — and the protocol carries no process-group id and no cgroup path, so "kill this context and its children" is not implementable from the fields that exist. Inside a container pid= names another PID namespace, so opening it locally names an unrelated process, and a run0 context's pid is root-owned, so the case a user most wants would fail with EPERM . Re-entering a container or remote host to open its working directory. Executing nsenter or ssh on the basis of a spoofable field is exactly the rule above being broken.

docs.text: Contour consumes OSC 3008 , the UAPI.15 hierarchical context signalling specification . A terminal connects a user with programs, and control of the program side is passed around while the user works: a shell invokes a command, run0 acquires privileges, systemd-nspawn enters a container, ssh connects to another machine. OSC 3008 lets each of those components tell the terminal that a new context begins, and carry metadata describing it. The value is not that this is more metadata. It is that it arrives without any configuration : systemd 258 and later ship a shell snippet that emits these sequences around every interactive command, so on such a system Contour learns command boundaries, exit statuses and working directories with no shell integration installed at all.
docs.title: OSC 3008 — Hierarchical Context Signalling

docs.text: OSC 3008 ; start= CTXID [ ; field=value ]... ST OSC 3008 ; end= CTXID [ ; field=value ]... ST start= initiates a context, updates one that already exists, or returns to one further up. end= terminates one. Contexts nest: the newest is active, and everything written while it is active belongs to it. Because ; separates fields, a literal semicolon in a value is written as the four characters \x3b , and a literal backslash as \x5c . Values are UTF-8 and are stored as sent.

docs.text: Progress indicator (OSC 9;4) # A long-running command — a package install, a build, a large download — knows how far along it is, but nothing outside it does. This extension lets an application tell the terminal, which then shows it where the user is already looking: the tab strip, the status line, and the OS taskbar. The sequence originates with ConEmu and is implemented by Windows Terminal, iTerm2 and Ghostty . Contour follows the same grammar, so an application already emitting it needs no changes. Syntax # OSC 9 ; 4 ; <state> [ ; <progress> ] ST <state> selects what the indicator says; <progress> is an integer percentage from 0 to 100. <state> Meaning Effect on the percentage 0 Withdraw the indicator Reset to 0 1 Running normally Set to <progress> , or 0 if omitted 2 Failed Set to <progress> if given, else unchanged 3 Busy, with no known completion Unchanged 4 Paused, or warning Set to <progress> if given, else unchanged The asymmetry is deliberate and matches the other implementations. State 1 is about the number, so omitting it means "at the start". States 2 and 4 are about the condition, so an application that only wants to mark a failure need not restate a percentage it already sent. State 3 has no meaningful position at all, and carrying the previous one across means an application can go busy and come back without losing the bar it had drawn. Examples # printf '\033]9;4;1;40\033\\' # running, 40% complete printf '\033]9;4;3\033\\' # busy, no percentage printf '\033]9;4;4;40\033\\' # paused at 40% printf '\033]9;4;2;80\033\\' # failed at 80% printf '\033]9;4;0\033\\' # withdraw the indicator A shell loop reporting real progress: for i in $( seq 0 10 100 ) ; do printf '\033]9;4;1;%d\033\\' " $i " sleep 0 .2 done printf '\033]9;4;0\033\\' Where it shows # The tab strip — a thin bar along the bottom edge of the tab whose active pane reported it. Green while running, amber when paused, red on failure; the busy state pulses. It is drawn under the tab label rather than beside it, so it costs the title no width and tabs do not reflow as applications start and finish. The status line — via the {Progress} placeholder, which renders as 45% , BUSY , PAUSED 45% or ERROR 45% , and collapses to nothing while no operation is in flight. Add it to a status line like any other placeholder: status_line : indicator : right : "{Progress:Bold} | {Clock}" The OS taskbar or Dock , on Windows, KDE Plasma and macOS, including while Contour is minimized. No extra setting is required. Progress from all tabs and split panes is combined per window on Windows and across the application's windows on KDE Plasma and macOS: a failure outranks a pause, which outranks a busy session, which outranks a running one — and among equals the least complete percentage wins, so the indicator reflects the work still outstanding. Background tabs and panes also contribute. Moving or closing a tab updates the indicator. KDE Plasma uses the Unity LauncherEntry D-Bus protocol and requires a matching installed desktop file. It shows percentages for running, paused and error states without distinct state colors; busy is represented by a full bar because this protocol has no indeterminate state. Other desktops implementing the same protocol may also display it. macOS overlays a bar on the application Dock icon, with red for errors, orange for paused work and a moving segment while busy. Show delay # The tab strip and desktop indicators wait 500 milliseconds before showing running or busy progress. If the application clears progress in that time, no bar appears. Percentage updates keep the original deadline. Paused and error states appear immediately. The status line shows progress as soon as it is reported. Change Progress show delay under Settings → Appearance → Tab bar , or set progress_show_delay in milliseconds in contour.yml . Use 0 for immediate display. Withdrawing a stale indicator # The terminal cannot tell a genuinely long operation from an application that died holding one, so by default the indicator persists until the application clears it with state 0 . That is what the sequence specifies, and what ConEmu and Windows Terminal do. A hard reset ( RIS ) also withdraws it, which covers the common case of a shell reset after a crash. If you would rather have the terminal give up on a silent application, set progress_timeout to a non-zero number of milliseconds. Applications using the protocol are expected to refresh it roughly once a second, so a value well above that — 15000 or so, which is what Ghostty hardcodes — is the useful range. # 0 (the default) disables expiry entirely. progress_timeout : 15000 Notes # A malformed sequence — an unknown state, a non-numeric percentage — is ignored, leaving whatever indicator was already showing. Withdrawing one the application still wants shown would be worse than dropping a sequence the terminal cannot read. A percentage above 100 is clamped rather than rejected: an application overshooting still means "finished". OSC 9 without a leading 4; is ConEmu's simple desktop notification, and still works: printf '\033]9;Build finished\033\\' . Only a first parameter of exactly 4 selects the progress indicator, so a notification whose text merely begins with a 4 is still a notification. Progress is per-session state, so it survives detaching and re-attaching in daemon mode : a client that attaches mid-operation adopts the bar already in flight.

docs.text: Private Use Glyphs # Contour draws a few glyphs that Unicode has no character for. Rather than inventing a second drawing channel for them, they are given codepoints in a Private Use Area and rendered by the same built-in box-drawing renderer that draws U+2500 – U+257F , the block elements and the legacy computing symbols. This page documents those codepoints so that other terminals, fonts and tools can render the same glyphs if they want to. Nothing here is a protocol: no escape sequence introduces these characters, and Contour never requires an application to emit one. The reserved block # U+10F000 – U+10F0FF — Contour Terminal private glyphs. The block sits in Supplementary Private Use Area-B (plane 16) rather than in the BMP's U+E000 – U+F8FF . That lower range is comprehensively claimed by Nerd Fonts — Powerline, Font Awesome, Devicons, Octicons, Seti, Material and others — and Contour already renders several of those assignments itself ( U+E0B0 – U+E0BE , U+EE00 – U+EE05 , U+F5D0 – U+F60D ). It also sits away from the start of a plane. An allocation that outgrows the BMP tends to land at the beginning of the next area it is offered, which makes U+F0000 — the first codepoint of plane 15 — one of the more contended places to put a block, not one of the safer ones. U+10F000 is near the far end of plane 16 instead, where no widely-deployed assignment reaches. Only the codepoints listed below are actually claimed by the renderer. The rest of the block is reserved for future use and deliberately falls through to the font, so that reserving a range costs nothing to anyone who is already using it. Assigned codepoints # Codepoint Name Glyph U+10F000 FOLD HEAD OPEN A square box containing a minus, with a stem descending from its bottom edge to the bottom of the cell. U+10F001 FOLD HEAD CLOSED A square box containing a plus. No stem. U+10F002 BLOCK RUNNING A small filled triangle pointing right, as U+25B8 ▸. U+10F003 USER MARK A filled diamond, as U+25C6 ◆. U+10F004 BLOCK FINISHED A filled disc, as U+25CF ●. U+10F005 BLOCK FAILED A diagonal cross, as U+2717 ✗. U+10F006 FOLD BODY A vertical line through the cell, in the stem's column, as U+2502 │. U+10F007 FOLD BODY END A vertical line from the cell's top to its middle, turning right to the cell's edge, as U+2514 └. U+10F008 FOLD HEAD OPEN HEAVY U+10F000 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F009 FOLD HEAD CLOSED HEAVY U+10F001 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F00A FOLD BODY HEAVY U+10F006 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F00B FOLD BODY END HEAVY U+10F007 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F00C FOLD HEAD OPEN HEAVIER U+10F000 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F00D FOLD HEAD CLOSED HEAVIER U+10F001 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F00E FOLD BODY HEAVIER U+10F006 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F00F FOLD BODY END HEAVIER U+10F007 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F010 BLOCK SUCCEEDED A light check mark, as U+2713 ✓. U+10F011 BLOCK FAILED DISC A filled disc with a diagonal cross knocked out of it: ✗ on ●. The fold column is drawn as line art at the current foreground colour, scaled to the cell: the box is square whatever the cell's aspect ratio, and every glyph of the column shares one stroke and one column, so that the head's stem, the body and its end meet exactly. The stroke is the cell's own line weight -- twice it for the heavy four, three times for the heavier four -- even where the gutter draws its glyphs two cells wide. The marks are filled shapes at the current foreground colour, anti-aliased, centred in the cell and spanning 60% of its shorter side, so they sit on the same line as the fold column's stem. What they are for # They form the head of Contour's fold column — the gutter drawn to the left of the grid, which marks each foldable OSC 133 command block: ⊟─ $ make -j8 <- U+10F000, the block is open │ [ 1/120] cc a.c <- U+10F006 │ [ 2/120] cc b.c └ ... done <- U+10F007, the block's last row ⊞ $ make -j8 <- U+10F001, the block is collapsed The body and its end look like U+2502 (BOX DRAWINGS LIGHT VERTICAL) and U+2514 (BOX DRAWINGS LIGHT UP AND RIGHT), and once were. They are Contour's own because of the two-cell gutter: a box-drawing character drawn two cells wide takes the doubled stroke of a DECDWL row, whose text is stretched to twice its width, while the head beside it does not -- so the body stepped out of the stem's weight at every head. Drawn here, the column has one stroke in either width. The head needs a codepoint of its own in any case. U+229F SQUARED MINUS and U+229E SQUARED PLUS are the box and its sign, but neither carries the stem that joins an open head to the body beneath it, and a head that did not connect would read as two unrelated marks rather than as one bracket down the side of a block. A box carrying a plus or a minus, rather than a triangle, because that is the fold control a reader has already met in editors, tree views and file managers. The marks share that column. A command that is still running heads its block with U+10F002 , a finished one with no fold control beside it with U+10F004 -- or U+10F005 when it failed -- and a row the user marked (vi mm ) carries U+10F003 . A failed command whose output folds draws its whole fold heavy, head and body, with U+10F008 to U+10F00B , so failure reads by shape as well as by colour -- collapsed too, where only the head is drawn. The fold under the pointer is drawn one step heavier again ( gutter.bold_on_hover ): heavy for a light fold, U+10F00C to U+10F00F for a failed one. The gutter's block column may be two cells wide ( gutter.block_column_width ); its glyphs are then drawn across both cells, each twice the size. The native chromes draw the block column as a rail instead: a bar in a strip of pixels between the gutter's cells and the grid, which marks a block's head with U+10F002 while it runs, with U+10F011 when it failed -- one glyph, so the cross is the page showing through the disc -- and with U+10F010 , only while the block is hovered or focused, when it succeeded. A row the user marked carries U+10F003 there too. The rail's marks are drawn two cells wide, sized to the row; the Terminal chrome keeps the glyph column above. Unicode has these four shapes at U+25B8 , U+25C6 , U+25CF and U+2717 (and the check at U+2713 ), but the gutter does not use them: the renderer's claim on a codepoint is global, so claiming those would draw every one a program writes -- the ● of systemctl status , a prompt theme's ▸ or ◆, DEC Special Graphics' ` -- as a gutter mark instead of in its font's own size and weight. Notes for implementers # These characters are produced by the terminal, for its own gutter . They are not part of any escape sequence, and an application has no reason to write one. A Private Use Area assignment is by definition not exclusive. Planes 15 and 16 are also used by some East Asian fonts for user-defined characters (GB 18030 and Big5 user-defined areas), so a document that already uses U+10F000 for something else will render as a fold head in Contour. Turning the gutter off ( folding.show_markers: false ) does not change that, because the glyphs are claimed by the renderer rather than by the fold feature — if this ever proves to matter in practice, the claim is one entry in BoxDrawingRenderer::renderable() . If you implement these in a font, note that Contour will still prefer its own rendition: the box-drawing renderer is consulted before font shaping, and font.builtin_box_drawing: false turns that off for all built-in glyphs, not just these.

U+10F004 BLOCK FINISHED A filled disc, as U+25CF ●. U+10F005 BLOCK FAILED A diagonal cross, as U+2717 ✗. U+10F006 FOLD BODY A vertical line through the cell, in the stem's column, as U+2502 │. U+10F007 FOLD BODY END A vertical line from the cell's top to its middle, turning right to the cell's edge, as U+2514 └. U+10F008 FOLD HEAD OPEN HEAVY U+10F000 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F009 FOLD HEAD CLOSED HEAVY U+10F001 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F00A FOLD BODY HEAVY U+10F006 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F00B FOLD BODY END HEAVY U+10F007 drawn at twice the stroke. U+10F00C FOLD HEAD OPEN HEAVIER U+10F000 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F00D FOLD HEAD CLOSED HEAVIER U+10F001 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F00E FOLD BODY HEAVIER U+10F006 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F00F FOLD BODY END HEAVIER U+10F007 drawn at three times the stroke. U+10F010 BLOCK SUCCEEDED A light check mark, as U+2713 ✓. U+10F011 BLOCK FAILED DISC A filled disc with a diagonal cross knocked out of it: ✗ on ●. The fold column is drawn as line art at the current foreground colour, scaled to the cell: the box is square whatever the cell's aspect ratio, and every glyph of the column shares one stroke and one column, so that the head's stem, the body and its end meet exactly. The stroke is the cell's own line weight -- twice it for the heavy four, three times for the heavier four -- even where the gutter draws its glyphs two cells wide. The marks are filled shapes at the current foreground colour, anti-aliased, centred in the cell and spanning 60% of its shorter side, so they sit on the same line as the fold column's stem.
docs.title: Assigned codepoints

docs.text: They form the head of Contour's fold column — the gutter drawn to the left of the grid, which marks each foldable OSC 133 command block: ⊟─ $ make -j8 <- U+10F000, the block is open │ [ 1/120] cc a.c <- U+10F006 │ [ 2/120] cc b.c └ ... done <- U+10F007, the block's last row ⊞ $ make -j8 <- U+10F001, the block is collapsed The body and its end look like U+2502 (BOX DRAWINGS LIGHT VERTICAL) and U+2514 (BOX DRAWINGS LIGHT UP AND RIGHT), and once were. They are Contour's own because of the two-cell gutter: a box-drawing character drawn two cells wide takes the doubled stroke of a DECDWL row, whose text is stretched to twice its width, while the head beside it does not -- so the body stepped out of the stem's weight at every head. Drawn here, the column has one stroke in either width. The head needs a codepoint of its own in any case. U+229F SQUARED MINUS and U+229E SQUARED PLUS are the box and its sign, but neither carries the stem that joins an open head to the body beneath it, and a head that did not connect would read as two unrelated marks rather than as one bracket down the side of a block. A box carrying a plus or a minus, rather than a triangle, because that is the fold control a reader has already met in editors, tree views and file managers. The marks share that column. A command that is still running heads its block with U+10F002 , a finished one with no fold control beside it with U+10F004 -- or U+10F005 when it failed -- and a row the user marked (vi mm ) carries U+10F003 . A failed command whose output folds draws its whole fold heavy, head and body, with U+10F008 to U+10F00B , so failure reads by shape as well as by colour -- collapsed too, where only the head is drawn. The fold under the pointer is drawn one step heavier again ( gutter.bold_on_hover ): heavy for a light fold, U+10F00C to U+10F00F for a failed one. The gutter's block column may be two cells wide ( gutter.block_column_width ); its glyphs are then drawn across both cells, each twice the size. The native chromes draw the block column as a rail instead: a bar in a strip of pixels between the gutter's cells and the grid, which marks a block's head with U+10F002 while it runs, with U+10F011 when it failed -- one glyph, so the cross is the page showing through the disc -- and with U+10F010 , only while the block is hovered or focused, when it succeeded. A row the user marked carries U+10F003 there too. The rail's marks are drawn two cells wide, sized to the row; the Terminal chrome keeps the glyph column above. Unicode has these four shapes at U+25B8 , U+25C6 , U+25CF and U+2717 (and the check at U+2713 ), but the gutter does not use them: the renderer's claim on a codepoint is global, so claiming those would draw every one a program writes -- the ● of systemctl status , a prompt theme's ▸ or ◆, DEC Special Graphics' ` -- as a gutter mark instead of in its font's own size and weight.
docs.title: What they are for

docs.text: These characters are produced by the terminal, for its own gutter . They are not part of any escape sequence, and an application has no reason to write one. A Private Use Area assignment is by definition not exclusive. Planes 15 and 16 are also used by some East Asian fonts for user-defined characters (GB 18030 and Big5 user-defined areas), so a document that already uses U+10F000 for something else will render as a fold head in Contour. Turning the gutter off ( folding.show_markers: false ) does not change that, because the glyphs are claimed by the renderer rather than by the fold feature — if this ever proves to matter in practice, the claim is one entry in BoxDrawingRenderer::renderable() . If you implement these in a font, note that Contour will still prefer its own rendition: the box-drawing renderer is consulted before font shaping, and font.builtin_box_drawing: false turns that off for all built-in glyphs, not just these.

docs.text: Program status (OSC 7501) # A program can tell the terminal what it is doing: whether it is working, finished, failed, or waiting for the user to approve something or answer a question. The terminal keeps the latest report of every program running in it, and shows it where the user will see it even when the tab is in the background. Contour implements the program-status protocol , revision 0.4. Syntax # OSC 7501 ; key=value [ : key=value ... ] ST OSC 7501 ; ? ST Pairs are separated by : . A value uses letters, digits and _ . , + / = - ; a pair holding anything else, a pair without = , and unknown keys are skipped, and a repeated key keeps its last value. Key Value Meaning state idle , working , done , blocked , error , clear Required. clear removes records. id segment(/segment)* Which record; absent for the root. build/test lies beneath build . kind permission , question , auth Why it is blocked; only with blocked . progress 0 .. 100 Percent done; only with working or blocked . app [A-Za-z0-9_.+-]{1,32} The program; inherited from the nearest ancestor when absent. title base64 UTF-8 A short label. msg base64 UTF-8 One line describing the status. A report replaces its record whole: a key it leaves out is cleared. Limits # A report that breaks one of these is discarded whole, and the records stay as they were: the whole sequence is at most 4096 bytes, a key at most 16; id is at most 128 bytes, 32 per segment and 8 segments deep; msg is at most 2732 bytes encoded and 2048 decoded, title 256 and 192; base64 must be valid (padding is optional); decoded text must be UTF-8 without control characters (C0, DEL or C1). Contour keeps at most 64 records per terminal , the minimum the protocol requires. A 65th evicts the record that was updated least recently, so a loop reporting fresh ids cannot grow the terminal. Lifetime # Records belong to the terminal, not to a screen: switching to the alternate screen and back keeps them, and so does a soft reset (DECSTR). A full reset (RIS) removes all of them. State Ends when working , blocked Replaced, cleared, the process exits, or a new shell prompt starts (OSC 133 A ) idle Replaced or cleared; Contour keeps it across a prompt done , error Replaced or cleared A close the user or a script asks for ends the terminal, and its records with it. Feature detection # printf '\033]7501;?\033\\\033[c' Contour answers OSC 7501 ; ? : states=idle,working,done,blocked,error : kinds=permission,question,auth ST before the primary device attributes reply. A terminal that does not support the protocol answers only the device attributes. Where it shows # The tab strip. A tab shows the most urgent record of all its panes: blocked, then error, then working, then done. Working (with its progress, when given) and blocked show always; done and error only while the tab is in the background. The badge's tooltip is the record's title, else its message, else its app, with invisible formatting characters (bidi overrides, zero-width characters) removed. The control API. contour ls --json lists each pane's records, and contour events --kind pane.programStatusChanged follows their changes. Daemon mode. The daemon keeps the records and mirrors them to every attached client. Contour does not derive program status from the progress indicator (OSC 9;4), nor the other way round: they are separate sequences with separate meanings. Examples # # A build: working at 40%, then finished. printf '\033]7501;state=working:app=cargo:progress=40\033\\' printf '\033]7501;state=done:app=cargo\033\\' # Waiting for an approval, with a message. printf '\033]7501;state=blocked:kind=permission:app=terraform:msg=%s\033\\' \ " $( printf 'Apply 3 changes?' | base64 -w0 ) " # Two regions of a deployment, then clearing both. printf '\033]7501;state=working:id=deploy/eu:app=deploy\033\\' printf '\033]7501;state=error:id=deploy/us\033\\' printf '\033]7501;state=clear:id=deploy\033\\'

docs.text: Save and Restore SGR attributes. # Feature detection # Use SGRSAVE ( CSI # { ) save the currently set SGR attributes, and SGRRESTORE ( CSI # } ) to restore the previously saved SGR attributes. Relation to xterm's XTPUSHSGR / XTPOPSGR # Both, XTPUSHSGR and XTPOPSGR are in its most basic form equivalent to SGRSAVE and SGRRESTORE , but the xterm extensions push and pop using a stack rather than save and restore using a simple storage location, and the xterm equivalent does allow pushing/popping only certain SGR attributes. This is needless functionality that should not be implemented by a terminal but rather in the applications itself.

docs.text: Semantic Block Query (DEC Mode 2034) # This extension provides a discoverable, machine-readable query mechanism that returns structured JSON blocks of semantic command data from the terminal. It is designed for programmatic consumers such as AI agents, accessibility tools, and automation scripts. Note Contour's own accessibility support — reporting the caret and the live prompt region to the operating system — does not go through this protocol and does not require mode 2034. It reads the OSC 133 line marks directly, because those are terminal memory and are recorded for every shell that emits them. This extension is for external consumers that want the command history as structured data. Prerequisites # This feature requires OSC 133 shell integration to be active in the running shell. The shell must emit OSC 133 sequences (A, B, C, D) to mark prompt boundaries, command output regions, and command completion. Feature Discovery # DEC Private Mode 2034 # Enable: CSI ? 2034 h (DECSM) Disable: CSI ? 2034 l (DECRM) Query: CSI ? 2034 $ p (DECRQM) -> CSI ? 2034 ; Ps $ y Where Ps in the DECRQM response is: - 0 = not recognized (terminal does not support this mode) - 1 = set (enabled) - 2 = reset (disabled) When enabled: - The terminal reports the command blocks whose command has not started yet: the prompt on screen at this point (a shell may enable the mode from its prompt hook), and every block after it. Contour records every shell's command blocks whether or not this mode is on (its gutter, sticky header and notifications read them), but a reader never sees a command that started before it enabled the mode, so enabling it is never a way to read back commands that ran earlier. - The terminal generates a session token and replies with a DCS containing the token (see Authentication below). - The query sequence CSI > Ps ; Pn ; T1 ; T2 ; T3 ; T4 [; Ph] b becomes available. When disabled: - Nothing is reported any more; commands started so far stay hidden even if the mode is enabled again. - The session token is invalidated. - The query sequence returns an error response. Authentication # When mode 2034 is enabled via DECSM, the terminal generates a 64-bit session token and replies with: DCS > 2034 ; 1 b T1 ; T2 ; T3 ; T4 ST That is: ESC P > 2034 ; 1 b T1 ; T2 ; T3 ; T4 ESC \ T1 .. T4 are the session token: four decimal integers from 0 to 65534, its four 16-bit parts. Every SBQUERY carries them back as its last four parameters, exactly as received (see Query Syntax below). There is nothing to convert. A part is never 65535: a terminal reads every larger number in a CSI parameter as 65535, so that value stands for all of them. An SBQUERY whose token carries a part of 65535 or more, or leaves a part out, fails authentication (status 3). Token Lifecycle # On DECSET 2034 : Terminal generates a fresh token and replies with the DCS token response. On SBQUERY : The token must be included as parameters T1..T4. Missing or invalid tokens produce error responses. On DECRST 2034 : The token is invalidated, and the commands started so far are hidden from every later session. On RIS : As on DECRST 2034. A hard reset returns every mode to its power-up state, this one included. On re-enable : A new token is generated; previous tokens are no longer valid. Security Note # DECSET normally does not produce a reply. Some terminal multiplexers (e.g. tmux, screen) may not forward the DCS token response to the application. In such environments, token-based authentication may not be usable. This is a known limitation. Query Syntax — SBQUERY # CSI > Ps ; Pn ; T1 ; T2 ; T3 ; T4 [; Ph] b Mnemonic: SBQUERY — S emantic B lock QUERY CSI with > leader, final character b (for "blocks"). Parameter Meaning Ps Query type (see table below) Pn Count parameter (default 1); for Ps 4, the id's low 16 bits T1..T4 The session token, as the DECSET reply carried it Ph For Ps 4, the id's high 16 bits (default 0) Ps Meaning Pn 1 Last completed command block ignored 2 Last N completed command blocks count (default 1) 3 Current in-progress command ignored 4 The block with id Ph × 65536 + Pn , in any state the id's low 16 bits A Ps of 0, like an omitted one, means 1. Any other Ps is answered DCS > 0 b ST , as a query with no data: a reader asking a question the terminal does not know never receives the answer to another. Ps 4 answers an older block a reader learned the id of from an earlier reply: finished, superseded, running or still at its prompt. A CSI parameter cannot exceed 65535, so the id travels in two halves, Pn = id & 0xFFFF and Ph = id >> 16 ; Ph comes after the token, which so stays at parameters 2..5. A block the reader may not see (its command started before the mode was enabled), or one the terminal no longer keeps, is answered DCS > 0 b ST , as is an id of 0, which no block has. A completed block is one the shell finished with OSC 133;D (or OSC 3008 end= ). A block that a newer prompt superseded without one -- the prompt of a nested shell, such as inside ssh -- is not reported. Response Syntax # The response is a DCS (Device Control String) with > leader and final character b . Success: DCS > 1 b {JSON} ST That is: ESC P > 1 b {JSON} ESC \ Error — no data or mode disabled: DCS > 0 b ST Error — authentication required (missing token): DCS > 2 b ST Error — authentication failed (wrong token): DCS > 3 b ST Status Codes # Status Meaning 0 Mode disabled, no data, or an unknown query type 1 Success with JSON payload 2 Authentication required (no token provided) 3 Authentication failed (invalid token) JSON Response Schema # The JSON of step 4 of the example session below, laid out with whitespace the terminal does not send; the values of the keys version 2 adds are an example of their own: { "version" : 2 , "blocks" : [ { "command" : "echo hello" , "prompt" : "user@host:~$ echo hello" , "output" : "hello" , "exitCode" : 0 , "finished" : true , "outputLineCount" : 1 , "id" : 4 , "cwd" : "/home/user" , "startedAt" : "2026-10-24T09:41:07.312Z" , "durationMs" : 4 } ] } Fields # Field Type Description version integer Schema version, currently 2 . blocks array Array of command block objects, ordered chronologically. command string or null The command line from OSC 133;C cmdline_url or cmdline , or -- when the shell sent none but marked its prompt end with OSC 133;B -- the text typed after the prompt. null when neither is known. Longer than 4096 bytes it is cut at a character boundary and ends in … . prompt string The prompt the command was typed at, the typed command included: the block's lines from the one OSC 133;A marked down to the one its output starts on. output string What the command printed: the block's lines from the one OSC 133;C marked to where OSC 133;D ended it. For a command still running, what it printed so far, down to the line the cursor is on. exitCode integer From OSC 133;D (or OSC 3008 end= ). -1 if unknown. finished boolean false for in-progress commands (Ps=3 query), true otherwise. outputLineCount integer Number of lines in output . id integer The block's id (version 2): what Ps 4 asks for. Valid within the current id epoch only -- the ids start over when they would overflow -- and not the block:<pane>/<serial> id of the control API . cwd string or null The working directory (OSC 7) the command started in (version 2). null before it started, or when none was reported. startedAt string or null When the command started (OSC 133;C), as RFC 3339 in UTC with milliseconds (version 2). null before it started. durationMs integer or null How long it ran, from OSC 133;C to its reported end, in milliseconds (version 2). null until it ended. Versions. Version 2 only adds keys, after every key of version 1, which keeps its spelling, place and meaning: a reader of version 1 reads a version-2 reply unchanged. A reader that needs id , cwd , startedAt or durationMs checks version >= 2 . prompt and output are read from the block's own lines, wherever they are in the scrollback, so neither ever carries another command's text. Lines that have scrolled out of the history are missing from them; once all of a block's lines have, both are empty. Text fields use JSON's native encoding for control characters (e.g. \u001b for ESC), which ensures the payload never contains a raw ST (ESC ) sequence. Example Session # At a user@host:~$ prompt, in a shell whose OSC 133 integration reports each command line ( cmdline_url ). Every printf is a command of its own, and so a command block of its own. # 1. Enable the semantic block protocol and capture the token printf '\033[?2034h' # Response: DCS > 2034 ; 1 b 41394 ; 50132 ; 58870 ; 1816 ST # Token values: T1=41394 T2=50132 T3=58870 T4=1816 # 2. Verify it's enabled via DECRQM printf '\033[?2034$p' # Response: CSI ? 2034 ; 1 $ y # 3. Run some commands ls echo hello # 4. Query the last completed command (with token) printf '\033[>1;1;41394;50132;58870;1816b' # Response: DCS > 1 b {"version":2,"blocks":[{"command":"echo hello","prompt":"user@host:~$ echo hello","output":"hello","exitCode":0,"finished":true,"outputLineCount":1,"id":4,...}]} ST # 5. Query the last 3 completed commands (with token) printf '\033[>2;3;41394;50132;58870;1816b' # Response: DCS > 1 b {JSON} ST, listing `ls`, `echo hello` and the printf of step 4, oldest first # 6. Query any in-progress command (with token) printf '\033[>3;1;41394;50132;58870;1816b' # Response: DCS > 1 b {JSON} ST, listing this printf itself, with "finished":false and "exitCode":-1 # 7. Query block 4, the `echo hello` of step 3, by the id step 4 reported (Pn = 4, Ph = 0) printf '\033[>4;4;41394;50132;58870;1816;0b' # Response: DCS > 1 b {JSON} ST, listing that block alone # 8. Disable when done (invalidates the token) printf '\033[?2034l' Implementation Notes # Token storage : Terminals implementing this specification should generate the session token using a cryptographically secure random number generator and store it for the duration of the mode being enabled. The token must be regenerated on each enable. Contour draws it from the platform's random device. Terminal multiplexers : DECSET does not normally produce a reply. Multiplexers and terminal proxies that intercept DEC mode sequences should be aware that mode 2034 produces a DCS reply and must forward it to the requesting application. CLI/tool integration : Tools should capture the DCS token reply immediately after sending DECSET 2034, and read T1 .. T4 from it (see Authentication ) before issuing any SBQUERY. Error handling : Consumers should check the status byte in every DCS response and handle status 2 (missing token) and 3 (invalid token) gracefully, e.g. by re-enabling the mode to obtain a fresh token. Capacity limits : The number of retained completed command blocks is implementation-defined. Consumers should not assume an unbounded history. Output encoding : JSON text fields use standard JSON escaping for control characters (e.g. \u001b for ESC), ensuring the DCS payload never contains a raw ST sequence. See Also # OSC 133 - Shell Integration
